KMT calls for DPP apology over nuclear power U-turn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:54 UTC
01:40:54 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) yesterday said that President William Lai (賴清德) should apologize for phasing out nuclear power, as regulators indicated they were close to approving the restart of Taiwan’s last operating reactor less than a year and a half after it went offline.
In a statement, KMT Culture and Communications Committee Director Chen I-hsin (陳以信) said the plans to return the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant to operation showed that Lai’s pledge to achieve a “non-nuclear homeland” by last year without electricity shortages had failed.
Chen said nuclear power was essential to industrial competitiveness, artificial intelligence (AI) development and energy security and that Taiwan Power Co’s (Taipower) pursuit of Ma-anshan’s reopening vindicated the KMT’s calls for a more pragmatic energy policy.
Photo: Tsai Tsung-hsien, Taipei Times
In contrast, the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) long-standing opposition to nuclear power was a “mistaken policy” that had cost Taiwan, Chen said.
The Nuclear Safety Commission (NSC) on Wednesday said that it had completed technical reviews of Taipower’s application to restart Ma-anshan, with approval pending final administrative procedures.
Taipower applied to restart the Ma-anshan and Guosheng nuclear plants in March, after amendments passed in May last year allowed for the licenses of decommissioned reactors to be extended for up to 20 years beyond their original 40-year operating limit.
Later yesterday, DPP caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) questioned whether Chen would also seek contrition from opposition politicians who campaigned against nuclear power, including New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜) and Hou’s predecessor, Eric Chu (朱立倫), both former KMT presidential candidates.
Speaking at a news conference at the Legislative Yuan, Chuang said that the DPP’s “nuclear-free homeland” policy reflected public safety concerns when it was adopted.
While rising electricity demand from Taiwan’s booming AI and semiconductor sectors had made a policy review appropriate, Chuang said it was premature to conclude that the government had decided to restart nuclear power.
Chuang said that voters, not political parties, would ultimately decide the issue through a referendum on scrapping the “nuclear-free homeland” policy to be held alongside November’s local elections.
Even if the referendum passes, restarting the Ma-anshan plant would still require clearing multiple regulatory and safety hurdles, including resolving the issue of nuclear waste disposal, he added.
The Ma-anshan power plant, in Pingtung County’s Hengchun Township (恆春), shut down its last — and Taiwan’s last — active nuclear reactor on May 17 last year.
The Guosheng plant, in New Taipei City’s Wanli District (萬里), shut down and entered decommissioning in March 2023.

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) on Wednesday accused the Control Yuan of halting the publication of civil servant property disclosures, while the watchdog blamed the stoppage on a lack of appointed members.
Writing in separate releases, the KMT and TPP caucuses accused the Control Yuan of stopping the publication of public disclosures in a bid to shield corrupt Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) officials.
The parties alleged that the Control Yuan suspended the publication to protect Overseas Community Affairs Council Minister Hsu Chia-ching (徐佳青), who it recently fined NT$100,000 for allowing her son to join a council-founded youth camp on the Pratas Islands (Dongsha Islands, 東沙群島).
Photo: Taipei Times
Since taking office five years ago, Hsu made 47 trips abroad for a total of 536 days, costing taxpayers NT$23 million (US$724,295), the KMT caucus said.
The Control Yuan in a news release said that it lacks legal authority to report on cases of corruption, as the legislature has not approved any new members to the constitutional branch of government.
It said the statements from the opposition parties are untruthful as the disclosure gazettes themselves are still being printed.
The gazette is a routine part of the Control Yuan’s operations, which is not affected by its lack of duly appointed members, the KMT caucus said.
“The Control Yuan was highly efficient in targeting [former] TPP chairman Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), but now excuses itself for not being staffed,” the caucus added.
The different treatment of Hsu and Ko shows that the body has a double standard benefitting DPP officials, it said, demanding that the gazette’s publication be resumed within the week.
The TPP caucus said that the lack of members did not affect the Control Yuan’s freezing of Ko’s assets.
The Control Yuan said that laws and regulations stipulate members must formally censure an official before the matter can be published in the gazette.
The Control Yuan has no members authorized to enable this process at the moment, it said.
The branch is legally designated to be in charge of enforcing the Political Donations Act (政治獻金法) and Recusal of Public Servants Due to Conflicts of Interest Act (公職人員利益衝突迴避法), which means it does not need appointed members to investigate Ko, it said.

Swiss woman recounts escape from Nepal floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:51 UTC
01:40:51 KST

Natalia Rjumin-Girardet, a Swiss national who narrowly escaped deadly flash floods in Nepal while making a spiritual journey to Mount Kailash in Tibet, said that “divine providence” saved her.
The 70-year-old yoga teacher was traveling by bus with a group of eight people of different nationalities along a road bordering the Bhotekoshi River when the disaster struck.
“Suddenly, I saw the [group’s] cook jump out of the bus window. Someone else opened the door and I saw a huge mountain ... in the fog,” Rjumin-Girardet told reporters by phone from a hotel in Kathmandu.
Photo: AP
Then she realized that the “mountain” was actually a “massive wave of water and mud.”
“I saw everyone start running, so I started running too,” she said, her voice trembling. “I think we had a minute, maybe two, to get out of the bus.”
The Russian-born woman with short, gray hair said that by luck, a small, concrete staircase stood right next to where the vehicle had come to a halt, allowing the group to get away.
Photo: AFP / Ludmila Yilmaz
After the stairs, “we ran” up a hillside, she said, adding that no one in the group remembered how they had reached higher ground, as they were all in a state of “shock.”
“Those stairs saved us,” she said. “We were incredibly lucky.”
Once she realized she was safe, Rjumin-Girardet said she turned around and saw the devastation below.
“I saw houses, cars and even buses being swept away by the wave,” she said.
“It was truly awful,” she said, adding that it was only later that the group understood the full scale of the disaster.
Their hotel and the entire village of Syabrubesi where they had spent the night had been completely destroyed.
According to the latest figures, rescue teams had recovered more than 1,100 bodies, while nearly 4,500 people were missing after the gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris triggered by a glacial collapse roared down the China-Nepal border on Wednesday last week.
The members of the group that Rjumin-Girardet was with, who had been on their way to make a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, see their survival as a “miracle.”
“It was divine providence that allowed the group to stay alive,” she said. “If we had arrived two or three minutes earlier or later, we might not have been lucky enough to be saved.”
She described how the survivors spent the first night after the flash flood huddled in a small barn on a hilltop, in the cold and rain.
“We hardly slept,” she said.
The next morning, a helicopter evacuated them to an area where military personnel took charge of them, before transferring them to Kathmandu.
Having lost her phone on the bus, Rjumin-Girardet was finally able to notify her loved ones that she was alive thanks to a friend who had her sister’s number.
Today, the group remains very close.
“For us, August 26 has become an important date, [marking] a rebirth,” she said.
Rjumin-Girardet, who founded Art and Peace — a Swiss association using art and creativity as tools for dialogue — said she did not yet know whether she would return to Switzerland or continue her journey.
However, she said she hoped lessons could be drawn from the harrowing experience.
“I would like everyone to have more compassion for others,” she said. “Perhaps our world could change a little for the better.”

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) yesterday vowed to strictly scrutinize the Cabinet’s NT$607.63 billion (US$19.13 billion) supplementary budget, blasting a massive bailout for CPC Corp, Taiwan as illegal and demanding the promulgation of the opposition’s drone industry act.
In response to the inclusion of military drone procurements in the supplementary budget, the KMT caucus called on the Cabinet and President William Lai (賴清德) to countersign and promulgate the opposition-majority legislature’s version of the drone budget.
For the government to request supplementary funds, it must first approve the regular budget allotted to the same projects, it said.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
This means the opposition’s National Defense Autonomy and Uncrewed Vehicle Industry Development Act (強化國防自主暨無人載具產業發展條例) must be countersigned before the lawmakers can discuss the supplementary budget, it said.
The NT$145.69 billion funding for arms, primarily drones, in the supplementary budget must be implemented in a manner consistent with the drone industry legislation passed by the KMT and the TPP, it said.
This means the Ministry of National Defense must prioritize domestically sourced systems and components to stimulate the rise of an indigenous drone industry fully supported by integrated domestic supply chains, the KMT caucus said.
The legislature is to scrutinize the government’s proposal for compliance with these conditions, it said.
The public and the Taiwanese drone industry overwhelmingly support the opposition’s drone act, the caucus said.
TPP caucus whip Jacky Chen (陳清龍) said that the Cabinet’s resort to proposing a supplementary budget proved that the government lied about the necessity of funding drones with a special budget act.
Using a supplementary budget to subsidize the CPC is not lawful under Article 79 of the Budget Act (預算法), which stipulates that such budgets can only be invoked if a major incident causes a state-run enterprise’s expenses to exceed the legal budget, he added.
No major incident caused the CPC to be in the red for six years straight other than its own unprofitability, he said.
The Cabinet is using 40 percent of its proposed supplementary budget on the CPC instead of funding defense or making meaningful increases to the salaries of police, firefighters and military service personnel, he said.

Canada’s battle to build a new global defense bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has thrown his weight behind a new global defense bank intended to help allies rearm, but other major economies have yet to commit just weeks before prospective members are due to sign up.
The Defense, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) has been seeking to raise about 100 billion euros (US$116 billion) and use the money to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defense projects. It would also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers. Alongside Canada, where the DSRB would be based, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine have pledged their support.
Two officials from countries involved in the project said that the DSRB had secured about 5 billion euros in commitments by last month. It is aiming for about 20 billion euros in paid-in capital and a further 80 billion euros it can tap when needed, one of them said. However, Germany, Britain and other G7 countries have so far declined to join, raising questions over whether the DSRB can achieve the triple-A credit rating it wants to help secure the lowest funding costs.
“To make a good impression on the ratings agencies, they would need to have several other substantial governments participating,” said William Perraudin, managing director at Risk Control, an analytics firm specializing in multilateral institutions.
Reuters spoke to eight people with knowledge of the discussions to join the bank. Some said that whether the DSRB can offer cheaper financing than highly rated national governments was a stumbling block for some potential members.
The amount of capital countries would need to commit while public finances are strained, the bank’s governance and overlaps with existing initiatives were also cited as factors. Canada said it is talking with many countries ahead of a charter signing that its lead negotiator for the DSRB, Isabelle Hudon, said on the sidelines of July’s Farnborough Airshow was planned for the autumn.
“We are proceeding at pace, developing Articles of Agreement and working with allies and partners alike to form a group of founding nations,” Canadian Ministry of Finance press secretary John Fragos said.
Speaking at Farnborough on a panel dedicated to defense investment, DSRB founder Rob Murray said the lender would help countries rearm to counter mounting security threats.
“We need 10 of them, frankly,” the former British Army officer and NATO innovation chief said.
European countries are increasing defense spending after US President Donald Trump demanded that they take on more of NATO’s burden, although few are close to meeting the alliance’s latest targets. Carney earlier this year called for an alliance of “middle powers” to respond to what he sees as the fracturing of the US-led world order.
The DSRB would “ensure that Canada and our allies have the capacity to meet the challenges of a more dangerous and divided world together,” he said in July.
Perraudin said the DSRB could use financial leverage separate from the balance sheets of already indebted nations to boost defense investment. However, to become a significant player, it would need additional sovereign backing beyond current commitments, he said.
While big European economies can already borrow cheaply, membership would ensure their domestic contractors can access the DSRB funding, said Linus Terhorst of the Royal United Services Institute think tank.
Five of the people with knowledge of the talks about DSRB membership cited potential overlap with other financing efforts, including the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program and Britain’s proposed Multilateral Defense Mechanism (MDM).
The EU launched its 150 billion euros SAFE defense financing program last year, while Britain is developing a MDM with the Netherlands, Finland and Poland focused on joint procurement.
One official also cited concerns about the upfront capital required from governments, as well as uncertainty over how projects would be selected. Larger countries have been asked to put forward about 1 billion euros, two people with knowledge of the plans said.
Murray said that this could be paid over three years and would in time return profits through dividends, while the DSRB would provide a more permanent institution for financing defense than SAFE and could work with any procurement method.
“If we do this properly, higher defense expenditure can generate technology, factories, skilled jobs, stronger supply chains and economic growth while simultaneously strengthening deterrence,” Murray said.
Canada hopes Britain could reconsider under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose minister of defense, Wes Streeting, described the DSRB at Farnborough as a “really interesting and innovative mechanism.” He also said he did not see the proposed defense bank and MDM as being in competition. Britain previously declined to join, citing concerns over value for money. According to his Downing Street office, Burnham discussed the DSRB alongside the MDM scheme with Carney in July and with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden during a visit last month to Kyiv.
“The UK joining would create pressure from German industry on the German government to join,” said Terhorst.
A German Ministry of Finance spokesperson said that its position on the DSRB had not changed since July, when it said it had taken part in DSRB talks as an observer and was reviewing the outcome. The Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that no decision had been made about participating.
British and German industry groups have lobbied their countries to join. Andrew Kinniburgh of Make UK Defense said companies risked being excluded from projects financed through the bank if Britain stayed out.
About a dozen banks, including JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank, have provided some US$10 million in funding or services in kind to help establish the DSRB, a person with knowledge of the matter said. The lenders, which could earn millions in fees arranging DSRB-funded projects, also backed an advertisement in the Financial Times newspaper saying the project had “the hallmarks of a future AAA-rated multilateral financial institution.”
JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank declined to comment.
Canada’s Hudon said at Farnborough that she was confident the DSRB could get a triple-A rating. Murray said a multilateral bank’s rating depends on many factors and often exceeds the average rating of members.
Ottawa is prepared to launch the bank with the current group of supporters, one person involved in the project said, with other countries free to join later. That could help cement the rating it wants.
“The creditworthiness of multilateral institutions is principally driven by the support of their core shareholders,” said Elisabeth Rudman, head of financial institution ratings at Morningstar DBRS.

16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

American Cole Houshmand yesterday took the Fiji Pro title ahead of Gabriel Medina in pumping conditions at the Cloudbreak reef, while in-form Canadian teenager Erin Brooks earned a second straight world tour title.
Californian Houshmand had lost six times in the first round this year, but turned his season around by beating reigning world champion Yago Dora in the quarter-finals and Medina in the title-decider.
His victory in the final was all the more impressive as Brazilian Medina scored a perfect 10 with his first ride of the final in a 1.8m to 2.4m swell.
Photo: EPA-EFE
“I went on the first wave and when I turned back, he was just getting blown out of a perfect wave. I was thinking ‘what have I done?’” Houshmand said.
Three-time world champion Medina failed to back up his first ride, and Houshmand ran out a 16.87-15.17 winner to take his third title in three years on the elite tour.
“I’m pretty speechless. It never really goes the way you expect it,” Houshmand said. “But if you just put your head down and work hard, and have faith, it’ll all work out.”
Medina’s second place moved him up to fourth in the standings, 6,840 points behind compatriot and championship leader Italo Ferreira with five rounds of the season to go.
Texas-born Brooks also landed a 10-point ride when the eighth stop of the tour kicked off last week and she kept up her fine form to claim back-to-back titles after her win at the Tahiti Pro last month.
The 19-year-old beat five-times world champion Carissa Moore 11.84-9.97 in the semi-finals and clinched her second Fiji Pro title when Australian Isabella Nichols was unable to compete after suffering an injury.
“I love Bella like a sister and I was so [devastated] to hear she got injured,” Brooks said.
“It’s been unreal,” she added of her last two events. “I was having a real shocker [of a season]. I was having some disbelief in myself. I’m just so grateful to be where I am right now.”
The two straight wins moved Brooks up to eighth in the women’s rankings, which are led by Hawaiian Moore.
The world tour next moves on to southern California for the Trestles Pro from Friday next week to Sept. 20.

Denmark warns of Russian sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

Russia is “actively” preparing sabotage operations against Denmark, particularly its defense industry, the head of the Danish intelligence service was quoted as saying yesterday.
The warning came after EU countries summoned Russia’s envoys and discussed fresh sanctions after an explosive-laden drone incident in Germany that the bloc’s foreign policy chief said bore the marks of “state-sponsored terrorism.”
Russia has in the past few months been accused of ratcheting up sabotage attacks against European backers of Ukraine.
Photo: Reuters
“The Russians are actively preparing sabotage operations targeting the defense industry in Denmark,” Emil Graesholm, head of counterintelligence at the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, said in an interview with newspaper Berlingske.
“It is fundamentally important that the defense industry, in the broad sense, take the necessary security measures so that it is able to protect itself,” Graesholm told broadcaster TV2. “Many actors in the sector are already actively working on this.”
Russian security services are seeking to recruit “completely ordinary Danes” for missions, he said.
The missions might, for example, involve taking photographs, and checking and reporting on access and security conditions around a facility, he said.
“We are talking about the methods, because they don’t need to look like a spy movie,” he told Berlingske.
Separately, Norwegian authorities on Wednesday seized a Russian vessel — the Professor Molchanov — in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at the request of Ukraine’s Naftogaz as part of a global effort to enforce a US$4.22 billion arbitration award stemming from Russia’s 2014 illegal annexation of Crimea and its seizure of Ukrainian energy assets.
In 2023, an arbitration tribunal in The Hague, Netherlands, ordered Russia to pay US$4.22 billion to the Ukrainian state-owned energy company for unlawfully seizing its assets in Crimea.
After Russia’s refusal to pay the award, Naftogaz has been petitioning national courts seeking court orders to seize Russian commercial assets.
“This is another important step towards restoring justice for Russia’s unlawful seizure of Naftogaz assets in Crimea. Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award. We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world,” Naftogaz chief executive officer Sergii Fedorenko said.
The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday called the seizure “piracy.”
Russian Minister for the Development of the Russian Far East and Arctic Alexei Chekunkov said that Moscow would challenge the ruling, saying the seizure of the vessel was “another example of Western countries’ legal nihilism and lawlessness,” Interfax news agency reported.

Data center spending to reach US$31.6tn by 2050
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:38 UTC
01:40:38 KST

Global data center spending is set to reach US$31.6 trillion through 2050 to meet the world’s growing appetite for artificial intelligence (AI), an investment boom with no precedent in history, PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (PwC) said in a report released on Wednesday.
Dwarfing projects such as the railways, Internet and electrification, spending on data centers could even hit US$50 trillion over the next two-and-a-half decades if AI adoption accelerates beyond PwC’s “central scenario” forecast, the firm said.
For comparison, US GDP is about US$30 trillion.
Photo: AFP
With consumers, companies and governments increasingly using AI, tech giants such as Microsoft Corp and Amazon.com Inc and smaller data center providers are setting up new computing facilities across the planet at a rapid clip. The bulk of the spending would go into what fills the data centers — hardware from companies such as global AI chip leader Nvidia Corp.
At the same time, the tech industry is trying to blunt a backlash against data centers that threatens to slow down the buildout.
At least 75 projects, worth about US$130 billion combined, were blocked or delayed by local opposition during the first three months of this year, according to research group Data Center Watch.
Protesters cite concerns about environmental impacts, resource consumption and more broadly how AI could upend employment and society.
The US would capture nearly half the projected data center spending, at US$15.1 trillion, PwC said.
The Asia-Pacific region would follow at US$8.2 trillion, Europe at US$5.6 trillion, the Middle East at US$1.1 trillion and Africa at US$255 billion of the cumulative capital expenditure, PwC’s inaugural Global Data Center Outlook showed.
“Railways. Electrification. The Internet. Each required enormous amounts of capital and defined an era,” the researchers said in the report. “The AI infrastructure cycle under way dwarfs all three. This one resets every four to six years — and shows no signs of ending.”
On an annual basis, global data center spending would increase from about US$800 billion this year to US$1.1 trillion in 2030 and US$1.8 trillion in 2050, PwC predicted.
China and India would drive the largest share of incremental demand, supported by large populations, rapidly expanding digital economies, and substantial headroom for AI to embed in business and consumer activity.
While global demand is strong, factors such as power availability, data sovereignty requirements and the flow of semiconductors would determine which regions capture the investments, PwC said.
Power would be the foremost factor that shapes where AI infrastructure investment occurs, it said.
Indeed, much of the forecast hinges on how fast reliable electricity supply for data centers can be established, the report said.
Affordable, reliable, and increasingly low-carbon electricity at scale is the hardest requirement for many markets to meet.
While the researchers’ projection assumes a fairly open trading system where chips move freely across borders, disruptions in semiconductor supply chains could cut global investment by nearly 20 percent, they said.
Meanwhile, a growing sovereignty push could redistribute, but not reduce, global investment.
“The US$31.6 trillion question isn’t whether the capital exists. It does,” the researchers said. “Nor is the question whether the demand is real. It is. The question is which regions, operators and institutions are positioned to capture it and which aren’t.”

Palau urges ‘unified’ China response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:38 UTC
01:40:38 KST

Palau’s president yesterday called for a “unified” Pacific response to a missile test by China in July, while Taiwan and its Pacific allies a day earlier at the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) reaffirmed their commitment to peace, stability and prosperity.
China gave only a handful of nations short notice before test-firing an intercontinental ballistic missile in July, sparking condemnation from several Pacific leaders.
The 18-member PIF being held in Palau was expected to release a communique after press time last night, with a formal response to the test possibly included.
Photo: AFP
Palau, which invited Taiwan to attend sideline events as an aid partner, urged the region to send a strong message.
“That’s definitely something that we’ll be discussing today [yesterday], and a unified Pacific voice is critical in getting Beijing to respect sovereignty, to respect transparency, and to be a responsible partner,” Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr told reporters.
“I think that’s the message that we should be sending to Beijing,” Whipps said. “So it’s important we have a unified position and we’ll work on that.”
He said that Beijing had “threatened and really disrespected” the region with the test of the rocket, which monitors said appeared to land in the ocean somewhere between the Solomon Islands, Nauru and Tuvalu.
“They never bothered to tell us that that’s what’s happening,” he said.
Beijing said the test launch was “a routine arrangement of China’s annual military training” and that “relevant countries were informed in advance.”
The PIF yesterday had a leaders’ retreat, during which officials were expected to hammer out the wording for a joint communique.
Meanwhile, Chinese Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo (錢波) said that there would be “consequences” after Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) attended the PIF opening ceremony.
On Wednesday, Taiwan and its three Pacific allies reaffirmed their commitment to peace, stability and prosperity in a joint statement.
The statement — which was signed by Lin, Whipps, Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine and Tuvaluan Prime Minister Feleti Teo — also expressed support for the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, a regional framework aimed at addressing shared challenges and promoting sustainable development.
The statement was signed during the 30th Taiwan/Republic of China Forum Countries Dialogue, hosted by Whipps alongside the PIF.
At the Taiwan forum, Lin exchanged views with the leaders of diplomatic allies on talent development and regional exchanges, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
Lin proposed integrating education, training, employment and skills assessment, drawing on Taiwan’s experience in vocational education to help its allies cultivate talent that meets the needs of their societies and industries, the ministry said.
The initiative aims to improve the employability of young people and build a stronger talent base for their countries’ long-term development, it said.
The leaders also explored the feasibility of using funds from allies to invest in Taiwan’s capital markets, and expanding cooperation in areas including finance, industry and economic development, the ministry said.
Although the international landscape has continued to change, Taiwan has remained committed to working with its Pacific partners in a pragmatic and mutually beneficial way to address shared challenges, Lin said.

====================================================================================================

Is China really a champion  of the global south?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:34 UTC
01:40:34 KST

China often leans into its “developing country” status, portraying itself as a defender of the global south’s interests and cultivating a close alliance with the Group of 77, which includes 134 countries from Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean. However, some have questioned whether China’s efforts to lead the global south are less about shattering the “status quo” and more about consolidating its power as the US disengages from the international system it built.
Determining China’s motivations requires a deeper understanding of its rivalry with the US. In 1820, Qing Dynasty China was the world’s largest economy, accounting for nearly one-third of world GDP in purchasing-power-parity terms, while the US economy was one-10th the size of the British Empire’s.
Then came China’s “century of humiliation.” While large parts of China were occupied by Western powers and Japan, the US economy grew at an extraordinary rate, becoming the world’s largest by 1903. In the wake of World War II, the US consolidated its economic hegemony by playing a central role in establishing the UN, the Bretton Woods institutions, and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the precursor to the WTO.
Illustration: Mountain People
In 1978, Deng Xiaoping (鄧小平) sought to reclaim China’s lost glory through his visionary economic reforms. By 2010, China’s economy had become the world’s second-largest (after the US) and, as of 2024, its share of global manufacturing had risen to more than 30 percent, while the US’ had declined to 15 percent, down from more than 50 percent in 1945.
This reversal of fortunes set the stage for the two countries’ ongoing trade war, which began when the US imposed tariffs on select Chinese goods in 2018 and left the WTO’s Appellate Body inquorate and unable to resolve disputes.
As a result, China’s trade surplus with the US fell from a peak of US$400 billion in 2018 to about US$200 billion last year, although many Chinese exports still reach the US through third countries such as Mexico and Canada. China has since accelerated its pivot to self-sufficiency, which includes developing resilient supply chains for critical technologies such as semiconductors, and weaponized its dominance in rare earths.
The general consensus within Chinese leadership circles is that “the East is rising and the West is declining,” as Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) famously declared in 2021, and that the US, suffering from “hegemonic anxiety,” is lashing out against its main rival.
However, the US’ decline should not be overstated. Despite its huge national debt, which surpassed US$40 trillion, and despite representing only 4 percent of the global population, the US, with a nominal GDP of about US$32 trillion, remains the world’s largest economy. Moreover, the US dollar has retained its dominance, accounting for about half of international payments.
The US is an overextended hegemon, and its decline would continue slowly, as other powers such as China assume more global responsibilities, but the US retains its hard and soft power. About 165,000 US military personnel are deployed in 178 countries. The US is home to 35 of the world’s top-ranked 100 universities and remains the top destination for immigrants. Tellingly, 55 percent of the US’ billion-dollar start-ups had at least one foreign-born founder. China, by contrast, is an extraordinarily homogenous and closed society.
The biggest battle between the US and China is for artificial intelligence (AI) supremacy. The two countries account for 90 percent of the world’s frontier computing power, implying that the winner of the AI race would gain an unassailable technological lead. China is quickly catching up, focusing on affordable models. This reflects the Chinese government’s growing emphasis on basic science: Its spending on research and development surpassed the US’ in 2024, while Chinese scholars published as many papers as American, British, German, and Japanese researchers combined last year.
Meanwhile, China has shown that it cannot be a credible leader of the global south. Rather, it is a reliable, if hardheaded, trading partner that pursues its own interests. The country’s cheap textile exports led to job losses across Africa, while its free-trade agreements with Chile and Peru have been criticized as extractive and contributing to deindustrialization. Equally important, China has been reluctant to transfer technology — especially the clean tech that has been a powerful driver of economic growth — to the global south.
In short, China is happy to preserve the “status quo.” At the US-China summit in May, officials eagerly sought US acknowledgment of China’s superpower status — more than they have ever sought global south approval. When the US intervened in Venezuela and, together with Israel, attacked Iran, China’s response was muted, seemingly because the country was more interested in avoiding a direct military confrontation with the US than in supporting its reliable oil suppliers (and, in the case of Iran, a BRICS+ member).
China also failed to veto a UN Security Council resolution condemning Iran’s attacks on Gulf countries. Still, many in the Global South see the sharp contrast between China and the US, which has vetoed at least 53 UN Security Council resolutions critical of Israel since 1972.
Under Xi’s leadership, Chinese diplomats have become “wolf warriors” who use aggressive tactics, including the threat of boycotts, to defend China’s interests. For example, senior African and Jamaican diplomats said that China threatened Zambia and Jamaica with aid cuts to secure the removal of their permanent representatives at the UN, who were championing Security Council reforms. Such crude bullying tends to alienate potential allies and betrays an extraordinary lack of understanding of how to wield soft power.
To be sure, the global south hopes to emulate certain elements of China’s rise, particularly its technological innovation and its success in lifting nearly 800 million people out of extreme poverty. However, China is ultimately a “status quo” superpower more concerned with the repression of dissent at home and the protection of its own interests abroad than with leading the development of an international system that works for all countries.
Adekeye Adebajo, a professor and a senior research fellow at the University of Pretoria’s Centre for the Advancement of Scholarship, is the editor of The Black Atlantic’s Triple Burden: Slavery, Colonialism, and Reparations.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Russia’s and Iran’s war efforts are being materially supported by Chinese supplies of drone components and missile fuels. So far in 2026, such Chinese support has enabled a 60 percent increase in civilian casualties in Ukraine caused by long-range Russian weapons such as missiles and drones from January to June 2026 compared with the same

MAC approves China travel for APEC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:34 UTC
01:40:34 KST

The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) yesterday said that it had conducted risk assessments and contingency planning for all government officials scheduled to attend APEC ministerial meetings in China this year, and has determined that they can proceed.
The council made the remarks as Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) is scheduled to attend the APEC Human Resources Development Ministerial Meeting in Nanjing on Sept. 21, making him the first minister to travel to China since President William Lai (賴清德) took office in 2024.
“So far, officials’ trips have gone smoothly. We think the overall risks this time would be manageable,” MAC Deputy Minister and spokesman Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) told a news conference in Taipei.
Photo: Chen Yu-fu, Taipei Times
Officials including Deputy Minister of Economic Affairs Chiang Wen-jo (江文若) and former chief trade negotiator at the Office of Trade Negotiations Yang Jen-ni (楊珍妮) have traveled to China to attend APEC-related meetings this year, Liang said.
Hung would enter China by presenting APEC’s invitation and following the organizer’s arrangement, without having to present a Mainland Travel Permit for Taiwan Residents, Liang said.
Hung’s participation and remarks at APEC already demonstrate the existence of the Republic of China (Taiwan), with no need for any additional declaration of sovereignty, he added.
Any interaction with Chinese officials during the meetings can proceed naturally, and Hung need not avoid or make a deliberate attempt to meet, he said.
“We hope that, as the APEC host, China will treat our delegation appropriately in accordance with existing practices and APEC rules,” Liang said.
Liang also responded to reports that a Taiwanese man was interrogated by Chinese immigration officers during a business trip to Shanghai due to his past work as an intern for Amnesty International.
China views international human rights organizations as engaging in anti-China activities, and Taiwanese who were participants of these groups risk being interrogated or persecuted, Liang said.
“This would cause people to censor themselves and avoid joining activities hosted by civil groups, constituting a major threat to Taiwan’s democratic system,” Liang said.
So far, about half of Taiwanese who were interrogated or detained during trips to China are current or retired civil servants, Liang said.
While China’s Taiwan Affairs Office tried to assure the public that they should not be concerned about its new entry and exit regulations, which are to take effect on Sept. 15, so long as they do not engage in criminal activities in China, the travel risks do not disappear, he said.
“They could still be interrogated for what they have done in Taiwan and elsewhere,” he said, adding that the best way to counter the problem is to disclose such incidents in public.
Liang said that the purpose of asking people to register trips to China is so that the government can provide timely assistance in case of emergencies.

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) yesterday said that it had deployed vessels to “monitor” Chinese ships operating in waters off the east coast.
The CGA said it dispatched vessels in response to a China Coast Guard announcement that it had carried out another “routine law-enforcement patrol” in waters off the east coast.
“The CGA firmly rejects China’s cognitive warfare campaign of ‘law enforcement in name, jurisdictional expansion in practice,’” it said on X.
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration
As of 11am yesterday, two China Coast Guard ships were “loitering and drifting” about 105 nautical miles (195km) and 74 nautical miles east of Green Island (綠島) respectively, it said.
It also condemned China’s actions that “sought to harass” Taiwan through maritime activities.
China carried out its first “law enforcement” patrol east of Taiwan in June.
Beijing has since dialed up pressure, deploying a record 244 coast guard, scientific research and other ships around the nation in July, data showed.
That compares with 55 ships detected in June, 30 in May and 58 in July last year.
In the first 21 days of last month, 152 vessels were detected.
About 60 percent were China Coast Guard ships, with research vessels and other government boats making up the rest.
The figures do not include Chinese warships, which China’s military deploys on a near-daily basis.

The CGA on Aug. 21 said it had warned off and shadowed a Chinese research ship sailing in sensitive waters near Taiwan, the third time the vessel had been spotted since May.

Injured penguins given vests to help them heal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:30 UTC
01:40:30 KST

Researchers in Chile have designed an unlikely new garment for injured penguins — snug red vests threaded with copper and zinc that they hope will help the aquatic birds heal faster.
Veterinarians have found success using such suits to treat injured dogs and cats. Now they are trying out the technology on Humboldt penguins in Chile, home to the largest concentration of the vulnerable species.
“For years, vests with microfibers containing elements like copper and zinc have been tested on pets, particularly dogs and cats, and have greatly helped in the recovery of skin wounds,” said Ignacio Idalsoaga, director of the Buin Zoo, a wildlife park on the outskirts of Chile’s capital, Santiago, where researchers took measurements of penguins to develop the first bodysuits.
Photo: Reuters
“We began to wonder — why can’t this be used on penguins?” Idalsoaga told reporters from the zoo on Wednesday.
The experiment comes as Chile’s Humboldt penguin population declines sharply. Chilean and international researchers surveying the country’s major breeding colonies in 2024 and last year found a 63 percent drop in active nests compared with the same sites three years earlier.
The birds face mounting threats, including entanglement in fishing nets, plastic pollution, disease outbreaks and competition with fisheries for food.
Now Humboldt penguins also find themselves in the crosshairs of one of the world’s most disruptive weather patterns, El Nino, which brings unusually warm waters to parts of the Pacific Ocean, making the cold-water fish that they rely on harder to find.
Hunger forces penguin parents to travel farther afield for food and leave their nests behind.
“Especially now, with all the problems caused by El Nino, we’re likely to see many abandoned chicks in the coming weeks, with injuries they suffer in the environment,” Idalsoaga said.
Wildlife clinics across Chile receive distressed penguins stranded along Chile’s coast, some cut by fishing nets or boat propellers, others weakened by a lack of food, said Tomas Pino, a veterinarian who runs Conservacion Humboldt, a nonprofit that rehabilitates injured marine animals in the country’s north.
Treating the injuries can be tricky. Penguins often twist their long necks to peck at gashes and pull out their own stitches, Pino said.
The vests prevent them from doing that while putting copper — of which Chile is the world’s top producer — to work as a salve.
Copper and zinc woven into the fabric inhibit the growth of bacteria and fungi. Zinc also stimulates the formation of new blood vessels, helping damaged tissue heal faster.
“We’ve seen that the penguins tolerate it quite well,” Pino said. “We noticed that from one day to the next, the wounds were in better condition with the vest.”

Taiwan hepatitis certification still on track: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:30 UTC
01:40:30 KST

A cluster of hepatitis C cases in New Taipei City would not affect the timeline for Taiwan’s application for WHO certification, Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Chuang Jen-hsiang (莊人祥) said yesterday.
Earlier this year, Taipei submitted its Taiwan Hepatitis C Elimination Report to the WHO Western Pacific Regional Office for a “gold tier” status for its efforts to eliminate hepatitis C ahead of the WHO’s 2030 global target.
The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) on Wednesday linked 11 acute viral hepatitis C cases to a clinic in New Taipei City’s Banciao District (板橋).
Photo: Lo Pi, Taipei Times
The cases had received intravenous nutritional injections at the Antai Songhe Clinic (安泰淞鶴診所) between January and last month, the agency said.
The CDC said it received a report on Aug. 12 about two cases of acute hepatitis C and immediately launched an investigation.
Chuang said more than 1,000 people are awaiting screening.
Hepatitis C has an incubation period of six months.
At the end of last year, the Ministry of Health and Welfare announced that Taiwan had achieved hepatitis C elimination ahead of schedule, with diagnosis and treatment rates exceeding 90 percent.
If clusters are detected early and treated, they would not affect hepatitis C elimination indicators or Taiwan’s application to the WHO, as confirmed cases are not expected to exceed 1,000, Chuang said.
If granted gold tier status, Taiwan would become a regional leader and join countries at the forefront of hepatitis elimination, such as Iceland, Australia and Egypt.
WHO criteria do not require Taiwan to completely eliminate new hepatitis C infections, and monitoring and active prevention and control efforts would remain necessary, the Health Promotion Administration said.
About 7.96 million people in Taiwan underwent hepatitis B and C screening between 2017 and June, while 184,000 people with chronic hepatitis C received treatment with new oral antiviral drugs, its data showed.

Reaching a milestone in Taiwan-Italy ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:27 UTC
01:40:27 KST

In a landmark moment of bilateral relations, President William Lai (賴清德) on Tuesday received Italy’s largest-ever cross-party parliamentary delegation at the Presidential Office.
The arrival of the 10-member delegation — headed by Italian Senate Vice President Gian Marco Centinaio — is the result of a gradual, bipartisan push within the Italian Parliament to elevate relations with Taiwan, and reflects Rome’s efforts to bolster its democratic alliances.
The mission is driven by strategic objectives: to translate shared democratic values into strong economic and industrial partnerships, safeguard peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, and project a unified Italian commitment to the rules-based international order, anchored in Centinaio’s core message that “helping Taiwan is helping the entire world.”
“Taiwan will continue to cooperate with Italy and other like-minded partners to uphold the rules-based international order and expand economic, trade and industrial collaboration,” Lai said.
His words reflect an alignment of views between the countries, which would serve as a launchpad to consolidate a vision based on preserving common values and implementing a strategy that enables both nations to achieve mutually tangible benefits across numerous areas of shared interest.
Taiwan is a high-value ally eager to deploy its strengths in semiconductors and high-tech innovation, supply chain resilience, cultural diplomacy, regional security, academic research and green technology.
Rome’s commitment to giving continuity to the hopes voiced by Lai is validated by the record-breaking scope of the mission to Taiwan and its cross-party composition.
This visit unfolds within a global environment defined by instability and uncertainty, where mounting tensions in the Taiwan Strait and security concerns across the Indo-Pacific region are viewed as increasingly urgent imperatives.
In the eyes of the Italian lawmakers, navigating these challenges demands a recalibration toward Taiwan. As one of the G7 nations most vocal in advocating for peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, Italy is uniquely positioned to play a leading role in firmly reiterating that any unilateral change to the “status quo” is unacceptable.
The visit confirms that, in an era defined by growing antagonism between democracies and autocracies, the Italian political spectrum has recognized the necessity of taking a clear stance to defend its core values, not only at home, but across geopolitical theaters worldwide.
By elevating engagement to a formal cross-party level, Italy is helping dismantle Taipei’s geopolitical isolation, sending an unambiguous signal that European democracies view cross-strait stability not as a localized dispute, but as a global imperative.
This diplomatic backing legitimizes Taipei’s standing on the international stage, as Rome’s visible support sends a clear message to the broader international community that Taiwan is a significant, permanent stakeholder in the global order.
The adoption of a similar posture by other European nations would further help Taiwan interact as a trusted peer fully empowered to shape the global policy agenda and drive international innovation.
Taiwan would benefit exponentially from a unified stance from Europe’s major economies, which would effectively neutralize Beijing’s strategy of diplomatic isolation, providing Taipei with the geopolitical coverage needed to execute bilateral trade, investment and technology agreements without fear of disproportionate economic retaliation.
Michele Maresca is an analyst at Il Caffe Geopolitico, an online international law journal, and the think tank Geopol21.

Chinese artists withdraw from biennale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:27 UTC
01:40:27 KST

Chinese artists withdrew from a major South Korean art show after organizers allowed “Taiwan” to be used in the name of the exhibition, officials said yesterday, as China issued a rebuke.
The Gwangju Biennale, one of Asia’s largest contemporary art events, is to open tomorrow, with its Pavilion Project bringing together artists from around the world at venues across the city.
The dispute began after Taiwanese artists said organizers had initially agreed to call their exhibition the “Taiwan Pavilion,” but in June changed the name to “NTMoFA,” the acronym for the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts.
Photo: Yonhap/AFP
The change was made “without the consent of the participating team, and brutally erased Taiwan from the poster,” the artists said in a joint statement last month, accusing organizers of political censorship.
Last week, the Gwangju Biennale Foundation reversed course and agreed to restore the name “Taiwan Pavilion.”
Chinese artists then halted preparations for their own pavilion, and yesterday the Chinese artists announced they would formally withdraw, local media reported.
A spokesperson for the foundation confirmed that the Chinese artists were withdrawing.
China’s consulate general in Gwangju said biennale organizers “openly allowed the Taiwan region of China to participate in the exhibition using a name that is completely inconsistent with its status.”
“This constitutes a serious violation of the one China principle,” it said. “We once again urge the organizers of the Gwangju Biennale to immediately rectify their wrongdoing.”
The South Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the “government’s basic position regarding Taiwan remains unchanged.”
The decision was made in the cultural and artistic sphere, and “is unrelated to the South Korean government’s position regarding Taiwan,” it said.
“We hope that this issue will not affect South Korea-China relations or exchanges and cooperation between the two countries,” it added.

Taipei, New Taipei to offer free bus rides on Sept. 22
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:26 UTC
01:40:26 KST

All bus services in Taipei and New Taipei City are to be free on Sept. 22 to mark World Car Free Day, the city governments announced yesterday.
A total of 5,842 buses operating on 719 routes across the two cities would participate, including early morning departures and late-night services continuing into the early hours of Sept. 23, officials said.
The initiative aims to raise awareness of alternative ways to commute and encourage people to break their driving habits, Taipei Deputy Mayor Chang Wen-te (張溫德) told a news conference.
Photo: CNA
All buses are to display signs indicating that rides are free, and ticket machines and fare boxes would be sealed, New Taipei City Transportation Department Director Chung Ming-shi (鍾鳴時) said.
The number of bus departures would be increased, although drivers would not be required to work overtime, officials said.
The Taipei and New Taipei City governments have allocated NT$30 million (US$944,733) and NT$20 million respectively to subsidize bus operators for the campaign, they said.
The free rides apply only to regular bus services. Sightseeing services are not included.

Nvidia to buy AI platform Hugging Face for US$12.9 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:24 UTC
01:40:24 KST

Nvidia Corp announced yesterday that it would buy artificial intelligence (AI) platform Hugging Face for US$12.9 billion, as the chipmaking giant seeks to diversify its hold on the AI sector.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) confirmed the deal — first reported by US media last month — in a statement on the company’s Web site.
"US$12.9 billion is what it took to close the deal, and it’s worth every single penny," Huang told US broadcaster CNBC after the deal was announced.
Photo: Jonathan Drake, Reuters
The price is a marked increase from the US$7 billion valuation that was the basis of initial negotiations with Nvidia late last year, according to US media reports.
Founded in 2016 in New York by three French entrepreneurs, Hugging Face — whose name is inspired by an emoji — describes itself as "the AI community building the future."
The company touts open models, which can be downloaded and modified, as opposed to closed models like those of rivals OpenAI or Anthropic PBC.
Huang said that Nvidia would not be changing Hugging Face’s core model with the acquisition.
"Hugging Face will continue to support open source and open weight models from across the ecosystem, from every model builder," he said, adding that it would "remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem."
According to Nvidia’s statement, the AI platform has more than 18 million users, who have created more than 3 million models and more than a million applications.
Speaking to CNBC, Huang said the company’s "vision was spot on" for being focused on open models.
"At a time when open models are accelerating, this is really a very, very delicate time, and we want to make sure that it has all the support necessary," he said.
Huang said open models were crucial for his company’s growth.
"Together we can scale open community even faster than they’re able to do today, which will be great for Nvidia," he said.
Hugging Face co-founder Clem Delangue said he, his two co-founders and the entire Hugging Face would remain on and join Nvidia as part of the new move.
"The goal really is to join Nvidia, to continue to run (an) independently neutral platform within the Nvidia team," he told CNBC.
The advent of AI agents capable of carrying out tasks autonomously has led to soaring demand for computing power.
To keep costs down, more companies and software developers are turning to open models, which are often cheaper than their closed alternatives.
Hugging Face has seen increasing traffic to its online software library, but was in the news for the wrong reasons in July when two OpenAI models broke into its internal systems.
The models were not authorized to do so and should have been operating in a closed environment, OpenAI said.
The incident fed worries that AI giants are unable to keep their own technology under control, with similar episodes reported by Anthropic and Moonshot AI Technology Co (月之暗面).

TPP’s Vivian Huang steps away from politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:24 UTC
01:40:24 KST

Former Taipei deputy mayor Vivian Huang (黃珊珊), a senior figure in the opposition Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), yesterday said that she would not run for office again.
In a Facebook post, Huang, who served as a TPP legislator, said that she had entered nine elections since the age of 28: six Taipei City Council races, two legislative elections and one Taipei mayoral race.
She also recalled campaigning multiple times for presidential and legislative candidates.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
Huang said that she had decided not to seek a sixth term on the Taipei City Council after falling ill in 2015, resolving at the time to live for herself and her family from then on.
However, she realized that her responsibilities were not yet completed and continued on her political path for another 10 years.
Huang said that she had completed her mission, having done her best and having no regrets.
She said her goal in politics had always been to “build a better Taiwan for the next generation.”
Although she would no longer seek elected office, she said she remains concerned about public affairs and would continue to participate in a different capacity.
Huang added that she would no longer have to weigh the value of her actions against their potential impact on an election.
She plans to return to the career she enjoys, learn new things and continue pursuing her dreams, she said.
She also said she would write about her experiences and thoughts, stand up for what she believes is right and do her best in whatever position she takes.
Huang won all six of her Taipei City Council races, serving in the role for more than 20 years, before becoming deputy mayor under TPP founder Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) in 2019.
She resigned in 2022 to run for Taipei mayor.
In 2024, Huang was the first candidate on the TPP’s party-list legislative slate.
She left the legislature this year after serving for two years, in accordance with the party’s policy of rotating its party-list lawmakers every two years.

Taiwan firms plan new US investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:23 UTC
01:40:23 KST

Taiwanese companies’ planned additional US$20 billion investment in the US would come mainly from semiconductor companies and their supply chains and artificial intelligence (AI) server-related businesses, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.
The new investment, on top of a US$35 billion pledge made by 20 firms that participated in the SelectUSA Investment Summit in May, reflects rising global demand for AI and semiconductors, as well as Taiwanese manufacturers’ growing interest in expanding in the US, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said.
US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick on Wednesday said in an interview with CNBC’s Squawk Box that Taiwan is expected next week to announce plans to invest an additional US$20 billion to US$30 billion in the US as part of a bilateral trade agreement focused on semiconductors, AI and energy.
Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
Robust semiconductor orders were also evident at the Semicon Taiwan trade show in Taipei this week, Kung said.
Event organizer SEMI has raised its forecast for global semiconductor revenue to US$1 trillion this year and US$2 trillion by 2030, from an earlier estimate of US$1 trillion by 2030.
Based on those figures, Taiwanese companies, which play key roles in advanced chipmaking and AI server manufacturing, must expand capacity at home and abroad, including the US, to meet rapidly growing demand, Kung said.
Regarding Lutnick’s remarks on potential tariffs on semiconductors, Kung said Taiwanese firms investing in the US could receive duty-free import quotas equal to 2.5 times their US production capacity under a memorandum of understanding on Taiwan-US investment signed on Jan. 15.
Taiwan’s major semiconductor firms and contract electronics makers have invested in the US, he said.
The ministry is also working with the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association (台灣電機電子公會) to develop technology parks overseas to help more suppliers and small and medium-sized enterprises expand into the US, he said.
Separately, regarding printed circuit board maker Unimicron Technology Corp’s (欣興) alleged breach of country-of-origin rules, Kung said the case is in judicial proceedings, and investigators and the courts would determine whether origin laundering occurred.
Origin laundering typically involves goods from China or elsewhere undergoing only minor processing in Taiwan or a third location before being relabeled for export to the US, without meeting substantial-transformation rules or a 35 percent value-added threshold, he said.
Taiwan’s standards apply to its own export controls, while US Customs and Border Protection makes the final determination on whether goods meet its country-of-origin rules, he said.
In contrast, the suspected May transshipment to China of servers equipped with Nvidia Corp’s advanced chips, involving three Taiwanese defendants, is an export-control issue, Kung said.
The government is considering amendments to the Foreign Trade Act (貿易法) or adding specific products to controlled lists to address the issue, with relevant agencies coordinating on the matter, he said.

German Navy announces first-time ‘secret’ tests of Israeli missiles from its frigates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:37:22 UTC
01:37:22 KST

MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. The German Navy successfully launched Israeli long-range tactical missiles from its surface ships in what it called a "historic" achievement, Commander-in-Chief Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack told the DPA news agency.
The missile in question is the LORA (LOng Range Artillery), which was developed and manufactured by Israel Aerospace Industries. According to the news agency, the missile has a range of over 500 kilometers. Israel has used the LORA on multiple occasions in combat operations in Lebanon and in its air-launched variant in Iran.
The manufacturer markets the LORA as a high-precision weapon that can be launched "from a mobile or naval platform" and "capable of striking strategic targets deep behind enemy lines." "Any detected target within the [missile’s] range can be destroyed in no more than 10 minutes," DPA noted.
However, the manufacturer provides slightly different specifications on its website. According to Israel Aerospace Industries, the LORA’s range varies between 90 and 430 kilometers.
Its launch weight is 1.6 tons, its length is 5.2 meters, and its diameter is 624 milimeters. The manufacturer also says that this single-stage solid-fuel missile uses GPS and an inertial navigation system, and its circular error probability relative to the intended target does not exceed 10 meters.
According to Kaack, the tests took place in the North Atlantic, in the waters between Ireland and Iceland. The tests, the preparations for which, according to the news agency, "were largely kept secret," involved two German frigates. The country’s Navy issued a warning about the upcoming launch 45 days in advance.
"Last night's successful ballistic missile launch was historic, and I am extremely pleased with this achievement," the Navy commander-in-chief told DPA, confirming the LORA’s compatibility with German surface ships. According to him, "the potential range [of the Israeli missile] exceeds anything we know of out there today."
"From the perspective of defending Germany and our [NATO] allies, this test marks a new chapter in terms of [enhancing] deterrence and the Navy’s combat readiness," Kaack added.
According to sources cited by DPA, two LORA missiles were launched during the tests. "Comprehensive" objective monitoring data, which, as the news agency noted, was collected during the tests, showed that both missiles reached their designated targets on the high seas.
The data, in particular, included not only the flight performance demonstrated by the missiles but also how difficult they were to detect on radar. It is currently being analyzed by relevant specialists.
DPA explained that the LORA missiles are delivered in special transport and launch containers, allowing them to be launched "relatively quickly" from surface vessels. According to the news agency, Germany's procurement of these missiles is part of the country's national rearmament programs launched following the start of the conflict in Ukraine.
DPA also emphasized that these Israeli munitions will be the second type of weapon at the disposal of the German armed forces with an effective range of more than 500 kilometers, after the Taurus cruise missiles. This will enable the German military to strike land targets at great distances.
Army Recognition recalled that Israel Aerospace Industries first demonstrated the capability to launch the LORA missile from a surface vessel during a series of tests in 2020. At that time, the missile was fired at targets ranging from 90 to 400 kilometers away. The news outlet noted that Germany increased the range of the target. Nevertheless, the missile proved its effectiveness.

Unlike Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham promises us that things will get better. And we must believe they can | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:36:05 UTC
01:36:05 KST

Of all the epithets thrown at a new prime minister, “people-pleaser” bounces off Andy Burnham. After all, the polls have him with a favourability rating of +13, making him the only party leader who scores above zero. His manner as he responded to all 125 of his questioners on his first Commons appearance this week had a warmth and empathy that his predecessor lacked. It’s a natural timbre, a good bedside manner for an uneasy country.
Keir Starmer’s rating as he left office was -36. He was defenestrated precisely because of his unpopularity. That baffled his allies, but his ratings crashed early into an electoral death zone from which no leader returns. His revenge comes in giving Labour a potentially awkward byelection confrontation with Zack Polanski: although, just as Burnham defeated the right in Makerfield, any candidate under his leadership stands a good chance of defeating the Greens in Holborn and St Pancras.
Starmer’s fall began soon after Labour’s landslide victory in July 2024 with his message of foreboding gloom in the Downing Street garden. The country faced an economic and societal “black hole”, he said, adding that “things will get worse before they get better”.
Burnham has avoided that kind of misery, on Tuesday making a promise to “unlock a feeling of positivity and possibility” in every part of the country. And why not? Hope is always better than despair. It has its own elevating power that can stimulate growth, social optimism and investment. Even in the face of coming storms, it’s better by far to have a leader who raises spirits in adversity.
The strongest El Niño on record, exacerbated by the stresses of the climate emergency, will hit the UK with tempestuously alarming weather through to early 2027. Equally alarming was that, even as Burnham spoke, the bond markets set off their own El Niño with their global sell-off raising interest rates across the world, especially on UK debt. Their preference for investing in AI companies over governments may be the wrong bet, amid warnings of this bubble bursting to the devastation of the global economy. And still there is no sign that Donald Trump will end his calamitous war with Iran and free the world from its economic blight.
Burnham, well-seasoned in the ways of politics, is fully armed against the cannonades from right and left. He’s all too familiar with the particular poison of most of the British press, for ever hostile to Labour. But the extra lashings of vitriol suggests the right are alarmed by his popularity. Here’s Tim Stanley, the Telegraph’s parliamentary sketch writer, on Burnham’s first Commons outing: “What a relief! The PM’s a dud. For a horrid moment I thought Labour had found a man who could flog socialism to simpletons, but Our Andy’s debut at the Dispatch Box – billed as make-or-break for the British Left – was met by embarrassed silence.”
Presumably, it reassures Telegraph readers to be fed exaggeration when both Reform UK and the Conservatives are on the slide. Farage is not recovering from the scrutiny over his astounding £5m gift, while the Tories languish even below their 2024 election result, which was their lowest since 1832.
They perk up at Kemi Badenoch becoming a little less unpopular. She is indeed more confident at PMQs, but her negative rating suggests she’s no people-pleaser. She leads her party downwards. My hunch is it’s not terminal: the Tories always resurrect, but only by shape-shifting to catch up with changing times, from which they periodically disconnect. But it won’t happen under her. Burnham is lucky to have an opponent swimming hard against the modern tide. Until the Tories repent, or at least recognise the catastrophic consequences of their Brexit, they won’t revive. Their anti-net zero climate extremism is bizarrely out of tune with a country that has just seen record heatwaves and which, Tory voters included, backs the zero emissions target.
Her “slashing” Britain’s welfare bill may be what people want, but it also acts as a reminder of the sheer cruelty of the Tories’ austerity years. And she is prone to tumbling into her own elephant traps. She thought she had a gotcha when she challenged Burnham as a spendthrift: what had he cut? “Tax is the simple answer,” he said, quick as a flash, citing two tax cuts in his first week.
His summer of goodwill defied Labour’s enemies, who enjoyed little success opposing capping bus fares at £2, scrapping the 5% VAT on energy bills or the creation of No 10 North, all of which were well received by the public. They will hope his pledge to end rough sleeping in England by Christmas fails. When faced with the prison overcrowding crisis, he did the unpopular thing and released prisoners. Unwelcome public advice from friends, including his former economic adviser Jim O’Neill, warning he must make cuts or tax rises has been picked up with glee by Badenoch. But oddly, she failed to mention his solution: end the ruinous triple lock on pensions.
Many people are pleased that he will set about capping political donations. Stella Creasy withdrew her strongly backed amendment to the representation of the people bill calling for a £500,000 cap, signalling her confidence in Burnham’s promised taskforce to draw up a plan. That’s a people-pleaser for a public disgusted with the squalor of cash swirling around Westminster. Another strongly backed amendment from Alex Sobel, to set up a national commission on electoral reform, was ruled out of the scope of the bill by the speaker, but the government confirmed it supports reform: it will be back and in the next manifesto.
That’s a good start. You couldn’t hope for better. Can he buck the trend of prime ministers haemorrhaging popularity within months? Storms ahead are threatening. But facing into the wind with optimism is the way to go.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Syria begins destruction of Assad-era chemical materials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:34:09 UTC
01:34:09 KST

Syria announced that it has begun destroying chemical materials found in the country under the supervision of experts from the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), marking what Damascus described as a major step since the fall of the former regime.
Speaking to the UN Security Council on Thursday, Syria’s Permanent Representative Ibrahim Olabi said the operation was the first effort of its kind on Syrian territory in more than a decade.
“I would like to announce before you today a historic moment,” Olabi said, referring to the start of the destruction process under OPCW oversight.
He said the operation demonstrated what diplomacy, political will and international cooperation could achieve, while stressing Syria’s commitment to accountability and cooperation with the international community.
Damascus vows accountability and security
Olabi said Syria was addressing the complex legacy inherited from the former regime in accordance with international law and standards.
He stressed that accountability was non-negotiable and said the destruction effort was designed to protect Syrians, prevent chemical materials from falling into the wrong hands and strengthen regional and international security.
“Every site that is secured, every ammunition that is identified, does not merely remove a danger to Syria but the entire world,” he said.
Delayed action due to Israeli attacks
Olabi accused Israel of repeatedly disrupting efforts to destroy the chemical materials, saying attacks had at times halted operations and forced the cancellation of OPCW visits.
He said the attacks had also endangered Syrian and international teams working to secure chemical sites.
“We cannot safeguard the security of the region if our security is exposed to attacks at the hands of Israel,” Olabi said, urging the international community to help create conditions that would allow the destruction process to continue.
US welcomes progress
US Deputy Ambassador to the UN Tammy Bruce welcomed Syria’s progress in dismantling remnants of the former regime’s chemical weapons program.
Bruce said the OPCW Executive Council had restored Syria’s rights and privileges under the Chemical Weapons Convention and noted that OPCW inspectors were in Syria to verify the destruction of Category 3 chemical weapons.
These include empty M4000 aerial bombs and Volcano rockets linked to past chemical attacks in Khan Sheikhoun and Ghouta.
Bruce urged UN members to support Syria’s efforts to eliminate chemical weapons and pursue accountability for those responsible, while honouring victims and survivors of chemical attacks carried out under the Assad regime.

The show must go on: Taiwanese opera star Wang Jin-ying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:33:06 UTC
01:33:06 KST

In the living room, an old-fashioned blue-green electric fan gently circulates the air. Wang Jin-ying is making chrysanthemum pu’er tea as a phonograph spills out the sounds of Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai, which she recorded when she was young. By nature impatient, she nonetheless leads a very structured life, with everything well organized and systematic. She has been this way throughout her more than 70-year-long Taiwanese Opera career, which has included performing, script work, and teaching.
From “deadbeat” to star
Wang Jin-ying was born in Xiushui, Changhua County, in 1946. Her family was very poor, so at the age of only three she was apprenticed to a Taiwanese Opera school to which her sister already belonged. Starting out as what she self-deprecatingly describes as a “deadbeat,” she made her first stage appearance at age six, and at 13 began performing in a “medicine show” troupe. From indoor theater performances and radio plays to television productions and the innovative Holo Taiwanese Opera Troupe, she has been involved in every important stage in the evolution of this art form.
Using her clear, resonant voice and expressive recitation skills, Wang became a household name for playing xiaodan (genteel heroine) roles. Over the course of the last two to three decades, she has shifted her focus to education as well as writing, editing, and preserving scripts, leaving the stage to younger performers.
The most important thing
For Wang, the format of Taiwanese Opera can change, but “singing and recitation skills” must never waver. She says that from a young age her teachers demanded that she voice her parts with clear enunciation, so that the audience could understand the plot and feel the characters’ joys and sorrows without the need for subtitles.
“Taiwanese Opera is drama through song, not just singing melodies.” She always reminds her students that they must use their voices to reveal their characters’ personalities: “The play must be present in the songs.” As she describes it, students must train their bodies to learn the necessary techniques until these become instinctive, so that as soon as they open their mouths the sounds are correct and precise.
At rehearsals, she corrects students syllable by syllable and line by line, sometimes having them repeat one sound for several hours. On the day of our visit, she has just finished 12 straight hours of class, and tells us slightly hoarsely: “Passing down a tradition is not just something that you talk about—it requires effort.”
Old scripts
Now in her 80s, Wang not only teaches classes and trains performers, she continues to edit and preserve old scripts and write new ones. She only learned to write Chinese characters at the age of 70, which she did expressly to write down dialogue and lyrics on her own.
Several years ago, she inherited a collection of precious old scripts entrusted to her by a dying uncle, including the long-lost opera Lu Mengzheng. She edited the lyrics and deleted anachronistic passages while preserving the core spirit of the work. She says: “Old scripts cannot just be left sleeping in storage—I want them to wake up and get to work!”
Wang provides her edited scripts to Taiwanese Opera schools and the younger generation free of charge, without asking for royalties.
Old operas, new listeners
Wang believes that the elegance and charisma of actors come from regular, routine self-cultivation. Therefore, when she teaches she not only teaches technique, but proper conduct. She also leads by example in all things, so that, for instance, she is never late for class and always dresses properly.
In recent years she has continued to collaborate with artists like Hsiao Mi (a prominent performer) and Ko Ming-feng (a veteran musician) to explore novel formats and broadcast platforms for Taiwanese Opera. One example is a Taiwanese Opera web series called Sister A Niau’s Century Old Store, which is available on YouTube. The aim is to make this genre accessible to more young people.
As our interview draws to a close, Wang says she is in a race against time to record every inspiration and pass along the techniques of Taiwanese Opera singing and recitation to the next generation. So long as people continue to learn these skills and perform classic scripts, Taiwanese Opera will live on into the future.
