US pressure on Iran starting to tell, as sanctions and blockade bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:32:22 UTC
01:32:22 KST

Breadcrumb
US pressure on Iran starting to tell, as sanctions and blockade bite
A U.S. campaign to throttle Iran's economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is growing increasingly difficult to withstand, three senior Iranian sources said.
Washington has in recent weeks sought to ratchet up the economic pressure on Tehran, in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that six months of conflict have so far failed to secure.
Although Iran's rulers managed to bypass sanctions for decades, the latest U.S. moves have left them in a far more sensitive position, with few remaining channels to secure foreign currency or buy goods, the sources said.
In particular, the effort to stop Iran from accessing international financing networks in other countries it has long used to keep its economy functioning poses a real and urgent threat, the sources said.
Any sign the economic campaign may break a months-long deadlock in the conflict will likely cheer U.S. planners, though Iran has also warned it could respond to the pressure with military escalation, raising the stakes at a key moment.
Petrol stocks low, currency collapses
The war has erupted back into open fighting this week, with U.S. attacks along Iran's Gulf coast prompting retaliatory Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Arab states.
Neither side has signalled it is ready to make the concessions demanded by the other, leaving the war in a costly stalemate - though one that may be shifting.
While more energy is flowing to international markets through the Strait of Hormuz despite Iranian efforts to continue disrupting the seaway, the U.S. blockade of Iranian oil exports has entirely cut off Tehran's main source of revenue.
Adding to Iran's problems, the economy was already deep in crisis before the conflict, with a cratering currency and spiralling inflation, while months of bombing have run up a massive bill to rebuild damaged industry and infrastructure.
Meanwhile, the country's financial squeeze is itself biting into Tehran's efforts to get around the sanctions regime, leaving less cash to pay the high premiums required to skirt sanctions illicitly, the sources said.
The rial has fallen to record lows over recent days and one senior source said Iran only has another two months' supply of gasoline, which has to be imported despite domestic oil production because of limited refining capacity.
Iran's rulers are keenly aware of the potential risks of an economic meltdown and the possibility of it reigniting the nationwide mass protests it put down in January by killing thousands of demonstrators.
"They are under very, very severe economic pressure. They're losing control of the Straits. It's really a question of if they choose to negotiate and I think they'll have to," said Ali Ansari, modern history professor at St Andrews University in Scotland.
The war is also entering a new phase, with each side trying to influence each other's politics.
Iran hopes the threat of inflation will deter the U.S. administration before midterm elections in November, while Washington aims to push Iranians to revolt, a senior Iranian official said.
Blockade, sanctions squeezing Tehran
The latest U.S. measures expanded secondary sanctions that target countries doing business with Iran in a bid to stop it clearing dollar transactions needed for both oil sales and to finance crucial imports of goods and raw materials.
That effort is making Iran's existing sanctions evasion networks - front companies, unregistered tankers and smuggling - too expensive to use, the three senior sources said.
Iranian crude loadings have fallen this month to about 260,000 barrels a day, from about 1.7 million a year earlier, according to data from commodity analytics firm Kpler, with only a trickle still moving off terminals for distribution by truck, train or smaller boats over the Caspian Sea.
Tehran says it still has tens of millions of barrels stored in tankers outside the blockade zone that it can sell, but the new sanctions mean intermediaries are stepping back or demanding more money, one of the officials said.
Total trade has fallen between 25% and 35%, with imports hit harder than exports, President Masoud Pezeshkian has said, one of several top officials warning in recent weeks about Iran's rapidly deteriorating situation.
U.S. pressure and Iran's own attacks have meanwhile disrupted one of the main conduits for Iranian trade - the United Arab Emirates, which said on August 19 that all commercial exchange and financial dealings with Tehran were halted until further notice.
“If those channels stay closed, a supplier wants cash, a deal is routed through another country and a shipment arrives later and dearer,” said an Iranian trader in Tehran who deals in imported goods.
The currency has collapsed in value from around 1 million rials to the dollar a year ago to over 2.2 million rials now.
The internal impact is very painful. Official figures put 12-month average inflation at 69.9% with food, beverages and tobacco prices rising at nearly twice that rate.
Official unemployment rose to 9.1% in the spring, while the number of those in work fell by about 450,000 from a year earlier amid a wider fall in labour force participation.
Even for those still in work, the average monthly salary of around $125 a month comes nowhere near meeting basic household spending requirements that come to around $450 a month according to official data.
"We are getting poorer every day," said Mahnaz, a 34-year-old private-sector employee in Tehran who asked that her family name not be used.

Reform’s media presenter worked for Chinese state propaganda channel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:30:46 UTC
01:30:46 KST

Reform UK’s top media presenter has worked for a Chinese state propaganda channel within the past year, the Guardian can reveal.
Ray Addison, who presents the political party’s in-house podcast and social media campaigns, fronted films about Xinjiang province – where the Chinese government is accused of committing genocide – for state media in September 2025.
In the videos, entitled Raymond’s Xinjiang Stories, some of which praise Chinese infrastructure, Addison described himself as a CGTN correspondent. The series was made after Addison left GB News in 2024, where he had worked as a news presenter and reporter.
Xinjiang province has attracted international attention because of alleged human rights abuses against the region’s Muslim Uyghur population by the Chinese state, including claims of forced labour, sterilisation, re-education and mass surveillance.
Addison’s work for China contrasts with the hard line Reform has taken on Chinese issues ranging from industrial relations to suspected Chinese state espionage within Westminster.
In a social media video posted by GB News in January, Nigel Farage said of the UK’s relationship with China: “I’m very, very nervous about the extent to which China has effectively spied on us, stolen many of our industrial secrets. I’m worried about the extent to which they’ve infiltrated, using money, British universities. We must be cautious about the relationship.”
The videos presented by Addison for CGTN are publicly available on YouTube and carry a warning stating that “CGTN is funded in whole or in part by the Chinese government”.
CGTN lost its licence to broadcast in the UK in 2021 after the regulator Ofcom determined it was ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party.
US goverments under both the previous Trump and Biden administrations have formally described China’s actions against the Uyghurs and other ethnic groups in the province as genocide. The UK government has not made a formal declaration but has noted concerns about alleged human rights abuses in the region. In 2021, British MPs voted to declare that China is committing genocide against the Uyghur people in Xinjiang.
Suella Braverman, now a Reform MP, has also made public statements to this effect.
On 14 January 2025, before she defected from the Conservative party to Reform, she posted on X: “China is committing genocide in Xinjiang, funding Putin’s war of aggression in Europe and has committed acts of cyber-terrorism against the British people.”
Addison is paid by Reform to produce content about the party and creates social media videos as well as presenting its The Reform UK Podcast. In recent days he has fronted the party’s social media promotion of its conference, which is being held in Birmingham.
The party has sought to capitalise on Farage’s fanbase by advertising its podcast on the basis of exclusive interviews with the party leader and other senior party figures.
Several countries have banned or limited imports of Chinese cotton from Xinjiang because of allegations that the regime uses Uyghur slave labour to process the material.
In one video posted on YouTube in September 2025, which appears to be filmed in Xinjiang, Addison describes the “gorgeous [cotton] fields all around me” and in solely favourable terms describes how technology is being used to boost cotton yields. He adds: “Xinjiang’s cotton story is no longer just about scale, it’s about transformation.”
Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, has said the party is concerned about a range of behaviour by the Chinese Communist party, including its threat to Taiwan.
“We are very anxious about multiple areas of what China is doing, and I think we need to be much stricter on it,” he told a podcast last year. Tice went on to say that the last Conservative government had been “too permissive” of China and called for the west to make it clear to China it would “come down like a ton of bricks” both militarily and economically.
Iain Duncan Smith, one of a number of British MPs and peers targeted by Chinese sanctions, criticised Reform’s engagement of Addison.
“There is a question of what due diligence will have been carried out. Everything in China is controlled by the state and if you have someone who has been employed by state media then that means they will have been employed by the state,” said.
Reform was aware of Addison’s work for a Chinese government-controlled media outlet before he was appointed. A spokesperson did not answer specific questions about its vetting process.
A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK stands by its critical comments regarding China. Ray has worked for a number of British media outlets such as GB News. China wants to back Egypt's push into AI. The US isn't happy.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:30:42 UTC
01:30:42 KST

Breadcrumb
China wants to help Egypt build out a local AI industry. The US isn't happy.
Egypt has emerged as unlikely battleground in the global AI race as China and the US vie for influence in the North African country.
News that Chinese tech giant Huawei had offered to take the lead on developing the country's AI datacentres surfaced just days before President Xi Jinping landed in Cairo for his first state visit in more than a decade.
The company has proposed exporting 1,408 of its most advanced Ascend 950-series chips to train AI models and 600 others for two clusters to run AI models after they're trained, Bloomberg reported on 26 August. It submitted a plan to build the datacentres inside 12 months, according to documents seen by the business news outlet.
The offer marks the first challenge to American AI dominance in the Middle East and if it goes through would be first known incidence of Huawei chips being exported abroad.
US companies have so far focused their efforts on lucrative markets in the Gulf, where the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain have received billions of dollars of investment in large-scale datacentres, cloud infrastructure and AI research institutions.
But news of Huawei's offer appears to have caused concern in the Trump administration, which is reportedly trying to rally American tech firms to consider a rival bid. The State Department is thought to have reached out to Microsoft and chip designers Nvidia and AMD to explore options.
Egypt, a country under-resourced in money and energy for AI development, has until now not been on Washington's radar. That it should now be the focus of conversations in Washington underlines the importance the Trump administration places on preventing Chinese AI from making inroads abroad.
Huawei's bid also hints at the role Beijing sees for AI as it tries to compete with the US in the Middle East and elsewhere. It dovetails with Xi's message this week to Arab capitals reeling from the US-Israeli war on Iran: Reject external interference and build a new security architecture.
Huawei has a longstanding relationship with Egypt, where it has for years worked on advanced technology projects including 5G, battery storage and cloud computing.
But it also trails far behind its American rivals in terms of international reach in AI and semiconductors. US export controls have drastically limited its access to cutting-edge technology, and though it is developing indigenous capabilities of its own, it is yet to challenge properly challenge America's dominance. Sealing the deal with Egypt would lay down a marker that proves that Chinese companies can compete with the America's tech giants.
China is vying for influence in other ways. In July it launched the first international body focused on AI development - World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation – which attracted signatures from 30 countries, mostly in the developing world. Beijing says the goal of the body is to ensure the development of advanced AI systems is inclusive and safe.
WAICO has been compared in some quarters to the US-led Pax Silica, an international initiative launched by the Trump administration last year to decrease reliance on Chinese supply chains.

What Dolly Parton Said in Her Last Interview Should Terrify Us
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:30:41 UTC
01:30:41 KST

Dolly Parton did so much in her life to help others. In her final days, I think she did one last thing that will help millions of people, if we pay attention to her warning and take action.
Just four days before she died, Parton said that she was being treated for health problems that she “didn’t pay attention to when I was watching over Carl.” She was talking about the years she spent caring for her husband through a long illness. The interview moved on to her upcoming projects, and that line went by so quickly that most people missed it. As we reflect on her death, I think it was a clear wake-up call to America.
This is caregiving in 2026. More than 60 million Americans are going through it, a 45% increase over the past decade. We are struggling in the shadows at great sacrifice to our own health and well-being, and caregiving rarely gets airtime as few people want to hear about it. Even worse, hardly anyone wants to talk about it.
In my mid-30s, I suddenly became a spousal caregiver for my wife through her cancer battle. It took an enormous toll on my own health, and woke me up to the harsh realities that millions of Americans face. I realized that supporting caregivers is one of the biggest unmet societal needs of our time, and I decided to dedicate the rest of my life to helping caregivers.
I left my thriving career as a hedge fund manager to build a social impact organization CareYaya, where I’ve worked directly to help thousands of caregivers, people taking care of their spouses and their aging parents, who are caring for loved ones through serious illness, dementia or disability. The toll that millions of us are facing is enormous and completely in the shadows.
But with our rapidly aging population, rising rates of dementia, cancer, and serious illness, all of which place a huge caregiving burden on spouses or adult children, I think now is a critical time to talk about caregiving, before it totally breaks our society. Parton’s death can be the wake-up call to change the societal narrative and bring about much-needed changes to support caregivers.
Parton’s own words suggest that for years, her health was going untended while she tended someone else’s, and that no one caught it. In October 2025, when posting a video to quiet fans who had begun to worry about her health, she said that while Carl was sick and after he died, “I didn’t take care of myself,” and that she had let things slide. A few months later in March 2026, opening the season at Dollywood, she said she had gotten “worn down and worn out.” And in August 2026, she said it a final time, only four days before she passed. For years, one of the most famous women in America was doing the unseen and unheralded work of a caregiver.
We have known for a quarter century that this work can literally kill the person doing it. In the Caregiver Health Effects Study, published in JAMA in 1999, elderly spousal caregivers who reported strain had a four-year mortality rate 63% higher than non-caregiving spouses.
Scientists like Janice Kiecolt-Glaser have mapped in detail the biology underneath this phenomenon. Give a caregiver and a matched non-caregiver an identical small wound, and the caregiver’s wound takes about nine days longer to close. Caregivers’ immune cells show accelerated telomere erosion, the hallmark cellular signature of faster aging.
When Blue Cross Blue Shield went into its own claims database and identified 6.7 million members who were caregivers, it found that caregivers had 26% poorer overall health than a matched benchmark. They were 64% more likely to have high blood pressure, 37% more likely to have major depression, and 34% more likely to have anxiety. Among Millennials, the so-called “sandwich generation” raising their children while managing an aging parent’s illness, the rates of hypertension ran 82% higher and hospitalizations ran 59% higher. The health care system can already see clearly what caregiving does to someone’s own health. It simply has not adjusted the way it responds to help caregivers.
Even when the person they’re caring for dies, the risk does not end, as a well-documented “Widowhood Effect” shows the surviving spouse has an excess mortality of over 30% in the first three months after the passing of their loved one.
So what’s the solution? We can start with making caregiving a diagnosis.
Let’s take high blood pressure as an example. It often causes no symptoms and does not hurt. Yet we screen for it, code it, track it, and treat it anyway, simply for one reason: it reliably increases your risk of dying early. That is the logic of preventative health care, to address the risk factor before it becomes an emergency.
By that standard, caregiving should be at the top of the list. It elevates blood pressure, depression, and inflammation, suppresses immune response, correlates with a measurable rise in mortality. And unlike most other risk factors, it is very obvious who might be affected.
The caregiver is often the person standing in the clinic exam room with their loved one, doing the paperwork and answering questions on someone else’s behalf. Yet currently, they are invisible to our health care system.
In my years as a cancer caregiver for my wife, taking her to dozens of appointments and treatments, I was never once asked how I was doing or how my health was holding up. Only 15% of caregivers have ever been asked by a health care provider how they are doing. Even on the mental-health side, clinicians still lack the diagnostic pathway to bill for supporting caregivers, so even if caregiver burden is documented, it’s not treated because it’s not billable. Our health care system can bill for almost anything these days, yet it cannot bill for one of the most common health exposures in American life.
What else would caregiver support look like?
If you know a caregiver, please stop texting, “let me know if you need anything.” An exhausted caregiver will never ask, and answering requires more work and inventing a task for you. Just name a day and a four-hour window, and show up. Bring food for them and take over the care duties for a few hours, so they can get a much-needed break to go watch a movie, go to their own doctor’s appointment, sit in a park, or take a nap.
If you are the caregiver, treat your own medical appointments as part of the job. Book them at the same time that you book your loved one’s. Tell one clinician on your care team that you are the caregiver, and ask to be checked on, too. That is information the system needs. And think about it as the announcement you hear when you board an airplane: “In the event of an emergency, please put on your oxygen mask before you help others.” If you don’t manage your own health, you may not be capable of helping your loved one.
As a country, we need to see caregivers, name the burden, and pay for it. Register caregivers alongside the patient, and screen them for physical health, mental health, and economic stability, with actual corresponding help. We should fund respite care and tax credits for caregivers. Unpaid family caregivers deliver over a trillion dollars of economic value in care every year, and we need to decide that’s worth supporting.
The next time a caregiver walks someone they love into an exam room, somebody in the room should ask how they are doing, write the answer down, and support them.
That is the memorial Dolly Parton earned, and the best way we can honor her legacy.

RABAT, September 3. /TASS/. Nearly 4,000 people who intended to illegally get into the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta on the African Mediterranean coast have been deported from the Moroccan city of Tangier located several kilometers from Ceuta, Moroccan law enforcement agencies said.
"In the past 20 days alone, the Tangier authorities have arrested and expelled more than 4,000 people from the region who had gathered in the city and its environs and were planning to cross into Ceuta," they said. "Most of those detained and deported from Tangier were young or minors, as well as migrants from African countries south of the Sahara.
"From 150 to 30 potential illegal migrant are arrested in one day, and up to 400 on the days when calls for a mass illegal crossing of the border emerge on social media," law enforcement said, adding that all the arrested Moroccans "are transported from the northern region to their places of permanent residence after their identities are verified."
According to earlier reports, the Moroccan authorities detained and deported from areas adjacent to Ceuta those who had tried to illegally reach Ceuta after the migration crisis in late July - early August. This figure "does not include those who entered Ceuta illegally during the mass border crossings and voluntarily returned to Moroccan territory or were returned as a result of coordination between Morocco and Spain," law enforcement said.
Tens of thousands of migrants managed to reach Spain’s Ceuta by swimming or walking around the breakwater separating the city from Morocco in late July. The Moroccan interior ministry said that around 40,000 people had tried to illegally reach Ceuta, and 1,135 others - Melilla. According to the Spanish side, around 72,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta, with nearly 70,000 of then having returned to Morocco. Data on the fatalities during the migration crisis vary: there are significant discrepancies between official figures and estimates from human rights organizations and local sources. The Moroccan side has officially reported 11 deaths, but according to the nongovernmental human rights organization Caminando Fronteras, at least 141 migrants died while attempting to reach the territory of the autonomous city.

Israel's Trojan Horse: Exporting instability via the Achilles Shield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:29:23 UTC
01:29:23 KST

Klaus Jurgens
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
- Klaus Jurgens is the director of Economyfirst Limited London.
"Moving Greece into a new reality" – this is how Defence Minister Nikos Dendias labelled his country's massive deal with Israel signed earlier this week. The deal involves 3.1 billion euros of investment in order to obtain Israeli air defense technology, including the medium- to long-range "David’s Sling." Granted, any nation has the right to defend itself against potential aggressors and prevention plays a central role—think of missile attacks, warplanes, or increasingly frequent drones. But observers might wonder: is Greece all of a sudden at the forefront of frontline states?
Let us quickly recall that the Achilles Shield project already existed before Monday’s deal – a total of 4.2 billion euros is earmarked for the entire program, yet with the bulk of it now flowing into Israel. Which brings us to the point: why now, and why buy from Israel?
From the Israeli perspective, securing Greece on board is highly opportunistic. As more and more European as well as non-European countries finally call a spade a spade and refer to Israel’s actions in Palestine as genocide, providing air defense systems to a NATO member state in the region is certainly aimed at diverting attention from just that: the killing of tens of thousands of innocent people. The deal fits nicely into Israel’s strategy of divide and rule – dividing public opinion abroad by falsely claiming the moral high ground and acting as the "good guys." But ever since Oct. 7, 2023, more and more critical voices have appeared, arguing that Israel's "right to exist" must not be misinterpreted as "Palestine has no right to exist." Besides, Israel continues to create regional instability by illegally invading free neighboring nations such as Lebanon. We can observe a pattern of escalating tension, and the Achilles Shield deal with Greece is part and parcel of that trend. One might actually argue that after last year’s agreement to buy 36 Israeli-made rocket artillery systems to the tune of $740 million, this week’s additional defense partnership underlines Israel’s intent to split opinion amongst NATO allies.
Exporting instability to NATO
And Greece is not the only state that attracts Israel’s attention: Finland will start using David’s Sling, an anti-missile system, by 2027. First Finland on board, now Greece. Do we detect a strategy here? Exporting Israeli air defense technology to more and more NATO member states is an attempt to project Israel as a peacemaker and ally, rather than an aggressor. Israel knows only too well that NATO is in a kind of soul-searching process due to new geopolitical realities, as well as trying to figure out whether a defense alliance should become a value-based organization or simply focus on its core aims. All this fits nicely into the above-mentioned approach of exporting not only defense technology, but instability too.
To make matters even more delicate: Monday’s deal would not have happened if Washington had said ‘no’. The technology at stake requires the USA to be consulted, as Washington has a say over third-party intellectual property transfer rights. So: we already have three NATO member states actively promoting the sale of Israeli air defense technology. Which leads us to a major issue – how is it possible that Washington allows Israel to transfer technology to other NATO member states with the clear knowledge that Israel is facing genocide proceedings at the International Court of Justice?
The remaining NATO member states would be well advised not to follow in Finland’s or Greece’s defense footsteps, so to speak. Whilst the ICJ proceedings continue, it seems inappropriate to finance the Israeli regime by offering it huge defense-industry deals and investments. For sure, safeguarding a nation's borders and territory is a legitimate undertaking. But there are other nations producing air defense systems, and not just Israel.
Economic illusions and hidden agendas
First, whilst the deal looks good on paper, it is no win-win situation at all. Out of the 3.1 billion euro investment, only a meager 25% will actually flow back into the Greek economy by means of involving Greek companies in the production of the air defense systems.
Second, would Greece not have been better advised to create additional employment at home instead of worrying about alleged and unproven threats against their nation?
And last but not least, could it be that by exporting technology to Greece, Israel maliciously wants to stir up public sentiment in Greece against the Republic of Türkiye? Israel is certainly worried about Türkiye as an ever more influential and democratic regional actor highly regarded in all four corners of the world.
Legitimate worries about global peace and stability are one thing, but exporting technology to be used as a Trojan Horse by Israel to divide Europe is something totally different. The EU, wider Europe, and NATO should not allow the latter to happen.

Amnesty International presents Stories That Resist, its first Virtual Museum—an immersive 360° experience that allows visitors to explore 65 years of campaigning, research and collective action in defence of human rights around the world.
Across five thematic galleries, visitors can explore more than 50 historical items, including emblematic objects from Amnesty International’s archives, campaigns that defined generations, photographs, videos, awards and testimonies from people who chose to act in the face of injustice.
“The history of Amnesty International is made up of people who refused to remain indifferent. This museum allows us to honour their courage, preserve the memory of our struggles and remind ourselves that every action, however small it may seem, can help transform a life,” said Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Americas.
The history of Amnesty International is made up of people who refused to remain indifferent. This museum allows us to honour their courage, preserve the memory of our struggles and remind ourselves that every action, however small it may seem, can help transform a life.”
Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Americas.
The museum offers visitors a closer look at some of the most significant moments and honours in Amnesty International’s history, including the story of the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to the organization in 1977 for its contribution to the defence of human rights.
It also features individuals and movements honoured with the Ambassador of Conscience Award, Amnesty International’s highest distinction, presented to those who have confronted injustice and used their voices and actions to inspire millions of people. Recipients include Nelson Mandela, Malala Yousafzai, Ai Weiwei, Alicia Keys, Greta Thunberg and the Fridays for Future movement.
Developed in the Americas, the initiative aims to introduce the movement’s history to new audiences and inspire more people and future generations to join the defence of human rights.
More than a digital archive, Stories That Resist is a space for memory, education and participation that demonstrates what can be achieved when thousands of people organize and act in the face of injustice.
The museum is available in English, Spanish and Portuguese, includes accessibility features for all visitors and can be explored free of charge from anywhere in the world.

What Each F-35 Variant Really Costs Right Now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:24:15 UTC
01:24:15 KST

The base cost of an F-35A, the Air Force variant of the Joint Strike Fighter, is going up 11.5 percent from $82.5 million to $92 million for the latest lots of the fifth-generation aircraft, Air & Space Forces Magazine has confirmed.
A spokesperson for the F-35 Joint Program Office gave cost estimates for each F-35 variant, averaged across Lots 18 and 19, in current-year dollars. A recent Pentagon acquisition report gave the estimates in 2012 dollars, when the program was rebaselined. The new figures give insight how inflation is affecting the program.
Manufacturer Lockheed Martin lists the price of F-35 variants for Lots 15 through 17 on its website.
The totals are average flyaway costs, which refer to all the basic costs it takes to produce one aircraft. The JPO confirmed those price tags include the cost of the jets’ engines and radars, which are provided to manufacturer Lockheed Martin as government-furnished equipment.
The cost of the F-35A went up the most in recent lots, at 11.5 percent, with the F-35B almost identical in terms of percentage growth. The F-35C went up the least, at just 8.5 percent.
But the F-35A remains the cheapest and least complex variant of the three. The F-35B—the short takeoff and vertical landing variant flown by the Marine Corps—is the most expensive and complicated, given its unique swiveling engine nozzle and hovering capabilities. And the F-35C, flown by both the Marine Corps and the Navy, is closer in price to the F-35B and has bigger wings than the F-35A to help with carrier landings, as well as folding wingtips to help with storage in close quarters.
The revelation of the price tags for the F-35s’ upcoming lots—the highest in the nearly $2 trillion program’s history—follows the Pentagon’s release of a modernized selected acquisition report which said the total estimated acquisition cost for the F-35, including both airframes and engines, had grown more than 10 percent to $536.2 billion.
The selected acquisition report, which was released in August, pointed to inflation and critical upgrades as causes of the F-35’s cost growth. But the report only included flyways costs for the three variants in 2012 dollars, leaving the full effects of inflation unclear.
Those costs were:
- $78 million for the F-35A, up 7.3 percent from the previous report in 2023.
- $110.3 million for the F-35B, up 10.5 percent from the previous report.
- $93.4 million for the F-35C, up 6.6 percent from the previous report.
The fact that the actual costs are seeing greater percentage increases could suggest inflation is having a significant effect on the jet’s price tag.
The JPO pointed to information in the selected acquisition report when asked for comment on the Lots 18 and 19 cost growth. Lockheed Martin said in a response to a query that the recent acquisition report shows the program is moving into full-rate production, resuming high-volume development deliveries, and growing globally.
“It also shows that the hard work has shifted from proving the basic aircraft to executiving major modernization, improving fleet readiness, and controlling long-term sustainment and integration costs,” a Lockheed spokesperson said.
The JPO had previously declined to release the cost for each variant in current-year dollars and said those numbers were considered controlled unclassified information. The office eventually released the figures after further queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The JPO and Lockheed Martin in September 2025 struck a final “definitized” deal for Lots 18 and 19, which would buy 296 fighters for nearly $24.3 billion. That deal was for just the airframe and did not include engine costs, meaning the average cost of just the airframe across all variants will be $82.4 million.

Poland says NATO allies ready to expand Warsaw's role in nuclear deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:17:45 UTC
01:17:45 KST

Jo Harper
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Poland has for the first time secured support from NATO countries to join an alliance program involving the delivery of nuclear weapons, Deputy Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski said on Thursday, as Warsaw seeks a larger role in NATO's nuclear deterrence.
"We want to participate in the programme for carrying nuclear weapons, which is part of nuclear sharing, and therefore increase our participation in NATO's nuclear deterrence," Zalewski told private broadcaster RMF FM.
"For the first time, we have reached the point where NATO countries want to include Poland in the programme for carrying nuclear weapons," he added.
Zalewski stressed, however, that the talks do not involve stationing nuclear warheads on Polish soil.
"There is currently no question of installing nuclear warheads anywhere other than where they are now," he said.
Under NATO's nuclear-sharing arrangements, US nuclear weapons deployed in Europe remain under American custody and control. Several NATO allies provide dual-capable aircraft capable of delivering nuclear weapons in a conflict, while other members contribute conventional forces, infrastructure, and logistical support.
NATO did not publicly confirmed that Poland is being admitted to an expanded role in these arrangements.
Zalewski's comments follow years of debate in Warsaw over whether Poland—which borders Russia's Kaliningrad enclave and Russian ally Belarus—should participate more directly in NATO's nuclear deterrence.
"If yesterday it was Georgia and today it is Ukraine, tomorrow it will be Poland," he said.
Poland has sharply increased defense spending and military capabilities since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, repeatedly calling for a stronger NATO and US military presence on the alliance's eastern flank.
NATO defense ministers said in June that the alliance would continue strengthening its nuclear deterrence through modernized capabilities, improved nuclear planning, and greater sharing of the responsibilities and risks associated with the mission.
Zalewski said separately that Poland and the United States were also discussing locations for permanent American military bases in the country.
"We are talking about permanent bases; we are talking about locations," he said, adding that Warsaw wants Washington to deploy some of its most advanced capabilities to Poland, including reconnaissance and cyber units.
Poland's government formally decided in June to pursue the establishment of a permanent US armed forces base on Polish territory.

The Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has questioned Donald Trump’s oil deal with Venezuela’s interim government, declaring that the country’s natural resources do not belong to “an illegitimate regime”.
In her first public comments since Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Venezuela last Friday, Machado walked a diplomatic tightrope between challenging the controversial agreement and trying not to rile the White House.
In a video posted on social media, the Nobel peace prize winner said: “Of course the United States is the principal partner Venezuela needs to fully develop its strategic potential. This is what the majority of Venezuelans believe … and it is something I’ve spent my whole life defending.”
However, Machado said the current occupants of the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas were “enemies of the US” and claimed they did not have the right or the democratic mandate to negotiate Venezuela’s natural resources. “The wealth of our subsoil does not belong to an illegitimate regime – it belongs to the Venezuelan people,” said Machado, recognising that supporters felt “sadness and anger” at being excluded from the decision-making process.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels – more than 65bn barrels of which are involved in the agreement.
Trump’s deal was struck with the un-elected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who took power in January after her strongman predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces.
Many observers expected Trump to replace Maduro with Machado, a conservative democracy activist who later gave the US president her Nobel prize award. But Trump instead backed Rodríguez, warning: “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price – probably bigger than Maduro.” Machado has been sidelined.
The White House claims the oil deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves.
Speaking outside the Miraflores palace on Wednesday, the US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said the aim was “to massively grow production and economic opportunities in Venezuela”. “President Trump has a clear mission in Venezuela. The mission is to bring peace, freedom, opportunity, and prosperity to everyone in Venezuela,” Wright told reporters.
But there has been widespread condemnation of what critics have called a predatory and colonial-style land grab. Machado’s supporters fear the deal makes Washington far less inclined to push for fresh presidential elections.
Machado’s movement is widely believed to have beaten Maduro by a landslide in the last such vote, in 2024, but he refused to accept the result and clung to power until his dramatic rendition on 3 January 2026.
On Wednesday, both Trump and Rodríguez brushed off questions about when an election might be held.
“You had a very powerful, very nasty dictatorship in Venezuela – and they’re just not going to be ready for it yet,” Trump told reporters, before adding vaguely: “But soon.”
Asked when an election would be held, Rodríguez said: “There will be an electoral process, but when Venezuela is ready.”
“I don’t set dates,” she added.

Drone production for Ukraine has begun in Germany. The German-American defense company Auterion and Ukraine’s Airlogix have already announced the production of the first drones, with a total of 5,000 drones planned. Handelsblatt reports, as cited by UNN.
Mass production of more than 5,000 long-range combat drones for Ukraine has begun in the Greater Munich area. The German government’s order is to be fulfilled by mid-2027

For the drones, Auterion supplies the software and operating system, while Airlogix supplies the hardware.

Why Russia’s Iskander-M Missile Still Relies on Western Chips for Its Most Critical Functions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:13:08 UTC
01:13:08 KST

- Category
- Investigations
Why Russia’s Iskander-M Missile Still Relies on Western Chips for Its Most Critical Functions
About 78% of the identified components in the inertial navigation system of Russia's 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missile are US-made, an independent analysis has found.
The Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO) reached that figure after examining the missile's inertial navigation system, a core element that fixes the weapon's position and tracks its movement in flight. The share applies to the components identified within that single analyzed system, not to the missile as a whole.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The parts NAKO traced are not peripheral. According to the commission, the chips perform critical functions—signal processing, analog-to-digital conversion, digital isolation, power management, and memory.
Where the components come from
Two US firms account for most of the American share. NAKO traced almost 40% of the identified US components to Analog Devices and roughly 12% to Texas Instruments, with the remaining 48% spread across 11 other manufacturers.
American suppliers were the largest but not the only foreign source. NAKO's breakdown of the identified components by origin ran as follows:
- American manufacturers accounted for 78% of the parts;
- Japanese suppliers made up 9.4%;
- Taiwanese firms, 6.3%;
- Swiss firms, 6.3%.
Russia's "import substitution"
Moscow has pressed import substitution across its defense industry, and NAKO acknowledged that Russia has replaced some foreign parts—mostly simpler, less sophisticated ones. The commission described the Oreshnik as its most localized missile to date.
Where systems demand high-precision signal processing and data conversion, though, the reliance on Western components persists.
That unevenness, NAKO argued, matters for sanctions design. Rather than trying to choke off every electronic part reaching Russia, the commission urged a focus on the components that specific weapons cannot function without.
Not an isolated case
The Iskander missile is not the only weapon of its kind. On August 10, 2026, specialists from Ukraine’s Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) demonstrated foreign components extracted from Russian missiles, drones, and other weaponry to Ukrainian diplomats.
As of August 2026, the directorate had identified 5,816 foreign components across 202 Russian weapons systems, it reported, alongside numerous Russian and Belarusian parts.
Among the samples were an American Nvidia Jetson Orin microcomputer taken from a Russian S-71M cruise missile and an inertial module carrying parts from Texas Instruments and Japan's TDK.
A presentation at the Office of the President of Ukraine last week underscored the same dependency. Ukraine's presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, pointed to the Kometa navigation module and components of autonomous inertial systems as critical units. The reliance extends beyond electronics to imported rocket-fuel components, carbon fiber, specialized resins, aluminum and titanium alloys, and high-precision machine tools.
Why it matters for sanctions
Russia’s access to Western microelectronics has come under greater scrutiny as its ballistic missile campaign expands.
Since the start of 2026, Russia has fired more than 500 ballistic missiles at Ukraine while also deploying North Korean KN-23 systems.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has assessed that Russia can build up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year and already holds 600 to 630 in its arsenal. He emphasized that Ukraine's forces are working to blunt Russia's military machine, though he acknowledged that the strikes continue.

Lebanon receives first detainee of five to be freed by Israel
Unknown

2026-09-03
16:10:12 UTC

Breadcrumb
Lebanon receives first detainee of five to be freed by Israel
Lebanon said it received a man on Thursday, freed as Israel announced it would release five people seized from the country's south, where it has fought several wars against Hezbollah in recent years.
The announcement came after Lebanon said its army received a man returned by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the first since Beirut called in August talks for the release of an initial group seized since the start of the 2024 war.
A source in the ICRC told The New Arab: "A humanitarian operation is currently underway, and to ensure the safety of everyone involved, we will not issue any further statements until after the operation is over".
"It was decided to release five Lebanese civilians who were arrested in areas under (Israeli army) control in southern Lebanon," the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement.
"After their interrogation was completed, it became clear that they are civilians who are not members of any terrorist organisation, have not engaged in terrorism, and there is no reason to continue holding them in Israel."
The Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) said the man, identified as Malik Ghazi, was currently undergoing medical examinations, noting he was not registered on the Lebanese Association of Prisoners' list of missing persons.
A source in the association confirmed to The New Arab that they were not aware he had been captured.
"We usually inform residents about the capture or disappearance of a person and follow up on the matter and document it, but this did not happen with Ghazi. We learned today of the kidnapping of three people from the town of Helta in the south by Israel, and we are trying to find out the fate of these people," the source explained.
A source in the Lebanese Army told The New Arab that more prisoners are set to be handed over in the coming hours, but no specific times or dates were given.
Lebanese authorities have not officially announced the number of citizens Israel seized during that war and the ongoing hostilities, but a list of more than 30 people has been compiled by their families and a committee working on their cases.
The list includes at least one Syrian national and several Hezbollah fighters.
Netanyahu's office said the decision followed "extensive efforts" by Israel and Lebanon to locate and return the bodies of leaders of Lebanon's Jewish community abducted and killed in the 1980s during the country's 15-year civil war.
After the latest round of Lebanon-Israel talks in Rome last month, a Lebanese official said Israel gave Beirut a list of individuals to demand the return of their remains.
The Israeli military said in August it recovered the remains of a soldier killed in eastern Lebanon in 1982.
'Humanitarian operation'
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency said that the Lebanese army received Ghazi earlier on Thursday, adding that he was taken to an army intelligence headquarters in the southern city of Tyre.
Ghazi's family, from the southeastern town of Ain Ata, said in October last year that they had lost contact with him after he had gone out to exercise.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam hailed the release in a statement, thanking "the American administration... for the efforts exerted in this regard".
He pledged to work "until the release of all our prisoners" and "the disclosure of the fate of the missing", as well as an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory.
Israel and Hezbollah have been engaged in hostilities since October 2023, when Tel Aviv launched the war on Gaza. What started as tit-for-tat attacks continued for a year before escalating into a full-blown war in 2024.
Hezbollah also drew Lebanon into the Middle East war two years later in support of its backer Iran after launching rockets at Israel, following joint US-Israel strikes on Tehran.
Israel responded with airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people.
The conflict has calmed since a US-Iran memorandum of understanding and a framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon agreed in June.
The Lebanon-Israel deal calls for the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from south Lebanon and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in "pilot zones".
A date has not yet been set for the next round of Lebanon-Israel talks, and Israel still carries out strikes on Lebanon while occupying parts of its territory.

CEA proposes mandatory storage for solar, wind projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:08:55 UTC
01:08:55 KST

Govt proposes phased storage mandate for new solar, wind projects from 2027, starting at 10% capacity with two-hour duration. (AI-generated image)
NEW DELHI: New solar and wind power projects may have to install battery storage alongside generation capacity from 2027, with govt proposing a phased storage requirement as part of revised technical standards for renewable energy plants.Under the draft regulations issued by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) on Thursday, ground-mounted solar and onshore wind projects commissioned after July 1, 2027 will have to install co-located energy storage equivalent to at least 10% of their installed capacity, with a minimum storage duration of two hours.This means a 100 MW solar plant would need at least 10 MW of storage capacity capable of storing electricity for two hours, or 20 MWh.The requirement will become more stringent for projects commissioned after July 1, 2029 and up to June 30, 2031. Such projects will have to provide storage equivalent to 10% of installed capacity but with a minimum duration of four hours. A 100 MW plant would therefore require 10 MW/40 MWh of storage.The move comes as the share of renewable energy in the power mix rises and the grid increasingly has to manage fluctuations in solar and wind generation.
While there is abundant renewable generation during solar hours, it can lead to curtailment due to insufficient evacuation capacity. Storage will allow surplus electricity to be stored and used during non-solar hours.More than 8,133 gigawatt-hour (GWh) of solar energy - equivalent to 1.5 days of the entire country's total power consumption or enough to power nearly 1.4 million homes for an entire year - was curtailed during the first quarter of the ongoing financial year as the grid could not absorb excess supply during daytime. “Large-scale deployment of battery energy storage systems and grid-forming inverters are crucial for integrating renewable energy into the grid,” said a new and renewable energy ministry official.The CEA has also proposed that renewable energy plants commissioned after July 1, 2027 have at least 15% of their inverters equipped with grid-forming control. All power conversion systems of battery energy storage systems will also have to have grid-forming capability.
Grid-forming technology allows power electronic equipment to help establish and maintain grid voltage and frequency, which becomes increasingly important as the share of inverter-based renewable generation rises.Stakeholders have been asked to submit suggestions on the draft Central Electricity Authority (Technical Standards for Construction of Electric Plants and Electric Lines) 2nd Amendment Regulations, 2026 by Oct 4.

"Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved by the countries involved in the conflict – Russia and Ukraine," he said.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told reporters in Kyiv: "I believe that we will now have a new dynamic in the peace efforts, with the return of this active phase of political and diplomatic engagement in many capitals around the world."

Since then, with the U.S. distracted by the Iran war, both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up long-range air attacks deep inside the other's territory.

"It is difficult for me to say right now to what extent these contacts are leading to a peace agreement, given the statements we have heard recently from Ukraine's top leadership," he said.

Russians skewer authorities for ordering citizens to register their chicken
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:06:55 UTC
01:06:55 KST

A government decree requiring registration of domestic birds, camels and reindeer took effect Tuesday, sending Russians to government service centres with live chickens in tow before authorities clarified that owners did not need to bring their animals anywhere.
A Russian government decree requiring owners of chickens, camels, reindeer and the like to register their animals took effect on Tuesday, triggering a wave of public mockery and a minor administrative crisis as Russians began turning up at government service centres with live birds.
Videos on social media showed people with chickens in tow waiting in queues, taking numbered tickets and lining up at counters. Some residents dressed their birds up before bringing them in.
Bloggers and social media users quickly compared it to the satirical fiction of Gogol, a writer who specialised in skewering the absurdities of Russian bureaucracy.
One widely shared video on Russian social media showed a chicken owner asking: "And if a chicken dies, should we call the police to investigate? What if it's aggravated murder?"
"I'm just imagining a fox or a weasel walking in... The police will be overwhelmed, and then the police will be running around with sketches of the chickens," the video said.
Social media users also asked ironically whether chickens would need death certificates and what maternity payments would be due for each new chick, a reference to Russia's state funding for births.
The so-called multifunctional centres — local one-stop-shop offices offering services such as issuing passports or registering property — in Kabardino-Balkaria were the first to break: on Wednesday morning they announced they no longer handled animal registration and told chicken owners to contact the regional veterinary authority instead.
Russia's Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance subsequently clarified that owners do not need to bring their animals anywhere.
Instead a veterinary officer will visit the premises, count the animals and assign them an identification number.
What in the bird is going on?
Under the decree, farmers with more than 10 domestic birds — including chickens, ducks, geese, turkeys, guinea fowl, quails and ostriches — must register them from 1 September this year. Smaller holdings have until 1 September 2029.
All camels and reindeer must also be registered with immediate effect. Once registered, animals are entered into the federal Horriot database, with details including species, breed, colour, sex, purpose and owner. Enclosures must be labelled.
For domestic birds, the identification number is assigned to the flock as a whole rather than to each bird individually.
Failure to comply carries fines of up to 1,000 roubles (€10) for private individuals and up to 20,000 roubles (€200) for commercial organisations, which also risk a 60-day suspension of operations.
Russian authorities said the register was designed to help track and control outbreaks of infectious animal diseases and to verify the origin of agricultural produce entering the food supply chain.
The decree's practical implications had not been clearly communicated before it took effect, which contributed to the confusion.

France pushes to keep UNIFIL in Lebanon as US rejects extension
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:05:22 UTC
01:05:22 KST

France is pushing to keep the UN peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon beyond its planned withdrawal, reopening a decision the Security Council made last year to end the mission, while the United States is firmly opposing any extension.
The issue returned to the Security Council in a closed-door discussion after Lebanon asked UN Secretary-General António Guterres to reconsider the timetable for dismantling UNIFIL, the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon.
Under the decision adopted last year, the force is due to begin a phased withdrawal in 2027 and ultimately leave southern Lebanon, transferring responsibility for security there to the Lebanese government and army.
France has now backed Beirut’s request to revisit that decision, arguing that the deteriorating security situation and ongoing contacts with Israel justify keeping the force in place longer.
The French ambassador did not present a written proposal or specify how long an extension should last. Still, raising the issue marked the first significant attempt to reopen a decision that had already been settled.
The United States strongly rejected the idea.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said Washington did not want to extend the mandate of a force it believes has failed in its mission, saying the United States would not repeat “the mistakes of the past.”
The American opposition is particularly significant because the current mandate had already been defined as UNIFIL’s final extension before an orderly withdrawal.
Several European countries expressed general support for the French position, while China and Russia, which had previously backed UNIFIL, did not take a position on the latest proposal.
Lebanese foreign minister reportedly receives security warnings
The diplomatic dispute comes as Lebanon’s Foreign Minister Youssef Raggi, a prominent Hezbollah critic and supporter of negotiations with Israel, has reportedly stopped appearing at his office after receiving security warnings.
Lebanese broadcaster Al Jadeed contacted Raggi about talks with Israel but did not receive a substantive response. When asked whether security warnings were preventing him from reaching his office, however, the minister reportedly answered in the affirmative.
Raggi has repeatedly clashed with Hezbollah and is considered one of the more outspoken Lebanese officials favoring direct political engagement over the conflict with Israel.
UN official links Hezbollah disarmament to Israeli presence
The UNIFIL debate also exposed a deeper disagreement over who bears responsibility for the continued instability in southern Lebanon.
Carlos Arnáu, the UN’s acting coordinator in Beirut, argued during the discussion that one reason Hezbollah has not disarmed is the continued Israeli military presence in Lebanese territory.
According to that position, Israel should withdraw first, after which the Lebanese army could consolidate control and create conditions for Hezbollah’s disarmament.
Jean-Pierre Lacroix, the UN under-secretary-general for peace operations, voiced a similar concern, warning against creating a security vacuum in southern Lebanon once UNIFIL leaves.
He said planning for the withdrawal was already underway but that major questions remained over what would follow, including the implications for regional stability and other UN operations in Lebanon.
France’s ambassador said after the meeting that he had received “positive reactions” from Security Council members and that Paris would continue working on the issue in the coming weeks and months.
The dispute therefore remains unresolved, with France, Lebanon and some European governments seeking to preserve the mission and Washington pressing ahead with its termination.
Israel: ‘No reason to go backward’
Israeli Ambassador to the UN Danny Danon rejected efforts to keep UNIFIL in place.
“UNIFIL failed for years in the mission assigned to it and did not prevent Hezbollah’s military buildup in southern Lebanon,” Danon said.
“The decision to end its mandate has already been made, and there is no reason to go backward. In the months remaining until the end of its activity, the force must focus on enforcing Resolution 1701 and disarming Hezbollah. Responsibility afterward will rest with the Lebanese government and the Lebanese army.”
An Israeli senior official likewise said Jerusalem opposed the creation of any new version of UNIFIL after the current mission ends.
“We oppose a new UNIFIL force,” the official said. “I would not be surprised if the UN secretary-general tries to recreate UNIFIL.”
The official said Israel and the Trump administration were aligned on the issue and had agreed that the United States could train elite units of the Lebanese army so that it could exercise effective control over the area after UNIFIL leaves.
Israel is also scrutinizing which countries might participate in any future monitoring arrangements, the official said, adding that governments seen in Jerusalem as acting against Israel should not be given a role.
Nearly five decades in Lebanon
UNIFIL was established in 1978 following Israel’s Litani Operation in southern Lebanon.
For decades, the force’s role centered largely on monitoring and reporting violations along the Blue Line, the UN-demarcated boundary between Israel and Lebanon.
After the 2006 Second Lebanon War, Security Council Resolution 1701 expanded its mandate, including support for the Lebanese army and efforts to prevent unauthorized armed activity in southern Lebanon.
Israel and the United States have long argued that UNIFIL failed to prevent Hezbollah from building extensive military infrastructure in the area.
The force currently includes roughly 10,800 troops and personnel from 47 countries.
Under the Security Council decision adopted last year, its withdrawal is expected to begin in 2027, after which responsibility for security in southern Lebanon is to pass exclusively to the Lebanese state.
During the withdrawal period, UNIFIL will still be permitted to conduct limited operations before leaving Lebanon entirely.

Nvidia strikes $12.9bn deal to buy AI platform Hugging Face
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
17:01:39 BST
01:01:39 KST

Nvidia strikes $12.9bn deal to buy AI platform Hugging Face
- Published
Nvidia has agreed to buy artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face in a deal valued at about $12.9bn (£9.5bn), one of the AI chipmaker's biggest acquisitions as it expands into software.
Hugging Face, founded in 2016, has become a popular online platform where developers and researchers can find, share and test AI models and tools.
It recently made headlines after rogue AI agents that escaped a testing environment appeared on its platform, raising questions about AI safety and oversight.
The deal would bring one of the world's largest AI developer communities into Nvidia and give it control of a leading open-source platform - an alternative to systems offered by OpenAI and Anthropic.
Nvidia is best known for making the advanced chips used to train and run AI systems. Demand for those chips has surged as companies race to build AI products.
The companies already work together to help developers use Nvidia's computing services through the platform.
According to the companies, Hugging Face is used by more than 18 million developers and hosts more than three million AI models. More than 200,000 companies use the platform, they said.
Nvidia said Hugging Face would remain open to developers and that users would not be required to use its chips or services.
Nvidia shares were up just under 1.5% at 17:30 BST.
Under the agreement, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors and offer up to $1bn in stock-based incentives to employees who join the company.
The deal could also help Nvidia expand its presence in AI software as some of its biggest customers, including Microsoft, Meta and OpenAI, develop their own chips.
Open-source AI models can be downloaded and adapted by users, unlike many AI systems that are controlled by a single company.
Supporters say the approach can make the technology more accessible to businesses, researchers and developers.
Yaël Ossowski, deputy director of advocacy group Consumer Choice Center, said the acquisition was "a vote of confidence in open AI" and suggested it could encourage competition by making AI tools more widely available to start ups and smaller companies.
The deal will be a "major victory for innovators and consumers worldwide" if Nvidia keeps Hugging Face open and accessible, he added.
The deal would also give Nvidia access to one of the world's largest AI developer communities as competition in the sector intensifies.
Founded by French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, Hugging Face also provides datasets, software tools and cloud services used to build AI applications.
Hugging Face is backed by investors including Amazon, AMD and Intel.

Only democratic government can provide stability for oil investors, Venezuelan opposition leader says
Sept 3 - Only a "serious, democratic government" can provide the stability needed by investors in Venezuela's oil sector, opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado said in a video message on Thursday.
International energy firms on Wednesday committed to expanding projects in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by interim President Delcy Rodriguez and U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
The signings, including by Eni, GE Vernova and Chevron, represent the latest effort by private companies to help revive Venezuela's struggling oil industry, which produces about 1.25 million barrels per day, far short of its 3 million bpd peak in the late 1990s.
The deals are separate from a Caracas-Washington deal that gives the U.S. access to 17 oilfields.
"The United States is the principal partner Venezuela needs to fully develop its strategic potential," Machado said in a video posted to X.

"We need to attract capital and sustained, long-term investment under conditions that provide profitability, certainty and security, while delivering a real reduction in Venezuela’s country risk," she added. "That is only possible with the legitimacy and stability provided by a serious, democratic government."
Machado, who has been outside Venezuela since late last year, when she left after living in hiding in order to receive her Nobel, has taken pains for years to develop close ties with the Trump administration, which removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid. His former vice president Rodriguez has been at a helm since.
U.S. officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has historically been close with Machado, have this week defended Washington's oil deal, casting it as part of a process to align Venezuela's energy industry with the U.S. while helping rebuild a nation ravaged by corruption, and said that the time is still not right for elections.

After 8 years in space, European spacecraft BepiColombo is finally nearing Mercury
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:00:29 UTC
01:00:29 KST

Mercury, the closest planet to the sun, is extremely difficult to study up close. In fact, just one spacecraft, NASA’s MESSENGER, has ever orbited the planet. But soon a second mission will begin exploring this rocky world to tease out new details about its surface, interior and interaction with our star. And on Thursday that mission—BepiColombo, a joint operation of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA)—took a critical step closer to beginning in earnest.
After an eight-year voyage in space, BepiColombo’s two component science orbiters, which will together observe Mercury, have split off from the spacecraft’s Mercury Transfer Module: the ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter were released and gave out a strong signal to Earth, according to an ESA livestream of the procedure.
The job isn’t done yet. Now that they’ve separated from the transfer module, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter will remain joined together until November, when they’ll enter orbit around Mercury. A month later, they’ll go on their separate orbital paths before full science operations begin next April.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The ESA orbiter will gather data on Mercury’s topography and interior structure and will put Einstein’s general theory of relativity to the test, while the JAXA orbiter will study the planet’s magnetosphere and magnetic field.
BepiColombo has already had a couple of close interactions with Mercury: it conducted flybys that used the planet’s gravity to help it get toward the proper position to accomplish its mission. During one such flyby in 2021, the spacecraft captured some photographs of the surface from just 199 kilometers (123 miles) away.

Harsh parenting predicts teenage depression and aggression through different types of repetitive thinking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:00:01 UTC
01:00:01 KST

Harsh disciplinary tactics like yelling and physical punishment predict a higher likelihood of depression and aggressive behavior in teenagers over time. A recent study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders indicates that these negative outcomes arise because adolescents get stuck in repetitive cycles of angry or sad thoughts. The research illustrates how a parent’s attempts to control behavior through strictness can ultimately harm a child’s psychological development.
Across the globe, many parents use psychological pressure or corporal punishment to manage their children’s behavior. In traditional Chinese culture, these methods are often viewed through the lens of family ethics and duty. Maxims suggesting that beating shows love and scolding shows care frame strict discipline as a form of parental responsibility. Psychologists Yanli Hou and Caina Li of Shaanxi Normal University wanted to test if this cultural acceptance buffers the harm of harsh parenting or if it still negatively affects youth development.
Previous research mostly examined these parenting tactics in Western countries using single snapshot surveys. The research team designed a longitudinal study to observe how family dynamics influence mental health over several years. They focused on a mental habit called rumination, which involves repeatedly dwelling on distressing feelings and their causes rather than finding solutions to problems. The researchers suspected that adolescents facing harsh punishment at home might develop ruminative habits as a way to process the stress.
Rumination generally takes two forms that serve distinct psychological functions. Sadness rumination occurs when a person obsessively thinks about feelings of loss, helplessness, or worthlessness. According to psychological theories of emotion, sadness usually prompts people to withdraw from a situation and retreat. Anger rumination happens when someone repeatedly focuses on perceived injustices and desires for retaliation. Anger typically energizes a person to confront obstacles and take action.
Hou, Li, and their colleagues tracked 878 junior high school students in China over three years. During the first year, the roughly twelve-year-old students completed questionnaires reporting how often they experienced harsh discipline from their parents. These behaviors included psychological aggression, mild physical punishment like pinching, and physical abuse like kicking. One year later, the students took a survey measuring how frequently they engaged in sadness and anger rumination.
During the third year, the researchers measured the students’ symptoms of depression along with their levels of reactive and proactive aggression. Reactive aggression involves lashing out in response to a perceived threat or frustration. Proactive aggression is planned, goal-directed behavior intended to assert dominance or harm someone else. By separating these measurements across three years, the team could track the sequence of emotional and behavioral changes.
The researchers first tested a model that separated the emotional pathways, looking at whether sadness and anger each predicted specific behavioral outcomes. They found that harsh parenting in the first year predicted higher levels of both sadness and anger rumination in the second year. From there, the pathways split as expected. Sadness rumination predicted symptoms of depression in the third year, while anger rumination predicted both reactive and proactive aggression.
When analyzing boys and girls separately, the researchers noticed distinct patterns based on social expectations. In many cultures, boys are socialized to be strong and unyielding, leading them to process stress through anger and aggression. Girls are often expected to be emotionally sensitive and relationship-oriented, which can make them more prone to internalizing stress as sadness. In the initial model, sadness leading to depression was a prominent pathway for boys, while anger leading to aggression was a highly prominent pathway for girls.
Next, the team tested a combined model to see how these emotional processes overlap in reality. Real-life emotions are rarely isolated, and people often experience sadness and anger simultaneously. When analyzing both types of rumination and both outcomes at the same time, sadness rumination emerged as a broader risk factor. In this combined analysis, sadness rumination predicted both later depression and aggressive behavior.
The specific link between anger rumination and aggression disappeared when the researchers accounted for the heavy overlap between sad and angry thoughts. This overlap suggests that dwelling on sadness drains a person’s cognitive resources. When a teenager is exhausted by persistent sadness, they have a harder time regulating impulses, making them more likely to act out aggressively. For girls in particular, prolonged sadness from harsh discipline appeared to intertwine with frustration, ultimately elevating the risk of reactive and proactive aggression.
The study relies on self-reported questionnaires, which depend on the students accurately remembering their parents’ behaviors and their own feelings. The students all attended private schools in a single geographic area, meaning the results might look different in rural communities or different cultural contexts. Because the researchers did not measure the students’ initial levels of rumination in the first year, the study cannot definitively prove that harsh parenting caused the repetitive thinking.
Future research could track these thought patterns more frequently, perhaps using daily diary applications, to observe exactly how angry and sad thoughts evolve over shorter periods. Researchers could also incorporate observations from teachers or parents to provide a more comprehensive view of the adolescents’ behavior. Despite these limitations, the findings suggest that parents should consider alternative disciplinary methods, as strict punishments correspond with long-term emotional distress and behavioral issues.
The study, “When love harms: Longitudinal effects of harsh parenting on adolescents’ depressive symptoms and reactive – proactive aggression,” was authored by Yanli Hou, Shengcheng Song, Ruonan Guo, and Caina Li.
