Russian House Shutdown: Decisive Move or Convenient Timing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:41:00 UTC
00:41:00 KST

Germany announced the closure of Berlin’s Russian House after attributing the attempted explosive-drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport to Russian state actors.
The Aug. 4 operation allegedly targeted a Ukrainian transport aircraft. Germany identified Russia as responsible less than a month later and announced that it would close the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and terminate the agreement governing the Russian House.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But what exactly is the Russian House, and how much does Germany’s decision immediately change?
Russia’s largest cultural center abroad
The Russian House is officially the Russian Center for Science and Culture. It belongs to a network operated by Rossotrudnichestvo, a federal agency under Russia’s foreign ministry.
Rossotrudnichestvo says it operates 87 foreign missions in 71 countries. The seven-story Berlin center, opened on Friedrichstrasse in 1984, has traditionally been the largest.
The complex contains approximately 29,000 square meters (7 acres) of usable floor space, including a 1,700-square-meter (18,300-square-feet) foyer, exhibition areas, concert halls, a cinema, a library and apartments. More than 100 people were registered as residents there in 2023.
Its official program includes Russian-language courses, concerts, films, exhibitions and events for Berlin’s Russian-speaking population.
“That is the official picture,” Berlin-based journalist and analyst Nikolai Klimeniouk told Kyiv Post.
Ukraine Fast-Tracks Interceptors for Jet-Powered Shahed
“In practice, it is a center of Russia’s so-called soft power and, in reality, propaganda. Its formal task is to promote Russian culture and Russian positions, as well as to work with the Russian-speaking diaspora and draw it toward Russia,” he added.
The EU sanctioned Rossotrudnichestvo in 2022, describing it as the Kremlin’s principal agency for projecting soft power and hybrid influence. The EU said it coordinated networks of Russian “compatriots” and influence agents, financed propaganda projects and spread revisionist accounts of history.
French authorities have gone further. Documents obtained by WDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung described the Russian House as cover for Russian intelligence services.
Nathalie Vogel, a research fellow at the Institute of World Politics in Washington, DC, whose research focuses on the role of intelligence agencies in combating Russian hybrid warfare, said both the Russian House and Bonn consulate were important components of Moscow’s intelligence presence.
“Both the Russian House, serving as an instrument for the clandestine establishment of operational agents, and the consulate in Bonn, acting as an espionage outpost in western Germany, constituted fundamental pillars of Russian intelligence-gathering activities within the Federal Republic of Germany,” Vogel told Kyiv Post.
Vogel said the allegations raised a second question: If German authorities knew about those activities, why did they not act earlier?
She also pointed to the 2016 establishment of Vladimir Yakunin’s now-defunct Dialogue of Civilizations Research Institute approximately 70 meters (230 feet) from the Russian House. Yakunin, a former Russian Railways chief and Putin associate, presented the institute as an independent platform for international dialogue. Critics described it as another instrument of Kremlin influence.
There is no public evidence that German politicians instructed the country’s intelligence agencies to disregard either institution.
Propaganda presented as culture
The Russian House’s political role was visible before the recent intelligence allegations.
Following Russia’s initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014, it hosted a photo exhibition produced by Rossiya Segodnya, the Russian state media group that includes Sputnik. The exhibition presented alleged Ukrainian military crimes against civilians.
In October 2022, the center screened an RT production titled “The Holocaust: Threads of Memory.” According to Klimeniouk’s investigation, the film portrayed Ukrainians as Nazis.
A Russian bookstore called Mnogoknig, or “Many Books,” opened inside the complex in December 2023. The store is a tenant rather than a formal department of the Russian House and belongs to a chain headquartered in Latvia.
Klimeniouk visited the shop in early 2024.
Among the products he found was a children’s soap-making kit featuring molds shaped like a grenade, pistol and Russian tank. The packaging displayed a masked soldier against a camouflage background.
The children’s section included “From Moscow to Berlin,” which reproduced Soviet myths about the Second World War, including the story of Panfilov’s “Twenty-Eight Guardsmen.” Archival evidence has established that Soviet journalists fabricated the supposed last stand.
The shop also stocked numerous novels from the Russian “popadantsy” genre, in which modern protagonists travel into the past and use their knowledge to strengthen the Soviet Union, prevent its collapse or defeat the West.
Other shelves contained works by Zakhar Prilepin, a prominent supporter of Russia’s war who served with Russian irregular forces in occupied Donbas, and Soviet nostalgist Yury Polyakov.
The store also carried opposition authors and queer literature unavailable in Russia. Klimeniouk argued that placing those books beside historical revisionism and military propaganda allowed the latter to be presented as simply another legitimate viewpoint.
Taking journalists to court
Klimeniouk published his findings in the “Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung” in April 2024.
The Russian House responded by taking the newspaper to court.
According to Klimeniouk, the center claimed that it had no connection to Rossotrudnichestvo, operated as an independent organization and did not distribute propaganda. It also objected to statements concerning the bookstore, although the article had explicitly identified Mnogoknig as a tenant rather than part of the Russian House.
The Russian House demanded corrections and an injunction preventing the publication of parts of the article.
It lost at the first instance and again on appeal, Klimeniouk said.
The legal claims nevertheless required extensive work by Klimeniouk and the publishing company’s lawyers.
“This is a clear example of how journalists can be intimidated through litigation,” he said.
“A large publishing company can afford that. A small publication or an independent journalist would face much more serious difficulties.”
Klimeniouk believes creating that burden was more important than winning.
“The message was straightforward: Regardless of what you write, if it is not complimentary, you will have to fight them in court.”
The case was not the only legal dispute involving the center.
Former Green Party lawmaker Volker Beck filed a criminal complaint alleging that its continued operation violated Germany’s Foreign Trade and Payments Act because Rossotrudnichestvo was under EU sanctions.
Berlin prosecutors opened an investigation but closed it in 2023, citing the diplomatic status of those responsible. Beck appealed the decision.
Ukrainian organization Vitsche has also held repeated demonstrations demanding the center’s closure.
A closure that takes 9 months
Germany has not used an emergency mechanism to close the Russian House immediately.
Its operation is governed by a bilateral agreement signed in 2011 and effective since June 2012. The agreement also covers the Goethe-Institut’s activities in Russia and renews automatically for five-year periods.
Either government can prevent another renewal by giving six months’ notice.
The agreement last renewed automatically in June 2022. Germany would have needed to submit notice in December 2021 to prevent that extension, before Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
The next notification deadline was already approaching on Dec. 6, 2026. Germany has now used that ordinary termination mechanism. The agreement will expire in June 2027.
The government is taking some immediate measures. Employees posted to the Russian House from Russia have been ordered to leave Germany, and events were canceled immediately after the announcement. The Russian Consulate General in Bonn must close by Sept. 18.
The large Friedrichstrasse building will remain Russian state property under a separate 99-year agreement signed in 2013.
For Klimeniouk, presenting the non-renewal as a severe new sanction exaggerates the decision.
“Germany is allowing the agreement to run out through the ordinary contractual procedure while presenting the decision as an act of exceptional resolve,” he said.
The announcement has also exposed Germany’s political divide over Russia.
Before the decision, Berlin AfD spokesperson Ronald Gläser demanded proof that the Russian House served as an intelligence center and called the closure debate counterproductive. He argued that the institution could eventually support renewed cultural and economic relations with Moscow.
After the Leipzig attribution, AfD foreign-policy spokesperson Markus Frohnmaier accused the government of applying a “double standard” by acting against Russia while failing to impose comparable consequences over the Nord Stream pipeline explosions.
The pro-Russian position is not confined to the far right. The left-wing BSW launched a petition to preserve the Russian House, while senior Die Linke lawmaker Dietmar Bartsch said the closures would not make Germany safer and could bring a larger war closer.
Germany has finally chosen to end the Russian House’s protected status. It has not, however, closed the center overnight. Its agreement can remain in force until June 2027, nearly five years after the EU sanctioned the Kremlin agency operating it.

Heidegger criticized Plato, alleging that all metaphysics is Platonism and that metaphysics is a misunderstanding and falsification of the question of Being. Is it possible to defend Platonism against this Heideggerian accusation? Three thinkers among Heidegger’s first generation of students answered this question affirmatively, and appropriated Platonic philosophy in order to respond to Heidegger’s critique and to criticize his thought more broadly. Antoine Pageau-St-Hilaire examines the Platonic critiques of Heidegger found in the works of Leo Strauss, Hans-Georg Gadamer, and Gerhard Krüger in the context from which they emerged, namely the intellectual constellation of Marburg as shaped by Marburg neo-Kantian Platonism and the philological innovations of Paul Friedländer. His rich study illuminates neglected aspects of the reception of Plato in the German tradition, and presents a new narrative of developments in post-Heideggerian thought.

How much oil is going through Hormuz? How data doesn’t match US claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:38:19 UTC
00:38:19 KST

How much oil is going through Hormuz? Why data doesn’t match US claims
Trump says the US is helping around 30 ships cross the waterway daily, but ship-tracking data suggests the number is far fewer.
The United States and Iran continue to make competing claims about who has greater control of the critical Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Washington claims the strait is open and that dozens of ships, carrying millions of barrels of oil, are passing through each day. US President Donald Trump claimed last month that the US was in “total control” of the waterway, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas is shipped during peacetime, but which has been closed since the US-Israel war on Iran began six months ago.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump says US sees ‘everything’ Iran does, threatens further attacks
- list 2 of 3USS Abraham Lincoln reaches Thailand after 9 months at sea
- list 3 of 3Saudi Arabia condemns deadly Iranian attack on tanker in Strait of Hormuz
Iran, however, says the strait remains under its control and is closed except to pre-approved vessels using its designated channels. It has warned that other ships attempting to transit risk being targeted.
So what is really going on in the strait – and what explains the divergent accounts?
What are the latest US claims about the Strait of Hormuz?
The US says shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has significantly increased in recent weeks.
Two US officials told CNN that 40 commercial ships carrying some 18 million barrels of oil passed through the strait under US military escort on Tuesday, in what would be a new wartime record.
Trump gave a similar figure on Monday, saying the US Navy was helping some 30 ships pass through Hormuz every night. He later said the waterway was “under USA control”.
In terms of oil, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that “at least 10 million barrels” were getting through the strait each day, with between 15 million and 17 million on Tuesday.
The assessment comes after US CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper claimed last week that the US military had cleared Hormuz’s transit lanes of sea mines.
Before the war began, an average of around 100 ships and 20 million barrels of oil are estimated to have passed through the waterway each day.
According to figures from PortWatch, this has fallen to an overall average of seven vessels since March.
What does Iran claim about the strait?
Iran has acknowledged that some vessels are getting through the strait, but insists it remains in control of the waterway.
Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Tuesday said “the enemy managed to get some ships” through Hormuz, but stressed that Iranian forces remain “in complete control of the strait and will not allow it to be opened”.
Ghalibaf accused the US of giving ships “false guarantees” about their ability to cross a southern route in Hormuz, warning that ships that try to do so would be targeted.
The following day, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed two oil tankers had hit mines and were disabled while trying to cross an “illegal route” in the strait. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, claimed an Iranian attack hit a Saudi oil tanker, killing two Filipino sailors.
What does shipping data show?
The latest ship-tracking data paints a different picture than the US claims, with far fewer vessels recorded as transiting the strait.
According to marine analytics firm Kpler, just six vessels crossed the strait on Wednesday, 11 on Tuesday and five on Monday. It put the 10-day average at 13 vessels per day.
Other ship-trafficking services show a similar pattern. Maritime data firm Lloyd’s List Intelligence recorded an average of around 12 transits per day from August 26 to September 1, though the latest data may be incomplete “due to a lag in identifying dark transits”, said the firm’s maritime intelligence and research director, Bridget Diakun. This means that some ships are switching off their tracking beacons.
From August 17-23, Lloyd’s List Intelligence recorded “about 14 non-Iranian-linked ships each day”, Diakun told Al Jazeera.
All these figures are far lower than the US claim that 40 ships transited the strait on Tuesday.
The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), which monitors threats to shipping in the region, said in a September 1 advisory that commercial traffic through Hormuz was “far below baseline”, despite a “modest uptick from recent lows”.
The advisory put the risk level for Hormuz at “severe”, citing a “continued risk of drifting or uncharted mines”, despite US claims to have cleared the strait of mines.
What explains the discrepancy?
Diakun told Al Jazeera that it is difficult to explain the gap between US-claimed transit figures and those recorded by ship trackers without insight into how the US tallies its own figures.
She said it’s possible the US includes smaller or non-cargo-carrying ships in its total, unlike Lloyd’s, which only counts “cargo-carrying vessels over 10,000 dwt [deadweight tonnage]”.
Eirik Hooper, a senior associate covering the ports and terminals sector for maritime research consultancy Drewry, also pointed to possible differences in how the US counts vessel transits.
“A US operational count plausibly includes everything that moved under or near naval protection: naval auxiliaries, offshore support and tugs, coastal and small craft [and] dhows,” said Hooper, noting that ship-tracking firm Kpler filters out such vessels “on size or cargo grounds”.
Hooper also said the US has access to “satellite, airborne and other sensor coverage plus its own convoy manifests”, which enables it to see vessels not immediately picked up by the normal automatic identification system (AIS) tracking system.
“By late August, the majority of Hormuz crossings were classified ‘dark’ or unknown by route, and AIS data counts often need to be revised to include vessels that switch off their transponders, with confirmed movements backdated,” said Hooper.
More generally, both the US and Iran have an incentive to play up their influence in the strait, the status of which has become a major sticking point in their six-month conflict.
Former US Ambassador Henry Ensher recently told Al Jazeera that he believes the latest cycle of US-Iran confrontation was likely triggered by CENTCOM’s claims to have de-mined that strait, and said “both sides would be well served to stop talking quite so much”.

Russia charges a children’s hospice founder with spreading ‘fakes’ about the military over a post condemning the war. She faces up to 10 years in prison.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:38:00 UTC
00:38:00 KST

Russia charges a children’s hospice founder with spreading ‘fakes’ about the military over a post condemning the war. She faces up to 10 years in prison.
Russian authorities detained Lida Moniava, head of the “House with a Lighthouse” children’s hospice, and charged her with spreading “fake” information about the Russian military motivated by political hatred (Article 207.3, Part 2, Clause D of Russia’s Criminal Code). Officers searched Moniava’s home on the morning of September 2 and brought her in for questioning at the Investigative Committee, Russia’s main law enforcement agency for major crimes. The charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
The criminal case stems from a post Moniava published on her Telegram channel on February 24, 2023, the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, her defense attorney Mikhail Biryukov told the independent Russian news outlet Mediazona. The post opened with the words: “For a year now my country has been sending missiles, tanks, and soldiers into Ukraine. For a year now, innocent people have been dying because of this.” Moniava went on to describe the killing of Ukrainian civilians, including young children, and urged readers to donate to a fund helping Ukrainian refugees who had ended up in Russia because of the war.
Moniava did not admit guilt during questioning at the Investigative Committee, and authorities are expected to ask a court to send her to a pretrial detention center. Biryukov said a hearing on her pretrial restriction is scheduled for September 3, after 5 p.m., at Simonovsky District Court in Moscow. Investigators have not yet filed the motion, but Moniava’s defense attorneys believe they will seek her pretrial detention.
The House with a Lighthouse foundation told Meduza it was awaiting news about Moniava, adding: “The work of House with a Lighthouse and its support for families continues as usual.”
A court fined Moniava 45,000 rubles in February 2026 under an administrative charge of “discrediting” the Russian military. The penalty stemmed from three posts on her Telegram channel in 2025. In one, she linked to a “Christmas Address to Friends” by Orthodox Christians in emigration, published by The Moscow Times, which spoke of “a terrible war unleashed by the Russian state.” In another, Moniava wrote about the killing of children in a Russian missile strike on Kryvyi Rih. In a third, she described the deaths of the Martynenko family in a Russian strike on Sumy.
After the fine, Moniava said she had no plans to leave Russia. She wrote on social media that the war is “evil” and “a terrible tragedy” that needs “to be stopped as soon as possible”:
I’ve also received a lot of advice to leave Russia. I suppose I should respond to that too. When Center E comes pounding at your apartment door, it is of course frightening. But just look at this picture of what a great shift Anya and I are having — a girl who spent 19 years living behind the walls of a state institution. If I leave, more children in palliative care will end up spending time in institutions and intensive care units. I doubt I could live happily in another country under those circumstances. So I’m not planning to emigrate. But I also can’t stay silent as if there’s no war. Living truthfully matters most to me.
Lida Moniava started volunteering in the oncology department of the Russian Children’s Clinical Hospital while still in school. “There I played with the children and helped supply the department with things like disposable materials, laundry detergent, and cleaning supplies,” she said. She continued helping at the hospital while studying at the journalism department of Moscow State University, then went to work for the Podari Zhizn (Gift of Life) foundation, which helps children with cancer and severe blood disorders. From 2008 to 2011, Moniava served as personal assistant to the foundation’s director, Galina Chalikova. After Chalikova died of cancer, Moniava became a coordinator of children’s assistance at the Vera foundation, which had just launched a program of targeted aid for terminally ill children.
Moniava went on to co-found the House with a Lighthouse children’s hospice with Nyuta Federmesser, who created the Vera foundation, and headed the charitable foundation of the same name, which supports children’s hospices in Moscow and the Moscow region and helps severely ill children and young adults up to age 30.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion began, Moniava launched a separate fund to help refugees from Ukraine, Russia’s border regions, and Nagorno-Karabakh. It suspended operations in September 2025.

The World Food Programme is standing by its partnership with Palantir, telling staff that the new deal with the controversial military contractor will save the organisation millions of dollars. But some WFPers have questions.
Inklings explores how aid works in the wilds of humanitarian hubs, on the front lines of emergency response, or in the dark corners of aid punditry.
It’s also available as an email newsletter. Subscribe here.
Today: WFP staff question Palantir renewal, the fundraising strategy behind ration cuts, and the pope’s moral challenge on data extraction.
On the radar |
WFP is defending its partnership with Palantir, the data analytics firm and military contractor. In a message shared with staff on 30 August, the agency acknowledged that it renewed its “partnership agreement” for five years in July, following ”extensive internal reviews covering operational value, data governance, privacy, and security”.
“WFP management acknowledges concerns that have been raised regarding work with Palantir,” the internal message states. “These have been carefully considered through a cross-divisional committee, including ensuring safeguards to protect beneficiary data.”
WFP has come under fire for its secretive relationship with Palantir, often seen as an AI arms dealer that espouses a techno-fascist, US-dominated worldview. While governments and the public in several countries are questioning or breaking ties with Palantir, mostly over data sovereignty fears, WFP has largely refused to discuss or even acknowledge basic details about its partnership.
Internally, some staff have described a culture of silence when it comes to Palantir. The 30 August message was a rare example of WFP management engaging with the unease about Palantir, said a staff member who shared the note with us.
That said, the message was seen as more of a shut door than an open discussion. Senior WFP management was also questioned about the Palantir renewal during a 3 September all-staff meeting.
The vibe from management, the staff member said, is ”that this is the way it is. This is our partnership and we don’t have any intentions to let it go. So you have to accept this fact and stop asking questions”.
- Quick recap: WFP trumpeted its Palantir partnership in 2019, but quickly clammed up as criticism grew. Chatter in and out of WFP for several weeks has been that the food agency would renew its contract. PassBlue and France24 reported in early August that the contract was on the verge of being finalised, despite “key privacy concerns” from an internal audit. WFP is the backbone of the international humanitarian sector’s logistics operations and is building its growth strategy around harnessing data and pioneering new tech. A May cyber-attack exposed data belonging to a vast majority of Gaza’s remaining population. WFP restarted data collection in Gaza in July, but has ignored or sidestepped many questions about the breach from media, aid partners, and donors. Israel’s military has used data and AI-enabled analytics to target and kill in Gaza.
A few more tidbits from WFP’s internal message to staff:
- Cost savings: The all-seeing data integration platform created with Palantir, known as DOTS, has led to $50 million in savings, WFP says. Aid groups (especially WFP) often cite efficiency and savings as a reason for tech experimentation – a trend that’s accelerating amid today’s aid cuts. WFP did not show the math behind the figure. 
- How WFP describes Palantir’s value: DOTS helps WFP “aggregate large volumes of disparate data across supply chain, logistics, and planning into one analytical view, where patterns and trends can be identified,” the internal staff message states. It lists five examples of how decision-making is sped up: designing food baskets, procurement, planning movement ahead of rainy seasons, reducing delays and costs, and tracking commodity disruptions en route.
- What WFP says about dependency on Palantir: Analysts say creating user dependency is built into Palantir’s business model, and that WFP is veering in this direction. WFP’s message to staff said the agency is avoiding so-called “vendor lock-in” by working with “nearly all leading software providers”. We’ve asked WFP which software partners help prevent reliance on Palantir, and what WFP has done to explore alternatives.
- What’s missing: The internal staff message highlights cost savings and data security, insisting that beneficiary data is protected and does not “connect to any Palantir technology”. It does not address core moral critiques about the company itself, and why a humanitarian agency is partnering with a military contractor that has supplied tech used by the Israeli military in Gaza or by ICE to target migrants in the United States, or that is accused of aiding and abetting a genocide.
- What WFP says: We’ve asked WFP to discuss these issues, and for more info about the contract renewal and partnership. The agency has mostly ignored repeated questions about Palantir and the May cyber-attack.
Cuts |
Fundraising by pipeline cuts: WFP seems more eager to talk about ration cuts than data breaches or Palantir. The agency said funding shortfalls will force it to halve the number of people receiving food assistance in the West Bank.
It’s a familiar message. For years, the agency has highlighted ration cuts across various emergencies, and it has often pointed a finger back at donors in press releases. Analysts say the strategy has often soured relations with key donors, calling it “last-minute fundraising drives based on threats of breaks in the food distribution pipeline”.
Today’s funding pressures are massive, but the practice pre-dates the sector’s donor retreat and the resulting financial crisis. Meanwhile, some who have relied on aid question why food rations seem to be the first thing cut when money is scarce.
Palantíri |
Here are a few more additions to the “everyone is talking about Palantir, except for humanitarians” file:
Protest: Code Pink, the feminist anti-war group, staged a protest at the offices of World Food Program USA last month. The US non-profit raises funds for the UN agency.
Manchester: The all-caps tech magazine, WIRED, reports on the English county that’s saying no to Palantir.
“Why everybody hates Palantir”: This Economist article has a more measured view than its click-y headline suggests. It notes that Palantir weakens its position “by overstating what the software has achieved”. But it also largely lines up behind the firm, questioning whether other companies can do what Palantir does (this Computer Weekly article reckons they can indeed).
Palantir v The Pope: WFP hosted Pope Leo XIV at the agency’s Rome headquarters back in June. A few days later, Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel called the pope “a Chinese communist agent” (he meant it as an insult) for calling for AI regulation. Thiel previously gave lectures on “the antichrist” in Rome, reportedly unnerving Vatican officials.
LOTR: The pope’s AI encyclical contains a Lord of the Rings reference (the Palantir company name is borrowed from the Tolkien novel, which is always a reassuring sign). The papal encyclical, BTW, also calls data extraction a new form of colonialism: “Those who control the health data of entire peoples – often collected under the pretext of aid, research, or innovation – possess a structural leverage over the future,” he warned.
“This looks absolutely rubbish”: London Review of Books has a long read on Palantir and the UK’s National Health Service.
“It’s just a waste of time”: The article’s co-authors have a slightly shorter summary on their Substack.

Panama Canal restricts traffic amid Hormuz crisis: Why this matters

Unknown Publisher

Panama Canal restricts traffic amid Hormuz crisis: Why this matters
Limits on the number of vessels in the canal could create shipping delays and increase freight costs.
While shipping remains severely disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz, shippers are facing new constraints at another strategic maritime chokepoint on the other side of the world: the Panama Canal.
From this week, the number of vessels permitted to pass through the canal per day will begin to fall because of low water levels, canal authorities say.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Asia looks to store oil, gas closer to home after Strait of Hormuz crisis
- list 2 of 3Trump suggests renaming Strait of Hormuz as Trump Strait amid Iran war
- list 3 of 3The US is gobbling up Venezuelan oil, but will it lower fuel prices?
Here’s what we know about the latest measures at the canal, which handles some 5 percent of global maritime trade, according to the Panama Canal authority.
What restrictions are being introduced in the Panama Canal?
From Thursday, only 34 vessels will be permitted to sail daily through the canal, which has traditionally been able to accommodate up to 40 per day.
On September 15, the cap will drop further to 32.
The Panama Canal Authority, the body which oversees the waterway, says the new limits are necessary as the country braces for lower water levels due to the El Nino weather phenomenon.
In the area of the canal, rainfall from May to August is down by 34 percent from its historical average, the authority said, adding that El Nino could cut it even more.
The authority has already implemented other water conservation measures, such as lowering the maximum draft – the vessel’s depth in the water – for the largest ships.
How significant is the Panama Canal for world trade?
Some $270bn of cargo passed through the canal in 2024, according to research by Al Jazeera. The passageway accounted for 40 percent of all US container traffic and 2.5 percent of all global sea trade.
This year, according to the Panama Canal authority, that has risen to 5 percent of all global sea trade, with 70 percent destined for or originating in the US.
Has traffic in the Panama Canal been increasing this year?
Yes.
At the end of June, Panama Canal administrator Ricaurte Vasquez Morales said more than 10,000 vessels had transited the canal over the previous nine months, up 5.2 percent from the same period a year earlier, driven largely by increases in container ships and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) carriers.
He also said the canal’s total vessel tonnage was 7.2 percent higher during the same period.
How has the Hormuz crisis contributed to this?
With Gulf producers unable to export as much oil through the Strait of Hormuz as they did before the war – about 20 million barrels of oil per day (bpd) – countries are increasingly turning to North and South America to make up supplies, driving more traffic towards the Panama Canal.
The effect has been particularly pronounced for crude oil exports from the United States, which leapt by 46 percent year-on-year to a record 61.6 million metric tonnes in the second quarter of 2026, according to global trade intelligence firm Kpler – equivalent to about 450 million barrels in total, or an average of about 5 million bpd.
Brazil, Argentina and Guyana have all posted record shipments of oil so far in 2026.
What impact will the new Panama restrictions have?
The rise in cargoes needing to be shipped through the canal is already creating a bidding war for transit slots in the canal.
While average auction prices for transit slots were $55,000 between October last year and February this year, the recent surge in demand has caused those prices to jump three-fold, according to the canal’s authority.
One South Korean ship paid a record $5.3m to pass through the canal on September 1, according to Bloomberg News.
Niels Rasmussen, chief shipping analyst at the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO), an international shipping association, said the canal’s new restrictions will put more pressure on shipping, pushing some vessels to reroute and make longer, more costly journeys around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.
“Reduced cargo capacity, combined with higher auction prices for transit slots, is likely to push freight rates higher,” Rasmussen told Al Jazeera.
Container cargo moving from Asia to the US’s east coast, as well as LPG exports from the US Gulf to Asia and the western coasts of Central and South America, could be particularly affected, he added.

FINCEN FILES
White House pick to run Venezuela oil deal under investigation in two countries
ICIJ’s 2020 FinCEN Files revealed that major banks flagged suspicious payments involving one of the Venezuelan tycoon’s companies, which remains at the heart of embezzlement investigations in Europe.
A massive oil deal between the U.S. and Venezuelan governments has revived the profile of Alejandro Betancourt, a businessman under investigation in Spain and Switzerland on suspicion of laundering billions of dollars out of Venezuela and into the European financial system.
On Monday, the White House announced details of a new deal with interim President Delcy Rodríguez giving the U.S. majority control over 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil. The deal comes after the January U.S. military seizure of former President Nicolás Maduro, who is currently jailed in New York.
Venezuela’s interim authorities granted North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a privately held company and the second-largest private Venezuelan oil producer, 100-year concessions – the permits that allow for the exploration and production of crude – for 17 oil fields, according to the press release. The deal guarantees the U.S. access to 20% of the crude with right of first refusal to buy the remaining 80%.
Betancourt, a Venezuelan who attended Boston’s Suffolk University, is a majority shareholder in NABEP, according to ICIJ partner El País. In 2018, the businessman was also under investigation in the U.S. for theft of more than $1 billion from Venezuela’s state-owned oil company, though no charges were ever filed.
As recently as May, Betancourt was living in the United Kingdom and fighting a Swiss extradition request over an investigation into alleged money laundering, the Financial Times reported. At the same time, authorities in Spain were also investigating his company Derwick Associates.
In 2020, BuzzFeed News’ and the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists’ FinCEN Files investigation revealed how Betancourt and several other young Venezuelan businessmen known for their ties to the government moved vast sums of public money, including funds intended for housing and other basic services, out of the struggling Latin American country. The reporting was based on a leak of thousands of suspicious activity reports filed by banks to the U.S. Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.
Data from the FinCEN Files showed that Derwick used accounts at JPMorgan to move at least $2.1 million in 2011 and 2012 and that the bank processed other transactions of undisclosed amounts for Derwick and its managers at least into 2013. The files also showed that transactions between 2009 and 2017 involving Derwick Associates and flagged as suspicious amounted to $7.6 million.
In 2018, the U.S. Justice Department charged a senior Derwick executive in an alleged $1.2 billion bribery and money-laundering scheme. Betancourt, who was in his 20s when he co-founded Derwick with a younger cousin, was cited in the criminal complaint as an unnamed co-conspirator, according to reports by the Miami Herald, an ICIJ partner.
In its statement about its new oil venture with Venuezela, the White House did not mention Betancourt as the owner of NABEP, nor did it make any mention of the businessman’s current and past investigations.

Why Ukraine’s drained Kakhovka Dam is strategic for Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:34:03 UTC
00:34:03 KST

Why Ukraine’s drained Kakhovka Dam is strategic for Russia
Small groups of Russian soldiers have been inching forward through the vast, drained Kakhovka reservoir since they blew up the dam in June 2023. Russian forces are infiltrating this “no man’s land” for reconnaissance purposes rather than for a future military offensive, said a military expert.
When the Russian Army exploded the Kakhovka Dam in June 2023, the landscape changed dramatically. The body of water, which was once so large that people living nearby sometimes called it a “sea”, caused catastrophic flooding downstream.
Upstream, the exposed basin experienced a dramatic transformation, with lush vegetation taking over the terrain. Tall weeds, tangled bushes and willow thickets sprouted from the soil that had been underwater for decades.
The changed landscape has become the theatre for a new type of combat between the Russian and Ukrainian armies. While drones have become ubiquitous across frontlines in Ukraine, they aren’t as helpful when it comes to spotting the enemy in the dense thickets of the former basin.
Several media sources have recently described the direct combat that has taken place in the boggy terrain. Ukrainian forces try to track and ambush Russian infantry units attempting to infiltrate the area by stepping into the tree line themselves to engage Russian troops in firefights.
Read moreIs the Kakhovka dam breach a hard blow to the Ukrainian counteroffensive?
“When it exploded, the reservoir mostly emptied out, leaving a narrower river and a reservoir bed,” said Emil Kastehelmi, a military analyst from the Finnish Black Bird Group, who is familiar with the Zaporizhzhia oblast. “Even in its narrower form, the Dnipro River is still a significant water obstacle that would be an issue for the advancing Russians to cross,” he added.
“The area of the dried-out riverbank should be considered as a no man’s land because it’s possibly easier for the Russians to enter,” said Kastehelmi. The expert spoke to FRANCE 24 about Russia’s presence in the former basin, which he said was only for reconnaissance purposes and could “not be the basis for a larger, more significant offensive”.
Why is the area of the drained Kakhovka reservoir strategically important for Russia?
This area basically forms a natural obstacle between the Ukrainian and Russian forces. Even though it is drained, some infantry movement around there is more possible than before. It’s still a very difficult area to operate in, especially when we’re talking about larger movements. It’s an area which separates the two counterparts, and the Ukrainians most likely want to keep it this way.
How are both sides adapting their strategy to this terrain characterised by a flourishing vegetation?
The forest there isn’t fully grown yet. So infantries can move somewhat concealed in the area, but it’s not the same as some older and denser forests. There’s also a certain type of vegetation that grows in these old riverbanks. It’s not like it could provide the same kind of shelter as actual forests.
Second, the area is full of smaller streams and ponds. It’s not an easy terrain where troops can move as freely as they do on solid ground. It’s different from the other types of terrain where the war is taking place.
Read moreFast and fearless: Baltic defence startups innovate to counter Russian threat
How is combat changing in this context?
There’s a limited amount of combat in the area. Smaller Russian infiltration and reconnaissance patrols operate in this area, just like Ukrainian ones. Yet these are smaller infantry detachments. Of course, Ukrainians may need to secure the area so that the Russians don’t get to the other side.
Yet then again, this place has some of the same realities as in some other directions. Reconnaissance drones fly around the area trying to spot enemies. Drone strikes against spotted enemies happen. It should also be mentioned that many frontline areas have been left untreated for a long time. Not only on the dried riverbank where a lot of vegetation has grown, but in many other frontline areas where farming hasn’t happened for years.
The Dnipro River – and the dam – lead up to Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine’s fifth largest city. Why is this southern Ukrainian city important for Russia?
The battle for Zaporizhzhia has been going on for a prolonged amount of time and there are active battles in some areas of the Zaporizhzhia oblast. The Russians have been trying to advance toward the city, but it’s really a difficult thing to do. They haven’t had much progress throughout the years.
The Russians have annexed Zaporizhzhia in their legislation; from the Russian point of view, it's a Russian territory. They currently hold something like 75% of the Zaporizhzhia oblast. So, the main part of this governmental area is occupied by the Russians. But some of the most important and difficult areas still haven’t been taken, and the front hasn’t moved much over the last few years.
Yet taking it [Dnipro] would be difficult because there is the river and the dam, which would be extremely hard to cross. It would be a very difficult operation to cross the river and deal with all the height differences and the dam area, especially in the age of ground warfare.
Ukrainians would hold on to it, especially the left bank of the river if the Russians got into the city. Zaporizhzhia is a city with around 700,000 people, or at least this was the case before 2022. The Russians haven’t had such a large urban battle in this war yet. If they were to get to Zaporizhzhia then a very gruesome and grinding urban battle would follow. It could take months if we compare look at how slowly things are progressing in towns that are 10 times smaller than Zaporizhzhia.
Yet Russian and Ukrainian reconnaissance teams have been playing a game of cat and mouse in the former basin?
They want to keep some pressure on the Ukrainians. They have the manpower to keep the pressure up in multiple areas at the same time. Losing a few squads to Ukrainian drones every now and then isn’t a big issue for the Russians. They can endure the losses and then force the Ukrainians to keep troops on the left bank of the river. They [the Russians] need to direct resources to conduct reconnaissance in the area. This is their strategy rather than forming an offensive and changing the situation in the area.

Many EU countries say tourist visas serve sabotage preparation

If the information is correct, it shows that visas can be used to enter the bloc by potential wrongdoers who intend to harm it, she added. Russia’s ex-combatants entering the EU is a risk flagged in a leaked threat assessment
"It is not normal": Russians in Europe while Russia bombs Ukraine

EU representatives said in July that the ban, kept separate from the tourist visa rules, was agreed in principle but still needed an evidence standard for refusing entry. The EU Council signs off after that, and the European Commission hoped at the time to finish by October.

Another European country transfers gold out of US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:31:16 UTC
00:31:16 KST

Another European country transfers gold out of US
The central bank of the Netherlands has become the latest country to move gold holdings out of the United States, announcing on Wednesday that it had transferred 86 tons of bullion to London. The bank described the move as “crisis preparedness” during a time of “increasing geopolitical unrest.”
The transfer was carried out between March and August. The bulk of the gold was moved from New York, with the rest coming from Canada. Only about 27 tons were physically transported across the Atlantic, while the remainder was accomplished through sales in the Americas and repurchases in London. Prior to the transfer, the Dutch central bank (DNB) had held 313 tons in North America.
“With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves,” according to a written statement by DNB Governor Olaf Sleijpen. “We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness.”
The DNB’s move comes after France’s central bank sold its remaining 129 tons of gold held at Federal Reserve vaults in New York between July 2025 and January 2026, leaving it with no bullion in the United States. The proceeds from the sale were used to purchase an equivalent amount of gold in Europe.
In 2017, under the first administration of US President Donald Trump, Germany’s Bundesbank announced that it had completed the transfer to Frankfurt of 300 tons of its gold held in New York. During Trump’s second term, several prominent German economists have called for the removal of the bank’s remaining holdings from the US.
Venezuela under President Hugo Chavez repatriated about 160 tons of its gold reserves from foreign banks, a move that was completed by January 2012. However, some 31 metric tons of Venezuelan gold are still held by the Bank of England. Efforts undertaken by then-President Nicolas Maduro to bring the bullion home were stymied by Great Britain, which did not recognize Maduro as the legitimate head of Venezuela’s government.
The DNB praised Bank of England-held gold as being “the world’s most easily tradable gold.” The Dutch central bank reported owning 612.4 metric tons as of the end of 2025, worth about €72 billion (about $84 billion).

Russia Church Official Wants Stalin-Era Divorce Rules Back as Demographic Fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:25:03 UTC
00:25:03 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Church Official Wants Stalin-Era Divorce Rules Back as Demographic Fix
A senior Russian Orthodox Church official proposed on September 2 reviving a Stalin-era Soviet decree to make divorce significantly harder in Russia, framing the move as a demographic necessity modeled after wartime policy, according to the independent Russian outlet Agentstvo.
Fyodor Lukyanov, chairman of the Patriarchal Commission on Family Affairs, Protection of Motherhood and Childhood, made the proposal at the Eastern Economic Forum during a session titled
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The Family as the Foundation for Preserving the Spiritual and Moral Values and Sovereignty of Russia," Lukyanov argued that abortion and divorce must be made economically disadvantageous and pushed to the social margins through a coordinated effort by the state and business.
"All citizens who were in a de facto marital relationship were required to register their marriage, indicating the duration of their cohabitation. Passports introduced a 'marital status' field. Differentiated taxation was introduced—income tax rates fell as the number of children increased.
The divorce procedure became more complex: two stages, a mandatory statement of grounds, the summoning of the spouse, and the calling of witnesses. This is not today's online divorce in our country," Lukyanov stated at the forum.
Lukyanov explicitly invoked Decree No. 118/11, issued by the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR in July 1944, arguing that the Soviet experience offers "a great deal of good that can be drawn upon given the current situation."
He noted that the USSR lost 26 million people during the Second World War and that the Soviet leadership responded with demographic measures—measures he argued Russia must now "retrieve and use." Under the 1944 decree, divorce required a court ruling rather than a simple registry office filing, and proceedings could include interrogations by prosecutors. The decree's provisions on marriage and divorce remained in force until 1965.
Lukyanov also raised questions about the official statistics on abortion, suggesting that a reported decline in their number reflects a fall in the population of women of reproductive age and possible manipulation of data.
He pointed to Russia's rate of recorded miscarriages—44% of pregnancies with an abortive outcome in 2024—and implied that clinics have a financial incentive to reclassify abortions as miscarriages under the compulsory medical insurance system, since the reimbursement rate for the latter is higher.
"Is this what happened to our women? Or is someone changing the statistics? Yes, most likely," he told the forum. Agentstvo noted that the 44% figure is calculated not from all known pregnancies but from those ending in an abortive outcome, a measure distinct from the World Health Organization's (WHO) standard reference range of 10–15%.
The proposal comes amid a deepening demographic crisis in Russia, with senior officials increasingly pressuring young people to have more children. In July, Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko demanded that young Russians start families early and have at least three children before turning 35.
Russia recorded 1.178 million births in 2025, below the previous post-Soviet low of 1.215 million in 1999, while births fell by another 17,000 year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026.

Russia Threw Six FPV Drones at Ukraine’s Armed Robot—It Completed the Mission Anyway
Ukraine’s Droid TW-12.7 unmanned ground vehicle survived five FPV drone strikes and completed its combat mission before a sixth hit finally disabled the platform, according to a DevDroid press release shared with UNITED24 Media on September 2.
Soldiers from the fire support company of Ukraine’s 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion deployed the UGV during a remotely conducted operation against a concentration of Russian troops.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
As the Droid TW-12.7 approached the position, two FPV drones struck the vehicle almost simultaneously. One of the hits damaged its aiming module, but the platform remained mobile and continued the mission.
Operators adapted to the damage by aiming in the direction of the weapon barrel and opened fire on the target. Two additional FPV drones struck the UGV during the engagement, but it remained operational long enough to complete its primary task.
The vehicle then began withdrawing and survived a fifth FPV strike while continuing to move. A sixth drone eventually disabled it on the return route.
DevDroid said the Russian troop concentration was cleared and enemy forces suffered losses. The entire operation was carried out remotely, allowing Ukrainian personnel to avoid direct contact with Russian troops.
“In this engagement, the enemy was able to stop the Droid only with the sixth FPV drone, but they still failed to prevent it from completing the mission. For us, this is what survivability means in practice: after being hit, a system must not simply remain mobile—it must retain enough functionality for its operators to complete the mission and achieve the intended result,” DevDroid CEO Yurii Poritskyi said.
The Droid TW-12.7 is a Ukrainian reconnaissance-and-strike UGV developed by DevDroid. It is equipped with a remotely operated turret carrying a 12.7 mm M2 Browning heavy machine gun, as well as an integrated ballistic computer and AI-assisted targeting functions.
The platform is designed to engage personnel, vehicles, and lightly armored targets while allowing Ukrainian troops to conduct dangerous frontline missions from a safer distance.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine is expanding its fleet of unmanned ground vehicles, aiming to produce at least 50,000 combat and logistics robots this year to reinforce infantry units and bridge manpower shortages along the frontline.

How many more missiles does Russia have — and can it keep firing them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:23:03 UTC
00:23:03 KST

How many more missiles does Russia have — and can it keep firing them?
Local residents and warehouse workers watch a massive fire burn at a commercial storage facility following a Russian drone strike in Boryspil, Kyiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 27, 2026. (Kostiantyn Liberov / Libkos / Getty Images)
Dmytro Shumlianskyi
Editor at Militarnyi
From the start of 2026 through the morning of Aug. 27, Russian forces fired at least 1,858 missiles of various types at Ukraine.
That figure alone, however, fails to show the whole picture. Over nearly eight months, Russia's missile campaign has changed character. After the large February salvos of cruise missiles, a significant share of which Ukrainian air defenses intercepted, Moscow has increasingly turned to massed attacks involving ballistic and quasi-ballistic weapons, which are considerably harder to intercept at a time when Ukraine faces a shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles.
Russia has identified that vulnerability and is exploiting it. Any engaged observer of the Russia-Ukraine war may now reasonably wonder just how long Moscow can sustain such a pace.
The numbers tell a story
To understand Russia's missile production and available stockpiles, it is worth first looking at how its missile campaign has changed significantly over the past several months.
After peaking at 296 missiles in February, Russian strikes briefly slowed in March and April before accelerating sharply in late spring: at least 235 missiles were used in May, 227 in June, 474 in July, and 195 during the first 27 days of August. Yet the more consequential change lies in what Moscow has been firing.
Ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles have increasingly dominated the campaign. Russia has used at least 794 Iskander-M, RM-48U, and KN-23 missiles since the beginning of the year, accounting for 43% of all missiles fired at Ukraine. After falling to 39 ballistic missiles in March and 61 in April, their use surged to 107 in May, 134 in Jun,e and 174 in July, followed by approximately 89 during the first 27 days of August.
The use of RM-48U missiles alone jumped from 15 a month during the first half of the year to 46 in the first 20 days of July.
Cruise missiles also remain a major part of the arsenal, with 866 used since January. Kh-101s account for 529 of them, or more than 61% of all cruise missiles fired. Their use has likewise intensified, reaching 119 in July after 111 in February, with at least 34 more launched in the first 27 days of August.
Kalibr use, though, has remained relatively low, with 126 launches since January and only eight recorded in August.
The summer also brought a steep increase in tactical and supersonic weapons. Russia fired 72 Kh-59/Kh-69 missiles in July, more than five times its previous 2026 monthly high, amid its campaign against Ukrainian ports and vessels in the Black Sea.
Zircon launches surged from just three in May to 15 in June and 24 in July, with another 15 recorded in August. Of the 80 Zircons used this year, roughly two-thirds were fired during the summer.
Onyx, meanwhile, was absent at all from the first six months of the year before Russia suddenly launched 25 in July and at least 16 more in August.
The same pattern is visible in the use of Kh-31 supersonic guided aviation missiles, whose principal variants are designed to target air-defense radar stations and other surface targets. Russia used 63 since the beginning of the year, including 27 in July alone, more than during the previous six months combined, and at least 17 more in the first 27 days of August.
Taken together, the numbers point to a deliberate intensification of pressure on Ukraine's already stretched air defenses, with Moscow increasingly drawing on weapons that are harder to intercept or can help suppress the systems protecting Ukrainian airspace.
For an engaged observer of the Russia-Ukraine war, that raises an obvious question: if Moscow is consuming its missiles at this rate, how long can it sustain the pace?
The production problem
Now, let's move onto the production picture.
Russia has been meeting or exceeding its targets for several key missile types. Its planned output of Iskander-M missiles has remained at 60 a month, yet it produced 65 in July.
Kh-101 production reached 87, against a monthly target of 72, while Kalibr output stood at 29, compared with a target of 26. A significant share of those newly produced Kalibrs, according to GUR deputy chief Vadym Skibitsky, is going towards arming Russian ships and submarines.
For Onyx and Zircon, the numbers are particularly strong: Russia's annual production plan of 60 missiles for Onyx had already been fulfilled by Aug. 3, halfway through the year. Zircon had a similar trend, with its production tempo running 57.1% above the annual target of 36 missiles.
Yet, quite importantly, the pace of expenditure has begun to catch up with (and in some cases outrun) production, particularly for these more heavily used systems. RM-48U production, meanwhile, remains at 40 missiles a month, according to both the April estimate and August plan.
Kinzhal is a different story. Russia's capacity was estimated at 10 missiles a month in April, but serial production has since been suspended as rocket fuel and other resources are redirected towards higher-priority ballistic missiles.
Kh-32 production has likewise been suspended, after an April estimate of up to eight missiles a month.
No less important are the stochpiles of these missiles. Russia entered 2026 with substantial reserves, though those stockpiles vary considerably by missile type.
Kh-101 reserves, for instance, have fallen from 150 missiles to no more than 100 despite almost continuous production, suggesting that missiles are moving rapidly from factories to combat units rather than piling up in storage. Iskander-M stocks have also declined amid the intense use recorded since May.
Zircon reserves appear to have fallen from up to 230 missiles in spring to around 120 by summer.
Kalibr remains relatively comfortable at more than 450 missiles. Onyx stocks are also substantial: Russia had used 41 by Aug. 27, even as it had already produced the 60 missiles planned for the entire year.
Some of those Onyx reserves are likely to consist of older variants that have proved less effective against ground targets, leaving room for gradual modernization. RM-48U stocks also remain significant and could partly offset the depletion of Iskander-M missiles, although at the cost of lower accuracy and a smaller warhead.
Kh-35 is harder to assess separately. The April estimate put the combined stockpile of Kh-29, Kh-31, Kh-35, Kh-58, and Kh-59 tactical missiles at up to 2,600, most of which are likely Soviet-era short-range Kh-29s.
There is, of course, some wiggle room in these numbers. Intelligence estimates are approximate, and production capacity on paper does not always translate directly into actual output. Even so, the direction of travel is becoming increasingly difficult to miss.
A war shaped by production
Russia's missile arsenal cannot be reduced to a simple question of whether it is "growing" or "depleting." The answer differs sharply by weapon, as we can see.
Zircons and the ballistic group of Iskander-M/RM-48U/KN-23 are being expended faster than they are produced during the most intense months. Kh-101s, by contrast, are being used at roughly the rate at which Russia can currently produce them.
Kalibr retains a large reserve because average output exceeds its use against Ukraine. Onyx stockpiles also remain substantial, although July and August brought a sharp increase in expenditure that has already surpassed the average production rate.
The Kh-35 appears only episodically in available reports, while the doubling of its July production target suggests that Moscow is prioritizing the weapon rather than confronting an immediate shortage. As a tactical cruise missile designed primarily for targets near the front, it may also be absent from public Ukrainian Air Force reporting.
Kinzhal and Kh-32, meanwhile, have shown insufficient effectiveness and have at least temporarily lost their priority status.
The conclusion we are left with is uncomfortable because it resists an easy prediction: Russia is unlikely simply to "run out of missiles."
It has established high production rates for almost every major missile type, including ballistic weapons. At the same time, a sustained and substantial expansion of its strike campaign would encounter a harder constraint: production for most of the arsenal has remained relatively stable over an extended period.
To increase the tempo of attacks, Russia would therefore have to make choices. It could pause strikes and accumulate reserves, draw down its remaining stockpiles, or rely more heavily on less accurate weapons such as Onyx and RM-48U, alongside subsonic Kalibr cruise missiles. Even the considerable Kalibr reserves are finite.
Additional ballistic missiles from North Korea could provide some relief, although supplies remain relatively modest, unless the Kremlin's friends in Tehran decide to lend a helping hand.
None of these constraints, unfortunately, guarantees a quieter winter. Russia can still accumulate a substantial arsenal for a renewed campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

====================================================================================================

ChatGPT soumis à de nouvelles règles européennes aux multiples angles morts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:16:34 UTC
00:16:34 KST

ChatGPT soumis à de nouvelles règles européennes aux multiples angles morts
Le chatbot le plus populaire au monde est désormais soumis à la réglementation stricte de l’Europe. Cependant, le fait de le classer comme moteur de recherche ne permet pas de couvrir bon nombre de ses principales fonctionnalités.
La décision de l’UE de réglementer ChatGPT en le considérant comme un moteur de recherche paraîtra logique à ceux qui l’utilisent comme tel. Mais qu’en est-il si vous l’utilisez comme un ami ? Ou comme un thérapeute ? Ou encore pour discuter des prochaines élections ?
Ce sont là quelques-unes des nombreuses nouvelles questions que l’avènement de l’IA générative soulève pour les régulateurs européens — qui, selon les experts, n’ont pas encore trouvé de réponses satisfaisantes.
Lundi, l’exécutif européen a classé ChatGPT parmi les “très grands moteurs de recherche en ligne” au titre du règlement sur les services numériques (DSA), lui imposant ainsi une série d’obligations en matière de transparence et d’atténuation des risques similaires à celles auxquelles sont soumis les leaders traditionnels du secteur, tels que Google et Bing (de Microsoft), qui comptent plus de 45 millions d’utilisateurs mensuels. La société mère de ChatGPT, OpenAI, s’expose à des amendes pouvant atteindre 6% de son chiffre d’affaires mondial annuel si elle ne respecte pas ces règles.
Advertisement
Toutefois, cette catégorisation est restrictive et ne s’applique qu’aux parties de l’outil qui font office de moteur de recherche, ce qui signifie que les conversations dans lesquelles le chatbot apporte sa propre contribution ne semblent pas être concernées. En application du DSA, la Commission aurait pu choisir de classer ChatGPT dans la catégorie des “très grandes plateformes en ligne”, qui s’applique généralement aux réseaux sociaux et aux plateformes d’e-commerce et qui impose des obligations différentes.
Pourtant, aucune de ces deux catégories ne reflète l’éventail des utilisations possibles des chatbots.
“ChatGPT est bien plus qu’un simple moteur de recherche, et il existe également des risques liés au chatbot lui-même qui échappent aux obligations les plus strictes [du règlement]”, a pointé Christel Schaldemose, députée européenne socialiste danoise, qui figurait parmi les principaux négociateurs de cette législation.
La députée européenne Christel Schaldemose a souligné les risques pour les enfants. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Elle a mis en avant les risques pour les enfants, “comme la dépendance affective et la conception manipulatrice ou addictive”, et a exhorté la Commission à préciser dans quelle mesure ces risques sont pris en compte par la réglementation en vigueur.
ChatGPT et ses concurrents font l’objet d’une polémique mondiale, car ils auraient contribué aux suicides tragiques d’adolescents, notamment celui d’Adam Raine, un jeune Californien de 16 ans, dont les parents ont engagé des poursuites judiciaires contre l’entreprise.
Les cas d’utilisation de chatbots basés sur l’IA pour une thérapie ou pour avoir de la compagnie ne sont pas marginaux : selon une étude récente menée par le secteur des assurances, pas moins de 60% des adultes dans le monde les utilisent à des fins thérapeutiques.
Advertisement
Un espace hybride
La législation actuelle sur les services numériques, adoptée en 2022, n’avait pas prévu l’essor des chatbots. João Pedro Quintais, maître de conférences en droit à l’université d’Amsterdam, décrit ChatGPT comme une technologie “hybride” qui combine les fonctions d’un moteur de recherche et d’une plateforme en ligne, ainsi que d’autres fonctions plus proches de celles d’un éditeur de ses propres contenus.
La qualification de “moteur de recherche” pourrait limiter la capacité de la Commission à contrôler la manière dont ChatGPT gère les risques liés non seulement à la santé mentale des adolescents, mais aussi à l’intégrité des élections ou aux contenus illicites.
Demander à ChatGPT de citer les noms des candidats à une élection locale devrait désormais relever du champ d’application du DSA. En revanche, une conversation entre un utilisateur et un chatbot sur le choix du candidat pour lequel voter, au cours de laquelle des informations erronées pourraient être diffusées, pourrait ne pas être concernée.
Il a fallu un peu moins d’un an à la Commission pour finaliser la classification de ce chatbot, ses équipes s’étant heurtées à des difficultés pour déterminer dans quelle catégorie le classer. Selon les experts, sans avoir consulté le texte intégral actant cette classification annoncée cette semaine, il est difficile de savoir exactement quelles seront les obligations d’OpenAI.
La qualification de “plateforme” aurait imposé à OpenAI des obligations supplémentaires en matière de modération des contenus au titre du règlement sur les services numériques, mais elle aurait aussi permis à l’entreprise d’échapper à une part importante de ses responsabilités. Le DSA, comme d’autres législations dans le monde relatives aux plateformes, s’articule autour du principe du “safe harbor”, en vertu duquel les entreprises ne sont pas responsables des contenus présents sur leurs plateformes, ceux-ci étant mis en ligne par les utilisateurs. Mais l’avènement des chatbots soulève la question de savoir si une conversation entre une personne et une machine peut être considérée comme un “contenu généré par les utilisateurs”.
Modèles et risques
Si l’attention portée par les autorités de régulation à ChatGPT en tant qu’application grand public est récente, la Commission surveille de près les modèles d’intelligence artificielle qui la sous-tendent via son règlement sur l’IA (AI Act).
Advertisement
OpenAI, la société mère de ChatGPT, ainsi que des entreprises telles qu’Anthropic et Gemini (de Google) développent ce que l’on appelle des modèles d’IA à usage général, capables d’effectuer une grande variété de tâches pouvant présenter des “risques systémiques potentiels”.
Depuis août dernier, au titre de l’AI Act, ces entreprises ont l’obligation d’“évaluer et d’atténuer” les risques que présentent ces modèles. La Commission a commencé à faire appliquer cette législation fin août, lorsqu’elle a cuisiné une série d’entreprises spécialisées dans l’IA sur leurs procédures de sécurité.
Auparavant, un groupe d’experts avait identifié quatre risques : la mise au point d’armes nucléaires ou biologiques, la perte de contrôle sur les modèles, des modèles d’IA hors de contrôle qui commencent à faire du piratage, ou encore des modèles se livrant à des manipulations à grande échelle.
Illustration d’un ami virtuel sur l’écran d’un iPhone. | Olivier Douliery/AFP via Getty Images
Mais aussi effrayants soient-ils, ces risques systémiques ne prennent pas en compte toute une série de problèmes potentiels, tant pour les utilisateurs que pour la société dans son ensemble.
“[Ces orientations] sont davantage axées sur ce qu’on appelle les risques existentiels que sur les risques pesant sur les droits fondamentaux”, a soulevé Daniel Leufer, responsable des politiques en matière de technologies émergentes chez AccessNow.
Il a fait valoir qu’avec la classification de ChatGPT au titre du DSA, il y a une chance “d’entrer dans les détails des choix de conception et de considérer ChatGPT davantage pour ce qu’il est réellement, à savoir un produit”.
Advertisement
L’intelligence artificielle ayant eu un impact aussi rapide et profond, la réglementation en la matière est encore en cours d’élaboration. Le député européen social-démocrate italien Brando Benifei, qui mène les travaux sur les questions l’intelligence artificielle au Parlement, a défendu l’approche européenne qui distingue la supervision des applications de celle des modèles d’IA, affirmant que ces deux cadres réglementaires peuvent se “compléter puissamment”.
Brando Benifei a toutefois reconnu qu’une supervision dans le cadre du DSA était “absolument nécessaire” pour protéger les personnes qui utilisent vraiment les outils d’IA, citant comme exemple concret les “dépendances dangereuses en matière de santé mentale” que certaines personnes développent à l’égard des chatbots compagnons.
“L’examen s’étend désormais du modèle sous-jacent à la manière dont ces services sont concrètement conçus et déployés.”
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

BERLIN, September 3. /TASS/. Germany has ruled out the possibility of transferring employees of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn to the embassy in Berlin, Russia’s Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev said in a message to compatriots living in Germany.
"On September 1, 2026, the Federal Government of the Federal Republic of Germany made the unprecedented decision to close the Russian Consulate General in Bonn by September 18, 2026, and to terminate the 2011 Russian-German intergovernmental agreement on the activities of cultural and information centers. This entails the closure of the Russian House of Science and Culture in Berlin by June 2027. Furthermore, all employees of the Consulate General and the Russian House, as well as their family members, are ordered to leave Germany immediately. The German side has rejected the possibility of transferring them to the embassy," the statement reads. It also notes that the State Duma elections on September 20 cannot be held at the Consulate General in Bonn.
The ambassador recalled that the Consulate General in Bonn was the last of five Russian consulates general operating in Germany. On May 31, 2023, Berlin demanded that Russia close four of its five consulates general in Germany - in Hamburg, Leipzig, Munich, and Frankfurt am Main.
"This latest unfriendly move by the German side, prompted by absurd and unsubstantiated accusations of Russia preparing acts of sabotage on German territory that have no basis in reality, will have an extremely negative impact on the embassy's ability to provide consular and legal services. Unfortunately, operational difficulties, especially in the initial period, are inevitable," the ambassador stated, adding that this was not Russia's choice.
Nechyaev assured that the Russian embassy would do everything possible to promptly rectify the situation and ensure consular access even in the most remote regions of Germany from Berlin.
On Tuesday, the German government officially blamed Russia for the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport and announced countermeasures. Specifically, it was decided to close the Russian Consulate General in Bonn by September 18. Other steps include the denunciation of the agreement on the activities of the Russian House in Berlin, tightening entry controls for Russians, and increasing pressure on Russia's so-called shadow fleet.
Russian President Vladimir Putin pointed out that Germany's new anti-Russian decisions, under the pretext of the drone incident at Leipzig Airport, are yet another grave error by the German authorities, contrary to the interests of their people. He believes these decisions are linked to the domestic political situation in that country, and in particular, the difficult situation of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Putin insists a new military draft is out of the question. The Kremlin said the exact same thing before the 2022 mobilization.
Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum, Russian President Vladimir Putin ruled out a new wave of military mobilization.
There is no scenario at this point that would require mobilization. This is an information attack by the adversary ahead of elections to the State Duma aimed at influencing the outcome. This is simply a deliberately orchestrated information operation.
Putin acknowledged that waging war is “a difficult, complicated matter” in which “a lot of problems arise,” but said having enough troops isn’t one of those “problems.”
It was the second time in a matter of days that Putin denied plans for a new mobilization. At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit on September 1, he dismissed talk of preparations for a post-election mobilization as “utter nonsense” and “an information attack on Russia.”
Sources for Meduza and other media outlets have reported since early summer that officials are weighing a new wave of mobilization. The reports come amid a steady decline in people willing to serve under contract in the armed forces and rising losses in the Russian military.
The Wall Street Journal reported in late August that, according to Western intelligence, the Russian military is conducting exercises rehearsing mobilization procedures. Sources for the outlet stressed that this reflects only practical preparation, and that no decision on mobilization has been made yet.
Putin is not alone — other officials have directly denied mobilization plans in recent weeks as well. Russia’s permanent representative to the U.N., Vitaly Nebenzya, said in mid-August that mobilization “is not planned and is not expected.” In late July, Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, called talk of mobilization “hogwash” and “a lying provocation.”
Russia’s last wave of mobilization was announced in September 2022, shortly after officials had denied plans to carry it out. That mobilization is officially still in effect — no presidential decree has ever formally ended it — though large-scale mobilization measures wrapped up within a few weeks in 2022.

Tunisia top court begins final hearing in mass trial of opposition figures

Breadcrumb
Tunisia top court begins final hearing in mass trial of opposition figures, despite condemnation from activists
The Tunisian Court of Cassation began hearing on Thursday the final appeal of dozens of opposition figures accused of plotting against the state, in a case condemned as political by activists.
In November, 34 defendants, many of them critics of President Kais Saied, were sentenced to up to 45 years in prison in an appeal trial, triggering sharp criticism from rights groups.
The court will either confirm the verdict or order a retrial.
A small crowd gathered Thursday morning outside the courthouse to support the defendants, an AFP journalist reported.
"This is a political case that the authorities have used to silence dissent and imprison figures from across the opposition," said lawyer Haifa Chebbi, whose father Ahmed Nejib Chebbi, 82, is among the defendants.
Chebbi and other lawyers have said they were only notified of the hearing on Monday, arguing it did not provide them with enough time to prepare the defence.
On Wednesday, lawyer and opposition figure Dalila Msaddek, whose brother Jawhar Ben Mbarek is on trial, condemned the proceedings, calling them nothing more than "the blatant implementation of political instructions".
Their father, leftist activist Ezzedine Hazgui, told reporters he was "proud" that Jawhar and other Saied critics were in prison.
"I am proud because they defended their country," said Hazgui, who was among the protesters outside the court.
"We oppose the coup and all forces hindering Tunisia's progress," he added, referring to Saied's power grab five years ago.
Saied was elected in 2019 after Tunisia emerged as the only democracy of the Arab Spring.
But in 2021, he staged a sweeping power grab, and human rights groups have since criticised a major rollback on freedoms.
Among the defendants in the mass trial were party leaders Issam Chebbi and Ghazi Chaouachi, as well as businessman Kamel Ltaief.
Amnesty International has urged Tunisian authorities to "rectify a travesty of justice that has upturned the lives of 34 prominent opposition figures, human rights defenders and lawyers who were convicted on unfounded charges".
