Rights groups urge US lawmakers to drop provision to deepen defense ties with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:11:17 UTC
00:11:17 KST

Rights groups urge US lawmakers to drop provision to deepen defense ties with Israel
WASHINGTON, Sept 3 - Dozens of civil rights and advocacy groups are urging Congress to scrap a defense bill provision that would deepen U.S.-Israeli military technology ties, according to a letter seen by Reuters, at a time of growing U.S. skepticism toward the longtime ally.
The provision would deepen cooperation between the U.S. and Israeli defense sectors by accelerating joint military technology development and other partnerships. The bill passed the House of Representatives in July and awaits Senate action.
The provision of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, known as Section 219, seeks to set up frameworks for joint ventures, licensing agreements and U.S.-based co-production partnerships with the Israeli industry.
In Thursday's letter addressed to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, 56 groups said deeper integration with Israel's defense sector would be "exceptionally dangerous" and urged lawmakers to remove the provision.
The groups include Amnesty International USA and the civil rights network National Lawyers Guild as well as Arab and Jewish advocacy groups.
"At a time in which American interests are increasingly diverging from those of Israel, and American public opinion is turning increasingly against unconditional support to Israel, creating new points of influence for Israel in the U.S. defense-technology ecosystem is exceptionally dangerous," said the letter, which has not been previously reported.
Israel is one of Washington's closest allies in the Middle East, and the two countries cooperate extensively on defense and intelligence issues. Supporters say deeper ties could help speed military innovation and technology development.
A spokesperson from the Israeli Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story.
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off U.S. military support within a decade. In a June letter to a U.S. congressman he wrote that the time has come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."
U.S. PUBLIC SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL DECLINES
U.S. public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of U.S. support for Israel.
The Islamist militant Hamas group, in an October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, killed nearly 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals and took hundreds hostage. More than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed in Israel's subsequent assault on Gaza, according to Gaza health officials.
The letter criticizes Israel for its potential violations of international humanitarian law in its war in Gaza and rising settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. It says such developments should prevent any discussion of deepening military ties.
A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion annual U.S. military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028 and conversations are under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
Some members of Congress have already tried to strip the provision from the fiscal 2027 NDAA. Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Democratic Representative Ro Khanna of California introduced an amendment to block it, but it did not make it into the House version of the bill.
Once the House and Senate write their versions of the NDAA, members of the two chambers work out a compromise version of the bill, which must pass both chambers - typically near the end of the calendar year - before it can be sent to the White House for President Donald Trump to sign into law or veto. German warship secretly fires ballistic missile in Atlantic
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:10:35 BST
00:10:35 KST

A German warship has fired an Israeli-made LORA ballistic missile during a live test in the North Atlantic, with the German Navy saying the launch demonstrated a strike capability with a potential range beyond anything it had previously operated.
German media reports, citing a German Navy spokesman, said two German frigates had deployed to waters between Ireland and Iceland for the test on Tuesday night. Images from the exercise show a containerised launcher positioned on the deck of a German vessel.
The messaging here could hardly be clearer. By disclosing a test that had deliberately been kept secret, NATO was sending a direct signal to Moscow: European forces are developing longer-range strike options, and not every capability will be visible before it is ready.
NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said the test had been kept secret until after it was completed and involved a German frigate firing the missile in the North Atlantic.
The command stated: “Kept secret. Now revealed. The German Navy just tested the Israeli LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.”
Kept secret. Now revealed. 🚀🇩🇪
The German Navy just tested the Israeli 🇮🇱 LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.
NATO 3.0 looks like this:
Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious… pic.twitter.com/K8x2JE61Gs
— NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum – JFCBS (@NATOJFCBS) September 2, 2026
It added: “NATO 3.0 looks like this: Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious capabilities and keeping a few cards close to the chest. Deterrence just got a little more interesting.”
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, Inspector of the German Navy, said: “With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we made naval history. I am extremely satisfied with this achievement.”
Kaack added that the system “can be successfully deployed from our units, and the potential range exceeds anything we have known before.”
In his original statement, the German Navy chief said the trial opened a new chapter for maritime deterrence and readiness, stating that the system could be operated successfully from German units and that its possible reach exceeded previous German naval capabilities.
The test was conducted with Israel Aerospace Industries’ LORA, or Long-Range Artillery Weapon System. According to IAI, the missile has a range of around 400 kilometres and an accuracy of within 10 metres, while NATO’s public account of the German test referred to a range of more than 500 kilometres.
Israel Aerospace Industries said the missile was launched from an operational German vessel equipped with a command trailer and launcher. According to the company, the missile followed its planned trajectory, navigated to the target and successfully struck it, with both the weapon system and missile meeting the objectives of the trial.
Boaz Levy, Chairman of IAI, said: “This is an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Israeli Ministry of Defense. The successful trial of the LORA missile, launched from a naval vessel and striking its target with exceptional precision, took place overnight in Germany – the country where the world’s first ballistic missile was developed.”
He added: “This trial demonstrates Israel’s technological strength and the unique cooperation between Israel and Germany. It marks another significant achievement alongside the deployment of the Arrow 3 system on German soil, further strengthening Germany’s defense and deterrence capabilities and deepening the strategic partnership between our two countries.”
IAI chief executive Guy Bar Lev said: “Israel Aerospace Industries is proud to take part in strengthening the strategic cooperation between the State of Israel and the Government of Germany. This significant milestone is underscored by the operational live-fire exercise (OPEX) of the LORA system, one of the world’s most advanced and combat-proven ballistic missile systems.”
The German Navy is using its OPEX initiative to trial technologies and operational concepts as part of its Marine 2035 and Beyond programme. The process is intended to allow new systems to be tested rapidly under conditions intended to resemble operational use as closely as possible.
The North Atlantic launch comes as Germany expands its investment in long-range strike and air and missile defence. The country has also begun fielding the Israeli-developed Arrow 3 ballistic missile defence system as part of its wider effort to strengthen national and NATO defensive capabilities.

Four imprisoned Palestine Action activists appeal ‘terrorism’ sentences
Unknown

Four imprisoned Palestine Action activists appeal ‘terrorism’ sentences
Supporters of those who participated in a raid on an Israeli weapons maker say the sentences set a dangerous precedent.
London, the UK – Four Palestine Action activists who were sentenced as “terrorists” are appealing against the ruling.
Charlotte Head, Samuel Corner, Leona Kamio, and Fatema Zainab Rajwani were found guilty of criminal damage “with a terrorist connection” following a raid, which was claimed by Palestine Action, on an Israeli arms factory in August 2024 in Filton, near Bristol.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Mark Ruffalo comments spark pushback against anti-Semitism ‘smear campaign’
- list 2 of 4As US seeks Gaza donor’s extradition, wife warns of ‘terrifying precedent’
- list 3 of 4Brazilian activist demands Tunisia release Sumud Flotilla organisers
- list 4 of 4Will the EU take action against Israel?
The sentencing marked the first categorisation of property damage as “terrorism” in British courts.
Human rights groups condemned the ruling in June.
“Uncontested, this judgement will also mark a flagrant departure from the rule of law in favour of foreign criminal actors and against and in the detriment of UK citizens,” said Shahd Hammouri, lecturer in international law and researcher of corporate war profiteering at the University of Kent, as she spoke on Thursday during a press conference in London, where supporters of the group announced the appeal.
“It will also set out a precedent that may extend to others who are protesting against grave violations of international law.”
At the time of the incident, Palestine Action was not a proscribed organisation.
Activists Head and Kamio were handed five-year sentences, while Corner, who was also convicted of grievous bodily harm without intent for striking a police officer during the raid, was given seven years and eight months. Rajwani, who at 21 is the youngest of the group, was handed a sentence of four years and eight months.
The appeal argues that the conviction violated Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), as Palestine Action was not a proscribed organisation at the time of the offence. It also argues that “the sentences were manifestly excessive” and violated the “principles of natural justice” as well as ECHR’s Article 6, which regards the right to a fair trial.
The mothers of Kamio and Rajwani, visibly emotional when describing prison conditions and futures their children may face, said they were proud of their daughters.
“She may be embroiled in this struggle for her freedom for another 20 years,” said Sukaina Rajwani.
Emma Kamio’s voice broke when stating, “[Leona] will be 50 years old…when she finishes her sentence”, referring to the decades of supervision that would follow time spent in prison.
Elbit Systems, Palestine Action’s main target, describes its drones as the “backbone” of the Israeli army.
The August 2024 Filton raid was carried out at its UK affiliate.
Palestine Action says it is “committed to ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. The group relies on direct action to disrupt flows of arms and military-related goods to Israel, stating that “If one action stops one weapon from killing a Palestinian, then it’s all worth it.”
James Smith, a doctor who returned eight days ago from Gaza, where he was providing urgent medical care, said it was “an honour” to support the activists.
Direct action efforts should be “understood alongside the sheer inability of healthcare workers to respond to the outcomes of these war machines”, he said, referring to Israeli quadcopter drones.
He referenced the shooting of a 10-month-old baby in Gaza by an Israeli quadcopter in April, 2024.
The activists known as the “Filton 24” have said they were targeting quadcopter drones produced by Elbit Systems during their raid.
When speaking of the activists, Smith noted the “first tenet” of medical best practice, saying, “Prevention is better than cure.”
People sentenced as “terrorists” are treated as dangerous and face scrutiny long after they leave prison.
Kamio said her daughter had worked with children at a nursery, facilitating outdoor, nature-based learning. While the nursery spoke highly of her, her mother said she feared that once released, she would not be able to work with children again because of enhanced checks.
In a statement, activists supporting the four said that they “would be subject to notification requirements for 15 years upon release” and that “such requirements include being obliged to notify police of any new device, bank account, address, holiday or relationship”.
In June, the case gained further prominence when Head’s lawyer, Rajiv Menon KC, was accused by Justice Jeremy Johnson of contempt of court by stating that Elbit Systems was “wined and dined in the corridors of power” and reminded jurors of their right to acquit based on conscience.
Menon now faces contempt proceedings; senior lawyers have criticised his prosecution.
“[Judge] Johnson did his worst,” Emma Kamio said of the sentencing.
In June 2025, the UK banned Palestine Action as “terrorist” organisation, making it a crime to be a member of or to express support for the group. More than 2,700 people have been arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 for protesting the ban.
The proscription, which came after activists spray-painted a Royal Air Force plane, placed Palestine Action on par with organisations like al-Qaeda, ISIL (ISIS) and extreme far-right groups.
Civil liberty organisations and United Nations experts have slammed the ban as an illiberal overreach.
Charlotte Head, in a letter written from prison, described the sentencing as “politically motivated to justify the proscription of Palestine Action”.
There is no date set for when the appeal will be heard, but lawyer Simon Natas said he hoped it would begin “in the coming months”.

====================================================================================================

Kemi the Valkyrie spoils for a fight and has the Russians in her sights | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:08:15 UTC
00:08:15 KST

There’s something about Kemi Badenoch making a keynote speech – everything she does comes billed as keynote these days – about defence that makes most normal people a little nervous. Because when Kemi talks about defence, what’s really on her mind is war. Starting one, if possible.
Kemi is never happier than when picking a fight. With herself, if no one else is around. You get the feeling that, left on a desert island she would be dreaming of Apocalypse Now. Flying low over the Mekong delta in a helicopter gunship, the Ride of the Valkyries playing through her earphones while she yelled: “I love the smell of napalm in the morning.”
Still, you can’t blame an opposition leader for opportunism. It’s the crumbs they live off. And the Tories reckon they have identified a Labour weakness. John Healey resigned as defence secretary a few months back over Keir Starmer’s reluctance to come up with a plan of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Now that Andy Burnham has appointed him chancellor, Healey seems suddenly rather reluctant to make the commitment he was asking of Rachel Reeves. Much happier to be pushed back to the longer-term goal of 3.5% by 2035, with the heavy lifting being done sometime, maybe never, after the next election. There are some decisions politicians choose to defer indefinitely.
It’s possible Healey will surprise us all and announce he is resigning again in protest at his own refusal to meet the 2030 target. But as of today he’s still very much in No 11 and, after some confusion at Wednesday’s prime minister’s questions, the government position is the 2035 deadline.
So Kemi and a few members of her shadow cabinet decamped to the slightly surreal setting of Scotland House London – the inside looks like a greenhouse and is about as sweaty – to tell the country it was 2030 or bust. If we delayed any longer, we would all be dead. If the Russians didn’t kill us, she would. The future of the world depended on her.
Andrew Griffith, Kemi’s new shadow chancellor, made the introductions. You’d have imagined he might be a little embarrassed about his part in writing the Liz Truss mini-budget and his vociferous support for it thereafter, but he isn’t a man much given to self-reflection. Rather, it’s as though he imagines he is doing us all a favour by sharing his brilliance. He started by paying tribute to his predecessor. Poor Mel Stride. Loyal but expendable. Kemi has just revealed her full shadow ministerial team and The Melster is about the only Tory MP not included in Kemi’s new shadow ministerial team.
Then came Kemi. Wake up, peeps, she said. We were as good as at war already. Cyber-attacks. Russian drones on Leipzig airport. A Russian attack on a Nato country nailed on for the next few years. She marvelled at Poland for its 300,000-strong army. That was the kind of country she wanted to lead. She forgot to mention that if she had been prime minister we would probably have been at war earlier this year. She had been all for joining Donald Trump’s war on Iran. It could have been us who killed some women and children at a wedding party this week. What an opportunity missed.
It was all very black and white. If we spent 3% we would all definitely be safe. The Russians and other hostile countries would immediately back off. But a penny less and they would attack for sure. They could spot weakness. So Kemi was preparing for war. She would not shy away from sending men and women to possibly pointless deaths. There would be many more corners of foreign fields that would be forever England.
Just as arbitrary was how this was all to be paid for. It’s almost become axiomatic in rightwing circles that the extra money for defence should be found by cutting the welfare bill. In other words, it’s the poorest and most vulnerable people who will be funding the military. This drew applause from the large audience. All of whom looked as though they were quite comfortably off and would therefore be spared the pain of making any sacrifices themselves. Which is exactly how they like it. That’s what makes them proud to be British.
When it came to the details of where the savings were to be made, Kemi came over all vague. Mumble, mumble. Moving on. Though most of us could have sworn that some of the cuts had already been announced last year and that she was effectively trying to spend the same money twice. But Kemi was adamant that Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, had been all over the details and that nothing had been left to chance. Which wasn’t quite as reassuring as Kemi had hoped.
There was also a commitment to save the money from a Chagos deal that had yet to be agreed and hadn’t even been spent. If I filled in my tax return with such creativity, HMRC would have some questions. But it’s the leader of the opposition and none of this may ever happen so none of this really matters. Kemi ended with a sneer at cheaper bus fares – why can’t people take taxis – and a whole list of taxes she would either abolish or cut. Weirdly, she didn’t think to end the pension triple lock, which most economists think is the only sane thing to do. The audience wouldn’t have been so keen on that.
All this was said with an effortless confidence. Even when she was talking nonsense and contradicting herself. I guess you could call that Kemi’s USP. Her answers to questions about why anyone should bother to listen – when it had been the Tories who had hollowed out the defence budget over the past 14 years – varied from the peace dividend, to everyone had done it, to it had been nothing to do with her and the Conservatives were starting again from scratch. Ground zero does a lot of heavy lifting for Kemi these days.
On one thing she was clear. Are we going to war? asked a reporter from the Express. Hell, yeah, said Kemi. Just watch me. She wouldn’t rest until every child could sleep safe in their bed while missiles were raining down across Britain. It was just a shame that for some kids, those beds might no longer be their own. Kicked out of their homes and forced into insecure accommodation the councils can’t afford. Still, I guess they can get used to a cardboard box. That will teach them to adopt welfare as a lifestyle.

Manchester synagogue attack: ministers seek to block MI5 files from inquest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:07:16 UTC
00:07:16 KST

Ministers are seeking to block intelligence material from being heard at an inquest into the death of two men killed in the 2025 Manchester synagogue attack.
Lawyers for Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, told a coroner on Thursday that disclosing the MI5 files would pose a serious risk to national security.
Melvin Cravitz, 66, died as a result of multiple knife wounds inflicted by the attacker, Jihad al-Shamie. Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a single police gunshot wound as he held the building’s doors shut against the terrorist.
A senior coroner is due to examine the deaths of the two men at the Heaton Park Hebrew synagogue on 2 October last year during Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
The full inquest will focus on al-Shamie’s background, as well as what the state knew about him before the attack. It will also examine security at the synagogue, the role of the state in assessing the risks to the Jewish community in Greater Manchester, and the response to the attack.
Mahmood told the Commons on 13 October that al-Shamie was “never referred to the Prevent programme, nor was he known to counter-terrorism policing or the security services”.
At a pre-inquest review on Thursday, barristers for the families of Cravitz and Daulby said they were concerned that the emergence of MI5 material “may contradict” that statement.
Anna Morris KC, representing Daulby’s family, said there had been a “demonstrable lack of candour” by the security services in other proceedings, including the inquiry into the Manchester Arena attack.
She said Daulby’s family were “concerned that this application [by the Home Office] and the information behind it may contradict statements made public by security services and counter-terrorism police that the suspect was not known to counter-terrorism police”.
The deaths of Daulby and Cravitz are being examined by Alexia Durran, the chief coroner of England and Wales, at Manchester coroner’s court.
Edward Pleeth, counsel to the inquest, told the hearing the government was seeking to withhold “potentially relevant security sensitive material held by MI5” and “potentially relevant security sensitive material held by counter-terrorism police”.
Pleeth said this unspecified material was judged by the government to “cause serious harm to national security” if it was disclosed publicly.
He said the inquest legal team was satisfied that the information was so sensitive it could not be aired even in a redacted form.
There was “no adequate alternative to complete non-disclosure”, Pleeth said, describing the concerns about its disclosure as “well-evidenced”.
Durran is now considering whether to ask the government to convert the inquest into a statutory public inquiry to allow the MI5 material to be heard in private.
Unlike public inquiries, coroner’s inquests cannot legally consider evidence given in secret hearings.
Neil Sheldon KC, representing the Home Office, described the MI5 material as a “discrete body of information” that had been “identified as relevant and has the potential to impact the inquest”.
The application to block the information from being heard publicly was not an “extreme approach” but was “cogent, compelling and supported by detailed analysis”, he told the court.
Victoria Ailes, representing Cravitz’s family, said his family had “questions in this entire area” and were concerned that this new material came after “statements by the secretary of state to the House of Commons [that al-Shamie] was not known to counter-terrorism police or the security services”.
Al-Shamie, a Syrian-born UK citizen, launched the attack while wearing what seemed to be a suicide vest. Before police arrived, the 35-year-old called 999 and pledged allegiance to Islamic State.
Last month, a man who conducted hostile reconnaissance at a military base alongside al-Shamie was jailed for life with a minimum term of 16 years, after admitting preparing acts of terror.
Mohammad Asim Bashir, 31, and al-Shamie travelled by car to the UK Defence Academy in Shrivenham, Swindon, in August last year, two months before the synagogue attack.
Bashir was identified when counter-terrorism officers searched al-Shamie’s mobile devices after the Heaton Park attack.
However, Greater Manchester police said last month that officers had seized his phones months earlier in 2025 after unrelated arrests, but that they were not examined until after the attack.
Another man, Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, was charged on 21 August with failing to disclose information in relation to the synagogue attack. Hakim, 49, pleaded not guilty at Westminster magistrates court. He is due to attend a hearing at the Old Bailey on 25 September.

US pressure on Iran starting to tell, as sanctions and blockade bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:06:14 UTC
00:06:14 KST

US pressure on Iran starting to tell, as sanctions and blockade bite
DUBAI - A US campaign to throttle Iran’s economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is growing increasingly difficult to withstand, three senior Iranian sources said.
Washington has, in recent weeks, sought to ratchet up the economic pressure on Tehran, in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that six months of conflict have so far failed to secure.
Although Iran’s clerical rulers managed to bypass sanctions for decades, the latest US moves have left them in a far more sensitive position, with few remaining channels to secure foreign currency or buy goods, the sources said.
In particular, the effort to stop Iran accessing international financing networks in other countries it has long used to keep its economy functioning poses a real and urgent threat, the sources said.
Any sign the economic campaign may break a months-long deadlock in the conflict will likely cheer US planners, though Iran has also warned it could respond to the pressure with military escalation, raising the stakes at a key moment.
Petrol stocks low as currency collapses
The war has erupted back into open fighting this week, with US attacks along Iran’s Gulf coast prompting retaliatory Iranian strikes at US bases in Arab states.
Neither side has yet signalled it is ready to make the concessions demanded by the other, leaving the war in a costly stalemate - though one that may be shifting.
While more energy is flowing to international markets through the Strait of Hormuz despite Iranian efforts to continue disrupting the seaway, the US blockade of Iranian oil exports has entirely cut off Tehran’s main source of revenue.
Adding to Iran’s problems, the economy was already deep in crisis before the conflict, with a cratering currency and spiralling inflation, while months of bombing have run up a massive bill to rebuild damaged industry and infrastructure.
Meanwhile, the country’s financial squeeze is itself biting into Tehran’s efforts to get around the sanctions regime, leaving less cash to pay the high premiums required to skirt sanctions illicitly, the sources said.
The rial has fallen to record lows over recent days and one senior source said Iran only has another two months’ supply of gasoline, which has to be imported despite domestic oil production because of limited refining capacity.
Iran’s rulers are keenly aware of the potential risks of an economic meltdown and the possibility of it reigniting the nationwide mass protests it put down in January by killing thousands of demonstrators.
“They are under very, very severe economic pressure. They’re losing control of the Straits. It’s really a question of if they choose to negotiate, and I think they’ll have to,” said Ali Ansari, modern history professor at St Andrews University in Scotland.
The war is also entering a new phase, with each side trying to influence each other’s politics.
Iran hopes the threat of inflation will deter the US administration before midterm elections in November, while Washington aims to push Iranians to revolt, a senior Iranian official said.
Blockade and secondary sanctions squeezing Tehran
The latest US measures expanded secondary sanctions that target countries doing business with Iran in a bid to stop it clearing dollar transactions needed for both oil sales and to finance crucial imports of goods and raw materials.
That effort is making Iran’s existing sanctions evasion networks - front companies, unregistered tankers and smuggling - too expensive to use, the three senior sources said.
Iranian crude loadings have fallen this month to about 260,000 barrels a day, from about 1.7 million a year earlier, according to data from commodity analytics firm Kpler, with only a trickle still moving off terminals for distribution by truck, train or smaller boats over the Caspian Sea.
Tehran says it still has tens of millions of barrels stored in tankers outside the blockade zone that it can sell, but the new sanctions mean intermediaries are stepping back or demanding more money, one of the officials said.
Total trade has fallen between 25 per cent and 35 per cent, with imports hit harder than exports, President Masoud Pezeshkian has said, one of several top officials warning in recent weeks about Iran’s rapidly deteriorating situation.
US pressure and Iran’s own attacks have meanwhile disrupted one of the main conduits for Iranian trade - the United Arab Emirates, which said on Aug 19 that all commercial exchange and financial dealings with Tehran were halted until further notice.
“If those channels stay closed, a supplier wants cash, a deal is routed through another country and a shipment arrives later and dearer,” said an Iranian trader in Tehran who deals in imported goods.
The currency has collapsed in value from around 1 million rials to the dollar a year ago to over 2.2 million rials now.
The internal impact is very painful. Official figures put 12-month average inflation at 69.9 per cent with food, beverages and tobacco prices rising at nearly twice that rate.
Official unemployment rose to 9.1 per cent in the spring, while the number of those in work fell by about 450,000 from a year earlier amid a wider fall in labour force participation.
Even for those still in work, the average monthly salary of around US$125 (S$158) a month comes nowhere near meeting basic household spending requirements that come to around US$450 a month according to official data.
“We are getting poorer every day,” said Mahnaz, a 34-year-old private-sector employee in Tehran who asked that her family name not be used. REUTERS

Belgium records nearly 3,000 deaths due to summer heatwaves
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
23:03:46 CST
00:03:46 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Belgium recorded nearly 3,000 excess deaths during three periods of high temperatures this summer, according to data released Thursday by the national public health institute, Sciensano.
Data from Sciensano's Belgian Mortality Monitoring (Be-MOMO) system showed that 2,035 deaths were recorded during the first heatwave from June 18 to July 3, representing an increase in mortality of 48.8 percent. The second heatwave, from July 4 to 17, saw 535 excess deaths, a 14.8 percent increase, while the third period of intense heat, from July 28 to Aug. 16, saw a 7 percent spike in mortality, or 365 deaths.
Sciensano said the first heatwave had the most pronounced impact on mortality, with a significant increase in deaths among people aged 15 to 64. This marked the highest excess mortality levels, both in absolute numbers and as a percentage, among heatwaves analyzed in Belgium since 2000.
The institute said the severity of the episode was linked to a combination of factors: the duration of the episode, the intensity of the heat and ozone concentrations.
It also said that maximum temperatures in Belgium had hovered around 30 degrees Celsius for 10 consecutive days from June 18, including three days near 35 degrees Celsius, while ozone concentrations remained above 100 micrograms per cubic meter for 10 consecutive days.
Be-MOMO monitors mortality from all causes by comparing observed deaths with the statistically expected number of deaths. The latest figures may still be revised as mortality data are further consolidated, Sciensano said. ■

CONAKRY, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Guinean Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah presided over the opening ceremony of the 12th African Conference on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights in Conakry on Wednesday.

Held under the theme "Sexual and reproductive health and rights of adolescents and young people in Africa in the face of multifaceted crises," the conference aims to promote the exchange of experiences and develop concrete responses to the challenges facing young people amid multiple humanitarian crises, the effects of climate change and declining funding for sexual and reproductive health services.
At the opening ceremony, Bah said that "Africa draws its greatest strength from its youth" and this strength "will only fully bear fruit if young people are educated, protected and healthy."
He noted that early pregnancy, unaddressed violence or delayed access to healthcare could lead to interruptions in schooling and undermine young people's prospects for the future.
"Sexual and reproductive health involves several dimensions of public policy: it concerns maternal health, education and the protection of women, equal opportunities and the quality of human capital," Bah said.
According to him, crises "amplify risks, disrupt services, keep young people away from health facilities and reduce intervention capacities," making prevention more difficult at a time when it is most needed.
He therefore called for concrete actions and policies capable of delivering tangible results in terms of the health and protection of young people.
Guinean Minister of Health and Public Hygiene Khaite Sall stressed that the rights recognized to young people should be translated into concrete actions and effective access to health services.
"Health is no longer considered a supporting expenditure, but a strategic investment in human capital and in the future of the country," she said.
According to Sall, the vision of the Guinean authorities is to advance the country toward universal health coverage while strengthening adolescents' and young people's access to local, confidential and respectful health services.
The minister also called for turning commitments into action so that sexual and reproductive rights would not remain merely principles enshrined in laws and policies, but could be effectively exercised by the people concerned.
According to the organizers, the 12th edition of the conference will focus in particular on sustainable financing for sexual and reproductive health services, adapting services to crises, combating gender-based violence, and strengthening young people's participation in decision-making. ■

Thousands of Ukrainian children still at risk in Russia as EU prepares new sanctions

Thousands of Ukrainian children remain under Russian control, facing indoctrination, militarisation and the loss of their identity, the Bring Kids Back UA initiative warned as the EU prepares new sanctions against those responsible for their deportation.
The head of the Bring Kids Back UA initiative has called for those responsible for Russia’s illegal deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to face prosecution, as the EU prepares new sanctions targeting another 27 Russian individuals and entities.
“Bring Kids Back UA has continuously called for all those responsible for Russia’s illegal deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to face prosecution, and we welcome this positive action from the European Union towards ensuring accountability for these crimes,” Maksym Maksymov told Euronews.
“Children who remain under Russian control continue to face the risk of indoctrination, militarisation and the erosion of their Ukrainian identity,” he said.
“There are still thousands of Ukrainian children who have yet to be returned home. The longer they remain under Russian control, the greater the risks they face.”
EU ambassadors reviewed the proposed listings on Wednesday at their first meeting since the summer recess.
“This is a humanitarian issue that concerns the entire international community. Every child who is returned demonstrates that coordinated international action can make a difference, while measures such as these send a clear message that these crimes will not go unanswered,” Maksymov said.
The new sanctions are being prepared ahead of a conference of the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children in Toronto, Canada, on 28-29 September.
“Through the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, governments and international partners can support efforts to secure these children’s safe return while strengthening the international mechanisms that protect children during armed conflict,” Maksymov said.
Brussels has previously targeted those involved in Russia’s deportation and forced assimilation of Ukrainian minors, with individual listings included in earlier sanctions packages.
In May, EU countries blacklisted 16 individuals and seven entities over the unlawful deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children, including their indoctrination, militarised education and unlawful adoption.
Following Wednesday’s presentation, further technical work is required to finalise the new listings, including legal checks intended to ensure they can withstand challenges in court.
The European External Action Service has also shared with member states a list of 1,600 individuals and entities directly contributing to Russia’s war effort, part of a broader shift away from large, sector-focused sanctions packages.
How many Ukrainian children are in Russia?
Ukraine has verified the deportation or forced transfer of more than 20,500 children, although the true scale is believed to be considerably larger.
Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab estimates the number may be closer to 35,000, while Moscow has openly suggested it could be as high as 700,000.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War has said that the true number is almost impossible to verify.
Euronews previously reported that Russia-installed occupation authorities in Ukrainian regions created an online “catalogue” of Ukrainian children, offering them for coerced “adoption” through the education department.
The minors were reportedly sorted and categorised so users could “filter” them by age, gender and physical characteristics such as eye and hair colour. The children were also described in terms of personality traits, with some labelled as “obedient” or “calm”.
Returning even one child can take years, from the moment Ukrainian authorities identify them until their eventual return home.
Almost every return so far has been mediated by a third state, notably Qatar, South Africa and the Vatican.
In March, the United Nations said that the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia constitutes a crime against humanity and a war crime.
“Bring Kids Back UA will continue working with our Ukrainian and international partners to ensure these children are returned safely to their families and their homeland,” Maksymov said.

Billionaires hoarding wealth while the rest of us struggle need to ask themselves: what would Dolly do? | Rebecca Shaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:00:48 UTC
00:00:48 KST

Since the moment the news broke that the great Dolly Parton had died, we have been inundated with all manner of Feelings. The internet is flooded with tributes to Dolly by people from all walks of life, who knew her personally or only from afar. There seems no end to the sharing of stories and thoughts about her, and in what feels like a miracle in this divided world, it has only been positive. Even on social media, where people tear down nice things like it’s their full-time job, I’ve seen nothing but adoration. She is not only beloved for her musical genius, but also for her generosity, her sense of humour, her support for other artists, her active care for marginalised communities, her attitude to living, her truly kind spirit.
I am one of these enthusiasts, of course. I have loved Dolly since I was a kid. I remember going to the Nashville country music museum in my 20s and seeing her handwritten lyrics for Jolene. A shiver went down my spine at the thought of 27-year-old Dolly writing that song, not knowing how far she would go, and the great good she would do for the world.
But after she died, and after a few days of reading every tribute with tears in my eyes, and both fists pumping, I decided that there was actually one important Feeling that has been missing from the discussion. That feeling is shame – and it is the shame that other millionaires, billionaires and (excuse me while I vomit a little in my mouth) trillionaires should be feeling.
We live in a world where the gulf between the rich and the poor has never been greater. We understand that the Earth and the majority of people on it are suffering more and more while an enormous amount of wealth and power is concentrated in the hands of a tiny elite. The wealthiest 10% of the global population owns 75% of all wealth. The poorest 50% holds only 2%. The individuals at the top could use tiny portions of their own fortunes to make the world so much better for everyone, and overwhelmingly they choose not to.
Dolly Parton’s life as a self-made millionaire was the antithesis of this. She has shown them all up with the power of her legacy. Every story about her kindness and generosity is an indictment on people who hoard their wealth. Those who use their resources to accelerate environmental destruction, escalate nonsensical culture wars, and invest in actual wars. Those who do everything they can to get richer with no consideration for the rest of humanity.
I suspect that a lot of Dolly’s desire to make life better for others came from the fact that she grew up in poverty. That experience provides perspective that you can’t have if you are born into wealth. She had a deeply ingrained understanding that there are more important things than watching your bank balance grow. She knew that money is the means, not the end. I can’t help but wonder if those who value profits over people saw this global outpouring of love for Dolly and thought about how they themselves might be remembered. I wonder if any had a brief moment of reflection, thinking about who would mourn their loss, or whether they had ever used their own privilege for good.
I know the answer is no. I know that you generally don’t become a billionaire by caring that much about other people. I’ve seen people say that Dolly didn’t hate anyone, and wouldn’t judge others like this. That she would keep her heart open to them. Well, I’m not Dolly Parton. Nobody is, but definitely not me. I do judge these people, and I think we all should. Dolly has shown us what is possible. She has shown us that humanity and grace and generosity can be real priorities for wealthy people.
Dolly had enough money to do whatever she wanted in life. She didn’t need more. This is true for all of the richest people on the planet. But Dolly saw the needs of others, and she responded. There are people who have enough to literally change huge aspects of society for the better, to make our world an easier place to live for everyone. But they don’t. If they don’t feel shame about that, we need to make them feel shame. We must not let them luxuriate in apathy as the world burns. We must demand more. The people hoarding wealth and resources need to start asking themselves: what would Dolly do?
- 
  Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in Sydney

35 years of Weimar Triangle
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
17:00:41 CEST
00:00:41 KST

35 years of Weimar Triangle
03.09.2026
On 3 September, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Radosław Sikorski took part in a jubilee meeting of the Weimar Triangle foreign ministers. In Weimar, the chief diplomats of Poland, France, and Germany adopted a declaration to mark 35 years of building trilateral relations and confirm the countries' determination and willingness to cooperate further.
During trilateral consultations, the heads of diplomacy, Radosław Sikorski, Johann Wadephul, and Jean-Noël Barrot, discussed key aspects of European and transatlantic policy. The ministers spoke about defence cooperation as well as countering disinformation, FIMI (Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference), and hybrid threats. They also raised the situation in the Middle East, especially at the Strait of Hormuz. Additionally, the top diplomats noted the significant dynamic of meetings within the Weimar Triangle. They stressed the potential of trilateral ties, notably in European policy, security, and digital, scientific, and space cooperation.
In the declaration adopted during the jubilee meeting, the ministers reiterated readiness to jointly counter threats to Europe’s security resulting from Russia’s aggressive and imperial policy. Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski underlined that Poland has backed Minister Wadephul’s response and decisions in the wake of Russia’s aggressive acts in the territory of Germany, including the decisions to close Russia’s consulate in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin.
We do not consent to the unpunished testing of our borders and to hostile acts taking place in our territories. We will not tolerate arson, railway attacks, and other provocations posing a risk to our citizens. Poland also summoned the Russian ambassador in order to express our firm opposition to the state-sponsored terrorism perpetrated by the Russian Federation. In fact, a problem of one of our allies is a problem of the entire NATO. Putin’s Russia remains one of the biggest security threats not just to Europe, but to the World Order altogether
- Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski said.
The top diplomats gave assurances of continued support to Ukraine in its fight. They agreed that there can be no secure Europe without sovereign Ukraine.
The partners confirmed their support for Poland’s position on increasing Europe’s competitiveness, including through building technological and economic independence, while maintaining partnership-based relations with the US. Also, the heads of diplomacies announced joint counteraction against disinformation and declared further enhanced cooperation.
Noting that regular trilateral political consultations are necessary, Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski invited his French and German counterparts to Poland for another meeting of the Weimar Triangle foreign ministers.
***
The Weimar Triangle format was set up in Weimar in 1991 by the foreign ministers of Poland, France, and Germany: Krzysztof Skubiszewski, Roland Dumas, and Hans-Dietrich Genscher. Its aim was to enhance cooperation between the three states and to overcome the divisions in Europe by integrating Poland into European and Euro-Atlantic structures.
Although the nature of that cooperation has evolved with time to keep up with the current challenges, the provisions of the 1991 Weimar Declaration on the Future of Europe have not lost their relevance. “We have a unique opportunity to further shape a new Europe, taking on shared responsibility in the spirit of human solidarity, conscious of our common destiny and drawing on the legacy of our shared values,” the ministers wrote. For 35 years now, the Weimar Triangle has proved its effectiveness through overcoming divides, building trust, and remaining open to dialogue.

Five killed, dozens more feared dead in boat adrift off Canary Islands

Five killed, dozens more feared dead in boat adrift off Canary Islands
Spanish migrant NGO says more than 80 people likely perished on the boat that left The Gambia 27 days ago.
The bodies of five people have been recovered after a boat carrying West Africans was rescued off Spain’s Canary Islands, maritime rescue authorities have said, as an NGO warns that dozens more may have perished.
Spain’s maritime rescue service Salvamento Maritimo said on Thursday that one of its boats rescued 44 men from a boat drifting some 120km (75 miles) south of the island of Gran Canaria on Wednesday evening.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Spain asks EU for help to process 5,000 Ceuta migrants amid local unrest
- list 2 of 3Spanish police evict hundreds of migrants from Ceuta beach to shelters
- list 3 of 3Ceuta mayor calls for migrant detention amid mass influx crisis
“Adverse weather conditions” initially prevented the retrieval of five corpses that remained on board before it was taken to the port of Arguineguin, the service said on social media.
Three survivors in critical condition were immediately evacuated by helicopter to a hospital on the island, while the remaining 41 people received care from the Red Cross.
All survivors were men, some underage, and came from Mali or Senegal, said Jose Antonio Rodriguez Verona, a spokesperson for the Red Cross in the Canaries.
But Helena Maleno, a spokesperson for the Spanish migrant aid NGO Caminando Fronteras, said on social media that 83 migrants and refugees had died, including three women and a baby girl, on a boat that left The Gambia 27 days ago.
The NGO compiles its data based on testimonies from migrants’ families and the official statistics of those rescued. Its tolls are often higher than the authorities’ figures.
A Salvamento Maritimo spokesperson told the AFP news agency that the other alleged victims “have not been found or rescued” and that the alternative death toll could not be confirmed.
It was unclear if more resources would be deployed to search for the other victims, she added.
Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo said the tragedy underscored the need for a state policy on migration.
“It is intolerable that lives continue to be lost. The Canaries cannot get used to or accept as normal the fact that the Atlantic continues to be a death trap,” Clavijo said on social media.
The Canary Islands are one of the main gateways into Europe for people fleeing poverty, conflict and persecution alongside Mediterranean routes to Italy and Greece.
The long journey from West Africa is one of the world’s deadliest, due to strong currents and the often ramshackle, overloaded vessels.
After peaking in 2024 at more than 46,000, arrivals to the Atlantic archipelago have fallen sharply thanks to tighter patrols and cooperation with countries of origin and transit.
A total of 5,163 migrants and refugees reached the Canaries by sea from January 1 to August 31, a 57 percent drop on the same period last year, according to interior ministry figures.

A culprit for corrosion may have been operating under our noses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Water droplets can do their own version of the electric slide. But instead of tearing up the dance floor, they may be wearing away at our cars, infrastructure and cultural heritage sites.
Water drops that become charged by sliding along a surface can then transfer their charge when they land on materials with the right electrical properties, including metals. This eventually drives the material to corrode, even when covered by a protective coating, researchers report August 26 in Nature. Water may also pick up charge in clouds, thunderstorms and waterfalls, so this effect might be widespread.
This work could pave the way for better anticorrosion coatings, says Stefan Weber, a physicist at the University of Stuttgart in Germany who was not involved in the study. Earlier work had shown that sliding along many surfaces causes water drops to become charged, but looking to sliding electrification as a source of corrosion represents a step forward, Weber says.
It’s electric
As drops of water slid down common surfaces, including leaves and a commercial kind of glass called polystyrene glass, they can pick up an electrical charge. In an experimental setup (left), when thousands of these drops landed on the Teflon-coated copper, they caused damage visible by microscope (bottom row; scale bar represents 100 micrometers).
Corrosion’s impact on the global economy is not trivial. This broad category of damage that includes rust cost the U.S. automotive industry alone more than $30 billion in 1999. Corrosion costs are not consistently tracked, but estimates put the global cost in the trillions.
Previous work attributed damage to the physical impact of water droplets, as well as small amounts of corrosive compounds like acid that they might contain. At first, it was not clear whether these electrified drops caused damage, says Zhongyuan Ni, a physicist at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research in Mainz, Germany. In early experiments, he could find no damage to a surface after hundreds of drops. “One day, I just let the experiment [keep] running. I forget; I [went] to drink coffee or something,” he says. When he came back, he found signs of damage that prompted him and his colleagues to investigate further.
With knowledge that thousands — not hundreds — of drops were needed to create observable damage, the researchers continuously released drops of water onto Teflon-coated copper surface samples. They imbued drops with charge by sliding them along common surfaces like leaves and construction materials. Each surface was tilted to ensure that water drops would land on the coated copper. For comparison, the team also released water drops directly onto Teflon-coated copper with no sliding.
All of the samples hit with sliding drops appeared damaged when inspected under a microscope, but not a sample hit with direct drops. A different microscopy technique used on a damaged sample revealed that the charged water drops had not only penetrated the Teflon, but reached and corroded the copper. The team observed similar deterioration on samples of polystyrene glass–coated copper and gold, showing that the phenomenon is not unique to Teflon-coated copper.
While these charged water drops could be in the clouds or sliding along your windshield, they should not scare you, Ni says. Their effects are small. But they add up for monuments, machinery and infrastructure that are exposed to the elements for years. Small charges shouldn’t be ignored, Ni says. Even if they’re tiny, “sometimes they will play an important role.”

Israel’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has drafted a plan to forcibly displace about 1.86 million Palestinians from the Gaza Strip over seven years, which he is expected to unveil Thursday as part of his election campaign, local media reported.
Ben-Gvir will present the public with a plan called "Disengagement 710," based on what it describes as "voluntary migration" from Gaza, the Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth reported.
The plan aims for 250,000 Palestinians to leave Gaza in its first year, 1.11 million within three years, and about 1.86 million within seven years, the report said.
Ben-Gvir plans to make the initiative a central part of his election campaign after "working on it for months," it added.
His Jewish Power party also plans to make adoption of the initiative a key demand in any negotiations to join Israel's next government, it also said.
The plan includes providing a destination country for each individual or family leaving Gaza, along with legal status, documentation, visas, travel funding, and initial housing.
It also includes vocational training, employment assistance, and support for up to 24 months, the report also said.
The plan is based on 12 principles, including what it calls "voluntary departure" and a requirement that "no one leave without a country prepared to receive them and provide them with regulated legal status," according to the report.
The plan further proposes "payments" to countries and entities involved in receiving those leaving Gaza based on "their performance, individual security screening and annual implementation targets."
It also calls for "monthly reports on the number of applications, approvals and departures," as well as "costs and the extent to which those leaving are integrated into their destination countries."
The plan would require an initial Israeli investment of 10 billion shekels ($3.1 billion) to establish and launch it, the report noted.
It also envisages an Israeli financing framework of up to 50 billion shekels ($15.6 billion), subject to international participation and agreements with destination countries.
More than 2.2 million Palestinians currently live in the Gaza Strip.
Israel's general elections are scheduled for Oct. 27. The current government is described as the most right-wing in Israel's history.
Israel launched its genocide in Gaza on Oct. 8, 2023. The offensive continued for two years, causing widespread destruction, while Israeli violations have persisted despite a cease-fire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025.

Hamilton hopeful Ferrari can win at Monza with engine upgrade

03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Lewis Hamilton said on Thursday that he remains confident Ferrari can compete for victory at the Italian Grand Prix as the team prepares to introduce an upgraded power unit at Monza.
The upgrade will be Ferrari's second on the power unit side this season after the team was granted two development opportunities under Formula 1's 2026 regulations.
The rules allow manufacturers whose internal combustion engines fall behind the leading power unit to make additional upgrades through the Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities system.
Ferrari was found to be more than 4% behind benchmark manufacturer Red Bull following the first review earlier this year.
The Italian team introduced its first upgrade at June's Austrian Grand Prix and will provide the second update to both Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at Monza.
"I think up until this point of the year we've been losing... even in the last race, on such a short circuit, we were losing four tenths a lap through the race, so that's a huge deficit and we've carried that through the year to this point," Hamilton said.
The seven-time world champion acknowledged that the upgrade would not eliminate Ferrari's entire performance deficit but welcomed the team's progress.
"This is a step forward. It's not the whole gap that we need, but we knew that would be the case. But to see bits coming each weekend, adding to the car, it's exciting to see that we are pushing. I strongly still believe that we've got what it takes to win," he added.
Hamilton enters the Italian Grand Prix third in the drivers' standings with 183 points, 59 behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes.
Antonelli is set to start from the back of the grid at his home race after exceeding his permitted allocation of power unit components.
Ferrari will race at Monza with a special livery commemorating the 30th anniversary of Michael Schumacher’s first Italian Grand Prix victory for the team in 1996.

Speaking in Kajiado County, Ruto accused Tata Chemicals Magadi of failing to sufficiently invest in the area despite operating at Lake Magadi for more than a century.

Ruto said his government had identified new investors to take over operations, arguing that Kenya should derive greater economic benefits from its mineral resources.
"We have said we are bringing in new companies. I have already sent them away," he said.
The president said two new companies would be brought in, with the government seeking increased investment, local processing and employment for Kenyans.
Tata Chemicals Magadi is part of India's Tata Group and operates at Lake Magadi, about 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the Kenyan capital, Nairobi. The company produces more than 350,000 tons of soda ash annually, exporting to markets including India, Southeast Asia, the Middle East and elsewhere in Africa.
The presidential announcement follows a July 28 government suspension of Tata Chemicals Magadi's mining operations over alleged non-compliance with Kenya's mining laws. Mining Cabinet Secretary Hassan Joho said at the time that operations would remain suspended until the company met its statutory obligations.
Tata Chemicals said last month that it had submitted all documents requested by Kenyan authorities and maintained that it had demonstrated compliance with regulatory requirements. It said the suspension was affecting about 500 employees as well as contractors, suppliers and surrounding communities.
The company's history at Lake Magadi dates to 1911, while a major mining lease with the Kenyan government was signed in 1928. Tata Chemicals acquired the operation in 2005 through its purchase of the UK's Brunner Mond Group.

EU suspension of Brazilian meat comes into force, despite ongoing talks with Brasília
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:54:43 UTC
23:54:43 KST

Brazil has yet to provide the necessary guarantees to allow an audit of its beef exports’ compliance with EU food safety standards, while inspections of poultry and honey imports are already under way.
The European Commission suspended imports of meat from Brazil on Thursday over concerns about antibiotic use, after Brasília failed to convince the EU executive that its products comply with European standards.
The move comes as Brazilian meat imports lie at the heart of opposition to the free trade agreement signed in January 2026 by the Commission with Mercosur countries — Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
EU farmers accuse Latin American producers of failing to comply with the bloc’s phytosanitary and food safety standards, arguing that this gives Latin American products an unfair advantage on the EU market.
“We have rules that ban antimicrobials or using antimicrobials for growth,” Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said. “On the 3rd of September, the list of countries that basically comply with our rules on antimicrobials comes into application.”
The spokesperson added that Brazil was not currently on the list, meaning its imports were suspended as of Thursday.
No guarantees for beef
The suspension, which resulted from a vote by national experts in May, covers beef, poultry, eggs and honey.
Imports of some products could resume following an audit of poultry and honey, launched on the basis of written guarantees of compliance provided by Brasília. The audit is expected to run until the end of the week, although the conclusions will take longer.
Hrncirova said no such guarantees had been provided for beef, adding that they must cover the animals’ entire life cycle, which is naturally longer for cattle.
Brazil’s ambassador to the EU, Pedro Miguel da Costa e Silva, told Euronews ahead of the summer that technical discussions with the Commission were ongoing. However, Brazil ultimately failed to prevent the suspension from taking effect.
Trade in agricultural products was the most contentious issue throughout the 25-year negotiations over the Mercosur agreement.
The deal was provisionally applied in May after the European Parliament suspended the ratification process with a legal referral to the European Court of Justice.

Trump congratulates Hegseth on ‘good job’ after deadly Iran wedding strike
Unknown

2026-09-03

23:51:53 KST

Trump congratulates Hegseth on ‘good job’ after deadly Iran wedding strike
US President Donald Trump has congratulated Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over the latest American strikes on Iran, despite one of the attacks hitting a wedding and killing several civilians.
Iranian authorities said two women and two children aged four and 16 were killed when a US munition hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province, on Tuesday. At least 67 others were wounded, many of them women and children.
According to weapons experts cited by AP and the New York Times, the fragments recovered at the site belonged to an American air-delivered guided munition, most likely a JSOW.
The Iranian Red Crescent has since asked the International Criminal Court to investigate the Kuhestak strike, while Iran’s UN envoy has urged the Security Council to condemn it.
US Central Command has said it is looking into the reports while insisting that American forces do not target civilians.
“You did a good job last night in Iran, by the way. You knocked the hell out of them,” Trump told Hegseth during an event at the White House on Wednesday. “We’re winning that one very big, by the way, in case you haven’t noticed,” he added, claiming that much of Iran’s naval and air capability has been destroyed.
Tehran responded to the latest wave of attacks by launching its own ballistic missiles and drones at US military facilities in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and the UAE, as well as Erbil in Kurdistan Region, Iraq.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later claimed to have killed “a number of enemy elements” and destroyed several drones in a missile and UAV attack on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base.
Kuwait acknowledged that its air defenses had intercepted incoming missiles and drones but reported no casualties. Jordan said ten of 13 ballistic missiles that entered its airspace were intercepted.
Tuesday’s wedding strike follows several other incidents in which US attacks have caused heavy civilian casualties in Iran. On the opening day of the war in February, a US strike hit an elementary school in Minab, killing 175 people, most of them children. On the same day, a US strike also killed at least 21 civilians, including seven children, in the southern Iranian city of Lamerd.
Tehran has accused Washington of war crimes throughout the conflict, reporting up to 3,000 civilian casualties since the US and Israel launched their campaign against the Islamic Republic in February.

It is also about fostering a culture of responsibility around water. JSJB places people’s participation at the centre of water management. It brings together communities, Panchayats, institutions and other stakeholders on locally appropriate solutions,” said the ministry in a statement.

A senior Russian air force commander was shot twice at close range in the Saratov region on Wednesday morning, in the latest of a series of attacks against Russian military officers on its territory.
An unidentified gunman on a motorbike fired twice at the officer as he was leaving a shop in the village of Probuzhdeniye in Engels district and fled. One bullet struck him in the face, the other in the torso.
He was taken to hospital in serious condition before being airlifted to Moscow for further treatment.
Telegram military blogger channels identified the injured man as Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, commander of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division of Russia's long-range aviation branch. Russian authorities have not officially identified him.
The ASTRA Telegram channel noted that Probuzhdeniye is listed as one of Varpakhovich's registered addresses.
The city of Engels — some 850 kilometres from Moscow — hosts the Engels-2 airbase, one of Russia's most significant strategic aviation facilities.
Bombing a hospital
Varpakhovich has been charged in absentia by Ukrainian authorities over the 8 July 2024 missile strike on the Okhmatdyt children's hospital in Kyiv.
Ukrainian investigators said he ordered the attack, which resulted in a Kh-101 cruise missile striking the hospital.
Two people were killed and more than 30 injured, including nine children. The building was partially destroyed.
Ukraine's Health Ministry said 627 children were receiving treatment at the hospital at the time of the strike.
Ukraine's Security Service published a statement on 31 August saying it had compiled evidence against two Russian military officials.
The second is Colonel Aleksandr Lutovinov, commander of a missile brigade in the 49th Combined Arms Army, who investigators said organised the 24 August 2024 missile strike on the Sapphire hotel complex in Kramatorsk.
A security adviser for Reuters news agency was killed in that attack, and five journalists were wounded.
The shooting in Engels is part of a series of gun and bomb attacks involving Russian military figures that has grown in recent weeks.
On 1 August, five people were killed and at least 19 wounded in an explosion at the Balzi Rossi restaurant in Moscow.
The presumed target was Colonel General Aleksandr Chaiko, commander-in-chief of the Russian Aerospace Forces, whom Ukrainian authorities have accused of organising massacres in Bucha following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Chaiko was also the commanding officer of Russian forces participating in the Syrian war on the side of ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad.
On 13 August, Russian Navy Captain First Rank Robert Shagiev was killed by an explosion in a street in Sevastopol. He was formerly the commander of Ukraine's submarine Zaporizhzhia. Shagiev was allegedly killed by a Russian national.
Last week, Air Force Lieutenant Colonel Sergei Sechkov was killed and his wife was taken to intensive care when an improvised explosive device planted in his car detonated in St Petersburg.
He was reportedly part of a Russian unit accused of attacks on civilians on the Slobozhanshchyna front in northeastern Ukraine.

Gaza flotilla coalition 'not deterred' by Israeli intimidation, aims to break blockade in October
Israel's assault on activists on a Gaza-bound flotilla earlier in May has "not deterred" plans for another attempt to break Israel's siege on the Palestinian enclave.
The Freedom Flotilla Coalition said on Tuesday that it would again sail from ports in Europe and make stops across the continent before making an attempt to reach Gaza in October.
Vessels began setting sail earlier in June and July, with vessel Handala II sailing around Scandinavia, and vessel Kate calling in Ireland, Germany and France.
"At every port, we will carry the demand that Palestinians be free to live in dignity," FCC Steering Committee member Zohar Chamberlain Regev said.
"In October, we intend to carry that demand and the solidarity of people around the world to Gaza’s shores," she added.
Since forming in 2010, the FFC has launched a number of attempts to break Israel's siege on Gaza, which has been in place since 2007.
The last attempt that occurred in May saw the mass abduction and detention of hundreds of activists by Israeli authorities, many of whom recounted torture, including beatings and sexual assault, at the hands of Israeli personnel.
A video published by Israel's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir taunting detainees was roundly condemned by several nations whose citizens were held, while the interception of the flotilla in international waters was condemned as violating international law.
Edward Digilio, an engineer from the US, said that "we know that sailing toward Gaza carries serious risks".
"But silence and inaction carry a much greater cost for Palestinians and the world," Digilio said.
"This mission is an expression of shared humanity and a refusal to accept the destruction of an entire people as normal," he added.
The FFC reiterated several demands to international governments ahead of their journey to Gaza, including for the safe passage of the flotilla to Gaza, and an end to Israel's obstruction of the entry of essential aid into Gaza.
The coalition also called for states to defend freedom of navigation in the event the flotilla is again intercepted, including through threats of diplomatic action, as well as using legal and economic means to end Israel's violations against Palestinians, and holding parties accountable for the detention of the flotilla's participants.

Aussie expert says hope still exists for those trapped in Nepal tunnels
Australian tunnel safety and disaster expert Arnold Dix has urged rescuers in Nepal not to give up hope of finding survivors inside the tunnels in the Upper Trishuli-3A hydropower project, where scores of workers are feared trapped underground days after a flash flood. 
“The operation at Trishuli 3A is proceeding as a rescue, not a recovery,” Dix, who is remotely assisting the operation, wrote on LinkedIn. Footage recorded around the time of the August 26 flood shows around 30 people moving toward and seeking shelter in the power station tunnels, he said. 
Dix said tunnels can remain comparatively stable after devastation above ground and may preserve breathable air and survivable spaces. “Silence is not evidence of death. It is only the absence of a signal,” he wrote, citing past rescues in Chile, 
Thailand, and India where people survived underground for days without contact. Rescue teams are still trying to reach workers at more than a dozen hydropower sites along the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor. At Trishuli-3A, a 93-member team is working with Chinese tunnel specialists, while teams from India and South Korea are assisting operations at other sites.

US hands over ancient sarcophagus fragments to Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:48:03 UTC
23:48:03 KST

Breadcrumb
US hands over ancient sarcophagus fragments to Lebanon
The United States on Thursday announced the return of Roman-era sarcophagus fragments to Lebanon that were looted from the southern city of Tyre and recovered by an FBI investigation.
The decorative, lead fragments were returned to the Lebanese consulate in New York on Wednesday, ahead of their repatriation, the US embassy in Lebanon said.
The recovery "reflects the strong US-Lebanon partnership in the fight against illicit trafficking of cultural property", the embassy said.
Lebanese Culture Minister Ghassan Salame said the fragments "were unearthed in the Tyre area during illegal excavations".
"The fragments bear distinctive artistic, decorative and technical characteristics typical of workshops that produced lead sarcophagus in Tyre, which were among the city's active and prolific workshops in antiquity."
According to the FBI, the antiquities "were stolen from illicit excavations in or around Tyre and were exported outside of Lebanon's borders".
The trade in looted antiquities is widespread in the Middle East. New York, one of the world's art capitals, is home to many wealthy collectors, galleries, and auction houses.
In December 2017, three ancient artefacts were returned to Lebanon, including a bull's head of Greek origin that had been exhibited at the Met Gala, valued at $1.2 million.
Salame said the Tyre region "is exceptionally rich in archaeological heritage" and "has recently suffered severe destruction" due to heavy Israeli strikes during the latest war between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah.
UNESCO, the United Nations cultural agency, added Tyre to its World Heritage in Danger list in July.

Russia's air transport authority reaches out to ICAO to discuss commercial flight safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:45:32 UTC
23:45:32 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) will interact with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) on maintaining the safety of commercial flights, head of the agency Dmitry Yadrov told reporters, adding that there have been no official contacts so far.
"If there was such a request, it must be considered by the ICAO Council, after which a decision may be taken to notify ICAO member states of the information contained in the request. We will surely talk with the International Civil Aviation Organization," he said on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency has not received any requests so far, Yadrov noted. "We have seen an ICAO commentary on that matter. However, there have been no official contacts so far. Obviously, we will also work on that issue with the Russian Foreign Ministry for them to join the matter as well," he said.
ICAO does not have the authority to close airspace over Russia, the agency’s head explained. "They can only make recommendations," he said.
Earlier, ICAO said in response to a request from TASS that the global risk of weapons being used against passenger aircraft was rising, adding that states should take more active measures to protect civil aviation from threats associated with armed conflicts. The organization considers it essential to share intelligence promptly regarding potential threats to aircraft and to conduct more thorough risk assessments for flights within national airspace. ICAO is also updating its recommendations on flight safety over and near conflict zones and is urging countries to make firmer commitments to protect civil aircraft.
Earlier, Russian President Vladimir Putin commented on Vladimir Zelensky’s "warning" to airlines regarding the danger of flying over Russia, saying that Moscow would find means to respond if the Kiev regime’s threats against civil aviation are carried out. Threats against civil aviation amount to an act of state terrorism, he stressed, adding that one does not negotiate with terrorists. In turn, Russian Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said that the ministry found solutions to ensure the safety of civil aviation and would not tolerate threats.
The Eastern Economic Forum is taking place on September 1-4 in Vladivostok on the campus of the Far Eastern Federal University.
