He helped build the surveillance system the FSB uses to spy on Russians. Then he escaped Russia with an archive of its internal documents. Here’s what he told iStories.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:41:13 UTC
23:41:13 KST

He helped build the surveillance system the FSB uses to spy on Russians. Then he escaped Russia with an archive of its internal documents. Here’s what he told iStories.
Journalists from iStories talked to Ivan Kirsanov, a 24-year-old programmer who worked at a company owned by the Citadel holding. The holding is the main developer of SORM, the FSB’s surveillance system. In 2025, Kirsanov left Russia and took with him an archive of technical documentation on SORM. He now lives in France on a student visa, works part-time as a shepherd on a farm, and is challenging the denial of his refugee status. Here is what Kirsanov said about himself, his work for the FSB, and the system used to spy on Russians.
What Ivan Kirsanov said about himself
Ivan Kirsanov grew up in Zelenodolsk, a small town near Kazan, in a large family: his father drove for a living, and his mother worked as a cleaner. He started teaching himself to code at 11, using YouTube videos, and it was there that he also came across videos by Alexey Navalny, which, he said, made him start “getting into the subject, taking an interest in politics.” In ninth grade, Kirsanov attended his first rally in Kazan: the “Voters’ Strike,” held after Navalny was barred from the 2018 presidential election.
Kirsanov was detained in 2021 at a rally against the politician’s arrest. He was fined, his college threatened to expel him, and prosecutors sent him written warnings. After officers from Center E spoke with him, he said he “finally understood” that if he kept doing “something like that,” it would “ruin” his life. “I understood that I would have to keep quiet, because I wanted to preserve myself,” the programmer said.
Alongside college, Kirsanov studied at School 21, the Russian franchise of France’s École 42 coding school. The program led to an internship — and soon after, a full-time job — at Sberbank, when he was 19. He finished college in 2022 and moved to Moscow, he said, to steer clear of the draft office. In 2023, he took a new job at MFI Soft, a company based in Nizhny Novgorod; at the interview, he was told the work involved the “Yarovaya package,” but Kirsanov said he “didn’t care.”
What the programmer said about working for Russia’s Federal Security Service
MFI Soft has developed technical equipment for the System for Operative Investigative Activities (SORM), the system Russia’s FSB uses to spy on Russians. The company belongs to Citadel, a holding that has acquired a series of firms supplying SORM equipment and software. Kirsanov joined MFI Soft in the summer of 2023 as a senior software engineer in the department handling internet traffic, where his job included refining code written by “FSB developers.”
Kirsanov said he initially took the FSB-linked job for the money, but later “started picking up on this general spirit: we’re doing something useful, fighting crime, writing great software, and with its help, they catch murderers and terrorists.” How useful SORM actually is for law enforcement work remains publicly unknown.
Kirsanov quit in 2024 after asking for a promotion and being told to wait. During his year working for the FSB, he said, he “barely grew as a programmer,” and management brushed aside his proposals for innovation. “If I had been promoted back then and given the chance to keep developing myself, I probably would have kept working there, climbing higher and higher up the career ladder, doing worse and worse things. I would have sincerely believed I was doing the right thing, just as I believed then,” Kirsanov reflects now.
Soon after quitting, Kirsanov decided to leave Russia. While preparing to emigrate, he said, someone tried to abduct him and take him to a police station. Kirsanov dropped to the ground outside the station, screamed for help, and threatened suicide. He was ultimately taken to a psychiatric hospital instead. After being released on a friend’s guarantee, he left the country, first for Serbia and then for France.
Kirsanov’s studies at École 42 allowed him to obtain a visa, and he lived off his savings for a while. Since the fall of 2025, he has been herding goats and picking strawberries on a farm. French authorities rejected his asylum application, saying they did not believe he faced a threat of persecution in Russia. Kirsanov plans to appeal the decision.
What we learned from the programmer’s account of SORM
Kirsanov gave iStories an archive of documents detailing exactly what happens to internet traffic as it travels from users to FSB officers.
Other journalists have previously reported on SORM’s capabilities, including Andrey Zakharov and Meduza. But as Zakharov says, “at the time we could only judge them by indirect signs.” The documents Kirsanov provided confirm those earlier conclusions — for example, how SORM “sees” Russians’ online activity.
Key takeaways:
- Most of the data on Russians’ online activity that SORM can collect is not especially useful, since a large share of the traffic is encrypted. Phone calls and text messages, however, are fully visible to the system.
- SORM can detect use of several popular messaging apps — Telegram, WhatsApp, IMO, Zoom, Viber, WeChat, and Discord — collecting metadata on calls made through them without revealing who the user is talking to or what they discussed.
- SORM cannot detect the use of Signal.
- Older, unencrypted services such as ICQ, Mail.ru Agent, and Jabber remain fully visible to SORM, and the Max messenger is likely just as transparent to the system, according to Zakharov.
- Users’ search queries on Google, and the search engine’s responses, are invisible to SORM, which can only tell that a user accessed the google.com domain. Google Meet and Google Drive both register to SORM simply as Google. The system can distinguish a Meet call from a Drive file upload only by indirect signs.
- SORM can identify some VPNs that run on the OpenVPN and PPTP protocols.
- Security officials likely cannot quickly decrypt traffic from many Russian services, including Yandex and VK, since they too rely on encryption, though the FSB can obtain data from Russian services through other channels.
- Only the FSB and developers have direct access to SORM. Kirsanov said that for one task, he captured the internet traffic of the operator Tele2 in Nizhny Novgorod. “I could analyze it, do whatever I wanted with it. Without any special clearance, I could effectively observe real people. In fact, every developer at the company could have had that same ability,” he added.
“Kirsanov confirms that a large part of the traffic recorded by SORM is junk. The equipment cannot decrypt data sent over HTTPS, which a large share of modern websites use,” Andrey Zakharov sums up.

The parties involved in a Kyiv shootout on Wednesday, Sept. 2, have offered differing accounts of the incident – one accusing the other of a Russian assassination plot, while the other alleging illegal kidnapping.
Initial reports suggest that officers from the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) engaged in a firefight with officers from Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) on the left bank of Kyiv on Wednesday over the disappearance of Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the incident and ordered an investigation by the State Bureau of Investigation (DBR) alongside the Prosecutor General’s Office.
The SBU has since accused Kaplunov of Russian collaboration, while Kaplunov has accused the SBU of kidnapping him illegally and fabricating the Russian plot as a cover-up.
Kyiv Post cannot independently verify the authenticity of reports from all sides.
Who are the SBU, HUR, and RDK?
The SBU is primarily responsible for domestic intelligence and counterterrorism activities, whereas HUR, as part of the military, is primarily tasked with foreign intelligence and reconnaissance.
The RDK is a military unit under HUR made up of Russian nationals fighting on behalf of Ukraine against Moscow.
SBU accuses Kaplunov of Russian collaboration
Soon after the incident went public, the SBU and the Prosecutor General’s Office published an identical press release accusing fighters from “one of the units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine” of hindering its investigation.
Russian Drones Hit Kyiv Region, Injuring 1 Amid Damaged Warehouses and Buildings
In a Thursday press release, the SBU then detailed its claims and the investigation itself, tying the case to an alleged attack prepared by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) against a Russian opposition leader who arrived in Ukraine for Independence Day on Aug. 24.
In it, an unnamed person widely believed to be Kaplunov was accused of working with the FSB to try to assassinate the unnamed figure, as well as “[eliminating] other military personnel of the Defense Forces of Ukraine in exchange for a monetary reward.”
The press release also includes a video of Kaplunov acknowledging contacts with the FSB, as well as screenshots of communications reportedly between Kaplunov and his FSB handler concerning the assassination plot that contains Nazi symbolism.
However, the SBU wrote that “no preventive measure was applied” given “ the recognition by this serviceman of contacts with the FSB of the Russian Federation and cooperation with the investigation.”
Kaplunov alleges illegal kidnapping and cover-up
Kaplunov has since been released and offered an entirely different account of the incident in an interview with New Voice of Ukraine, suggesting interagency rivalries.
According to Kaplunov, he was taken from his home on Aug. 23 by men who claimed to be police officers and was put into a black BMW car, where he was then transferred between multiple vehicles and detention facilities, with his eyes covered.
The RDK had reported Kaplunov’s disappearance and appealed to authorities for help, while New Voice of Ukraine published a video of Kaplunov’s detention on Thursday, after the interview was published.
Kaplunov then said he identified his kidnappers as SBU officers due to “how they described themselves during [their] exchanges.”
He also said he was interrogated and alleged that the SBU – including acting SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad – was trying to “discredit” HUR’s Tymur special forces unit and Kyrylo Budanov, the former HUR chief who now heads Ukraine’s Presidential Office.
However, Kaplunov said his abductors did not use physical force on him, save for the initial abduction.
Kaplunov said he was later told that he would be returned to his residence after over a week of abduction, though he was unaware of the abductors’ plan to conduct a search of his apartment, he said.
Upon their return, a gunfight ensued, and he was freed by soldiers from the Tymur special forces unit, who were supposedly monitoring his residence after his disappearance.
Commenting on his video confession shared by the SBU, he claimed in the interview that he did so under duress. He added that the SBU also attempted to implicate his commander, Dmytro Ivanov.
“While I was in that difficult situation, I really did fully agree with their version that I had been in contact with the FSB and later shifted that communication to my immediate commander, Dmytro. But in reality, nothing like that happened,” he said. “I went along with it because of the situation I was in and because of psychological pressure.”
No charges have been brought against Kaplunov at the time of publication.
What did HUR say?
HUR itself has remained quiet on the incident, though its Tymur special forces unit has accused the SBU of kidnapping.
On Thursday morning, the agency made a brief announcement warning of a “targeted disinformation campaign” to “discredit” the agency.
But the evening prior, hours after the shooting went public, Tymur – the commander and the unit’s namesake – sent a video response to Radio Liberty and accused the SBU of kidnapping Kaplunov “in broad daylight” and unlawful attempts to arrest his unit.

New EU border system triggers hours-long queues at Brussels Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:40:56 UTC
23:40:56 KST

Non-European travellers arriving at Brussels Airport faced waiting times of up to three hours at border control during peak morning hours on Thursday due to the rollout of the EU's new Entry/Exit System (EES) and a seasonal surge in returning holidaymakers.
Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens confirmed the delays to Dutch-language public broadcaster VRT, noting that non-European passengers experienced three-hour queues upon arrival. By contrast, European citizens using automated passport-control gates experienced shorter wait times, generally between 30 and 60 minutes.
The delays stem largely from the implementation of the EES, a digital border-management system that electronically registers non-European nationals entering and leaving the Schengen Area.
The system replaces physical passport stamps with biometric checks, including fingerprints and facial scans.
"The registration requires more steps and time per passenger. As a result, waiting times build up rapidly during busy periods," Franssens said.
Although the Belgian government deployed additional Aviation Police personnel ahead of the summer season to staff all available control booths, the airport reported that the extra workforce has proven insufficient during high-volume periods.

BIRMINGHAM, England — European diplomats are quietly courting Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, as the party gathers for its annual conference this week — with several EU countries sending representatives for the first time.
Germany, Italy and Spain are among the nations dispatching officials to the party’s conference in Birmingham, as capitals begin to grapple with the prospect of Farage’s party entering government.
“There are more [diplomats] attending this year, probably, because embassies realize more and more Reform UK is a political party that we have to take seriously, and it’s good to have contacts across political parties,” one EU diplomat, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic engagement, told POLITICO.
Advertisement
“This is how we get a better understanding of the policies and ambitions [of Reform], and also our way to share our views, [for example] on the importance of European cooperation,” the diplomat added.
Farage’s party has seen a decline in public support over the course of 2026, but is still neck-and-neck in the polls with the governing Labour party, which is enjoying a polling bounce after the appointment of Andy Burnham as prime minister in July.
Unwinding the reset
A Farage government would pose challenges for the European Union.
Reform has pledged to unwind the “reset” deals that the Labour government is negotiating with Brussels — and renegotiate the post-Brexit trade deal. It also wants to revisit the U.K.’s migrant returns deal with France, while removing EU settled status for welfare claimants and student loans for foreign nationals.
Tensions between the EU and Reform have remained high over the last year, with the bloc considering a so-called “Farage clause” designed to protect the reset from being rolled back by a future government. Farage, however, has already warned he would “not honour any clause.”
Berlin, Rome and Madrid aren’t the only capitals sending delegates in an effort to improve ties with the party.
Advertisement
Representatives from Denmark, Norway, Finland, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Ireland, the Netherlands, Poland, and Romania are also expected to descend on Birmingham’s National Exhibition Centre for this week’s conference, according to multiple people familiar with embassy plans.
Officials attending this year are largely political affairs officers and other diplomats, rather than the ambassadors themselves — a signal that European capitals are looking to establish contact with Reform without elevating the engagement to the highest diplomatic level.
“As an embassy, it’s our responsibility to monitor all domestic developments in the host country,” a second EU diplomat said. “For that reason, we aim to follow as many party conferences as possible, either in person or through other means.”
Staying away
However, one notable European nation appears to be keeping its distance.
France will not be sending representatives to this year’s conference, two EU diplomats told POLITICO — as Reform UK invites Jordan Bardella, president of France’s far-right National Rally, to address Farage’s supporters on Friday.
The French embassy did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.
Advertisement
French President Emmanuel Macron visited Downing Street on Thursday morning for his first bilateral meeting with British prime minister Andy Burnham, before heading to the British Museum to see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition, which has returned to England from France for the first time in more than 900 years.
Reform’s conference is expected to draw around 2,000 more attendees than last year, according to internal figures.
Reform declined to comment on the increased embassy engagement.

Lives on hold: Young Iranians watch their futures slip away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:40:11 UTC
23:40:11 KST

Share & more
The past six months of bombs, geopolitical tensions and the looming threat of a wider conflict have created a suffocating sense of uncertainty for many Iranians. And it’s not just about the airstrikes. Young people say the period since the US and Israel first struck their country in late February has been one of anxiety-inducing limbo, with their futures put on hold indefinitely.
The New Humanitarian spoke to five young Iranians in the capital, who shared what it feels like to be trapped, watching their best years slip away. From cancelled weddings and crushing unemployment to never-ending news updates and the vanishing of simple pleasures, their stories offer a window into what it is like to live through a war that has taken away their ability to plan for tomorrow.
In Tehran and across the country, fresh US and Iranian strikes this week were a stark reminder that, after half a year of bombing and a war of words between the US and Iran, ceasefire talks remain stalled. The Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut, while the core issues driving the conflict remain unresolved.
Iranian citizens have been left bracing for hostilities to resume at any moment. In the 40 days after the US and Israel launched attacks in late February, more than 3,500 people – including hundreds of civilians – were killed, according to the Iranian government.
While Iran’s economy has struggled for years amid sanctions, US economic pressure and the war have compounded the pain. Iranian officials have put the economic damage from the war at more than $270 billion, though the figure is a preliminary estimate. Inflation reached nearly 88% year-over-year in July with the rial hitting a record low on 2 September, while sweeping corporate budget cuts have triggered mass layoffs; more than a million people in a country of 87 million are believed to have lost their jobs.
Even when the skies over Tehran are quiet, the five young people whose words are featured here – Ziba, Nima, Fatema, Sima, and Amir Ali* – say the agony has shifted beyond the bombing itself. What weighs most heavily now is the paralysis of not knowing what comes next.
Names have been changed due to security concerns, and words have been translated, condensed, and edited for clarity.
Ziba, 27, watched her wedding plans fell apart
“Every major milestone in my life has been frozen”
My morning routine now begins before my feet even touch the floor. The very first thing I do when I wake up is grab my phone and open my main news channels. I have to scroll through everything posted overnight. The news cycle here changes by the minute. You might go to bed reading that a diplomatic agreement is imminent, only to wake up and find out that infrastructure was bombed while you were sleeping. I have to know exactly what reality I am waking up into.
The initial shock we felt when this first started has morphed into something else, but there are still moments that completely rattle me. It’s terrifying when I go outside and see massive lines of people panic-buying fuel at the petrol stations. I look at them and think, “What will happen to the city if they strike tomorrow?”
My nights are consumed by a different kind of anxiety. A few months ago, I didn't even know what [the live online flight tracker] Flightradar was. Now, before I can attempt to sleep, I am on the app monitoring the airspace over the Middle East. I check to see if civilian planes are still flying over Iran, or if flights are still landing in Israel. If I see commercial planes in the sky, I tell myself it's safe enough to close my eyes.
Even our family group chats offer no escape; they are a constant stream of terrifying rumours. Someone will forward a fake message claiming a nuclear strike is coming tonight, alongside advice to hoard food or buy power generators.
To cope with the overwhelming dread, I downloaded half a dozen mindless puzzle games on my phone. But the stress gave me such severe insomnia that I used to wake up multiple times a night just to check the news. Now, I have to take sleeping pills. When the anxiety becomes too heavy, I put on a podcast and play the puzzle games for hours, waiting for the medication to finally make my eyes heavy enough to sleep.
Every major milestone in my life has been frozen. My fiancé and I got engaged exactly 40 days before this recent wave of conflict began. We were deep into planning the wedding, but it completely fell apart. How can you book a venue, buy a wedding dress, or put down deposits when you don’t know if a war will break out tomorrow? We have stopped all planning and will probably just move into our apartment quietly without a celebration. It breaks my heart because I had to let what was supposed to be one of the best nights of my life go.
Even my smallest daily joys have vanished. I used to be obsessed with online shopping and skincare routines. I haven't bought anything in months. I am literally scraping the last drops out of my old makeup containers. Every time I think about restocking, I stop myself. I need to hoard every rial in case the economy collapses and I get laid off. And honestly, what is the point of a skincare routine if a war breaks out?
When I hang out with my friends, the panic has been replaced by a heavy numbness. Six months ago, we took every threat seriously. Now, if someone reads a headline out loud about an impending attack or a peace talk, we just laugh. We have become completely desensitised. Underneath that numbness is a profound grief. The prime years of our youth — the years we should be growing and experiencing life — are being destroyed by the egos of global powers who do not care about regular people.
Nima, 21, fears his attempt to leave Iran has set him back
“The sheer terror of being completely left behind”
For the past two years, my life has been defined by a single, obsessive goal: to emigrate from Iran by the time I turn 21. I took a massive risk and dropped out of university to make this happen. I work in video production and editing now, and every decision I’ve made since leaving school – every late night staring at editing deadlines, every rial I’ve desperately managed to save, every expensive language class I’ve paid for – has been dedicated to preparing for a visa interview at the French embassy and securing a way out. But since the conflict escalated last year, and with this endless, agonising cycle of ceasefires and new threats, my carefully constructed roadmap has been thrown into absolute chaos.
The uncertainty we are living through isn't just an abstract political talking point on the news; it is a solid brick wall standing between me and my future. I am supposed to be finalising my paperwork right now, but I wake up every morning paralysed by questions I cannot answer. If I am finally ready for my visa interview next month, will the foreign embassies in Tehran even be open? Are they quietly evacuating their diplomatic staff right now? Will any country even issue visas to young Iranians right now, or are we considered too high-risk? You just don’t know, and that not-knowing is suffocating.
The uncertainty we are living through isn't just an abstract political talking point on the news; it is a solid brick wall standing between me and my future.
Beyond the geopolitical anxieties, there is the grinding financial exhaustion of trying to survive here. Every single day, just staying afloat becomes harder. The economic fluctuations are tied to the military news cycle. You walk into a local shop and suddenly a pack of cigarettes is exponentially more expensive because of a headline about a potential strike; tomorrow the tension might ease and the price drops slightly, only to shoot up again the next day. We live completely at the mercy of breaking news alerts.
My absolute deepest fear is the very real possibility of losing on both fronts. I sacrificed my university degree for this emigration dream. I held back from fully committing to long-term career progression in the local video industry because I was saving all my energy and resources for a life abroad.
If this state of violent limbo drags on, what happens to me? I won't have my degree, I won't have advanced my career here, and I won't have successfully emigrated either. It’s the sheer terror of being completely left behind, stuck in a void. That is the heaviest burden I carry right now: the creeping realisation that while I wait for the world to decide our fate, my youth is just slipping through my fingers.
Fatemeh, 26, is being squeezed by inflation, job losses, and rising rents
“Watching the prices skyrocket day by day has been terrifying”
The first direct hit I took when the conflict escalated was deeply personal. My partner and I used to work together, but as the economic panic set in, our company began downsizing, and he was laid off. Almost overnight, we were forced into a long-distance relationship. The emotional toll of losing that daily proximity, combined with the crushing stress of his sudden unemployment, put a massive strain on both of us. But that was only the beginning.
Then came the hyperinflation. Watching the prices skyrocket day by day has been terrifying. To give a specific example: During the height of the tension, I wanted to buy a pair of sneakers that cost around four million tomans ($20). Before I could save enough, the price shot up to nearly seven million.
Food prices have increased by 100%. I’ve had to completely eliminate things from my grocery basket that I used to buy without a second thought. Something as simple as a tub of ice cream or snacks? I don’t even walk down those aisles in the supermarket anymore. I just can't justify the cost.
But the absolute hardest blow has been the threat to my basic security: my housing. The inflation resulting from these cycles of war and peace has forced everyone into survival mode. I am working much more now than I was before the conflict just to stay afloat. My roommate realised that staying in a fixed-salary job like she had was financial suicide, so she decided to pivot to doing skincare and facials because service prices and wages inflate and shift alongside the economy.
We live in central Tehran, in a neighbourhood filled with students and bookstores. It’s not the right demographic for premium beauty services. So she decided to move to west Tehran, to a neighbourhood where people have more disposable income. Her plan is to rent a one-bedroom apartment and convert half of it into a skincare studio.
Her decision left me completely stranded. The relentless inflation has wiped out my ability to save anything. I am left hovering between the earth and the sky. I don't have enough money for a new deposit. If I want to find a place of my own, I will have to drown myself in loans and borrow from everyone I know. Even then, my monthly rent will increase by 100%.
The scariest part is the logic behind my roommate's move. From the outside, taking such a massive financial risk in this unstable economy seems insane. But she firmly believes that if she doesn't make this leap this year, she will never be able to do it. The future looks so overwhelmingly dark and unpredictable that her mentality is literally now or never. She is convinced things are going to get so much worse that soon, even taking a risk will be impossible.
Sina, 20, lost the job he hoped would lift his family out of poverty
“A relentless exercise in overthinking”
I come from a lower-income, working-class family. My father is a labourer who has done gruelling physical work his entire life just to feed the family. For a brief moment, I truly thought I was going to be the one to break our family's cycle of poverty.
I had worked hard and managed to land a great, professional job. It was my golden ticket to pull myself up, build a real career, and finally change my social standing. But when the threat of war escalated and the economic shock hit, budget cuts followed immediately. I was one of the first people laid off, and my entire trajectory collapsed.
For the past five or six months, my existence has been reduced to desperately searching for work. I have sent out between 150 and 200 résumés. I’ve gone to countless interviews, but the answer is always the same. Because of the geopolitical situation and the shrinking economy, companies aren't hiring; they are completely frozen or downsizing.
Waking up every day as an unemployed 20-year-old in Tehran is a relentless exercise in overthinking. You wake up with nothing to do but obsess over what is going to happen next. Will prices go up again? You set a goal to save money to buy something basic, and by the time you reach that amount, the item has become drastically more expensive.
But the absolute hardest part is the sheer humiliation and guilt of losing my financial independence. I try to strip my expenses down to the bare minimum so I don't run out of the little money I have left. But sometimes, when I hit absolute zero, I have to ask my father for cash just to get by. At 20, with the pride of a young guy who thought he had finally made it and was supposed to start helping his family, it is a crushing feeling. Having to ask a tired, aging labourer for money just so you can buy a coffee? It completely destroys your dignity. I look at how hard he works, and the guilt eats me alive.
My biggest fear for the next year is that the inflation will spiral so far out of control that we won't be able to afford breathing. The most normal routines from a year ago are now impossible luxuries. Going out for dinner or to a cafe is something you can maybe do once every 10 days now; if you did it every night, your entire month's salary would vanish in two weeks.
People ask if I am afraid of a war breaking out. Honestly, no. I am not afraid of things coming to a head and our fate finally being decided. What genuinely terrifies me is this endless, paralysing limbo where my youth is wasted, and I am dragged right back to the bottom.
Amir Ali, 26, has seen his ambitions shrink after losing his job
“My only strategy is to do absolutely nothing”
At first, I told myself I wasn't bothered by the sound of missiles or the endless talk of war. But slowly it crept into my psyche and took over everything. My baseline level of stress has skyrocketed. I find myself becoming aggressive, snapping at things that used to be completely normal. There is this constant, heavy feeling that my basic safety is under threat.
But honestly, the hardest part isn’t the threat of war itself; it’s the absolute uncertainty. It’s the sheer paralysis of not knowing. You wake up in the morning and ask yourself, “What will happen today?” You check your phone and the news says things are calming down. Half an hour later, a new headline breaks, warning that everything is about to get worse. That relentless whiplash strips the life out of you because it makes it impossible to make a single long-term decision.
“The hardest part isn’t the threat of war itself; it’s the absolute uncertainty.”
The most immediate blow I took from the conflict was to my livelihood. I lost my main job and the steady income I relied on. That single event derailed every plan I had for the future. I had been diligently saving money for months just to upgrade my car. I wasn’t going to buy something luxurious, just a normal step forward. But with the economic shock and my lost wages, that plan evaporated. I couldn't pull the trigger.
Now, just changing my car feels like the absolute ceiling of my ambitions. Buying a house? That is a total pipe dream. Unless you have some miraculous exception, no one can buy property here on a normal salary anymore. Even the thought of getting married has been completely taken off the table. The inflation is so aggressive and the costs are so astronomical that you just give up. I genuinely don't know what to do anymore.
People ask if I have ideas to start a business or invest if things ever quieten down. The truth is, our economic environment is so deeply unhealthy and unpredictable that starting a business feels like walking into a trap.
In this climate, my only strategy is to do absolutely nothing – just freeze, keep my head down, and try to protect the little I have. You can't get a bank loan, because how can you commit to monthly repayments when you don't know if you'll have a job next week? That shadow hangs over every daily routine. I am terrified of being laid off again because no position is secure. And the saddest part is that it’s not just me. Look at anyone in my friendship circle. We are all deeply exhausted, trapped in this exact same limbo, totally clueless about what to do with our lives.

Two new British support ships named at Appledore
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:38:46 BST
23:38:46 KST

The second and third ships in the Royal Fleet Auxiliary’s new Fleet Solid Support programme will be named RFA Reliant and RFA Resourceful, with the names revealed as the keel was laid for first-of-class RFA Resurgent at Appledore in North Devon, the Royal Navy has said.
The three ships are being built to provide ammunition, stores and other supplies to Royal Navy vessels at sea, including the UK’s aircraft carriers. Sections of the vessels are being constructed at Navantia facilities in Appledore and Cadiz, as well as in Belfast, before being transported to Harland & Wolff’s Belfast facility for final integration.
Commodore Sam Shattock, head of the Royal Fleet Auxiliary, announced the names of the remaining two ships during the keel-laying ceremony for RFA Resurgent, which took place on Merchant Navy Day.
He said: “Today represents the moment when vision becomes reality, when plans and drawings come to life, effectively becoming the ship’s birthday.”
On the name of the first vessel, he added: “RFA Resurgent’s name speaks of renewal, resilience and the ability recover stronger from challenge.”
“Those qualities are reflected not only in the ship itself, but also in the people who will design, build, support and ultimately sail her.”
As part of the keel-laying ceremony, a coin was welded to the keel of RFA Resurgent by a Navantia UK apprentice, continuing a shipbuilding tradition marking the formal start of construction.
Each Fleet Solid Support ship will have a core RFA crew of 101, with accommodation for a further 80 personnel when required. Those additional personnel could include teams operating helicopters and boats or carrying out other specialist roles.
The vessels are intended to replenish Royal Navy ships with munitions, supplies and provisions while at sea. The Royal Navy says they will also be able to support wider operational activity, including counter-piracy and counter-terrorism missions and operations alongside allied forces.
The design also includes energy-efficient technologies intended to reduce power consumption. The ships are being built with the ability to use low-carbon, non-fossil fuels and future sustainable energy sources, with the Royal Navy saying the design is intended to allow the vessels to achieve Carbon Zero status by the end of their planned 30-year operational lives.
RFA Resurgent revives a name previously carried by a merchant vessel converted into a fleet replenishment ship in 1957. That ship remained in service until 1979 and supported a Joint Services scientific expedition to the Indian Ocean in 1975.
The name RFA Reliant has previously been used by three vessels, including stores and air stores support ships and a helicopter support ship. The most recent Reliant was a merchant vessel taken into naval service in 1983 and used during the multinational deployment to Lebanon in 1984, including during evacuation operations. She was sold in 1986 after being replaced in the helicopter support role by RFA Argus.
RFA Resourceful is a new name for the RFA, selected to follow the adjective-based naming convention of the class. The Royal Fleet Auxiliary previously operated an armament stores ship named RFA Resource, which served between 1966 and 1997 and received battle honours for the Falklands and Kuwait.
The Fleet Solid Support programme is also intended to support investment in UK shipyards, apprenticeships, skilled employment and domestic supply chains, while combining work in Britain with construction and expertise from Navantia’s Spanish facilities.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Thursday threatened to target Iran’s infrastructure and energy facilities if Tehran launches an attack on Israel, warning that Israel would return Iran to “the Stone Age and darkness.”
Speaking at a Defense Ministry ceremony ahead of the Jewish New Year, which begins Sept. 11, Katz claimed there are indications that Iran’s severe economic pressures and fears of an uprising and the collapse of its government could push it to take “desperate measures.”
“Any Iranian attack on Israel will free us from all limitations. We will strike all infrastructure, including energy infrastructure, and return Iran to the Stone Age and darkness,” he said.

The developments come amid renewed military escalation between the US and Iran at the start of September, after the pace of attacks had eased for about a month.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said Tuesday that it launched a wave of strikes against targets linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, including air defense systems, radars, naval capabilities and communications facilities.
Iran responded with missile and drone attacks targeting sites used by US forces in the region.

Washington and Tehran had reached a framework for de-escalation in June through Qatari and Pakistani mediation, but hostilities resumed amid continued disputes over the Strait of Hormuz and reciprocal military operations.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The only way to stop Russian drone terror is to create the same on their territory at points that are painful for them,” Kovalenko said.
He rejected suggestions that a single technological solution could immediately close Ukraine’s skies to Russian drones and missiles.

Ukraine Fast-Tracks Interceptors for Jet-Powered Shahed
According to him, the Ukrainian Armed Forces are already creating increasing problems for Russian airports. He predicted that continued disruption would affect Russia’s economy and the quality of life of its population.

Satellite warfare against drone operations
Kovalenko predicted that competition over satellite capabilities would become increasingly important as remotely controlled drones develop.

In response, future space forces would increasingly focus on disabling hostile satellites to protect people and infrastructure on Earth, Kovalenko said.
He warned that this technological competition could directly affect Ukraine and other European countries because Russia is also developing capabilities in this area.
“The technological race will continue,” Kovalenko said, urging governments and the public to be realistic about the limitations of air defense and the evolving nature of drone warfare.

Russian Black Sea attacks, low Danube waters push EU to seek alternative routes for Ukrainian grain exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:36:54 UTC
23:36:54 KST

The European Union is discussing export support with Ukraine and its neighboring countries, including through so-called solidarity lanes, Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen told Bloomberg on 2 September.
Strikes in the Black Sea have curtailed exports from both Ukraine and Russia, while low water limits how much grain vessels can carry on the Danube, Ukraine’s main fallback when sea traffic slows. Wheat and corn prices are at multiyear highs, and the Bloomberg Agriculture Spot Index jumped by more than 13% in August, its sharpest monthly rise in over a decade. Hansen said the EU’s role as a major food exporter means drought-driven production losses could cause shortages elsewhere.
Created after Russia's full-scale invasion, the solidarity lanes carry Ukrainian exports by road, rail, and river through neighboring countries when Black Sea shipping is disrupted.
The European Commission is separately weighing relief for drought-hit EU farmers. Hansen urged governments to use flexibilities in the Common Agricultural Policy, the EU's farm-subsidy system, including exemptions for circumstances beyond farmers' control, emergency fertilizer aid, and earlier payments, but proposed no new measures in a letter seen by Bloomberg. EU agriculture ministers are due to discuss the drought in Ireland next week and in Brussels later in September.
Russian attacks squeeze Ukraine’s export routes
Low water is only one obstacle to Ukraine’s southern export routes. Russia has repeatedly attacked ports and transport links along the Danube and on Odesa Oblast’s Black Sea coast. Some Ukrainian farmers have sold wheat below production cost as port prices fell, leaving less money for the next sowing.
Romania detected more than 100 drones during seven attacks on Danube ports in mid-August, interim Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruță said. Russia struck Izmail, Ukraine's largest Danube port, three times in August. The 29 August attack killed one person and destroyed five grain trucks, Odesa regional authorities said.
Ukraine and Moldova have pursued a rail corridor through Moldova to Constanța, Romania’s main Black Sea port, as an alternative. Moldova later halved transit tariffs through 31 December. Ukrainian officials estimate the corridor could handle around 10% of Ukraine's grain exports, Reuters reported.

Russian Strategic Bomber Chief Reportedly Shot in Engels, Home to Tu-95 and Tu-160 Fleet
A Russian Aerospace Forces officer was shot in the torso and face by a gunman on a motorcycle near Engels, home to one of Russia’s most important strategic bomber bases, Russian media outlet Mash reported on September 3.
The shooting took place in the settlement of Probuzhdenie near Engels in Russia’s Saratov region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Mash, the assailant approached a private house on a motorcycle while wearing a helmet and opened fire on the officer.
One bullet struck the officer in the torso, and another hit him in the face, leaving him seriously wounded.
The officer’s driver was also injured in the shooting but managed to escape and hide. He later returned to the scene and called an ambulance, according to the report.
According to preliminary unconfirmed information, the shooter might have hit Russian Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, commander of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division of the Long-Range Aviation of the Russian Aerospace Forces.
Doctors subsequently removed the bullets from the officer. He was reported to be in serious condition and was being prepared for transfer to Moscow aboard a specialized medical aircraft.
The location is particularly notable because Engels hosts a major base for Russia’s strategic aviation.
Varpakhovich’s command has also been directly linked to one of Russia’s most notorious missile strikes on Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Security Service says that on July 8, 2024, Varpakhovich issued the combat order for a Kh-101 cruise missile strike carried out by aircraft from the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division. One of the missiles hit Kyiv’s Okhmatdyt Children’s Hospital during a massive Russian barrage across Ukraine.
The European Union has also formally identified Varpakhovich as commander of the Engels-2-based division responsible for the Kh-101 strike on Okhmatdyt and sanctioned him over his role in actions supporting Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.
His division operates the long-range bombers that Russia has repeatedly used to launch cruise missiles at Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Engels-2 has long been associated with Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers, aircraft Moscow uses to launch long-range cruise missiles against Ukraine.
The Tu-95MS remains one of Russia’s principal air-launched cruise missile carriers. Although the aircraft is based on a Soviet-era design, part of the fleet has undergone modernization to the Tu-95MSM standard.
The upgrade introduced new engines, navigation and avionics equipment, an updated defensive suite and the ability to carry as many as eight Kh-101 or Kh-102 cruise missiles on external pylons.
According to estimates cited by Ukrainian defense analysts, Russia’s fleet as of 2024 consisted of approximately 31 Tu-95MS aircraft and another 27 upgraded Tu-95MSM bombers.
The aircraft are particularly difficult for Russia to replace. Production ended in 1992, meaning losses or severe damage permanently reduce a fleet built more than three decades ago.
Tu-160 strategic bombers have also operated from Engels and are used as long-range missile carriers in Russia’s military.
Previously, Ukraine’s Security Service struck a Russian Tu-95MS strategic bomber at Engels, home to a key base for Moscow’s long-range aviation fleet used to launch cruise missile attacks against Ukraine.

The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation announced that it had delivered the system for Ukrainian aviation after purchasing it through a joint fundraising project with ride-hailing company Uklon.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Video released by the foundation shows the remotely controlled weapon installed on a helicopter and operating against Russian aerial targets.
“We are complicating flights for Russian Shaheds. The video shows the remotely controlled Khyzhak combat module, which the Foundation delivered for aviation. The Khyzhak is built around a 7.62 mm PKT machine gun and provides full 360-degree horizontal rotation, while the weapon can elevate as much as 75 degrees vertically.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry has already codified the system and cleared it for use by the Armed Forces.
The stabilized mount is designed to maintain accurate fire while the platform carrying it is moving. According to the ministry, the weapon system can also use compatible 7.62 mm ammunition of both Soviet and NATO standards.
What makes the Khyzhak particularly versatile is its modular architecture.
The system can be fitted to unmanned ground vehicles, installed in fixed defensive positions, mounted on conventional vehicles or integrated with maritime platforms. The version shown in the latest footage represents an airborne adaptation of the same basic concept.
The module also incorporates artificial intelligence-assisted target recognition and tracking.
Its software can automatically detect and follow aerial targets, including drones, reducing the workload on the human operator and helping keep the weapon aligned with fast-moving threats.
That capability allows the Khyzhak to be used against small FPV drones as well as much larger Shahed-type UAVs at relatively close range.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Satellite images taken after the attack show at least four sites of intense burning across the refinery complex, indicating multiple drone impacts.
According to Dnipro Osint, the strikes caused significant damage to technical overpasses and columns associated with the AVT-4, AVT-5, and AVT-1 primary crude-processing units. A vacuum gas oil hydrotreatment unit used in secondary refining was also damaged.
The extent of the damage has forced the refinery to completely suspend operations while repairs are carried out, Dnipro Osint reported.
The Kstovo refinery, operated by LUKOIL-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, has an annual processing capacity of approximately 17 million metric tons of crude oil. According to Dnipro Osint, the facility accounts for up to 11% of Russia’s gasoline production.
Before repeated Ukrainian drone strikes, it produced about 5 million metric tons of gasoline and more than 5 million metric tons of diesel per year, along with roughly 2 million metric tons of fuel oil and around 500,000 metric tons of bitumen.
The August 26 operation also targeted a major Wildberries logistics center in Russia’s Tambov region. Ukrainian defense technology company Fire Point said FP-1 long-range drones were used to strike both the logistics hub and the Kstovo refinery.
Initial reports of a fire at the Wildberries facility in Kotovsk emerged shortly after 1 am, with local residents reporting at least 10 explosions before a major blaze broke out at the site.
The reported shutdown in Kstovo comes as Ukrainian strikes continue to disrupt operations at other major Russian refineries. Russia’s Kirishi oil refinery in the Leningrad region, the country’s second-largest by processing capacity, also suspended all crude processing following a Ukrainian drone attack on August 30.

New school year: Which EU countries pay their teachers the most?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:31:21 UTC
23:31:21 KST

It's back-to-school time again, and teachers and their unions are reigniting the debate over stagnant wages and recurring staff shortages. But which countries pay teachers the best?
The salaries of school staff, and in particular teachers and school heads, make up the largest single cost in formal education, yet teachers in most European countries are often considered underpaid relative to their level of education.
Some studies put teachers' starting salaries at around 40% less than the earnings of other professionals with a tertiary education, and while the gap narrows as they reach the top of the payscale, a stark geographic divide across Europe persists.
In the 2024/2025 school year, Luxembourg was the EU country that paid teachers the most across most of the education levels they taught at, for both those at the beginning and the peak of their careers.
That's according to Eurydice, the European Commission-funded education information network.
The Grand Duchy paid professionals at the start of their careers between €55,000 and €62,000, while it paid €97,000 and €109,000 at the top of their careers.
The Netherlands and Germany came in second place, depending on the education level the teacher works at and what stage of their career they are in.
On the other hand, Slovakia, Czechia and Hungary were the EU countries that paid teachers the least at the top of their careers.
Depending on the education level that the teacher taught at, Slovakia paid their employees between €18,000 and €22,000, while Hungary and Czechia paid up to €27,000.
Meanwhile, teachers in Greece and Slovakia earned the least at the start of their careers, with salaries of up to €17,000.
How long does it take for teachers to reach their peak career?
Career progression is often linked to teachers' roles and responsibilities, years in service, age, qualification level, and general performance.
It takes teachers in 11 EU countries between 31 and 40 years to reach the top of their career, depending on the education level, according to Eurydice.
Only in Denmark and Finland do teachers need up to 10 working years, depending on the education level.
As teachers progress in their careers, so too do their salaries grow, and this is a crucial factor in determining the education profession's attractiveness and retention rate.
It's something that not just teachers benefit from: better salaries for teachers also tend to lead to improved learning outcomes for students, according to a 2025 OECD study.
Eurydice figures say that teachers in Cyprus, Portugal, the Netherlands, and Slovenia will see the biggest salary jump among EU countries between the start and peak of their careers.
The debate on teachers' salaries and their progression has gained renewed interest in France, after the education ministry recently said on its website that a national education teacher received on average €3,090 net per month in 2024.
However, this figure reflects an average of all teachers' possible statuses: school teachers, certified teachers, associate professors, and more elite professors.
In addition, contract teachers, who represent 8% of the teaching staff, were not counted in this average, even though they are the lowest paid.
Furthermore, French teachers are among the five EU countries where salaries failed to keep up with the cost of living crisis, decreasing by 0.61% between the 2023/2024 and 2024/2025 school years, according to Eurydice.
In the EU, only Romania (-6.34%), Slovakia (-4.07%), Italy (-1.60%), and Belgium's French Community (-0.71%) ranked lower than France.

Iran struggles to restrict Hormuz traffic after US strikes hit maritime capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:30:10 UTC
23:30:10 KST

The Islamic Republic’s ability to surveil the Strait of Hormuz and lay mines in the vital waterway has likely been significantly degraded by American attacks, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed, noting that increased oil flows through the strait on September 1 suggest Iran is having difficulty preventing some commercial vessels from using the southern route.
United States officials told Axios on Wednesday that approximately 40 vessels carrying millions of barrels of oil transited the strait on September 1.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright also confirmed that oil tankers transported over 17 million barrels of oil through the strait on August 31, the highest volume of oil exports through the waterway since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.
The figure of 17 million barrels is close to pre-war levels, which averaged 21.6 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2025.
These developments, according to ISW, suggest that Iran is having difficulty preventing some commercial vessels from using the southern route.
Additionally, ISW reported growing indications that Iranian forces are facing operational constraints preventing them from efficiently identifying vessels and laying mines in the strait.
IRGC turns to alternative methods as Hormuz surveillance is degraded
According to ISW, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) recently attempted to use shore-based rocket launchers instead of fast-attack craft to deploy mines.
It has also reportedly used fast-attack craft to physically identify vessels because Iran has only a few functioning radars capable of covering the southern route.
ISW assessed that these less-optimal methods suggest that US strikes have degraded some of Iran’s maritime surveillance and mine-laying capabilities.
Though the IRGC has repeatedly claimed that vessels are striking naval mines in the strait, ISW’s assessment of the claims likely forms part of an effort to preserve the perception that the southern route remains dangerous. US Central Command previously reported that US forces had cleared naval mines from the strait.
CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said last week that US forces had cleared an effective pathway for ships to leave the Persian Gulf, adding that the mines had been “highly degraded.”
However, Ebrahim Zolfaghari, an Iranian military officer and spokesman, claimed on Wednesday that new mines had been laid.
“During last night’s operation, more naval mines were laid along the illicit routes south of the Strait of Hormuz. The only thing CENTCOM could do in response was rename the strait using Photoshop,” he wrote on X/Twitter. “Problem solved! You can just use Photoshop to get the oil tankers through, too!”
Iran appears to be investing in rebuilding its radar systems, ISW noted, citing a claim by US President Donald Trump that Iran had nearly rebuilt some of its radar systems before the US struck them again on September 1.
CENTCOM strikes targets on September 1
CENTCOM confirmed that its September 1 strikes targeted Iranian air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities, and communications sites.
ISW noted that Iran is likely to continue attempting to reconstitute these capabilities because control of the Strait of Hormuz remains one of Tehran’s core objectives.
With Iran’s radars degraded, ISW suggested that the regime would seek alternative ways to attempt control over the strait.
An unnamed American source told Saudi-based Al Arabiya on Wednesday that CENTCOM’s Tuesday night strikes were a preemptive response to the Islamic Republic considering disabling undersea cables.

The White House has signaled that it has no interest in making a deal with Iran; it also doesn’t trust Iran. Despite this, some reports have claimed that the US prefers to keep the conflict contained and has no desire to see it escalate. This means that, should the US seek to appease Iran, it will have to tread carefully.
Meanwhile, Israeli officials warn of possible escalation and have warned Iran against attacking Israel. As such, the region’s politics remain volatile, and many sensitive issues related to Iran remain unresolved.
There are plans for Syria to serve as a means of transferring oil to the Mediterranean. However, a recent report at Reuters noted that “Iraq’s plans to export oil via a pipeline through Syria to avert future disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz will likely require four years of construction and cost at least $15 billion.” The report added that the idea was receiving “initial support for feasibility studies from a consortium including Chevron.”
In June, the Syrian Petroleum Company signed a deal with ConocoPhillips and energy firm Novaterra to rehabilitate gas fields in Syria. The deal will also pay for development of a new gas field.
In July, ConocoPhillips posted that it had “announced it has agreed to terms with BP to acquire a 42% interest in BP Energy Company of Kirkuk Limited, supporting the ongoing redevelopment of four large-scale, currently producing oil fields in the Kirkuk area of northern Iraq. The agreement is expected to be signed as part of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s official visit to Washington, DC.”
There is an old pipeline from 1952 that links Iraq’s Kirkuk with Baniyas in Syria. However, it will take time to repair it and restore its relevance. Until then, Iraq and other countries will need to ship energy supplies on land.
The Washington Post noted that “day and night, 5,000 hulking trucks carrying oil from the Persian Gulf rumble across this stretch of barren desert as if in a caravan snaking its way toward the Mediterranean Sea.”
Damascus seeks international partnerships amid reconstruction push
This week, Syria focused on economic advancement and outreach to other countries. For instance, around 50 companies from Saudi Arabia participated at a fair in Damascus.
“Around 1,000 entities and companies from 60 countries are participating in this year’s Damascus International Fair, which runs through September 4,” Syrian state media noted.
In addition, Syria met with delegations from Denmark and Germany. “Foreign Affairs and Expatriates Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani met on Wednesday with a delegation from Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development, headed by State Secretary Niels Annen, to discuss ways to strengthen economic and development cooperation between Syria and Germany, and support national recovery and reconstruction priorities,” SANA state media added.
Syria’s president also met with the German delegation. “President Ahmad al-Sharaa held a roundtable meeting at the People’s Palace in Damascus with Annen and a number of heads and managers of German companies and members of the Syrian-German Business Council,” SANA added.
Syria is also working to rehabilitate the Mezzeh airport and use it for civilian aircraft. In the past, Mezzeh had been used by the Assad regime’s military.
Regarding the energy trade, The Washington Post article noted that “the trucks began shuttling between the refineries of southern Iraq and the Syrian port of Baniyas in April, initially as an experiment by Iraqi oil exporters seeking to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz after cargo traffic in the waterway was stopped by the US-Israeli war with Iran.”
The article quoted Ahmad Qubbaji, the deputy chief executive of Syrian state-owned Syrian Petroleum Corporation. It said that the company will operate the new pipeline and that Qubbaji noted that the “final contract is expected to be signed in September by a consortium that includes Houston-based Chevron, TotalEnergies of France, and Syrian and Qatari investors. The group is discussing security measures, including using drones and other advanced surveillance technology, to monitor the pipeline, which will also have security backing from the United States.”
From Venezuela to Syria, Trump pursues new energy corridors
Trump’s support for Syria as an oil transfer hub comes in the wake of a major deal in Venezuela. The White House posted on August 31 that “in the biggest oil deal in world history, President Donald J. Trump has secured US majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela – vastly expanding our current US territorial proven reserves of roughly 46 billion barrels. This deal secures our energy dominance for the next century –all at zero cost to the United States.”
The White House added that “the deal, signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, gives the US government powerful governance rights, economic ownership, and guaranteed low-cost off-take from a new private Venezuelan oil champion, which will be the second-largest private oil company by reserves in the world.”
This comes as the US helps tankers move through the Strait of Hormuz. The US Central Command (CENTCOM) is working to keep the strait open despite Iran’s threats.
This week, Gulf News reported that 40 ships had been able to move through the strait. “CENTCOM escorts record 18 million barrels of oil through Hormuz as US-Iran strikes flare,” Gulf News said.
Whether it’s through the Strait of Hormuz itself, or through Venezuela or Syria, the US is focused on one thing: securing a feasible route for energy trade.

BIRMINGHAM, England — France’s Jordan Bardella and Britain’s Nigel Farage will on Friday lock arms on immigration policy, but the limits to their love-in are becoming clear.
The two anti-immigrant populist leaders face opposition within Bardella’s far-right party, the National Rally, over Farage’s controversial proposal to enlist the Royal Navy to help repel immigrants trying to reach the United Kingdom on so-called small boats and return them to France.
Bardella, the president of the far-right National Rally, is expected to back Farage’s plan in a speech in English at Reform UK’s annual conference in Birmingham. He will outline how the two populist parties can jointly tackle illegal cross-channel migration, according to advisers to the duo.
Advertisement
The 30-year-old MEP had previously suggested he could support the so-called pushbacks — but that was back in December, when it looked like his mentor Marine Le Pen would be knocked out of the French presidential election due to an embezzlement conviction and Bardella would be running in her stead.
Le Pen’s revised sentence, giving her a surprise shot in the 2027 race to replace President Emmanuel Macron, has changed the equation. Le Pen, who is campaigning as a clear front-runner according to multiple polls, is seen as less ideologically flexible than Bardella.
One National Rally official, who, like others quoted in this piece, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about private policy discussions, cautioned that France and the U.K. would first have to sign a treaty and share the burden of sending migrants back to their countries of origin. Two advisers to the French far-right party skirted the issue altogether, saying it would not be a problem if the National Rally takes charge — because once in power, they’d so dramatically reduce immigration into France that there won’t be any small boats trying to reach English shores.
“We’re going to reduce immigration. There won’t be lots in Calais,” said one of the advisers.

Advertisement
Jean-Yves Camus, a far-right specialist at the Jean-Jaurès Foundation, concurred, saying that Bardella’s promises sound like “science fiction.”
“The Calais region is a Marine Le Pen stronghold. I don’t think Bardella realizes the impact of what he is proposing for areas that see a lot of migrant arrivals,” said Camus.
Still, Farage’s Reform UK and Bardella’s National Rally are trying to project ideological alignment on the need to drastically reduce immigration in both their countries.
Nigel Farage as he speaks during a press conference in London, on August 10, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
“It’s very important for [the National Rally] to build links, to show that you are listened to by people abroad,” said a former French official who knows the far-right party well.
Advertisement
The populist odd couple
Farage and Bardella aren’t the most obvious pair. One is a 62-year-old, tweed-sporting rabble-rouser and the other a carefully dressed, well-prepared politician who just entered his thirties.

For Farage, that means trying to neutralize the new threat from a further-right party called Restore, while Bardella tries to make the National Rally more business-friendly, despite no longer being the party’s nominee for president.

Bardella’s team was just as flattering in return, with an adviser to the National Rally president confirming they want closer cooperation with Reform.

“Farage is a political force of nature. He succeeded in the two ambitions of his life: Brexit and ending the two-party system in the United Kingdom,” the aide quoted above said. “We want Reform in power.”

Fund management giant Blackstone, the world’s largest alternative asset manager, led a $27 million investment round into Israeli cybersecurity start-up Huskeys, the company announced on Wednesday.
The company was founded in 2025 by IDF’s Unit 8200 alumni Itai Gafni (CEO) and Roy Weisfeld (CTO), and focuses on reducing the risk posed by agentic traffic (traffic produced by AI models instead of humans).
The company explained that, according to its estimates, 70% of internet traffic will be generated by AI agents as of 2027, and organizations will need to differentiate between legitimate customers using agents and malicious attacks.
“Artificial intelligence has changed the way the internet operates, bringing enormous opportunities alongside new security risks and the potential for lost revenue,” said Gafni.
“We believe that, in the near future, most identities operating on the web will be autonomous agents, and organizations will need a new infrastructure capable of identifying, securing, and managing them,” he added.
Company offers solutions to AI internet threats
The company explained that its Virtual Patching system allows Huskeys to identify when an AI agent is trying to breach a system and generate a rapid response within minutes, while a development team can work on it after the situation is brought under control.
Additionally, the company is developing an intelligent platform that centralizes all its clients' security solutions and products and enables rapid monitoring and response.
“Huskeys has built a platform designed to operate across any enterprise network, from the smallest and simplest to the largest and most complex, while advancing a new category for modern internet traffic,” said Adam Fletcher, Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) at Blackstone.
The company said the Blackstone investment marked its first early-stage cybersecurity investment, alongside strategic investments from Okta and Zscaler, and participation from Shlomo Kramer and Yishai Yuval’s Skinos Ventures and Merlin Ventures.
Senior executives from Cloudflare, Palo Alto Networks, Intel, Check Point, AWS, Microsoft, and Google, actor Assi Cohen, and mentalist Lior Suchard also invested in the company.
“We believe the company is well-positioned to redefine how organizations manage network security, and we are pleased to support Huskeys as it continues to develop its product in this important category,” Fletcher added.

Scientists assess nature conditions after cleanup mission on Alexandra Land
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:27:13 UTC
23:27:13 KST

MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. Experts at the Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of Geography found that the nature of the Alexandra Land Island in the Arctic retains its natural conditions: the experts found no toxic water pollution or traces of petroleum products, the Institute's press service told TASS.
"Having studied results of the comprehensive assessment we can speak with confidence about the remaining background ecological condition of the Alexandra Land Island. The rare excess concentrations of a number of metals are not related to anthropogenic pollution, as they reflect the natural geochemical processes in the region. It is fundamentally important to take this into account when planning any activities in the Arctic," the press service quoted leader of the Institute's Hydrology Laboratory Ekaterina Kashutina as saying.
The purpose of conducted study was to understand current conditions of the island's nature, to see whether there remain consequences of human economic activity, and to check how effective the earlier cleanup was. Additionally, it was important for scientists to determine which changes are associated with pollution and which are natural for that part of the Arctic.
During different seasons in 2024, experts examined the island's snow, ice, meltwater and lakes using 80 indicators. They checked the content of nitrogen and phosphorus compounds, various metals and petroleum products, and also assessed whether water could have a toxic effect on living organisms. None of the two used bio tests have shown a toxic effect.
The study showed that traces of economic activity remained only in ice-free areas. The ice domes, which occupy about two-thirds of the island's area, do not have signs of the kind. The obtained results confirmed the earlier cleaning was effective: the accumulated damage to the natural environment has been largely eliminated.
Why increased metal content is not recognized as pollution
In some locations, the scientists have found multiple increases in concentrations of copper, aluminum and iron. Those indicators were recorded in areas where meltwater comes into contact with the ground, as well as in lakes where surface runoff enters the water.
Researchers say those high rates are not related to human activity, as they are the natural composition of the region's soils and waters. The data is important in assessing the Arctic territories' conditions: they allow taking into account the area's natural features without mistaking them for the effects of pollution.
Generally speaking, the content of nitrogen, phosphorus, and metal compounds in snow, ice, and water did not exceed the maximum permissible concentrations, nor have the scientists found contamination with petroleum products.
The research results are published in the Izvestia RAS. Geographical Series journal.

Russia straps two small attack drones to wings of its long-range Gerans and releases them deep inside Ukraine. It rarely works, Flash says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:26:47 UTC
23:26:47 KST

Russia has been bolting small FPV attack drones to the wings of its long-range Gerans and releasing them deep inside Ukraine, far behind the front. The tactic may now have reached Kyiv Oblast, where an FPV drone was recently recorded, though it is not confirmed that a Geran delivered it, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, the president's adviser on defense technologies, told UNIAN. A Geran drop is one of the versions being weighed.
A Geran (the Russian-built version of Iran's Shahed-136) can fly hundreds of kilometers, so bolting short-range FPVs to its wings carries them far past the front line before release. Russia has done the same with its Molniya and Gerbera drones, and in May Euromaidan Press reported FPVs delivered this way, turning up dozens of kilometers from the border, on the ground, and even on the roofs of apartment buildings.
A year-old experiment, still rare
"The Russians have been running these experiments for a while. They attach two FPVs above the wings and drop them," Beskrestnov said.
He last recorded the tactic a week ago in Konotop, in Sumy Oblast, where Russian forces held two such drones on a carrier's wings and released them.
Until now, he added, it had shown up only on conventional Gerans. Holding an FPV on a jet-powered Geran is far harder because the speed is too high for a clean release, "but technologically it's entirely possible," Beskrestnov believes.
Ukrainian air defenders have brought at least one carrier down: in March, the Darknode anti-Shahed unit destroyed a Geran carrying two wing-mounted FPVs over Ukrainian airspace before it could release them, Militarnyi reported.
Low yield, mostly a scare tactic
Russia uses the tactic sparingly, and by its own measure, it does not work well.
"If you look at the number of successful strikes they've had with these FPVs, it's small," Beskrestnov explained, because controlling a drone dropped this way is difficult.
The FPVs carry no large warhead, and the launches often serve mainly to terrorize civilians, he said.
The dropped drones are usually flown over ordinary mobile networks rather than through a relay mounted on the carrier.
"There's an ordinary SIM card, and they control the FPV through it," Beskrestnov said, adding that Ukraine has been recording the practice on and off for about a year.
