Expiring emergency migration laws could be key to unlocking Hungary's EU fines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:26:39 UTC
23:26:39 KST

Brussels and Budapest are exploring whether letting two temporary Hungarian migration laws lapse – without softening border policy – could provide a path to ending the EU's €1m-a-day fine imposed on Hungary, but experts remain doubtful it will be enough to satisfy the ECJ.
Phasing out two temporary Hungarian migration laws could provide a route to ending the European Union's €1m-a-day fine against Budapest, according to people familiar with talks between the Hungarian government and the European Commission.
The move would not require Prime Minister Péter Magyar to soften Hungary's migration policy, Euronews understands – an idea he has repeatedly stressed as a non-starter even as he pushes Brussels to lift the penalty.
Hungary has lost €910m since the European Court of Justice (ECJ) ruled in 2024 that Viktor Orbán's government had persistently failed to apply EU standards in its treatment of asylum seekers.
In the aftermath of the 2015–16 migration crisis, Hungary effectively barred asylum seekers from lodging claims on its territory by erecting a fence along its border with Serbia, building prison-like transit zones, and pushing migrants back into Serbia. Budapest also declared that asylum seekers must apply for international protection while still in Serbia.
Magyar, who succeeded Orbán after April's elections, has called on European counterparts to resolve the fine, but vowed to keep his predecessor's contested migration policy in place.
The two measures under scrutiny are the "state of crisis due to mass migration", renewed roughly every six months since 2015 and used to deviate from several EU legal provisions – due to expire on 7 September unless extended – and a separate 2025 law requiring asylum seekers to register their intent at a Hungarian embassy abroad before applying in-country, which is set to lapse at the end of the year.
"It's a very difficult thing," Magyar said at a press conference on Thursday. "It's something that tests lawyers. It might just be necessary for something to come into effect for one day, then we tick this off, the one million euro fine is abolished, and then the next day an equally strict, slightly differently functioning regulation comes into effect."
The prospect that both measures could be allowed to expire is seen by some in Brussels as a potential step forward.
"It's for Hungary and the court to see what can be done," said European Commission spokesperson Markus Lammert. "What we can do from the Commission's side is engage closely with the Hungarian authorities on the matter."
"We expect an early resolution of the suspension of the €1m-per-day fine imposed under the previous Hungarian government," Magyar said on Wednesday, following a meeting in Budapest with European Council President António Costa.
"I emphasised that, in light of what happened in Ceuta this summer, Hungary will continue to maintain the necessary legal environment and physical border closure to stem illegal migration."
Magyar also met European People's Party leader Manfred Weber to discuss the matter, and called for the fines to be reimbursed through the EU's next seven-year budget.
"We expect our efforts to be recognised at the European level," he said.
Doubts remain
Even so, experts remain doubtful this would be enough to halt the fines.
"Amending the migration-related laws adopted in 2015–16 would have been an opportunity to avoid the fines," EU law expert Tamás Lattmann told Euronews.
"The only way to place any kind of cap on the fines would have been for the government, at the moment the provisions of the Migration Pact entered into force, to declare that Hungarian law and EU standards were now aligned on key points – meaning the underlying legal violation had ceased, and the penalty clock would stop running. But that did not happen."
The EU's Migration Pact, designed to strengthen external borders and share responsibility for asylum seekers among member states, entered into force over the summer, but Magyar has rejected its application in Hungary.
He has also repeatedly called on the EU to reimburse the fines already paid, a request that is technically and legally unworkable. Following the ECJ ruling, the fines accrued were deducted directly from funds earmarked for Hungary.
"I find it quite shameless that Magyar wants reimbursement of fines for a violation of EU law that has not been resolved at all," said Tineke Strik, the Dutch Green MEP who serves as the European Parliament's rapporteur for Hungary. "Granting reimbursement of fines imposed by the court would also mean the EU itself undermining or discrediting its own judgments."
On Tuesday, Magyar said Hungary would seek credit for the fines imposed so far during negotiations on the new EU budget. Technically, the EU is not prepared to label any funding as reimbursement for past fines, as this would risk sending the wrong message.
Poland has previously lost hundreds of millions of euros in funding over ECJ fines linked to its judicial reforms.
However, officials involved in the budget talks say "everything is possible," and Hungary could still negotiate additional resources for border protection – resources it could present domestically as a political win.
Another option under discussion is for the EU to rename or informally reallocate existing funding lines earmarked for Hungary in a way that could support Magyar's messaging at home.

Rise of far-right leader Roberto Vannacci challenges Meloni as she celebrates Italian milestone
Unknown

2026-09-03

23:25:25 KST

Giorgia Meloni’s government has become the longest-running in Italy since the second world war – a milestone the prime minister is determined not to let pass unnoticed.
In the port area of Bari, the capital of the southern Italian region of Puglia, where Meloni hosted the G7 in 2024 and where she spends her summer holiday, preparations are well under way for a festival-style showcase of her rightwing administration.
On Friday, there will be food trucks, water stations and traditional Puglian light shows as part of celebrations to entertain an expected crowd of 10,000 people bussed in from across Italy. Militants from the youth wing of Meloni’s far-right Brothers of Italy party have fanned the city’s squares and beaches for days, handing out flyers promoting the celebrations while wearing T-shirts featuring the official slogan: Il Governo più stabile, l’Italia più forte (the most stable government, the strongest Italy).
Meloni, who just a few weeks ago was booed at the opening ceremony of the Mediterranean Games in Taranto, farther south in Puglia, will address the audience in the evening, surrounded by her coalition allies – Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League, and the conservative Forza Italia’s Antonio Tajani.
“This moment will be written in the history books,” said Michele Picaro, a Brothers of Italy MEP and former Bari councillor. “We are the longest government in the history of the Italian Republic and this must be celebrated.”
Beneath the triumph, however, the outlook for Meloni is less settled. True, she has enjoyed a political stability that eluded her predecessors. Brothers of Italy is still the country’s biggest party. But in recent months, the political landscape has shifted with the emergence of a challenger – not from the left or the centre, but from someone who is even further to the right than Meloni.
Since its launch in February, Roberto Vannacci, a former army general, has seen his far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, rise to about 8% in the polls, surpassing his former compatriots in the League months ago and this week eclipsing Forza Italia, too.
Vannacci first entered the public eye in 2023 after self-publishing a book filled with racism, homophobia, Islamophobia and antisemitism. The subsequent backlash cost him his army job, but propelled him to the top of the bestsellers list. Helped along by ample coverage in the Italian press, he capitalised on the notoriety and in 2024 was elected as an MEP for the League, later leaving Salvini’s party to set up his own.
“I read his book because I always think you need to know the enemy,” said Giulia Pastorella, an MP and vice-president of the small centrist party Azione (Action). “And I thought, this is exactly the kind of thing you might hear people talking about in the bar. Here’s a military man, who is really a mirror of the worst impulses of people. The scary thing is, I think he’s genuine and not a PR construct.”
Vannacci’s policies, such as they are, are extreme. Futuro Nazionale’s recently published manifesto says that “abortion is not a right” and calls for gay people to be banned from TV between 6am and 11pm so children aren’t exposed to what it describes as “homosexualist” content. It also proposes introducing military education in high schools and a “remigration” plan to remove irregular immigrants and foreign nationals who commit crimes.
On foreign policy, Vannacci has campaigned to stop weapons and financial aid to Ukraine, saying if he could choose between Vladimir Putin or the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he would choose Putin.
In July, he organised a “Futuristic Triathlon” in the northern seaside town of Sanremo, billed as an event to “temper the mind and body” in an echo of the fascist aesthetics and themes of the Mussolini era.
Far from being a treated as a pariah, however, Vannacci’s party has proved moderately successful, luring defectors from the three main ruling coalition parties. It is also actively courting disillusioned voters from the Five Star Movement, a key ally in a broad but perennially fractious leftwing coalition led by the Democratic party.
For the government, he represents a dilemma. Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy has neofascist roots, has governed more moderately than many had expected, cultivating a pragmatic and, crucially, pro-Ukraine image abroad while still deploying hardline rhetoric on choice occasions for domestic audiences.
That positioning, however, has left a vacuum on the far right that Vannacci has exploited. The question now is: how will Meloni respond? Until now her ruling coalition had mostly coasted along, propped up by a strong parliamentary majority. Her government is largely regarded to have been fiscally prudent, but has steered clear of major structural reforms. Instead, it has heavily focused on security and continues to vigorously expand legislation on law and order.
“This government has wasted the huge occasion that stability gave them,” said Lia Quartapelle, an MP with the Democratic party. “None of the core issues have been addressed – we have stagnant productivity and growth, salaries that have lagged behind for many years and an education system that is not up to the pace.”
Pastorella said a focus on foreign policy had also contributed to Vannacci’s success. “Meloni hasn’t really done much at home but has been very present abroad,” she added. “The Italian electorate is tired of talking about foreign policy and would rather discuss national politics – this is precisely what Vannacci has understood.”
Picaro batted away questions about recent polls. “This is a government that is more used to working than looking at percentages,” he said, citing lower unemployment, reduced irregular immigration, cutting taxes for the self-employed and an initiative in the south to boost entrepreneurial investment.
Pastorella said that, far from being strong and stable, Meloni had struggled to keep her coalition united while dealing with various scandals, including ones that led to a tourism and a culture minister being forced to resign.
With the possibility of an election as early as April, time is now of the essence for the prime minister. In recent weeks she has pivoted back to hardline rhetoric, most notably in her reaction to the influx of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta.
She is also trying to push through a highly contentious electoral law that would give a majority bonus to any alliance winning more than 42% of the vote, which critics say is aimed at increasing her group’s chance of victory.
If Vannacci continues to strengthen, Meloni might be tempted to accommodate him before the vote, a move that would risk repelling moderate supporters. Or she could clinch a post-election pact to maintain power, resulting in what many both inside and outside Italy would see as a frightening shift to the extreme right.
As government supporters head to Bari, Alessandro Cattaneo, an MP with Forza Italia, thinks it won’t come to that. “We in Forza Italia believe that Vannacci is too far removed from our political culture,” he said. “It would not be possible to govern with him … the coalition needs to continue to work seriously for the remainder of this administration and explain better to people what we have done. The best antidote to the extreme right is to show our seriousness.”

Agents of chaos: Zelensky’s security services trade accusations after Kiev gunfights
The gang-warfare-style clash between Ukrainian security agencies that left three troops shot in Kiev and shocked the country is being spun into competing narratives by the rival parties involved.
Depending on which one of Vladimir Zelensky’s security agencies is speaking, the central figure in the conflict is either a hired gun working for Moscow, or a brave Ukrainian combat officer who was illegally detained for over a week by rogue Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) agents.
What triggered the scandal?
The gunfight on Wednesday morning followed the disappearance on August 23 of Stepan Kaplunov, a reported white supremacist and senior officer in the so-called Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK), a militia commanded by notorious neo-Nazi Denis “White Rex” Kapustin, under the patronage of the Ukrainian Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
This week, armed SBU and HUR combat units exchanged gunfire in eastern Kiev, in what was later revealed to have been a standoff over an alleged SBU search of the missing RDK officer’s apartment.
What excuses has the SBU offered for taking the HUR’s man?
On Thursday, as the scandal over the shooting escalated, the SBU accused Kaplunov of participating in a Russian government plot to assassinate a “leader of Russian opposition movement” on Ukraine’s Independence Day, which was marked on August 24.
The agency released a video in which Kaplunov, wearing sunglasses, “confessed” to cooperating with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), along with several screenshots it claimed had been taken from a messaging app on his phone.
Despite claiming to have foiled the alleged plot, the SBU said it chose not to seek Kaplunov’s formal arrest – a striking admission given that he was effectively being accused of treason.
What did Kaplunov claim he discussed with the “Russians”?
If authentic, the screenshots show the RDK officer – wanted for terrorism in Russia – discussing contract killings in Ukraine.
A test job worth $50,000 targeting “not a general or a politician” could have secured him a retainer that would pay him as much as $300,000 per week, his interlocutor wrote.
The alleged Russian connection was described as a “businessman from border areas” who was the son of someone important, “deals with FSB, etc.” and knew the client.
Where is Kaplunov now?
Kaplunov is presumably at a HUR safehouse, having been released after the debacle erupted across social media. In keeping with standard PR procedure, he subsequently gave an interview to a Ukrainian media outlet.
A decorated officer who has fought with Ukrainian units since 2014 and joined the RDK in 2023, where he serves as the RDK’s deputy commander for combat operations, Kaplunov now claims that the SBU had forced the confession from him, to manufacture legal grounds for searching his apartment.
He claims to have spent ten days in two secret SBU detention facilities, bound, blindfolded, and held incommunicado. He credited a HUR formation nicknamed “Timur’s special unit” – reportedly an umbrella structure for the RDK and several other militia groups working for military intelligence – with securing his release “by force.”
All three personnel injured in the shooting were Timur’s men, Kaplunov said.
“Timur” is the callsign of a man Kaplunov identified as Dmitry Ivanov. He stressed that Ivanov, rather than White Rex, is his direct commander.
“We are all a big family, and ‘Timur’ himself, our commander, will never leave anyone behind, not a soldier nor a commander, he will stand up for everyone,” Kaplunov said.
He blamed “historic competition” between the SBU and HUR for the confrontation and alleged that his “abduction” had been intended as a way to get to Ivanov.
What has the HUR said?
HUR has warned it is being targeted by a smear campaign and urged journalists who receive “dubious information” to report the leaks to law enforcement.
In an interview while wearing a face mask, “Timur,” accused the SBU of unlawfully detaining Kaplunov. He claimed that HUR personnel and the SBU’s Alfa commando unit had peacefully resolved the confrontation before another group of SBU agents arrived at the scene and opened fire.
Were there any repercussions for the agencies?
An embarrassed Zelensky, facing military, economic, demographic, and reputational collapse, fired Oleg Khramov from his position as head of the SBU section responsible for protecting state secrets, although it was not immediately clear whether he had any involvement in the scandal.
Both agencies have suffered a serious reputational blow for the second time this year.
Earlier, Ukrainian investigators accused an active HUR operative and a police officer reportedly serving clandestinely for the SBU of masterminding the Monaco bombing that seriously injured exiled Ukrainian businessman Vadim Ermolaev and members of his family in June.
The principal perpetrator was allegedly murdered by the masterminds after she returned to Ukraine.
Are SBU and HUR rivals?
Both agencies were overhauled with CIA assistance following the Western-backed armed coup in Kiev in 2014, according to media reports.
The SBU is currently run by Aleksandr Poklad, the agency’s acting head and former deputy head, whose promotion has yet to be confirmed by parliament.
Kirill Budanov, now the head of Zelensky’s office, previously commanded HUR before a corruption scandal forced the Ukrainian leader’s previous chief of staff, Andrey Yermak, to resign last year.
Budanov and Poklad reportedly have had strong personal animosity since 2022, when the SBU summarily executed banker Denis Kireev, an undercover HUR agent. Poklad allegedly orchestrated the killing.
Is Zelensky in control of SBU and HUR?
Zelensky’s ability to maintain control over Ukraine’s competing centers of power remains in question. His presidential term expired in 2024, and he has remained in office under martial law without holding another election.
The Ukrainian government has been battered by corruption allegations, with Western-backed anti-graft investigators regularly bringing cases against people close to Zelensky.
In the most recent example, last month a deputy head of Zelensky’s office was accused of laundering several bags of cash to pay bail for a former energy minister who himself faces graft allegations in a separate case.
The Ukrainian military is also under increasing strain as Zelensky has failed to secure additional supplies of Patriot interceptor missiles, the weapons Kiev badly needs to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
Despite the shortage, he ordered mass strikes in July on Russian cargo ships and retail warehouses, prompting overwhelming retaliatory strikes.
This week, Zelensky also threatened foreign airlines operating in Russia, claiming that Russian airspace belongs to Ukrainian kamikaze drones now.
With the situation rapidly unraveling, it remains unclear what people trained to spy, sabotage, abduct, and kill on behalf of the state might choose to do next.

Siberian crane population's database to be generated at national park in Yakutia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:24:52 UTC
23:24:52 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. A data base on conditions of the Siberian crane, listed in the Red Data Book, with a map of the species distribution across the region will be generated after research at the Kytalyk National Park in Yakutia's Arctic Zone, the national park's representative, research engineer at the Institute of Biological Problems of the Cryolithozone (the Russian Academy of Sciences' Siberian Branch) Sergey Sleptsov told TASS during the Eastern Economic Forum.
The research will continue for two years, from 2026 to 2027. It is funded by a grant from the Presidential Foundation for Nature. "As part of the project, we plan to generate a new database on the Siberian crane population, their nests with coordinates. The database would include a description, location of sites and photographs taken there. Later on, this would allow scientists to carry out further monitoring," the scientist said.
Similar studies were conducted several decades ago - from the 1990s to 2008, he continued. When creating the map, scientists used only data from the cranes' ringing. This summer, while working on the new map, it was for the first time that specialists used drones as they surveyed an area of more than 800,000 square kilometers.
"As of July, the Poyang Lake National Nature Reserve in China and Russia's Zeya Nature Reserve signed cooperation agreements under the project," the expert said. "In May, we began ground expeditions that finished in July, and two observation towers have been built. We have also organized educational events for residents and school students, and we have used drones to take video," the scientist added. In-house processing of the data obtained off drones will continue for next five months.
The project also involves the launch of a mechanism between protected areas of the Russian Federation and China to assess measures to protect Siberian cranes along the entire flight route and to create conditions for bird monitoring at nesting sites.
Siberian crane is the world's third most rare crane species. The birds nest only in Russia. They have two disparate populations - the West Siberian (Ob) and the East Siberian (Yakut). The East Siberian population has grown to about 5,500 birds over recent decades, though it still remains critically low for the species' long-term survival. The bird takes an important position in the culture of the North's low-numbered indigenous peoples inhabiting its breeding area. People in Yakutia say the Siberian crane (or white crane) is a sacred bird, and it is also a bird of happiness.
About the project and the national park
The Kytalyk National Park in Yakutia was established in December 2019 under the Ecology National Project. The national park's total area is more than 1.8 million hectares. The main protected species is the Siberian crane. The Siberian crane population's 70% is located in the specially protected natural area of the Kytalyk National Park in Yakutia's Allaikhovsky District.
The latest data from the autumn count on the Siberian crane flight in Yakutia and from the winter counts in China indicate an increase in the bird population. As the number increases, it is necessary to identify changes in the distribution of individuals in the nesting area.
The project's leader is Arkady Semenov, Director of the Lena Pillars National Park, which manages the Kytalyk National Park.
About the forum
The Eastern Economic Forum is running in Vladivostok from September 1 to 4 under the theme "The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People." The event's organizer is the Roscongress Foundation, with TASS as its general information partner.

The Czech Republic is preparing stricter travel rules for Russian diplomats - media
Kyiv • UNN
The Czech Republic, together with its intelligence services, will change the procedure for reporting trips by Russian diplomats. The new rules are intended to strengthen control.
The Czech Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in cooperation with the intelligence services, is preparing a project to change the notification procedure—the rules governing the movement of Russian diplomats. These rules are to better correspond to the needs of the intelligence services. Petr Macinka, the Czech foreign minister, said this after an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland, answering a question about whether the Czech Republic would tighten the rules following the drone incident at Leipzig Airport, UNN reports, citing Radio Prague.
"For many months, we have been assessing the situation. We saw the number of similar cases, understand which people are involved and for what purpose they travel. It turned out that there are not that many such cases. However, we know that the system has certain shortcomings that should be corrected," Macinka said, adding that it is only a matter of time before the Czech Republic makes these changes.
In addition,
The publication notes that the system of mandatory notifications about the movements of Russian diplomats provides the countries of the European Union with information about their travel within the Schengen Area. It also allows states to tighten the regime by granting or rejecting requests for individual trips.
At present, the Czech Republic requires Russian diplomats only to give prior notification. At the beginning of June, Petr Macinka said that a possible tightening of the regime would be discussed at the next meeting of the Security Council.
The obligation to report the movements of Russian diplomats around Europe, Petr Macinka recalls, has been in effect in all EU countries since January. Only Estonia has introduced a stricter regime, he said, adding that a hybrid system operates in other countries.
Reports that Germany may restrict entry for Russian diplomats emerged after Berlin officially held Russia responsible on Tuesday for the August incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport, where an explosive-laden UAV was discovered. According to media reports, the suspects in the attack are a Russian national with a Latvian passport and a Belarusian national with Russian citizenship. Moscow denies its involvement in the incident.
"Germany is understandably planning certain steps to make its position clear, but at the same time, they say that they are not at all interested in escalating the situation with Russia," the head of the Czech Foreign Ministry commented.
We remind you
As of January 25, 2026, the EU introduced an obligation for employees of Russian diplomatic missions in Schengen Area countries to report their entry into the territory of other EU states, except for the country of their accreditation. EU countries may also choose a stricter procedure—authorization, which requires the ministry's approval before the diplomat arrives in the country.
In January, Petr Macinka faced criticism for introducing softer rules—notification rather than obtaining permission for travel.

Rs 5,070-crore bet: Can ‘floating solar’ power India’s next renewable leap?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:23:19 UTC
23:23:19 KST

India’s floating solar push could unlock vast water bodies while boosting clean power, storage and energy security. (File photos)
India’s solar energy expansion is entering a new phase, with floating photovoltaic projects emerging as a potential answer to two of the country’s biggest renewable energy challenges: limited land availability and the need for more reliable power generation.The Union government’s approval of the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY) on July 31, 2026, marks a major push in that direction. According to the Press Information Bureau (PIB), the scheme will support 5,000 MW of floating solar photovoltaic capacity on reservoirs and other suitable inland water bodies, backed by energy storage systems with a minimum two-hour storage capacity.With an overall financial outlay of ₹5,070 crore, the scheme will be implemented from financial year 2026-27 to 2030-31. The government says the programme could help reduce pressure on land resources, improve grid reliability and open another avenue for India to expand its renewable energy capacity.
From solar experiment to energy powerhouse
India’s solar sector has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past decade. According to government data, installed solar capacity has risen from approximately 3 GW in 2014 to 162.15 GW as of June 30, 2026, representing more than a fiftyfold increase.
The expansion has been supported by large-scale solar parks, rooftop installations, solar-powered agricultural pumps, competitive bidding and policies designed to strengthen domestic manufacturing.
Floating solar opens a new frontier for India’s clean energy push.
The government said India added 44.61 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025-26, almost twice the 23.83 GW added in the previous financial year. During the same period, total non-fossil fuel capacity reached 283.46 GW, including 274.68 GW from renewable energy sources.The latest policy push towards floating solar builds on this broader expansion, while attempting to use a resource that conventional solar projects do not require: water surfaces.
A 5,000 MW floating solar bet
The PM-SSY is designed to support 5,000 MW of Floating Solar Photovoltaic projects with co-located Energy Storage Systems, according to the PIB.The storage component will have a minimum capacity of 10,000 MWh, equivalent to two hours of storage for the planned 5,000 MW floating solar capacity. This is intended to help states manage periods of peak electricity demand and address one of the central challenges associated with solar power, its variability.
Floating solar could turn India’s water bodies into power hubs.
Floating solar panels are mounted on buoyant structures and deployed on reservoirs, lakes, ponds and other suitable water bodies. Instead of competing with agriculture, settlements, forests or other land uses, the technology allows electricity generation from water surfaces.The government estimates that India currently has around 700 MW of floating solar capacity. The PM-SSY would therefore represent a substantial increase in the country's floating solar footprint.The scheme is based on an assessment by the National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE), which estimates that India has around 102.18 GWp of floating solar potential across reservoirs and suitable inland water bodies.
Why put solar panels on water?
The attraction of floating solar goes beyond saving land. Floating photovoltaic systems can benefit from the cooling effect of water, which can improve the operating efficiency of solar panels compared with installations exposed to higher temperatures on land. Research cited in the supplied material indicates that floating systems can generate between 0.6% and 4.4% more energy than comparable land-mounted installations, although actual performance varies according to site and technology.The panels can also shade portions of water bodies, reducing exposure to sunlight and potentially lowering evaporation. This could be particularly relevant in water-stressed regions where reservoirs are used for irrigation, drinking water or hydropower.
From reservoirs to renewable power, India’s solar shift is going afloat.
The scale of the potential benefit depends on factors such as climate, the percentage of the water surface covered and the characteristics of individual reservoirs.Floating solar can also be paired with existing hydropower infrastructure. Solar generation can use existing transmission connections, while hydropower or pumped-storage facilities can provide a means of balancing variable solar output.This combination could become increasingly important as India adds more renewable capacity to its electricity grid.
India already has floating solar experience
India is not starting from scratch. Some of the country's largest floating solar installations are already operating or under development. The Omkareshwar floating solar project in Madhya Pradesh, located on the Narmada River reservoir, is designed for a capacity of 600 MW and is among the country's most prominent floating solar developments.Other major installations include NTPC's 100 MW floating solar project at Ramagundam in Telangana, built on an ash pond near its thermal power station, and a 92 MW project at Kayamkulam in Kerala.These projects demonstrate how floating solar can be deployed on different types of water bodies, including reservoirs and water surfaces associated with existing industrial infrastructure.The experience is particularly relevant as the government seeks to expand floating solar beyond individual projects and create a larger national programme.
A global technology moving rapidly
Floating photovoltaics are no longer a niche technology. The first floating solar installation was developed in Japan in 2007, while larger projects began appearing during the following decade. Global installed capacity expanded rapidly, rising from around 1 GW in 2018 to 13 GW in 2022, according to figures cited in the supplied material.Asia has been at the forefront of this expansion, with China developing some of the world's largest floating solar installations.In 2022, China added a 320 MW floating photovoltaic facility in Dezhou, Shandong, developed by Huaneng Power International. Earlier large projects included installations at reservoirs and former mining sites.
The technology has also expanded beyond inland water bodies. Offshore floating solar remains comparatively young, but pilot projects have been developed in marine environments, including installations in the Maldives and the North Sea.The economics of floating solar have also improved. While floating projects once carried a substantial cost premium over conventional solar, costs had moved closer to land-based systems by 2020. However, the supplied research indicates that installation costs remained around 10-25% higher in 2023, largely because of additional anchoring and mooring requirements.
The land question gives floating solar an edge
Land availability is becoming an increasingly important consideration as India expands renewable generation.Large solar parks require substantial tracts of land, and acquiring suitable land can involve competing demands from agriculture, settlements, conservation and other economic activities.Floating solar offers an alternative by allowing electricity generation on existing reservoirs, industrial ponds, irrigation basins and other artificial water bodies.
Harnessing sunlight without consuming precious land.
India’s conventional solar expansion has already demonstrated the scale required to meet national targets. Large projects account for 118.79 GW of installed solar capacity, while grid-connected rooftop systems contribute another 27.88 GW, according to the government.Floating solar can add another layer to this mix without necessarily requiring comparable amounts of terrestrial land.The potential is especially significant around existing hydropower reservoirs, where solar generation can potentially share transmission infrastructure and complement hydropower generation.
Storage could solve solar’s biggest problem
The PM-SSY's storage component is particularly significant because India's solar expansion is moving into a phase where generation capacity alone will not be enough.Solar power is produced primarily during daylight hours, while electricity demand can remain high after sunset. Energy storage can help shift some of that generation to periods when it is needed most.Under PM-SSY, every supported floating solar project is expected to be associated with energy storage of at least two hours. The government expects this to help states manage peak demand while improving the reliability of renewable power.The combination of floating solar, existing reservoirs and energy storage could therefore create a model that goes beyond simply adding more generation capacity.In locations with hydropower or pumped-storage infrastructure, the relationship could become even more valuable. Water reservoirs can potentially function as part of an integrated renewable energy system, allowing solar generation to be balanced through stored water or battery systems.
The environmental equation remains complex
Floating solar's environmental advantages need to be considered alongside its potential risks.Partial coverage of water surfaces can reduce evaporation and sunlight penetration, potentially helping to conserve water and limit some forms of algal growth. However, extensive shading can also alter aquatic ecosystems.The environmental impact depends heavily on the type of water body, the percentage of its surface covered, the depth and movement of the water, and the design of the floating system.Marine floating solar presents additional challenges. Anchoring, mooring and installation activity can disturb sediments and potentially affect benthic ecosystems. Large installations can also alter the amount of sunlight reaching seagrass or coral habitats.This means floating solar cannot simply be treated as a zero-impact alternative to land-based solar.For India, where reservoirs can serve multiple purposes including irrigation, drinking water, fisheries and hydropower, careful site selection and long-term ecological monitoring will be important as deployment expands.
Floating solar joins a much bigger solar ecosystem
The government's floating solar push comes against the backdrop of a broader policy architecture that has driven India's solar growth.The National Solar Mission, launched in 2010, helped establish long-term targets, while the Solar Parks Scheme and Green Energy Corridor programme addressed infrastructure and transmission challenges.The Solar Parks Scheme has supported 54 parks with a combined sanctioned capacity of 39,188 MW, according to government data as of February 2026.The Green Energy Corridor, meanwhile, is intended to move renewable electricity from generation-rich regions to major demand centres. The programme had enabled evacuation of 24,567.8 MW of renewable energy through strengthened transmission networks as of February 2026.Competitive bidding has also transformed the economics of solar power. The government says solar tariffs fell from around ₹18 per unit in 2010 to ₹2.44 per unit at the Bhadla Solar Park auction in 2017.The expansion is now increasingly being supported by domestic manufacturing. Solar module manufacturing capacity grew from 2.3 GW in 2014 to around 172 GW as of March 31, 2026, according to the PIB.
Rooftops and farms are driving the next wave
India's solar transition is also becoming increasingly distributed. The PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, launched in February 2024 with an outlay of ₹75,021 crore, is aimed at expanding rooftop solar among households. More than 43 lakh households had been solarised by June 2026, according to the government.In agriculture, PM-KUSUM supports solar pumps, decentralised solar generation and feeder solarisation. Nearly 11.49 lakh off-grid solar pumps had been installed, while more than 15.89 lakh agricultural pumps were covered through feeder-level solarisation, according to government figures cited in the supplied material.Together, rooftop solar and PM-KUSUM contributed substantially to distributed solar capacity additions during FY 2025-26.Floating solar now offers another form of distributed geography, not necessarily through small installations, but by making productive use of water bodies that already exist.
The next test is scale
India's solar story has moved from building capacity to integrating that capacity into a more complex electricity system.The country's Panchamrit commitments include achieving 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, alongside the longer-term goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2070.Floating solar is unlikely to replace conventional ground-mounted or rooftop solar. Instead, its significance lies in expanding the range of locations where solar generation can be developed.The government's estimate of 102.18 GWp of floating solar potential suggests that water bodies could become an important part of that expansion. PM-SSY's 5,000 MW target is only a fraction of the assessed potential, but it could provide a large-scale test of the technology.The scheme is also expected to create 16,000-17,000 full-time equivalent jobs and support domestic manufacturing of floating structures, photovoltaic cells and modules and energy storage systems, according to the PIB.
If the technology can deliver reliable generation while limiting ecological disruption and managing its higher installation costs, floating solar could become an important component of India's renewable energy mix.For a country attempting to add hundreds of gigawatts of clean capacity while balancing land, water, transmission and reliability constraints, the next solar frontier may not necessarily be another field of panels on land.It could be the reservoirs already sitting at the heart of India's power and water infrastructure.

His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life.

The rebels welcomed an Iranian plane to Yemen's capital Sanaa, setting off a spate of attacks. They later announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships and territory.
Another military source said most of those killed on Thursday were on the frontlines between the government-held coastal city of Mokha and the inland city of Taiz, while the others died in clashes near the Red Sea coast.

"We also thwarted an attack with two booby-trapped boats that exploded near the port," he said.
Last month, Yemen's information minister Moammar al-Eryani warned that the Houthis were plotting to seize land along the Bab al-Mandab strait, which would allow them to further threaten the vital shipping artery.
The Houthis do not control the coastal areas bordering the strait, but they hold the key port city of Hodeida north of Mokha and have repeatedly attacked Saudi ships in the Red Sea.

The world is forgetting how to fear nuclear war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:21:33 UTC
23:21:33 KST

The world is forgetting how to fear nuclear war
For decades, mutual deterrence among major powers provided the world with a degree of predictability, with the nuclear factor lying at the heart of this system since the middle of the last century. The great powers restrained one another and, in doing so, restrained themselves.
They understood that overly ambitious geopolitical adventures could carry unacceptable risks, thus “strategic stability” was the reassuring term given to what was, in reality, the capacity for mutual destruction. International institutions grew around this balance like mushrooms around a tree trunk, but beneath all the agreements and diplomatic language lay something much simpler: the fear of the consequences of a direct conflict between major powers. Now, however, that system is falling apart.
Many posit that the problem is precisely the loss of fear as political elites have ceased to believe that nuclear war is genuinely possible and hence the declining restraint we see in the conflict in Ukraine, in the Middle East and, potentially, in Asia.
The apparent solution is therefore to remind everyone just how terrifying nuclear war would be. Restore the fear, the argument goes, and states will once again exercise restraint and become ready to negotiate new rules. There’s logic to this, but there’s also an enormous danger.
What happens if nuclear weapons are actually used? Either they produce precisely the catastrophe humanity has feared for eight decades, with irreparable consequences, or something quite different happens, such as there’s terrible destruction, but the world does’t end and the weapon doesn’t even guarantee victory.
In that case, nuclear weapons could cease to be primarily a political and psychological barrier and become simply another means of warfare, albeit an extraordinarily powerful one. Would this restore fear? Or would states instead accelerate the development of nuclear weapons designed for more effective battlefield use? Well, in the present atmosphere of growing recklessness, either is conceivable.
Nuclear weapons are the most powerful weapons humanity has invented and they were created to fight wars, but we discovered that they could perform another function by preventing the largest and most destructive wars from occurring at all. Today, however, perceptions seem to be returning to their starting point that a weapon is a weapon, even when it is nuclear.
Yet expecting weapons to solve the problems between states places impossible demands on them, particularly when warfare itself is becoming increasingly asymmetrical and all-pervasive.
States are finding it harder to hold on to what they can’t afford to lose. The erosion of borders, once celebrated as one of the great achievements of liberal globalization, is acquiring a much more alarming character.
The digital world is borderless by definition as drones cross dividing lines with increasing ease and mew technologies steadily undermine the ability of states to control and defend their territory and, in extreme circumstances, even to define where meaningful borders lie.
States won’t simply accept this loss of control, so every action produces a reaction, which means the struggle will become fiercer. More importantly, the battlefield will increasingly encompass almost every sphere of human activity.
Under such conditions, what does “strategic stability” even mean, and how can it be maintained?
War itself increasingly resembles not a means of resolving conflicts but a permanent form of interaction, even coexistence and there may be no decisive victory or defeat, but only repeated attempts to exhaust an opponent economically, militarily, politically, and psychologically.
However, prolonged attrition produces two contradictory effects. States become more experienced and capable of enduring confrontation, but at the same time, fatigue accumulates, along with the temptation to end an apparently endless struggle by reaching for the most decisive and destructive argument available.
The world is losing the systemic safeguards that once limited such impulses and it increasingly resembles a hunting ground during open season.
So what, then, can we hold on to? For now, perhaps only common sense and an accurate assessment of the relationship between our ambitions and our actual capabilities. It’s a fragile lifeline, but it may be enough to prevent us from feeding the flames and instead keep us clear of them.
At least until the value of restraint, including self-restraint, is once again understood by everyone.
This article was first published by Russia in Global Affairs, translated and edited by the RT team

As Iran’s military targeted US bases in the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes by the US president, Israel’s defence chief warned that economic pressures from the sanctions could lead Tehran to escalate to more “extreme measures”.
“This morning, the army hit the satellite communication systems, equipment depots and fighter aircraft hangars of the terrorist US army at the Ahmad al-Jaber air base in Kuwait with missiles and drones,” the Iranian military said on Thursday in a statement carried by state television.
The “location of forces and radar systems of the child-killing US army at the Al Minhad air base in the UAE were also attacked by missiles and drones of the army”, it added.
In a post on X, Kuwait’s ministry of defence said its air defences had intercepted missile and drone attacks during a “blatant Iranian aggression”.
The Kuwaiti statement came after the US allies Bahrain and Jordan said their air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks on Wednesday.
Fighting between the US and Iran has increased this week after the US hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, claiming that Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway.
The latest flare-up in the conflict comes amid little evidence that the Trump administration is succeeding in advancing its nebulous war aims either on the battlefield or via mediation, despite the US president’s repeated claims to have opened the strait of Hormuz to oil traffic.
Instead, traffic through the key maritime passageway remains far below prewar levels, with oil prices remaining stubbornly elevated ahead of US midterm elections. Oil prices jumped again on Thursday after the Iranian strikes.
Among the weapons Iran has used this week is its Kheibar Shekan medium-range ballistic missile system. The cheap and accurate missile can be launched within minutes and has become a staple of Iranian strikes.
The rocket’s solid fuel motor means it does not require lengthy fuelling. It can be deployed very quickly to avoid detection and can be armed with a powered and steerable final stage to help beat anti-missile systems.
Despite claims by the Trump administration that Tehran is running out of rockets, Iran continues to fire missiles that are considerably cheaper to produce than the US interceptors used to shoot them down.
Iran has claimed as recently as the end of August that it maintained both missiles stockpiles and the ability to manufacture them.
“Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said.
“However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran’s missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued.” Mohebbi’s characterisation of Iranian missile stockpiles could not be verified.
The continued strikes came as Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said that while the new US economic sanctions appeared to be effective, the increased pressure could lead Tehran into extreme measures.
“We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps,” Katz said at a ceremony for defence ministry employees.
The hawkish minister reiterated the threats against the Islamic Republic that he has made in recent months.
“An Iranian attack on Israel will free Israel from any existing constraint,” he said. “We will strike all of Iran’s national military and civilian infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and push Iran deep back into the stone age.”

In a statement, the company condemned the attack and said specialized teams have secured the site and taken necessary measures. It confirmed that fuel operations, distribution, and supply were continuing normally without interruption.

Libya relies heavily on its oil sector for government revenues and domestic energy supplies, while its major oil facilities and fuel distribution networks have often been disrupted by security incidents and armed clashes. ■

Malaysia moving towards diversified, efficient energy transition, says official

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia is moving towards a diversified and efficient energy transition that balances its energy security, affordability and sustainability while strengthening long-term competitiveness, Malaysian Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said on Thursday.
Even as it manages this transition, Malaysia's oil and gas sector will continue to play an important role in the economy, with natural gas in particular projected to remain a major component of the primary energy mix through 2050 as renewables are scaled up, he said at the Oil and Gas Asia 2026.
Akmal also cautioned that excessive dependence on any single energy source would leave the country vulnerable to external shocks. "The objective is not simply to replace one energy source with another," he said, stressing that diversification should give Malaysia more options, reduce exposure to disruptions and create new sources of economic value.
He explained that stronger regional energy links will also be critical, pointing to the ASEAN Power Grid as a means of facilitating cross-border electricity trade, supporting renewable integration and improving regional resilience.
He added that Malaysia will require a stronger electricity grid, greater energy storage and deeper integration between energy, industrial and digital infrastructure, with private capital expected to play a larger role in financing the transition. ■

Africa CDC says too early to declare DR Congo Ebola outbreak under control
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
22:10:37 CST
23:10:37 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said Thursday that it remains too early to declare the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) under control, despite signs of stabilization in recent weeks.
"We're still early to say that we're controlling the whole outbreak," Wessam Mankoula, an Africa CDC official, told an online press briefing.
According to the latest government situation report published Thursday, the DRC had recorded 6,250 confirmed cases and 3,039 deaths as of Sept. 1, with a case fatality rate of 48.6 percent. A total of 1,439 patients have recovered. The outbreak has affected 60 health zones across six provinces.
Four health zones have interrupted transmission after reporting no new cases for more than 42 days, while another five have gone between 21 and 42 days without a new case. Transmission, however, remains active in 51 health zones, Mankoula said.
"For the last two weeks, we are seeing a decline in the number of cases," Mankoula said, cautioning that "it's very early to say we have sustained decline in this outbreak."
Mankoula also warned that more than 60 percent of deaths recorded over the past seven days occurred in communities, pointing to continued delays in detection and challenges in seeking medical care.
The current outbreak, declared in May, has since become the country's largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic on record and the second-largest globally, behind the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

China's service trade posts steady expansion, as travel, transport lead export growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
22:10:26 CST
23:10:26 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's trade in services maintained steady growth in the first seven months of 2026, as the export of travel and transport services drove more than half of the overall export expansion, official data showed Thursday.
The country's services trade totaled nearly 4.45 trillion yuan (about 655.8 billion U.S. dollars) during the period, up 8.3 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
During the period, services exports rose 17.1 percent year on year to over 1.77 trillion yuan. Services imports reached 2.67 trillion yuan, up 3.2 percent from a year earlier. The country's services trade deficit narrowed by 176.33 billion yuan from a year earlier to 900.25 billion yuan.
A breakdown of the data showed travel and transport services emerged as the two export growth drivers. Travel services exports surged 27.7 percent, while transport services exports rose 27.1 percent. The two categories contributed 22.1 percent and 29.9 percent, respectively, to the overall growth of services exports.
Knowledge-intensive services also remained a pillar of China's export mix. Trade in such services, which include telecommunications, information technology, finance, intellectual property and other business services, increased 6.6 percent to 1.96 trillion yuan, accounting for 44.1 percent of the country's total services trade.
China has intensified policy efforts to boost service sector development. The outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) and this year's government work report both made specific arrangements for this sector.
In April, the State Council issued a guideline on advancing the expansion and quality upgrading of the sector. According to the guideline, China aims to make marked progress in high-quality service sector development by 2030, with the total scale of the sector exceeding 100 trillion yuan by then, while more competitive and influential "China services" brands will be cultivated. ■

====================================================================================================

Xinhua Headlines: Across rivers and ridges -- China ensures school access for children
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
22:10:24 CST
23:10:24 KST

* In 2022, a 268-meter-high elevator and an aerial cable car system came into service, giving children from the deep mountains a "sky shuttle" to the clifftop school. A second elevator, rising 288 meters, opened at the end of July this year as visitor numbers grew.
* Across China, governments are tailoring school transport to local needs, finding different ways to close the distance between home and school.
* The efforts, backed by national policy, reflect a broader commitment -- ensuring that geography does not determine a child's access to education.
KUNMING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- At age 12, Lei Xin had already mastered a skill most adults would never attempt: navigating a treacherous cliffside trail in the dark -- not for adventure, but to go to school.
For years, reaching school meant a three-hour trek for Lei and his peers from Nizhuhe Village in Xuanwei City, southwest China's Yunnan Province. The village sits at the bottom of the Nizhu River Grand Canyon near the border with Guizhou Province, while their school is perched more than 500 meters above them on the cliffs.
Children used to leave home well before sunrise, often returning exhausted. For parents, the daily trek was a source of constant worry.
Now, the most daunting stretch of the route Lei once took to school can be covered in just 57 seconds, with a new 288-meter-high cliffside elevator whisking students up the canyon wall at five meters per second.
Lei's story is not unique. Across China's vast, often rugged frontier regions, millions of children face long, perilous journeys to school. From sheer cliffs to winding rivers, the obstacles vary, but so do the solutions. The efforts, backed by national policy, reflect a broader commitment -- ensuring that geography does not determine a child's access to education.
CROSSING EVERY DIVIDE
Guanzhai Primary School, perched on the cliffs above, serves children from surrounding mountain communities, including four in Nizhuhe Village.
Cut off from the school above by sheer cliffs, the children had to follow a rudimentary trail carved into a rock face hundreds of meters high. Narrow and steep, strewn with loose gravel, the trail had sections barely half a meter wide. The steepest stretches required them to climb by hand.
"Back then, I wasn't afraid my child would be tired. I was afraid something might happen to him on the way," said Zhao Suzhen, the mother of Lei, who had accompanied him along the treacherous trail countless times over the years.
The change came with the development of the Nizhu River Grand Canyon scenic area. In 2022, a 268-meter-high elevator and an aerial cable car system came into service, giving children from the deep mountains a "sky shuttle" to the clifftop school. A second elevator, rising 288 meters, opened at the end of July this year as visitor numbers grew.
Together, the two elevators can carry up to 1,200 passengers per hour, significantly boosting the scenic area's capacity while eliminating the congestion that once forced students to compete with tourists for rides during peak seasons.
Now, the entire journey from the village to school takes about 30 minutes. Students take a shuttle bus to the foot of the cliff, ride an elevator, then continue by cable car to reach the school.
On Aug. 30, as many primary and secondary schools across Yunnan welcomed students back for the new semester, Lei once again boarded his unusual ride. Stepping into the new elevator, he watched the numbers on the display tick upward.
"The first elevator takes 90 seconds. This one, 33 seconds faster," he said, sharing his calculation. "I feel like an immortal carrying me through the sky."
Free for local students and villagers, the "sky shuttle" also features dedicated student passages, with police officers and staff on hand during peak hours to keep the children safe. By the end of August, the service had safely carried nearly 1,000 student trips between the village and school.
More than 500 km away from Puli Township, which administers Nizhuhe Village, another group of children in Yunnan began the school day on the water.
At a ferry crossing in Banda Village of Bo'ai Town, located in a reservoir area, village official Liang Guoyou arrived early in the morning to help students board. One by one, the children stepped onto a ferry that carried them across the water. It's their version of a "school bus."
The journey was not always this secure. "Years ago, privately operated ferries lacked unified standards, and safety was a constant concern," Liang said. Since 2021, local authorities have worked with schools, parents and transport officials to build a coordinated school transport system. Seven dedicated ferries now serve 12 crossings across the township for 329 primary and secondary school students and preschoolers.
For 55-year-old ferryman Wei Jinlin, the difference could not be starker. "When I was young, getting to school meant walking nearly 20 kilometers to town," he said. "Now the children can take the ferry. It's much safer and far more convenient."
According to local authorities, the ferry routes have safely carried students more than 147,000 times over the years, covering over 70,000 kilometers in total.
Across China, governments are tailoring school transport to local needs, finding different ways to close the distance between home and school.
In March, mountainous Chengkou County of southwest China's Chongqing Municipality launched a "Hope Line" school bus service, with 33 dedicated routes now in operation. The service uses fixed routes combined with flexible pickup points to tackle the "last mile" challenge for students living in scattered rural communities.
In Panxi Town, Guizhou, authorities faced similar challenges reaching students scattered across remote areas and recently surveyed the travel needs of 121 students before launching three customized school bus routes. Four vehicles now connect eight villages, providing point-to-point service during school hours.
BEYOND SCHOOL RIDES
The impact, it turns out, goes far beyond the ride to school.
Li Zhiguang, principal of Guanzhai Primary School, said that as the "sky shuttle" has made the journey less daunting and physically demanding, students become more cheerful, confident and engaged in school life. "They are more willing to speak up in class and eager to explore the wider world," Li added.
They also have more time for the things they enjoy. "Now I can use those hours saved on the journey to read and exercise," said Wang Sichun, a third-grade student at the school, her voice bright.
The benefits ripple outward. The "sky shuttle" has also enabled local co-development of education and rural revitalization.
As the canyon's scenery and cliff elevators attracted more visitors, Zhao turned part of her home into a three-story guesthouse with 12 rooms. During peak season, bookings can be made weeks in advance. "Now I can look after my children while earning a living without leaving my hometown," she said.
More villagers are following suit, opening guesthouses, selling local specialties or working as guides. Official data show that Puli Township now boasts 46 guesthouses and 159 specialty restaurants, with tourism supporting nearly 3,500 jobs.
Cai Xiong, chairman of the company behind the elevator project, grew up in the mountains himself and watched generations of children make the arduous climb to school. "I know how difficult the journey can be," he said. "I hope the 'sky shuttle' can give them a safer way to school, so they can focus on their studies, pursue their dreams and one day give back to their hometown."
Yang Bin, a professor at Yunnan Normal University who has long studied education development in western China, praised the local approach of repurposing cultural tourism infrastructure for public educational services.
"This is not merely an improvement in transportation infrastructure. It is a safeguard of rural children's right to education, ensuring that frontier children truly have access to equitable and quality schooling," Yang said.
He added that better educational conditions also support rural revitalization by helping to retain population and stabilize communities, providing a lasting social foundation for tourism and other industries.
The efforts are now finding institutional backing. A national plan to build a strong country through education by 2035 calls for advancing high-quality, balanced compulsory education and greater integration of urban and rural education, while narrowing gaps among regions, schools and student groups.
Earlier this year, China issued a plan to accelerate agricultural and rural modernization during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), calling for stronger basic public services in rural areas. It specifically requires more balanced compulsory education and better conditions for rural schools, including necessary small-scale village schools and kindergartens.
Yang noted that these efforts can help address the longstanding challenges in rural education and narrow the urban-rural development gap. "The road to school is, in many ways, the first step toward educational equity," he said. ■

03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Sweden faces a “high threat” linked to Russian hybrid warfare targeting support for Ukraine, the head of the country’s Military Intelligence and Security Service (MUST) said on Thursday.
Thomas Nilsson said Russia is conducting advanced hybrid warfare against NATO countries, including Sweden, with the aim of creating insecurity, dividing allies and weakening their support for Ukraine.
“They want to make us insecure, they want to divide us and they want us to stop our support for Ukraine,” Nilsson told Swedish public broadcaster SVT.
His remarks came after Sweden’s National Security Council met Wednesday to discuss an explosive-laden drone discovered at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport in August, an incident German authorities attributed to Russia.
Nilsson described the incident as a hybrid attack that had raised the threat to a “more dangerous level.”
“It was a drone that was armed with explosives, so we can assume that the intention was for it to explode,” he said.
Nilsson said Sweden was prepared for a similar scenario and was carrying out protective measures to secure activities related to its support for Ukraine, including those involving private companies.
“There is a high threat to our Ukraine support, which also includes private companies and other elements,” he said.
Although Sweden is currently not considered a primary target, Nilsson warned that Russia could quickly change its priorities and begin identifying targets in the country.
He said Germany, Poland, and the Baltic states remain the main targets of Russian hybrid operations.
The warning came a day after Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service said Russia was preparing sabotage operations against the Danish defense industry, particularly companies connected to Copenhagen’s military support for Ukraine.
According to the Danish intelligence service, Russian intelligence services have approached Danish citizens with offers to photograph warehouses, monitor factory deliveries, or carry out arson attacks.

Türkiye's inflation cools slightly to 31.51 pc in August

ANKARA, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye's annual inflation eased slightly to 31.51 percent in August, down from the previous month's 31.75 percent, as consumer prices edged up 1.84 percent month-on-month, the Turkish Statistical Institute announced Thursday.
The decline marked the third consecutive month of cooling price growth.
Türkiye's annual inflation eased to 30.89 percent at the end of 2025 before rising to 32.6 percent in May, as food prices surged due to adverse weather conditions earlier this year and higher energy costs linked to geopolitical tensions.
Türkiye has been struggling with high inflation for nearly a decade.
The country's gross domestic product (GDP) expanded just 2.3 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, down from 2.5 percent in the previous quarter, and well below the government's medium-term program target of 3.8 percent for the year, according to official data released on Aug. 31.
Türkiye is finalizing its new three-year economic Medium-Term Program for 2027-2029, which will be unveiled in September alongside the 2027 central government budget rollout. ■

Key milestone reached for future Navy support ship as names of sister ships announced
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:08:50 BST
23:08:50 KST

Key milestone reached for future Navy support ship as names of sister ships announced
RFA Resurgent's keel laying ceremony took place at Navantia UK's Appledore shipyard today, as her sister ships' names, RFA Reliant and RFA Resourceful, were revealed during the ceremony.
- RFA Resurgent, the first of three new Fleet Solid Support ships, begins to take shape with keel laying as names for sister ships, RFA Reliant and RFA Resourceful, are announced.
- The Fleet Solid Support programme is expected to create around 1,200 UK shipyard jobs and hundreds of apprenticeships, boosting sovereign shipbuilding in Navantia UK’s Appledore and Belfast shipyards.
- RFA Resurgent is due to enter service in the early 2030s, supporting Royal Navy vessels at sea including carrier strike group operations.
The Royal Navy’s ability to operate further and for longer at sea took a step forward today, as a key milestone was reached in the build of the first of its future solid support ship fleet.
RFA Resurgent, the first-in-class of three new Fleet Solid Support (FSS) ships being delivered to the Royal Fleet Auxiliary (RFA), had her keel laid today. Held at Navantia UK’s Appledore shipyard, the keel laying ceremony marked the point at which RFA Resurgent’s structure formally begins to take shape. The names of her sister ships, RFA Reliant and RFA Resourceful, were also announced during the ceremony by the Head of the RFA, Commodore Sam Shattock.
The FSS programme will see around £100M invested into Navantia UK’s shipyards in Belfast and Appledore, Devon - creating 1,200 jobs and hundreds of apprenticeships and supporting reindustrialisation.
Once in service, RFA Resurgent and her two sister ships will deliver munitions, spares, food and other essential supplies to Royal Navy vessels at sea, allowing the fleet to remain deployed for longer, including in support of carrier strike group operations.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:
  The Royal Fleet Auxiliary are the backbone of our Royal Navy and these new ships will keep our navy ready to operate at range for longer.
Seeing the steel cut for RFA Resurgent last year was a proud moment, and today’s keel laying shows real momentum behind this vital programme.
This investment is helping bolster UK shipbuilding, backing thousands of skilled jobs and apprenticeships in Appledore, Belfast and beyond.
A specially commissioned coin was placed within the ship’s structure and will be presented to the Captain and crew when the ship is ready to sail - in keeping with tradition.
Keith Bethell, Director Maritime Environment at the NAD Group, said:
  Today’s keel lay is a significant stride forward in delivering the support our Royal Navy needs to operate at pace and at range, wherever it is needed.
Through the NAD Group’s work procuring this capability alongside Navantia UK and the wider supply chain, we are proud to be supporting our armed forces and backing British shipbuilding and skilled jobs.
Each ship will have a core RFA crew of 101, with accommodation provided for an additional 80 personnel operating helicopters, boats, or performing other roles when required. Delivery of the first Fleet Solid Support ship is on track, with RFA Resurgent expected to enter service with the RFA in the early 2030s.
Commodore Sam Shattock, Head of the RFA, said:
  Today’s keel laying marks another important step in the delivery of RFA Resurgent and the wider Fleet Solid Support programme. Seeing construction progress here in Appledore demonstrates the momentum behind a project that will provide the Royal Fleet Auxiliary with world-class capabilities to sustain Royal Navy operations across the globe.
The commemorative coin placed beneath the keel continues a proud maritime tradition, linking this modern programme with generations of shipbuilders and seafarers who have gone before us. I am delighted that apprentices from both Navantia UK and the Royal Fleet Auxiliary have been part of this occasion, representing the future of UK shipbuilding and the future of the RFA.
Construction of ship modules is now taking place at Navantia UK’s Appledore yard, along with its Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast and Navantia’s yards in Spain. Final assembly, integration and trials of the ships will take place at their Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast.
Donato Martínez, CEO of Navantia UK, said:
  Today’s keel laying marks the formal start of assembly of the first Fleet Solid Support ship and an important moment for Appledore, where shipbuilding has returned to a yard with more than 170 years of history.
FSS is rebuilding sovereign industrial capability in the UK, creating skilled jobs, developing apprentices and strengthening the supply chain for future naval programmes, including the autonomous and uncrewed platforms of the future Hybrid Navy.
This milestone shows what sustained investment and close partnership between government and industry can deliver, and we are focused on maintaining that momentum as the first ship takes shape.
This programme forms part of the Government’s Defence Investment Plan and its wider £298 billion investment in Defence.

The billionaire financier Leon Black did not appear on Thursday in front of the House oversight committee for a scheduled deposition about his ties to Jeffrey Epstein, and has instead launched a lawsuit against the committee arguing that it does not have the authority to compel him to turn over non-disclosure agreements.
Black was a top Epstein client over several years, and the committee is investigating the men’s relationship as well as the existence of any NDAs to which Black is a party.
Black’s name has come up repeatedly in the Epstein files. He has repeatedlydenied any wrongdoing and has said that heregrets dealing with Epstein.
Black’s lawyers said in a statement on Thursday morning announcing the lawsuit: “The Committee is on a fishing expedition that oversteps its authority and completely ignores its responsibility. This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr Black. We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power.” The lawsuit, filed in the US district court for the District of Columbia, seeks to stop the committee from enforcing its subpoenas.
In the statement, they added: “We want to reiterate that Mr Black had no awareness of the criminal activities that led to Epstein’s arrest in 2019.
“Mr Black never abused a woman,” they said. “He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein.”
In a statement on Thursday, Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the oversight committee, called for Black to be held in contempt after his refusal to appear.
“By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two congressional subpoenas,” said Garcia.
“His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable,” Garcia added. “We must hold him in contempt immediately.”
The new development on Thursday, comes as Black first appeared before the committee in June for a transcribed interview, but the testimony ended abruptly after members from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. That day, James Comer, the Republican who chairs the committee, issued two subpoenas to Black, one demanding he produce “all non-disclosure agreements to which he is a party”, and another to appear before the committee again.
In August, in a letter to Black’s attorney, Comer threatened to hold Black in contempt if he refused to comply with the committee’s subpoenas or refused to appear for his deposition, which had been scheduled for 3 September.
On Thursday morning, Comercriticized Black in a statement, though stopped short of signaling a contempt vote.
“It’s a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people,” Comer said. “Our deposition is moving forward this morning for the record and there will be an empty chair for Mr Black. I will speak with our members about next steps.”
Earlier this week, ahead of Black’s scheduled deposition, over a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abuse urged Black to comply with congressional subpoenas.
“Black’s use of NDAs underscores why Congress must scrutinize the agreements in his possession and determine whether they shed light on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and others in Epstein’s orbit” the survivors wrote.
“If Black continues to withhold responsive records or refuses to comply with the committee’s demands, Congress should use every tool available to enforce its subpoenas,” they added.
Black’s lawsuit alleges that the two subpoenas issued to him are “invalid to the extent they exceed” the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection to OGR’s legislative purpose”.
“Additionally, the subpoenas would also expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee,” the suit says.
