ECHR drops remaining individual human-rights complaints against Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:06:25 UTC
23:06:25 KST

PARIS, September 3. /TASS/. The European Court of Human Rights has dropped the remaining individual complaints alleging human rights violations in Russia, citing a lack of resources and saying the issues raised had already been sufficiently addressed.
"The Court considered that it was no longer necessary to examine the remaining individual applications against Russia as they concerned issues that had already been sufficiently addressed and that the significant judicial resources required for their continued examination could not be justified," the statement said. "An individual examination of each of these applications would have required significant further resources, potentially at the expense of other applications requiring adjudication in respect of other States."
The decision concerns applications unrelated to military conflicts or inter-state disputes, as well as those that cannot be examined under a simplified procedure. The court stressed that it could restore an application to its list if the circumstances justified doing so. As of September 2022, when the ECHR considers Russia to have ceased to be a party to the European Convention on Human Rights, 15,800 such individual applications were pending, "the majority of which have been processed."
For now, the court plans to consider only applications concerning events outside Russia’s borders as recognized by the Council of Europe, as well as inter-state applications. More than 5,500 individual applications concern events in Crimea and Donbass, while another 150 cases have to do with the events of the 2008 armed conflict with Georgia. The court’s press service described these cases as a priority and said that a special Conflicts Unit had been established within the court’s Registry to ensure their swift examination.

Travelers face up to 3 hour waits at Brussels Airport amid new EU border system rollout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:06:07 UTC
23:06:07 KST

Melike Pala
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Non-European travelers arriving at Brussels Airport faced waiting times of up to three hours at border control during peak morning hours on Thursday due to the rollout of the EU's new Entry/Exit System (EES) and a seasonal surge in returning holidaymakers.
Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens confirmed the delays to Dutch-language public broadcaster VRT, noting that non-European passengers experienced three-hour queues upon arrival. By contrast, European citizens using automated passport-control gates experienced shorter wait times, generally between 30 and 60 minutes.
The delays stem largely from the implementation of the EES, a digital border-management system that electronically registers non-European nationals entering and leaving the Schengen Area. The system replaces physical passport stamps with biometric checks, including fingerprints and facial scans.
"The registration requires more steps and time per passenger. As a result, waiting times build up rapidly during busy periods," Franssens said.
Although the Belgian government deployed additional Aviation Police personnel ahead of the summer season to staff all available control booths, the airport reported that the extra workforce has proven insufficient during high-volume periods.

US-Türkiye friendship 'incredibly strong,' says US deputy chief of mission to Ankara
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:06:04 UTC
23:06:04 KST

US-Türkiye friendship 'incredibly strong,' says US deputy chief of mission to Ankara
'Strong relationship' between US, Turkish presidents provides foundation for broader cooperation, Alyce Abdalla says during 1st visit to Türkiye's quake-hit Hatay province
Lale Koklu and Fatma Zehra Solmaz
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
HATAY/ISTANBUL
'2027 will mark 100 years of formal diplomatic relations between US and Republic of Türkiye. ... I am really excited to be here at this moment'
The friendship between the US and Türkiye is currently “incredibly strong,” Deputy Chief of Mission at the US Embassy in Ankara Alyce Abdalla said, pointing to the close relationship between the leaders of the two countries.
Abdalla made the remarks to Anadolu while visiting Türkiye’s southern Hatay province to inspect reconstruction work at the Antakya Greek Orthodox Church, which was destroyed in the Feb. 6, 2023 earthquakes and whose rebuilding has been supported by the US.
Noting that she began her diplomatic assignment in Türkiye around two weeks ago and that Hatay was the destination of her first visit, Abdalla said she was very excited to be in the country.
Describing Türkiye as “an extraordinary place to work,” Abdalla assessed the friendship between the two countries.
“The friendship between the United States and Türkiye right now is incredibly strong, and it is true when we talk about our leaders. (US) President (Donald) Trump and (Turkish) President (Recep Tayyip) Erdogan had a historic meeting in Ankara in July during the NATO summit," she said.
"That is just a wonderful setting for me to come and start here as deputy chief of mission, and I am very excited about it," she added.
Abdalla described the relationship between the two leaders as "incredibly positive" and said it could serve as an example for the broader US-Türkiye bilateral ties.
"Right now, we have that strong relationship between our leaders, and we are working hard throughout the mission (in) Türkiye to make sure that that friendship is reflected throughout our work," she said.
Abdalla said she hopes to meet as many people and visit as many places as possible during her assignment in Türkiye.
Türkiye-US diplomatic relations to mark centennial
"Next year, 2027, will mark 100 years of formal diplomatic relations between the United States and the Republic of Türkiye," she said, adding that she was "really excited to be here at this moment."
"I hope that we can use the next year to further strengthen our relationship and think about the ways in which we can work together going forward," she added.
'I was just really struck by the strength and resilience of the people here, ... it is just inspiring'
Abdalla also received information about efforts to rebuild the Antakya Greek Orthodox Church, located on Saray Street in the Antakya district and destroyed in the earthquakes.
The work is being carried out by Türkiye’s Culture and Tourism Ministry and Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, with support from the US Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation and the World Monuments Fund.
Visiting the site, Abdalla said seeing the traces of the earthquakes firsthand and witnessing the scale of the destruction while touring Hatay had deeply affected her.
"I was really struck by the level of the damage when I walked on the ground today. It made me understand how really terrible those earthquakes were back in February 2023. I could tell that so much work has been done," she said.
Abdalla said she was also deeply impressed by the resilience shown by the people of the region.
"I was just really struck by the strength and resilience of the people here, to have that kind of destruction happen and then to recover and be focused on the future and rebuilding, it is just inspiring," she said.
Abdalla said the US Embassy was pleased to contribute to recovery efforts by funding emergency stabilization work at St. Paul Church and the Antioch Synagogue, while working with Türkiye's Culture and Tourism Ministry to support the local community in the aftermath of the devastating earthquakes.
Cooperation to return stolen cultural artifacts to Türkiye
Abdalla said the US has also provided various forms of support for efforts carried out with Türkiye to protect cultural heritage.
She noted that the two countries also cooperate on the return to Türkiye of historical artifacts that were illegally taken abroad.
"We are also very committed to working with Türkiye on returning stolen objects to Türkiye," she said.
"We have just recently signed a renewal of the US-Türkiye Cultural Property Agreement, and this is a way in which we can work with the Turkish government to make sure that objects that were stolen from Türkiye are returned to the Turkish people," she added.

Local media reported that while the SBU was searching an apartment linked to the investigation, HUR officers arrived and shots were fired; three HUR officers were injured.

In a separate statement, the SBU said its officers had come under armed attack while conducting an investigation and they had used their weapons in response.
On Thursday, the SBU released a video of the Russian national fighting for Ukraine who had been arrested last month. In the video, the man says he was contacted by a person from Russia acting for Moscow’s intelligence agency who wanted to recruit him to assassinate Ukrainian defence personnel and other individuals. The man’s lawyer told local media that the video had been recorded under pressure and was being released to “whitewash” the shootout. The man has since been released from SBU custody.
Hours after the shootout, Zelenskyy fired the SBU’s head of the department for the protection of state secrets, Oleh Khramov.
“Shooting here in Ukraine is permitted only at Russian occupiers, in defence of Ukraine. Our state will never regard any other shootout as acceptable,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post.
The incident comes at a delicate moment for Zelenskyy. He has recently faced down calls from a sacked defence minister to hold wartime elections. The demand, from Mykhailo Fedorov – whose dismissal triggered a wave of protests – was the biggest challenge to Zelenskyy’s authority from inside Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion.
Zelenskyy also recently sacked a presidential deputy chief of staff amid reports she was being investigated in connection to an alleged money-laundering scheme.
The president said the shooting on Wednesday needed to be investigated by both the SBU and the HUR. Ukraine’s main investigative agency has also opened an investigation.
In a separate incident, a 71-year-old man was shot outside a medical clinic on Thursday morning in Kyiv and remains in a “serious condition”, according to the the Kyiv city prosecutor’s office. An investigation has been launched into an attempted murder.
The shootings come as Kyiv withstands an intense period of Russian bombardment. Air raid alerts have been active for extended periods in the daytime as well as overnight in the capital. Across the country, at least five people were killed in strikes on Wednesday night. Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles.
Ukraine has also increased its use of long-range drones to target deep into Russian territory. This week Zelenskyy said that Russian airspace was becoming unsafe for commercial airlines because of the growing number of drone attacks.
On Thursday, Russian media reported that the military officer who ordered a missile strike on the Okhmatdyt children’s hospital in Kyiv in July 2024 had been shot. Maj Gen Nikolai Varpakhovich was reportedly shot twice by an assailant riding a motorbike and wearing a helmet. The officer remains in a critical condition.

Badenoch says UK must prepare for possible war by 2030
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:03:05 BST
23:03:05 KST

Kemi Badenoch has said Britain must increase defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030, warning that the country could face a major conflict within the next four years and arguing that higher military spending can no longer be delayed.
In a speech on Britain’s defence on Thursday, the Conservative leader linked the spending requirement to Russia, cyber attacks, threats to critical infrastructure and wider instability, while setting out the case for the £10 billion annual increase in defence spending announced by her party.
Badenoch said: “Before the summer, Keir Starmer was given intelligence that Russia could launch an attack on NATO as soon as 2030. Not enough politicians in Parliament have fully appreciated what that means. By that of course I mean Labour politicians. What this means that within the next 4 years, the UK could be at war with the world’s biggest nuclear armed state. Because under Article 5, an attack on any NATO country is an attack on all of them.”
She also referred to Russian naval activity around Britain and threats to undersea infrastructure, saying: “Vladimir Putin has called Britain Russia’s number one enemy. Russian warships have been sailing through the English Channel and the undersea cables which power our internet and power our entire information and communication network have come under threat. People may not see it in their day to day lives, but hostile states are constantly pushing the boundaries with unconventional warfare.”
Badenoch argued that national security needed to encompass more than conventional military forces, pointing to cyber security, energy infrastructure and national resilience.
She said: “National security is not just about tanks, boots on the ground and planes in the air. It is about our cyber defences, it is about our energy security, it is about our country’s resilience. National security does not just happen we also have to pay for it, and that means spending more money on defence.”
The Conservative leader compared the UK’s position with increased defence investment elsewhere in NATO, citing Poland’s expansion of its armed forces and higher German defence spending. She also referred to Greece already spending around 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence.
Badenoch said: “Being an island might make us feel safer, but it does not prevent conflict from coming to us. And let’s be honest, conflict is coming. We must act now. Because the defence of the nation is the first duty of government.”
She called for defence spending to rise every year until reaching 3 per cent of GDP by 2030, saying: “We need to increase our defence spending every year so we can get to 3% of GDP by 2030, anything after that is too late.”
The Conservatives have proposed increasing annual defence expenditure by around £10 billion by 2029/30 compared with current government plans. The party says the increase would be funded through welfare reductions and reallocating money from other areas of government expenditure, including civil research and development, the British Business Bank and the National Wealth Fund.
Badenoch said: “Finding the money to pay for defence means making tough choices, it means making difficult trade-offs.”
She added: “We have now completed our work to get to 3%.
“And today my team have set out our plan to remove the housing benefit and remove the VAT exemption for Motability, alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos Deal,
“And repurposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target.
“And let’s be clear, 3% is the minimum our country needs to stay safe.”
The speech also connected defence policy with the wider state of the economy, with Badenoch arguing that Britain’s ability to sustain greater military expenditure depends on controlling borrowing and public spending.
She said: “Defence is not separate from the economy. Fiscal responsibility is part of national security.”
Badenoch also repeated the Conservative proposal for a £17 billion Sovereign Defence Fund, which the party says would support military readiness and investment in the British defence industrial base.
The Labour Party was approached for comment on Badenoch’s remarks and the Conservatives’ defence spending proposals, but had not responded at the time of publication.
Closing the defence section of her speech, Badenoch said: “Russia will attack a country it thinks is weak. It will not attack a country it knows is strong.
“We need to be strong. If you want peace, you prepare for war.”

====================================================================================================

Male politicians show a spike in care-oriented language during peak periods of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:00:59 UTC
23:00:59 KST

A recent analysis of parliamentary speeches during the Israel-Hamas war indicates that lawmakers who frequently express a moral duty to care for others are more likely to propose constructive, repair-oriented policies. The findings suggest that female politicians consistently use more care-based language, while male politicians tend to increase their expressions of care primarily during periods of peak conflict. The study was published in the Journal of Applied Psychology.
“From a research perspective, we know surprisingly little about leadership when it arguably matters most — during high-strength events such as crises, let alone wars,” Alexander D. Stajkovic, a professor of management at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and Kayla S. Stajkovic of the University of California, Davis, told PsyPost. “Most leadership research has been conducted in relatively calm, low-stakes settings, yet crises are precisely when leaders face consequential decisions under remarkable uncertainty and human suffering.”
In political settings, leaders navigate intense pressures, especially during times of crisis. The central focus of the new study is a concept called ethics of care leadership. This is a leadership approach where officials balance their traditional strategic duties with an active, publicly voiced concern for the welfare of those affected by their decisions. Rather than treating care as just a personality trait, this framework views caring for others as a moral obligation that can be expressed through everyday political language and debate.
“Care for others and strength in responding to crises should not be treated as opposites in leadership,” the researchers explained. “Ethics of care leadership is not about softening or stepping back from the difficult responsibilities of the job — it is about carrying out those responsibilities while remaining attentive to the people affected by them.”
Historically, political leadership during security threats has been associated with masculine traits like toughness and dominance. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2016 found that the public tends to prefer male over female leadership when worried about terrorism. However, expectations and approaches appear to be shifting.
A 2020 study by the Stajkovics found that U.S. states led by female governors experienced fewer COVID-19 deaths early in the pandemic, with an analysis of public briefings showing that these women expressed more empathy and confidence than male governors. Interviews with members of European parliaments from a 2026 qualitative study also indicated that many lawmakers increasingly view cooperative, interpersonally sensitive behavior as a core part of good leadership, alongside traditional assertiveness.
To understand how these dynamics play out in real-world crises, the authors examined how ethics of care leadership functions during high-strength events. These are situations that create sudden upheaval and carry massive consequences for human life, such as a war. Because high-strength events unfold in waves of varying intensity, they offer a way to track whether leaders maintain a consistent moral orientation or adapt their language as the crisis escalates and stabilizes.
“Instead of treating ‘the war’ as one flat backdrop of a high-strength event, we coded each month as either a peak or sustained-high event-strength period,” the researchers noted. “That allowed us to examine not just ‘Does care matter during a crisis?’ but ‘Does care rise and fall as the crisis itself rises and falls?’ — a question that is difficult to answer without 16 months of continuous, real-world data.”
For the study, the researchers analyzed the language used in the Israeli Knesset between October 2023 and January 2025. During this 16-month period, they examined roughly 5.2 million words spoken by 152 legislators across 140 plenary sessions, which are meetings attended by all members of the legislative body.
“What makes the findings especially compelling is the setting,” the researchers pointed out. “These were not participants responding to a hypothetical leadership scenario. They were elected leaders speaking during an actual, ongoing war, tracked continuously over 16 months rather than at a single moment.”
Using natural language processing software, a branch of artificial intelligence that allows computers to read and analyze human text, the team measured how often lawmakers used words associated with care and moral concern. They also extracted 4,143 distinct policy suggestions from the transcripts.
A machine learning program, trained on examples coded by human reviewers, classified each of these policy suggestions as either constructive or combative. Constructive suggestions focused on repair, social inclusion, and long-term problem solving, while combative suggestions relied on blame, punishment, and escalation. The researchers also categorized each month of the conflict as either a period of peak intensity, marked by new escalations or major disruptions, or a sustained period, where the conflict continued without major novel developments.
The analysis indicated that higher expressions of care-based leadership were associated with a greater likelihood of proposing constructive policies.
“The effects are meaningful, but they should not be read as deterministic,” the Stajkovics noted, meaning one factor does not strictly guarantee an outcome. For every one-unit increase in a speaker’s care expression score, the odds of them making a constructive suggestion increased by 43 percent.
The data also pointed to differences in how men and women communicated. Overall, female legislators expressed higher levels of care-based leadership than male legislators throughout the 16 months. This higher expression of care indirectly explained why women were more likely to offer constructive policy suggestions.
However, the context of the event altered these patterns. During peak months of the conflict, expressions of care increased across the board. Notably, male politicians showed a much sharper increase in care-based language during these peak periods than female politicians did, narrowing the gender gap.
“One might expect the most threatening periods of a war to push leaders toward greater toughness, aggression, or emotional restraint,” the researchers said. “Instead, we found that male leaders tended to increase their expressions of care more sharply during exactly those periods.”
They explained that men face social pressure to appear tough, making it feel socially costly to openly express care. “But when suffering becomes visible and the stakes become extraordinarily high, the situation may provide a kind of ‘contextual license’ for men to express greater care,” they added. “In other words, extreme circumstances may temporarily loosen what society considers appropriate leadership behavior for men.”
The researchers also grouped the politicians into three distinct profiles based on their language. One group consistently showed low care expression, another maintained a stable and moderate level of care expression, and a third group showed highly responsive care expression that spiked during peak crisis months. Politicians with a stable care profile were the most likely to continue offering constructive policy suggestions even during peak months, acting as a steadying force during escalations.
A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 looked at whether female leaders causally reduced objective crisis outcomes like COVID-19 mortality rates, finding no statistical difference. The current research focuses on a different aspect of leadership, measuring gender differences in legislative speech and the expression of care during parliamentary debates rather than attempting to track objective crisis outcomes.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting the results. Because the study relies on observational data from political speeches, it cannot establish that expressing care directly causes a politician to adopt constructive policies. Instead, it highlights a strong association between the two factors.
“First, we would caution against reading this as showing that women are inherently more caring, or inherently ‘better’ leaders than men,” the researchers noted. “Women expressed more care on average, but men’s expression of care increased more substantially during peak-intensity periods. That is difficult to reconcile with a story in which care is simply a fixed trait of women.”
“‘Constructive’ should not be read as meaning anti-war, politically liberal, or the objectively correct policy,” they clarified. “We are studying the form of the proposed solution, not making a judgment about who is right in the conflict.”
It is also worth noting that what politicians suggest in a speech does not always translate into final legislative action. Parliamentary voting is often heavily influenced by party alliances and coalition requirements, meaning a leader’s verbal suggestions offer a window into their moral priorities in debate rather than a guarantee of how a law will be passed. The specific political and cultural context of the Israeli Knesset during a war also means these patterns might look different in other countries or during different types of emergencies.
“An interesting next step would be to examine how broadly these patterns generalize beyond war,” the researchers said. “War is an extreme case, but the features that make it a powerful test — novelty, disruption, high stakes, and consequences for human welfare — also characterize events such as natural disasters, public-health emergencies, humanitarian crises, and organizational crises.”
“If care were simply a luxury of leadership — something leaders could afford only when circumstances were easy — we would expect it to disappear as the crisis intensified,” they concluded. “We found close to the opposite. Expressions of care increased during peak periods, and leaders who expressed more care were more likely to put constructive alternatives into the conversation. Even in circumstances defined by conflict and polarization, escalation is not the only leadership response.”
The study, “Ethics of Care Leadership Expressions During a High-Strength Event: A Gendered Analysis of Combative Versus Constructive Policy Suggestions During the Israel–Hamas War,” was authored by Alexander D. Stajkovic, Kayla S. Stajkovic, Jenny M. Hoobler, and Frederick P. Morgeson.

Extra funds push Taiwan’s defence spending past NT$1 trillion for the first time
The island’s cabinet approves supplementary budget, with heavy investment in missiles, drones and classified programmes
Taiwan’s cabinet approved a supplementary defence budget of NT$145.7 billion (US$4.6 billion) on Thursday, pushing the island’s total defence-related spending for this year above NT$1 trillion for the first time.
The additional funding is expected to raise this year’s overall defence spending from 3.32 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) to about 3.83 per cent, the highest level in decades.
The supplementary budget, which still requires legislative approval, is aimed at plugging gaps left after opposition lawmakers cut NT$470 billion in May from an eight-year NT$1.25 trillion special defence package proposed by the government.
Two classified programmes would account for NT$64.5 billion.

Denmark exposed Russia&apos;s preparations for sabotage to disrupt defense deliveries to Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:59:55 EEST
22:59:55 KST

Denmark exposed Russia's preparations for sabotage to disrupt defense deliveries to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
PET warned about Russian plans to disrupt defense deliveries to Ukraine in Denmark. Possible methods include arson and recruiting citizens.
In Denmark, the authorities uncovered plans and preparations for Russian sabotage aimed at stopping supplies for Ukraine’s defense. UNN writes about this, citing dpa.
What was the target
Defense industry companies linked to military aid for Ukraine have become among the main targets, the head of counterintelligence at the Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET), Emil Gresholm, told the Berlingske newspaper on Wednesday.
"The main goal is to stop specific supplies for Ukraine’s defense," Gresholm was quoted as saying.
"At the same time, the goal is to intimidate us so that we no longer support the Ukrainians or expand our own defense capabilities," he said.
Intelligence services usually operate in the shadows, but Gresholm said the threat was specific enough to warrant a public warning.
"The choice of targets and the preparations are so specific that we consider it necessary to issue a public statement that this is a threat that must be taken seriously," he told Berlingske.
What methods does Russia use
Gresholm named arson as one of the possible objectives of Russia’s plans and called on defense industry companies to strengthen their security measures.
According to Gresholm, Russia is also trying to recruit "ordinary Danes" for its plans, often without their knowing that they are working for Moscow.
"This may include photographing or filming companies or facilities that could later be used in sabotage plans," he said.
He urged people in Denmark to be suspicious if they are approached with such requests.
As stated, PET expects the threat to continue growing "in scale and complexity."
"It is directed against Ukrainian defense manufacturers in Denmark," Gresholm said.
"But we see that the Russians are generally interested in Denmark’s defense industry," he added.
Additional information
Europe records that Russia is intensifying its so-called "gray zone" operations against European countries that support Ukraine. These include sabotage, arson, cyberattacks, espionage, violations of airspace by drones, and the recruitment of operatives through social media.
Among other things, as reported in the Western media, Russia has launched a new wave of attacks on European weapons manufacturing plants.
The Czech counterintelligence service, in particular, warned about one-off Russian agents who may attack facilities providing aid to Ukraine.

The officer was hospitalized in serious condition. The Telegram channel Dosye Shpiona (“Spy’s Dossier”) identifies the victim as Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, commander of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division within Russia’s Aerospace Forces’ long-range aviation branch. That information has not been officially confirmed.

Ukraine’s Security Service and the country’s Prosecutor General’s Office announced August 31 that they had named Nikolai Varpakhovich a suspect in absentia. Investigators believe he personally ordered the missile strike on Kyiv’s Okhmatdyt children’s hospital on July 8, 2024. At the time of the strike, the hospital had more than 600 patients and roughly the same number of staff members. Two people were killed.

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russia’s non-resource non-energy industrial exports rose to $58.8 billion in the first half of the year, Russian Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov told reporters on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
"According to the plan, this year we must reach a total non-resource non-energy export volume of $155.25 billion, with industrial sectors accounting for $116.95 billion of that amount. In the first half of 2026, industrial non-energy export increased to $58.8 billion," he said.
Alikhanov named chemical products, particularly mineral and chemical fertilizers, metallurgy and precious metals, light industry, pharmaceuticals, perfumes, and cosmetics, among the key sectors driving the growth in manufactured goods exports.

Moreover, export support centers, overseen by the Russian Industry and Trade Ministry with the support of the Russian Export Center, have now been integrated into the unified exporter support system. This will allow us to work more effectively with regional exporters," the minister added.
Russia increased its non-resource non-energy exports by 11% last year, establishing itself as a reliable supplier of high-tech products, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin reported earlier.
The Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) is being held on September 1-4 in Vladivostok on the campus of the Far Eastern Federal University. The main theme of the EEF in 2026 is "The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People." The event is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Government of the Russian Federation. TASS is the general media partner.

Putin says he strikes Ukraine so it "won't feel like" attacking his refineries
Russian leader Vladimir Putin is trying by all means to convince that Russia's war against Ukraine has no impact on his country's economy and that his forces are allegedly carrying out "retaliatory strikes" against Ukraine so that it "won't feel like harming" Russia.
Source: Russian propaganda agency TASS; Telegram channel Astra, with reference to Putin's statement at the plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum
Details: "There is a second method (of combating Ukrainian armed forces attacks – ed.). To carry out retaliatory strikes so that they won't feel like harming us. That's all," Putin said.
He also attempted to convince the audience that Russian air defence had allegedly repelled all drone attacks on oil refineries the night before last. According to Putin, drones had attempted to attack three oil refineries at the time.
He also claimed that only 10% of repair work on oil refineries remains to be completed.
It should be noted that Ukraine attacks Russian military factories that manufacture weapons used to strike Ukraine, Russian airfields from which Russian fighter jets take off, and oil refineries that supply fuel to the Russian military.
Why this matters: Russia invaded Ukraine and occupied the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and parts of Donbas as early as 2014.
In 2022, Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, attacking peaceful cities and towns across the country with missiles and bombs during the night.
Notably, in the early days of the full-scale invasion, Russian propagandists actively circulated claims that "Russia would take Kyiv in three days", while Russian soldiers advancing on the capital carried parade uniforms with them, intending to march down Khreshchatyk, the main street of Kyiv, after those supposed "three days".
However, as of late summer 2026, Russian forces have still failed even to reach the administrative borders of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts.
Russian forces attack residential buildings, schools, warehouses and shopping centres in Ukraine daily with drones and missiles, killing civilians.
Throughout this period, the Russian authorities have invented various justifications for starting the war, claiming, among other things, that NATO intended to attack Russia and alleging the existence of "biolaboratories" in Ukraine. Their claims have even extended to absurd stories about "combat mosquitoes" and a "dirty bomb".
In August 2026, Putin's adviser invented yet another reason for starting the war – claiming that Ukraine had allegedly been planning an invasion of Russia on 8 March 2022, so Moscow decided to pre-empt it by attacking first.
Russian authorities also try by all means to downplay the damage that the war they launched against Ukraine is inflicting on Russia itself and its citizens. On 19 August, Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes on industrial and logistics facilities are causing damage to the Russian economy but attempted to assert that there are allegedly "no critical consequences and there will be none".
At the end of June, following a series of attacks on Russian oil refineries and fuel problems in many regions of Russia, Putin insisted that the damage from Ukrainian strikes was allegedly "not critical". At the same time, he declared the need to increase the production of air defence systems to protect these facilities and improve the work of structures responsible for downing drones.

The Schalke 04 forward also recalled his goal against Wales and Bosnia and Herzegovina's playoff victory over Italy in Zenica in March, which secured qualification for the 2026 World Cup.
"And that is how I want to experience my final night representing my country: with all of you by my side, wearing the shirt I have loved since I was a boy - and the shirt I will love for the rest of my life," he added.

Libya's Tripoli oil depot targeted by suspected drone amid fuel crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:54:44 UTC
22:54:44 KST

Mohammed Ertima and Ikram Kouachi
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Libya's Brega Petroleum Marketing Company said Thursday that the Tripoli oil depot was targeted by a "flying object suspected to be a drone" that fell next to one of the fuel tanks, with no injuries reported.
In a statement, the state-owned company strongly condemned the attack, saying it “occurred early Thursday after the flying object, suspected to be a drone, entered the depot's airspace and fell next to one of the tanks.”
No casualties were reported in the incident, it said.
Specialized teams and relevant authorities immediately began taking necessary measures and securing the site, according to the statement.
The company reassured citizens that fuel operations, including distribution and supply, were continuing normally and that the incident had not affected operations or the fulfillment of scheduled orders for fuel stations.
It called for a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances of the incident, identification of those responsible and the necessary legal action against them.
The targeting comes as cities and areas across Libya have been facing a severe fuel shortage for about a week, resulting in long queues at distribution stations, some stretching more than 5 kilometers, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
In the second week of August, vital facilities, including oil storage tanks, water desalination plants and power generation facilities in the city of Zawiya, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) west of Tripoli, came under near-daily attacks by explosive-laden drones.
On Tuesday, the interior minister and head of the National Unity Government's committee tasked with addressing the fuel and gas crisis, Imad Trabelsi, announced the closure of 490 fuel stations, saying investigations had shown that they were being exploited in smuggling operations.
He said about 365 stations had been authorized to operate based on actual needs.
Trabelsi added that the committee would continue efforts to combat fuel manipulation and its sale on the black market, saying those benefiting from such operations make profits at the expense of Libyan citizens and the national economy.
Libya has been facing a political crisis amid the presence of two rival governments.
The first is the Government of National Unity, headed by Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh and based in Tripoli, which administers western Libya. The second is headed by Osama Hamad, appointed by the House of Representatives in early 2022 and based in Benghazi, which administers eastern Libya and most of the country's south.

La Maison Blanche fait pression sur les entreprises américaines pour qu’elles boycottent le sommet spatial de Macron
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:54:43 UTC
22:54:43 KST

La Maison Blanche fait pression sur les entreprises américaines pour qu’elles boycottent le sommet spatial de Macron
Alors que l’administration Trump a exhorté les géants américains du secteur à ne pas venir à Paris, le ministre français de l’Enseignement supérieur et de l’Espace a déclaré, ce jeudi, que l’Amérique était “la bienvenue” au sommet.
Donald Trump participe à une réunion bilatérale avec le président français Emmanuel Macron en marge du sommet du G7 à Évian le 15 juin 2026. Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images
La Maison Blanche a fait pression sur des entreprises spatiales américaines afin qu’elles n’assistent pas au sommet spatial organisé à Paris la semaine prochaine — une initiative qui a plongé les dirigeants de ces firmes dans une grande perplexité.
Jeudi 27 août, un cadre du Bureau de la politique scientifique et technologique (OSTP, en anglais) de la Maison Blanche a fait savoir à plusieurs grands groupes, dont SpaceX, Stoke Space, K2 Space et Astra, lors d’un appel privé, que la participation à cet événement français au Grand Palais pourrait s’apparenter à un soutien tacite aux positions européennes, d’après deux industriels et un membre de cabinet au fait de l’appel.
Advertisement
Si la Maison Blanche a assuré que la décision finale revenait aux entreprises, ces mêmes interlocuteurs estiment, eux, que l’exécutif a bien tenté de décourager toute présence au grand raoût, auquel plus de 120 pays doivent participer. Ces sources ont requis l’anonymat afin de pouvoir s’exprimer librement.
Selon les sources précitées, le responsable du Bureau de la politique scientifique et technologique a, lors de l’appel, affirmé aux représentants du secteur que la France ne s’était pas concertée avec les États-Unis au sujet du sommet. Il a en outre accusé le pays de “pratiques anticoncurrentielles” et laissé entendre que les tables rondes de l’événement n’étaient pas conçues pour intégrer le point de vue américain, ce qui risquait de nuire à l’industrie américaine. Il s’est enfin inquiété de la présence de la Chine à l’événement.
Sollicité par POLITICO, l’Elysée renvoie à la réaction de Philippe Baptiste, ministre français de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Espace et ancien patron du Cnes, publiée sur X ce jeudi matin. “L’Amérique n’est pas seulement la bienvenue — nous vous voulons là, a-t-il écrit. Les entreprises américaines, les scientifiques et l’administration sont tous les bienvenus. Nous travaillons en étroite coordination avec mon ami Michael Kratsios [conseiller science et technologie de Donald Trump].”
L’industrie spatiale dans l’inconfort
L’OSTP, qui supervise les orientations nationales en matière de science et de technologie, a organisé cet échange afin de répondre aux questions sur la position des États-Unis à l’égard de ce sommet, a expliqué un responsable de cette administration, qui a requis l’anonymat, pour décrire l’objectif de l’appel avec les acteurs du secteur. Il martèle qu’aucune consigne précise n’a été donnée.
“L’administration Trump continue de collaborer avec ses alliés et partenaires dans le domaine spatial”, a-t-il ajouté. “Nous nous réjouissons à l’idée d’avoir des échanges fructueux lors du Sommet spatial sur des priorités clés, notamment les missions scientifiques, les programmes d’exploration et la sécurité spatiale.”
Advertisement
A l’issue de l’échange de jeudi dernier, les exécutifs des grands groupes concernés étaient dans l’expectative quant à leur participation, ou non, au sommet, selon un représentant d’une de ces entreprises.
“L’Europe est un marché important pour nos entreprises mais pas autant que le marché américain, a-t-il ajouté. Les entreprises spatiales américaines se trouvent désormais dans la position délicate de devoir décliner l’invitation avec élégance.”
SpaceX, Stoke Space, K2 Space et Astra n’ont pas donné suite aux sollicitations de POLITICO.
Le spatial, en enjeu de souveraineté en Europe
Malgré les inquiétudes de l’administration concernant l’événement, des responsables de l’OSTP, du département d’État, du département du Commerce et de la NASA participeront tout de même au sommet.
Du 9 au 10 septembre, le sommet doit accueillir des délégations nationales, des agences spatiales, des chefs d’entreprises, des scientifiques et des cadres militaires.
L’événement “vise à favoriser un dialogue franc et direct, ainsi qu’à présenter des perspectives et des pistes de travail et d’action à travers des discussions de haut niveau, des annonces et des ateliers”, selon un site du gouvernement français, qui précise que le sommet sera placé sous le sceau d’une “réflexion stratégique sur l’avenir de l’espace”.
Advertisement
La présidente de la Commission européenne, Ursula von der Leyen, a également prévu de livrer un grand discours lors du sommet, comme le relatait récemment POLITICO.
Ce sommet intervient alors que l’Europe cherche à renforcer sa souveraineté en matière spatiale tout en réduisant sa dépendance à l’égard des États-Unis. Emmanuel Macron a présenté, en novembre, une nouvelle stratégie et annoncé une augmentation de 4,2 milliards d’euros du budget de la défense spatiale d’ici à 2030, portant le total des dépenses dédiées à ce secteur à 10,2 milliards d’euros.
Laura Kayali a contribué à cet article depuis Paris. Il a été initialement publié en anglais par POLITICO en anglais et adapté en français par Nicolas Cossic.

Farage bids to arrest Reform UK's decline after bruising summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:54:30 UTC
22:54:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Nigel Farage bids to arrest Reform UK's decline after bruising summer
If a week is a long time in politics, then a year is a very long time indeed.
Reform UK heads into its 2026 conference facing a very different set of circumstances than it did a year ago.
Twelve months earlier, the right-wing, anti-migrant insurgents were riding high in the polls, bolstered by the polycrisis in Keir Starmer's Labour government and a stagnating Tory party.
Reform leaders were eagerly presenting Nigel Farage as the country's prime minister-in-waiting and the party as having broken the Labour-Conservative duopoly's stranglehold on British politics.
May's local elections appeared to provide evidence of the party's thesis. The vote saw them pick up almost 1,500 council seats and take control of 14 local authorities, making the party bigger than ever.
It may also prove to be the high watermark of the party's popularity.
The Reform Spring has since given way to a summer of disquiet, if not outright discontent, amid scrutiny over Farage's finances, rumours of insider discord, and a reinvigorated Labour Party.
Questions over Farage's financial arrangements began gaining traction in the media in May after details emerged over an undeclared £5 million gift from billionaire investor Christopher Harborne. Several weeks later came an investigation by The Times that revealed his ties to convicted fraudster and cryptocurrency gambler George Cottrell. Farage says he didn’t break any rules but has been placed under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner.
His response to the allegations was to dramatically hand in his notice from parliament and trigger a by-election, before lying low from the media spotlight. This proved to be a major own goal. Other parties' refusal to participate in the race denied him his showdown against "The Establishment", leaving him instead to fight an absurd head-to-head against Count Binface. Though he easily retained his Clacton seat, the race has not made the questions go away and he remains under investigation by parliament.
Meanwhile, Labour's defenestration of the historically unpopular Keir Starmer in favour of the TikTok-savvy everyman Andy Burnham has led to a rapid reversal of the party's fortunes, displacing Reform at the top of the opinion polls. Farage, who built his public image as a relatable "man of the people", now has a charismatic competitor speaking to the concerns of his party's core supporters in deindustrialised, left-behind Britain.
Even before Labour anointed the 'King of the North' as the country's new prime minister, Starmer's bid to out-Reform Reform had begun to dilute the Farage's signature pledge to radically curb migration. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's crackdown on asylum seekers has seen applications fall by a fifth over the past year, while the number of boats crossing from France has fallen to six-year lows, recent data has shown.
The party also faces a challenge to its right in the form of Rupert Lowe's Restore Britain, an ethnonationalist offshoot for whom Reform is too moderate on migration. Lowe's demands for the mass deportation of millions of migrants not only threatens to eat into the party's voter base but has triggered the defection of one of its most powerful international supporters, far-right tech agitator Elon Musk.
There have also been whispers of behind-the-scenes strife, chiefly involving the party's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf, who was rebuked by Farage earlier this month after calling former Tory defence secretary Ben Wallace a "traitor".
That the party's momentum has stalled is evident in recent opinion polls, which have put Reform in second place behind Labour. More in Common's latest survey this week delivered the party's worst result in 18 months, putting it in third place: four points behind Labour and one behind the Conservatives.
A recent YouGov survey found that 71% of the public would use at least one negative term to describe Farage, with "racist" and "liar" being the most popular. Meanwhile, two-thirds of Britons do not see Farage as prime ministerial - including more than a quarter of Reform voters. For a party so built around the personality of one man, the figure does not make for pretty reading.
As delegates gather in Birmingham, party officials will be keen to portray this as a temporary hiccough, a bump in the road to victory at the next election. Farage will hope to rekindle the rockstar entrance of a year ago and put the turbulent summer behind him by cultivating a Reform versus The Establishment siege mentality.
His lieutenants have announced new policies as he continued to lie low ahead of the event. Deputy leader Richard Tice vowed to restrict migrants' access to social housing. Robert Jenrick declared plans to slash the welfare state. Foreign nationals would be banned from accessing almost all benefits. Will this be enough to quieten the murmurs of dissent?

Ukrainian intel agencies in Kyiv firefight: What happened and why?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:54:02 UTC
22:54:02 KST

Ukrainian intel agencies in Kyiv firefight: What happened and why?
Three intelligence officers were wounded in shootout that Zelenskyy has described as ‘absolutely disgraceful’.
A shootout between two of Ukraine’s top intelligence agencies has wounded at least three security officials, highlighting internal divisions within Kyiv’s security establishment.
On Wednesday morning, a gunfight broke out between Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR), a military arm which handles foreign intelligence, and the State Security Service (SBU), which focuses on domestic intelligence and counterterrorism activities.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3EU ministers in Ireland tackle Israeli settlement trade and Ukraine defence
- list 2 of 3Russia to close Goethe-Institut centres as Germany tensions escalate
- list 3 of 3‘An impasse’: EU ministers fail to break deadlock over Israel and Ukraine
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the incident “an absolutely disgraceful situation”.
What’s behind the feud between SBU and HUR, and how significant is it?
What happened?
According to Ukrainian media reports, the incident between Kyiv’s top intel agencies took place in the capital’s Dniprovskyi district after the SBU took Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RVC) that fights for Ukraine, into custody. RVC is a subordinate of HUR.
Ukraine’s Prosecutor General’s Office said in a statement that SBU officers had received orders to prevent a “terrorist act” from Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
“During a search at one of the addresses, a group of individuals carried out an armed attack on the SBU operational-investigative group,” the statement added.
“They tried to prevent the conduct of investigative actions and blocked the passage of law enforcement officers with cars,” the statement noted, adding that the attackers belonged to “one of the units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.” According to local media reports, the attackers were part of HUR.
Ukraine’s Presidential Adviser Dmytro Lytvyn also confirmed the involvement of SBU and HUR in the shootout.
But the commander of HUR’s special unit “Timur,” in an interview with Radio Liberty/Radio Free Europe, accused the SBU of kidnapping Kaplunov “in broad daylight”.
The commander added that the SBU was the one which opened fire on HUR officers at the scene.
Taras Borovskyi, a lawyer representing Kaplunov, told Ukrainska Pravda that one HUR officer was shot in the leg, bleeding and in hospital. The second officer, he said, is also in a serious condition in the hospital, while the third officer is only slightly injured.
Who is Stepan Kaplunov?
Kaplunov is a Russian native who moved to Ukraine after Moscow annexed Crimea in 2014, according to Ukrainian media reports.
After serving in the Ukrainian armed forces, he joined the RVC in 2022 and has since been defending Ukraine in its war with Russia.
While Kaplunov is still a Russian citizen, Moscow added him to its list of “terrorists and extremists” because of his support for Ukraine.
Kaplunov told Radio NV on Thursday that he was abducted and interrogated over suspicions that he might be in touch with Russia’s FSB Security Service, according to The New Voice of Ukraine site.
How have Zelenskyy and his government responded?
In a statement on Telegram, Ukraine’s president said he had spoken to the country’s Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who is investigating the incident with the State Bureau of Investigation.
“There must be accountability – including personnel decisions by the heads of the security services regarding the individuals involved – and internal investigations must be conducted within both agencies,” he said in the statement.
“Here in Ukraine, the only time shots may be fired is at Russian occupiers in defence of the country. Our state will never tolerate any other kind of shootout as something permissible,” he added.
Zelenskyy has since dismissed Oleg Khramov, the head of the SBU’s Department for the Protection of State Secrets.
Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office and a former HUR member, called for a “thorough and impartial investigation,” according to the RBC-Ukraine news agency.
“It is important to ensure a thorough and impartial investigation, but no one has the right to kidnap servicemen with impunity, open fire on the streets of our cities, give and carry out criminal orders,” he said.
How significant is the recent security shakeup?
The incident comes as Ukraine shakes up its security establishment amid the escalating war with Russia.
In January this year, Zelenskyy removed Vasyl Maliuk as the head of SBU, shifting him to focus directly on warfare missions against Russia.
Zelenskyy also named military intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov as his new chief of staff and announced that Foreign Intelligence Service chief Oleh Ivashchenko will replace Budanov as head of the HUR.
“Ukraine needs greater focus on security issues, the development of the Defence and Security Forces of Ukraine, as well as on the diplomatic track of negotiations, and the Office of the President will primarily serve the fulfilment of these tasks of our state,” Zelenskyy had said.
In July, Zelenskyy also fired Oleksandr Syrskii as the country’s commander-in-chief, appointing Mykhailo Drapatyi to lead the military.
The move came after six days of protests in the capital, Kyiv, caused by the removal of Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who had previously clashed with Syrskii.
According to a report by Carnegie Politika, the media and analysis platform of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin, Zelenskyy’s security reshuffle “suggests a deliberate effort to tighten political coordination across the institutions that control coercive power”.
“The replacements come after anti-corruption investigations once again began reaching senior figures around the president, reviving tensions between the presidential administration and independent anti-corruption institutions,” the report noted.
“Whether this will translate into renewed pressure on the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine remains to be seen, but the personnel changes clearly strengthen the presidential administration’s ability to shape the relationship between the security services and Ukraine’s law-enforcement architecture,” the report added.
Zelenskyy’s allies have also been accused of corruption.
Last November, a corruption scandal involving Zelenskyy’s business partner, political allies and a cast of presumed wrongdoers who profited from a nuclear power monopoly roiled Ukraine.
The agencies, Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), released video and audio recordings in which the group appears to use nicknames and codewords to discuss bribes and kickbacks amounting to tens of millions of dollars.
Zelenskyy, whose anticorruption presidential campaign resonated with voters in 2019, tried to curb the autonomy of both agencies in July after they opened investigations into his allies and former business partners. But he backed down after massive popular protests.

Russia, Indonesia pledge deeper cooperation at Vladivostok forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:52:59 UTC
22:52:59 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto have agreed to strengthen bilateral cooperation during a meeting on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
On Thursday, Putin described Indonesia as one of Russia's key partners in Southeast Asia and said bilateral trade volume expanded by more than 12 percent last year.
"Indonesia is one of Russia's key partners in Southeast Asia, and we have been linked by friendship for many years. Trade is developing; it is growing; last year it was over 12 percent plus," he said.
Putin also highlighted the free trade agreement between the Eurasian Economic Union and Indonesia, as well as cooperation between Moscow and Jakarta through the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the UN, and other international platforms.
Prabowo said Indonesia regarded Russia as an important partner and welcomed the development of bilateral relations to the level of a strategic partnership last year.
"Our relations are growing very strongly, including in trade and economic cooperation, and we are ready to further strengthen our relations," he said.
The Indonesian president said the two countries shared an interest in expanding cooperation across the Pacific, particularly in maritime affairs and connectivity.
"We are part of the Pacific, and for us, cooperation in the field of maritime cooperation and connectivity is very important," Prabowo said.
‘A natural gateway’
The meeting was the second between Putin and Prabowo this year. Putin said their personal contacts reflected the strategic nature of relations between Russia and Indonesia.
The Indonesian president told the forum during his address that the country serves as a "natural gateway to ASEAN," providing access to approximately 680 million people.
"For the Eurasian business community, Indonesia serves as a natural gateway to ASEAN. We are the region's largest market, a central player in the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), and now, a free trade partner," he said, according to state-run news agency Antara.
Prabowo also said that the free trade agreement will give Eurasian producers access to a market of over 290 million Indonesian consumers, while noting that it will open access for Indonesian producers to the five Eurasian Economic Union member states, including Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Russia.
Prabowo additionally proposed that Indonesia and Russia set a "clear challenge" to double their trade within the first review period of the agreement.
The bilateral trade between Russia and Indonesia stood at around $5 billion in 2025, up 21.7 percent from 2024.

Number of Iranian military personnel reported killed by US strikes this week rises to 13
DUBAI, Sept 3 - Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported on Thursday the deaths of six more military personnel from U.S. strikes this week, bringing the military death toll to at least 13.
The U.S. strikes on Tuesday were the most extensive for weeks. In the latest report on military deaths, Tasnim said six members of the regular military, including three pilots, had been killed in southern Iran. It gave no additional detail on the location.
Tasnim had earlier reported that Tuesday's strikes had killed three members of the paramilitary Basij on Lavan Island in the Gulf, with their funeral taking place in southern Iran on Wednesday.
The strikes also killed four members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' (IRGC) Aerospace Force in western Iran, according to a statement by the guards published on Wednesday.
Iranian military casualties in the conflict that began in late February have been reported periodically, without official confirmation of overall tolls.
The war, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, has left thousands of people dead, the vast majority of them in Iran and Lebanon.
On Wednesday, an Iranian health ministry official said on X that from August 30 to September 2, 18 people had been killed, including four people attending a wedding, and 142 had been wounded, drawing renewed attention to the civilian death toll.
Tasnim has also reported that U.S. strikes on southern Iran on Sunday, which followed a month-long lull in clashes, had killed three people. Two were identified as members of the IRGC Navy by Iran's Nournews outlet.
The U.S. has reported 18 military personnel killed and more than 750 wounded in the war. REUTERS

- Category

548 Drones Target Moscow Region in One of Largest Attacks in Two Years, Russia Says
Russia reported one of its largest drone attacks on the Moscow region in two years, with Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin announcing on September 3 that 548 UAVs had been directed toward the capital region between 8:00 a.m. on September 2 and noon on September 3, according to Russian state media outlets TASS and Interfax.
Interfax reported Sobyanin's statement in full, which was published at 12:22 p.m. on September 3. TASS characterized the attack in a separate post as one of the largest in the Moscow region over the past two years.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Between September 2 at 08:00 and September 3 at 12:00, 548 UAVs flew toward the Moscow region," Sobyanin wrote in his channel on the Max messenger. "The majority were destroyed at distant frontiers. 143 drones were destroyed on the approach to Moscow."
The figures emerged from a series of incremental updates published through the night and into the morning of September 3. Interfax reported that Sobyanin initially announced 10 drones shot down on approach to Moscow, a figure that later climbed to 27, then 37, then 86, before the final midday tally reached 143.
Russian authorities offered no independent breakdown of drone types, flight paths, or intercept locations to allow the claims to be independently verified.
The 143 drones destroyed near Moscow represent roughly one in four of the total figure claimed for the entire region; Russian officials stated only that the remainder were eliminated "at distant frontiers," without further detail.
The attack also disrupted civilian aviation. Russia's federal aviation authority, Rosaviatsia, reported operational changes at Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports, according to Fontanka and Regions.ru, with potential knock-on effects on flight schedules across all three facilities
Vedomosti also confirmed the disruptions, citing Sobyanin's statements on air defense activity.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned international airlines, insurers, and aviation operators that Russian airspace was becoming increasingly unsafe because of drone activity linked to the war.
He argued that Moscow’s failure to properly notify carriers about aerial hazards was effectively closing its own skies, stating that “the Russian sky will de facto be closed.”

Russia has accused Norway of an “act of piracy” after Norwegian authorities seized the Russian research vessel Professor Molchanov in Svalbard, escalating tensions over a legal dispute involving Ukrainian energy company Naftogaz.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said on Thursday that Moscow viewed the seizure as part of what she described as a broader deterioration in Western approaches to maritime affairs.
“For decades, maritime law was the guiding principle in maritime affairs. Today, everything has been mixed up, everything has been discarded, and they have simply embarked on genuine piracy,” Zakharova said on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
Vessel seized over Naftogaz claim
Norwegian authorities seized The Professor Molchanov on Wednesday while it was docked in Barentsburg, Svalbard, after a court granted Naftogaz the right to seize the vessel, according to the Governor of Svalbard.
The Nord-Troms District Court issued the order as part of Naftogaz’s efforts to recover funds linked to assets it says were expropriated by Russia in 2014.
The vessel has been ordered to remain in Barentsburg until the governor or the court decides otherwise.
Moscow denounces ‘degradation’
Zakharova described the seizure as “horrifying” and a “degradation,” arguing that it represented a retreat from established international maritime practices.
The dispute adds another layer to tensions between Russia and Western countries over property, sanctions and legal claims stemming from the conflict involving Russia and Ukraine.

South Africa fires deputy crime-intelligence chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:49:14 UTC
22:49:14 KST

South Africa fires deputy crime-intelligence chief
South Africa’s police service has fired Crime Intelligence deputy head Major-General Feroz Khan after he failed to appear for an expedited disciplinary process.
In a statement issued on Wednesday, SAPS (South African Police Service) said Khan was deemed dismissed in terms of the SAPS Discipline Regulations after failing to attend proceedings before the senior officer responsible for the disciplinary matter.
“The South African Police Service confirms the dismissal of Major General Feroz Khan from the Service,” the police said. SAPS reiterated its commitment to accountability and professional conduct, stressing that all members, regardless of rank, are subject to the same disciplinary framework.
“SAPS reiterates its commitment to accountability, discipline and professional conduct within the organisation. No member, regardless of rank or position, is above the law or the applicable disciplinary framework,” the statement read.
The police added that, because the matter has been the subject of legal proceedings, it would continue to respect court processes and would only provide further information where legally permissible.
The dismissal comes a day after Khan suffered a significant setback in the Labour Court when his urgent application to halt the disciplinary process was struck off the roll.
Judge Connie Prinsloo found that the court lacked jurisdiction to hear the matter and that Khan had failed to establish urgency. The ruling effectively cleared the way for SAPS to continue with the internal disciplinary proceedings.
Khan’s legal team had argued that the disciplinary hearing proceeded in his absence while he was receiving medical treatment following a shooting in Johannesburg in June. However, the court did not consider the merits of his case, focusing instead on jurisdiction and urgency.
Khan, who served as deputy national head of SAPS Crime Intelligence, has become one of the most prominent figures in South Africa’s ongoing policing crisis.
He has been repeatedly linked to allegations of political interference within SAPS and has been named during proceedings before the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry, which is investigating claims of corruption, criminal infiltration and political interference in law enforcement.
Khan remains under subpoena by the commission, although his appearance has been delayed because of medical concerns. Separately, Khan is facing criminal charges alongside Gauteng Hawks head Major-General Ebrahim Kadwa and businessman Tariq Downes.
The trio are accused of defeating the ends of justice and contravening the Precious Metals Act over allegations that they facilitated the release of a businessman found in possession of an unwrought gold bar in 2021. All three have denied wrongdoing and are out on bail pending the continuation of their criminal case.

Who are the ‘Hilltop Girls’ behind Israel’s ‘soft settlement’ strategy?
Young Israeli women are adopting an ostensibly peaceful, domestic lifestyle on West Bank hilltops to quietly expand illegal outposts and realise a vision of a ‘Greater Israel’.
A radical movement of young Israeli women is leaving civilian life and education behind to live in rudimentary hilltop tents across the occupied West Bank.
Dubbed the “Hilltop Girls”, this group champions a strategy of “soft settlement”, replacing weapons and military patrols with seemingly mundane daily activities.
By portraying their presence as a natural, family-oriented social project, they aim to legitimise the gradual seizure of private Palestinian land and the establishment of new outposts.
So who are these young women?
The latest version of the ‘Hilltop Youth’
The women are in many ways an extension of the Hilltop Youth a radical religious Zionist group that emerged in 1998 when then-Israeli Foreign Minister Ariel Sharon urged settler youths to seize West Bank hilltops to preempt final status negotiations.
While the broader movement is infamous for orchestrating deadly pogroms and seizing territory by force, the female offshoot embraces an ideology geared towards establishing a “Greater Israel” that extends beyond historic Palestine to include Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and the Arabian Peninsula.
Social media settlers
To normalise their presence, the Hilltop Girls heavily rely on social media.
Outpost accounts publish promotional videos aiming to move away from the more violent images associated with marauding Israeli settlers, who are often backed and shielded by the country’s security forces.
The female settlers claim they do not kill Palestinians or assault landowners, but merely cook and hang laundry like any other group of women.
But their end goals are similar – to establish the so-called Promised Land, including through the extension of Israel to the occupied West Bank. Their presence in the West Bank is no less illegal than that of violent extremists. And they too are transforming Palestinian pastoral land into fully-fledged settlements in violation of international law.
Strategic expansion
The Maoz Esther and Or Ahuvia outposts, located northeast of Ramallah, serve as prime examples of this systematic expansion.
Established in 2006 as a small youth outpost, Maoz Esther was demolished and rebuilt multiple times before expanding into what is now known as the “Girls’ Hill”. By 2025, it housed 17 families and more than 50 children, exceeding the size of the neighbouring 950-dunam (235-acre) Kochav HaShahar settlement.
Similarly, the Or Ahuvia outpost, established in 2023 near the Ofra settlement, reflects a broader vision to create a massive settlement bloc. The ultimate goal is to connect more than 20 outposts to Ofra, creating an integrated network capable of absorbing thousands of families in the future.
State complicity
While Israeli police occasionally dismantle these outposts on camera, rights activists describe these operations as a coordinated theatrical display.
According to the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem, most outposts enjoy direct support from the state and the army, with the women immediately rebuilding structures as soon as police depart. Logistically, these outposts are supplied with water, electricity, private road networks and military protection by the Israeli Civil Administration.
Furthermore, the government provides nearly $40m in food and clothing subsidies to Hilltop Youth members.
The movement enjoys unprecedented legislative and political cover. In early 2025, the Knesset advanced a bill proposed by the “Land of Israel” lobby to allow Jews to purchase land in the West Bank freely, ensuring these acquisitions remain protected even in the event of future political agreements.
Politicians like far-right Ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir actively support these outposts, while Defence Minister Israel Katz recently boasted to his party: “I cancelled, on my own initiative, all administrative orders against settlers in the West Bank.”
The human toll of this ideological expansion is devastating. Between January 2025 and May 2026, the United Nations recorded at least 2,806 settler attacks, averaging five incidents a day.
Prominent Hilltop Youth leader Elisha Yered recently summarised their violent strategy on a podcast, stating: “We’re very proud of initiating friction; even the army is in friction.”
In 2026 alone, systematic settler pogroms displaced nearly 2,000 Palestinians, prompting both the UN and the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs to reiterate that these relentless land grabs fundamentally undermine the possibility of a viable Palestinian state.
