I own six guns. Here’s how to talk to conservatives about firearms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:30:39 UTC
22:30:39 KST

I have six guns in my house.
The first was a vintage Winchester 12-gauge. It was the winter of 1990, and my husband and I had just moved from an urban block in north-west Philadelphia to a 100-year-old farmhouse in Appalachian Virginia, where my family goes back seven generations.
That spring, we started sitting out back every night with the two outdoor dogs and 13 feral barn cats we had adopted since moving in. Invariably, our new neighbor Jimmy would drive by and stop for a beer.
One evening in March, the three of us looked up to see a bat flying out of the old attic. Then another, and another. We stopped counting at 100. Since our only access to the attic was through a 2ft hole in the closet ceiling, we installed a door in the hallway with a drop-down ladder.
After clearing out countless piles of hidden guano, we began to worry about histoplasmosis – not to mention rabies – as the vexatious critters clawed at the edges of the new entrance, trying to squeeze their way into the house. By mid-summer, we still had not succeeded in humanely relocating what was clearly a firmly established colony.
In exasperation, we turned to our newfound repository of rural knowledge – Jimmy – who brought over his old shotgun and suggested we shoot in the air to scare them away. The bats made an immediate 180 and proceeded to chase after the shot, as if they were tracking down moths and mosquitoes.
We lost no bats, but we did gain a gun.
Our second came the next fall. As with many rural homesteads, when the Department of Transportation straightened out the road decades earlier, they located it 20ft from our front porch. My husband was out of town a good bit that summer, and someone set up a ratty old trailer at one end of our two-mile, gravel road. An abandoned farmhouse sat at the other end, and a group of single male squatters moved in.
Foot traffic grew between the two, and we suspected meth was changing hands. While I was alone one night, a particularly rough-looking fellow from the trailer stumbled up the front steps to “borrow the phone”. That weekend we took a trip to Walmart and added a 20-gauge Remington youth model to our collection.
When my mom died 10 years later, I inherited her old BB gun and Remington 22; my husband also inherited one of each. He says the two childhood BB guns don’t really count, but I think they do.
When I told a second amendment-supporting friend about our collection, she said: “You need to lock them up or get rid of them.”
I don’t disagree.
In rural America, guns are a fact of life. But the preventable deaths that come with unsecured firearms don’t have to be.
That is why, for the past two years, I’ve been working with liberal volunteers to find common ground with conservative gun owners, beginning with something remarkably simple: giving away gun locks.
As national director of Community Works, a program of the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative, I bring together volunteers across political differences to address practical needs in their home communities.
Progressives won’t gain traction in rural areas by showing up at election time and asking people to change their politics. We have to earn trust year-round by acting locally alongside our conservative neighbors to make things better for everyone: cleaning up rivers, repairing homes, distributing food – even saving lives.
When working shoulder-to-shoulder with fellow volunteers one day, it’s harder to turn around and demonize them the next. National depictions of Democrats as godless baby-killers or Republicans as gun-waving racists just don’t hold up when those same folks are standing next to you handing out diapers and school supplies, or packing food for students in the free-lunch program.
Promoting gun safety put that concept to an unusually difficult test. Guns, after all, are one of the subjects widely considered unbridgeable in rural politics.
I was aware of that when I asked volunteers to hand out free gun locks in some of Virginia’s most conservative counties. I also knew the stakes: firearms are the leading cause of death among American children and teenagers, killing 2,581 children under 18 in 2023 alone.
But decades of polarization have made it near impossible to agree on even the simplest measures. Liberals caricature gun owners as uneducated rednecks or reckless young men stockpiling AR-15s; gun owners see liberals as bleeding hearts determined to confiscate their weapons. But keeping guns away from children seemed like the one place where we might meet.
The Gun Aware Project (Gap) was founded by Karen and Nick Fischer after a local high school murder-suicide in 2023. Gap organizes free gun-lock distributions during fall back-to-school events in public schools, and volunteers from Community Works were eager to help.
One of the first distributions took place in Giles county, on the West Virginia border. There, a growing number of residents support seceding from Virginia and joining West Virginia, in part because they believe Virginia’s new gun laws threaten their second amendment rights.
It would be easy to dismiss such a group with the “ignorant hillbilly” stereotype, except for the fact that my physical therapist and her doctor husband were thinking about joining. Despite the gun lobby’s success in pitting gun owners against those who aren’t – always leading to bigger gun sales – the “sides” are often more fluid than we’ve been led to believe.
Maybe that’s why the Giles county sheriff’s office, a strong defender of second amendment rights, agreed to collaborate with the Gun Aware Project. Sheriff W Morgan Millirons issued a statement describing firearm safety as part of responsible gun ownership.
To date, Gap has given away more than 4,000 locks, 1,000 of those to local departments like Millirons’. Volunteers have spoken with more than 15,000 people in a four-county area. No proselytizing – just sharing storage safety information along with the locks.
The Fischers say they have been surprised by the number of people in NRA hats and camo who say: “I really like what you’re doing, we need to protect our kids.” The second most common response is more what they expected: “I have a right to have a weapon. Why are you people trying to take it away?”
Attuned to the rural gun culture in which they are operating, the Fischers acknowledge the second amendment, and then redirect the conversation back to safety.
Karen explains that removing the magazine from a semi-automatic firearm does not necessarily unload it: a live round may remain in the chamber, something most children – and even some gun owners – do not realize. After listening to Karen, and learning the locks were free, one woman asked for enough locks to secure 12 guns, saying it would be a Christmas gift to her husband.
“The issue is not about taking away the second amendment,” says Nick. “The issue is how we deal with living with the second amendment.”
In the same vein, the goal of Community Works is not to overcome, or try to change, rural culture. It’s about understanding, respecting and learning to live alongside our conservative rural neighbors.
Early research suggests the approach may be working. More than 4,400 surveys were conducted before and after the launch of Community Works in six pilot counties in Virginia and Georgia, along with nearby counties without the new program.
According to the study’s author, the Colby College social scientist Dr Nicholas Jacobs, residents in participating counties became less influenced by national partisan divisions and more likely to judge parties by how well they governed locally. They began to view local Democrats as distinct from national party stereotypes, instead judging people based on their contributions to the community.
What we did not foresee is that Community Works would also change the way rural Democrats viewed and interacted with their communities.
One Democratic volunteer who helped to hand out gun locks at a rural high school event reflected: “I was actually kind of scared to do this in gun country. I thought they’d call me ‘woke’ and walk right on by. But all the kids and parents were really nice, and they totally agreed with me about gun safety.”
Her apprehension was understandable. For generations, rural people – and particularly Appalachians with guns – have been portrayed as violent and backward. If you’ve seen the 1972 movie Deliverance or the more recent Netflix series Justified, you know what I’m talking about.
Historically, the Appalachian hillbilly stereotype was created in the late 1800s by “local color” travel writers to sell their stories to urban readers. Shotguns, moonshine, bad teeth and dirty overalls were all part of the image. The timber, coal and railroad industries soon adopted the negative caricature as justification for their abusive exploitation of Appalachian landowners.
It worked. By successfully casting their victims as ignorant, uncivilized and dangerous – as “other” – the corporate profiteers were given societal sanction to deceitfully extract natural resources that then reaped them huge returns in urban centers.
Since then, urban and suburban liberals have been told over and over again to be wary of folks born and raised “country”, especially those with guns.
Such was the case when White Rural Rage: The Threat to American Democracy, was released in 2024. With captions proclaiming “[w]hite rural voters are the most dangerous and anti-democratic group in the United States,” the authors promoted the more sensational aspects of their research on numerous morning talkshows.
In one 40-second soundbite, they accused white rural voters of being racist, xenophobic, anti-immigrant and anti-gay, leading to their conclusion that white rural rage was the greatest threat to American democracy. At the time, the city-based authors received a good deal of backlash from Appalachian and rural advocates for their use of tropes and stereotypes to sell their book.
I often use my son’s friends as a barometer for gauging declarations I read about conservative rural white folks, especially young white males. Born and raised here, my son’s a country boy just like his friends, but unlike him, they were raised in families that have voted Republican for decades. Not even FDR or JFK were able to carry the vote in our county. Kids here wear camo and seed caps, drive pickup trucks, and skip school the first day of hunting season. They are also some of the nicest, most respectful, young people I know.
From where I stand, the idea of white rural rage as the driving force behind the downfall of democracy is just one more example of the perpetuation of stereotypes that divide the rural working class from our counterparts and natural allies in the cities.
Now, instead of the timber, coal and railroad barons benefiting, we have tech and software billionaires and corporate giants, including gun manufacturers, who wield massive control over information and commerce.
And just as in the late 19th century, it’s to the advantage of these new titans to keep the rest of us separated and blaming each other for school shootings and the price of gas and groceries, as in, “you got what you voted for.”
I’d like to think we’ve learned something in 150 years: that by working together across lines of geography, race, class, party and even guns, we might build a more equitable future.
For myself, after handing out scores of gun locks to my neighbors, I’ll be donating half our guns to a local effort called Groceries Not Guns, and safely storing the others using my brand new locks.
- 
  Meredith Dean is the national director of the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative’s Community Works program. Previously, she served as chair of her local Democratic party, field director for a congressional campaign, and was the founding director of a non-profit dedicated to empowering Appalachian women to actively engage in democracy

Ukraine takes the war to Russia’s space programme in tactical shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:30:28 UTC
22:30:28 KST

Ukraine takes the war to Russia’s space programme in tactical shift
From Moscow to Plesetsk, Ukraine appears to be trying to hit infrastructure that powers Russia’s war from space.
Kyiv, Ukraine – Russian Aerospace Forces (RAF) chief Aleksandr Chayko barely survived a blast that killed his son-in-law.
Chayko, who turned 55 in the last week of July, was reportedly having a belated birthday party on August 1 at a high-end Italian restaurant in central Moscow.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Is Trump wooing Russia again – and why?
- list 2 of 4Germany accuses Russia of failed drone attack on Leipzig airport in August
- list 3 of 4Can Ukraine’s drones shut Russian airspace? What that means for airlines
- list 4 of 4‘An impasse’: EU ministers fail to break deadlock over Israel and Ukraine
But the celebration was cut short, as an unidentified woman carrying a homemade bomb tried to enter the restaurant. She was stopped by a security guard, according to Russia. The explosive in her bag detonated, killing at least five people.
The Kremlin did not confirm the casualties, but blamed the attack on the “bloody tentacles” of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s government.
Kyiv has not commented on the attack.
Russia’s space programme in the firing line
Chayko helped lead Russia’s intervention in Syria and commanded Russian forces north of Kyiv in early 2022.
Ukraine has accused him of war crimes.
In May, President Vladimir Putin appointed him commander-in-chief of the RAF that controls the military component of Russia’s space programme.
The RAF’s satellites and ground-space facilities have been used for gathering intelligence, navigation, and supporting the coordination of ground troops and drone and missile attacks.
These facilities are located mostly in western Russia, and new Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles are capable of striking them.
“Key factories are few, and they all are within the reach of Ukrainian missiles,” Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher with Germany’s University of Bremen, told Al Jazeera.
“These attacks may result – and certainly will – in the problems with all of Russia’s space programme, including specifically civilian and international programmes,” he said.
‘Long-range sanctions’
In late June, Ukrainian drones hit the giant space communications centre in the leafy, tranquil town of Dubna outside Moscow that managed reconnaissance satellites and processed military data.
The strike damaged a 32-metre (105-foot) satellite antenna, hardware modular complexes, central control consoles and technical buildings.
“Our long-range sanctions against Russia for this war once again reached the Dubna space communications centre,” Zelenskyy said on June 30.
Russian authorities said an unspecified building in Dubna was damaged and a six-month-old baby died.
Ukrainian drones also struck three smaller space communication centres in western Russia and annexed Crimea.
“These centres are very expensive, very labour-consuming from the viewpoint of construction,” Anatoly Zak, a United States-based author and one of the foremost experts on the Russian space programme, told Al Jazeera. “It’s very difficult to transfer their functions to another infrastructure” because they manage geostationary satellites “tied” to a certain location.
So far, there have been no signs that the satellites lost orbit or became unmanageable, but “behind the scenes there are for sure serious communication problems”, Zak said.
Ukraine attacks ‘when there’s a fully-fuelled rocket on the launchpad’
On August 23, swarms of Ukrainian drones flew more than 1,800km (1,120 miles) to reach Russia’s northwestern Arkhangelsk region.
Some 40 drones were downed, regional authorities claimed, but at least two reached the area near Plesetsk, Russia’s military cosmodrome, or spaceport, and launchpad for intercontinental ballistic missiles and rockets carrying military satellites.
No harm was done. A day later, Roscosmos, the state-run space corporation, reported the successful launch of a rocket with unnamed “military satellites”.
The timing of the Ukrainian attack – along with two more strikes earlier this year – was calculated to strike a booster rocket that had just been fuelled and lifted for takeoff.
“There have been three attempts to air-raid Plesetsk, and not just air-raid, but air-raid at the moment when there’s a fully-fuelled rocket on the launchpad that is about to start,” Zak said.
The attempts were serious enough to be publicly reported to Putin.
“Our [Ukrainian] ‘friends’ did everything to make this launch not happen,” Dmitry Bakanov, head of the Kremlin-run Roscosmos space agency, told Putin in April.
At least a dozen drones are necessary to damage Plesetsk’s launch table or rocket assembly shop, according to Pavel Luzin, an analyst with the Jamestown Foundation, a think tank in Washington, DC.
The military satellites launched from Plesetsk are part of the Rassvet (Dawn) satellite fleet designed to rival and replace Starlink satellite modems by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company, Moscow claimed.
The world’s most launched spaceship
Sputnik 1, the Earth’s first artificial satellite, was the size of a fitness ball, and had nothing but a radio transmitter and three silver-zinc batteries inside.
The “Sputnik moment” was the US’s realisation, after the Soviet Union launched the first satellite in 1957, that the USSR had taken the lead in space technology and science.
But Sputnik 1 was launched on a modified R-7 – the world’s first intercontinental ballistic missile, designed to carry a hydrogen bomb across continents. The same rocket technology that could deliver a nuclear warhead into the US had been repurposed to put a satellite into orbit.
The R-7 became a prototype of the Soyuz booster rockets, the world’s most launched spaceships that made Soviet and then Russian launches routine and precise, unlike US launches of space shuttles.
“Rain or shine or sleet or snow don’t matter,” Mark Bowman, deputy director of NASA’s human spaceflight programme, told this reporter in 2007 at the Baikonur spaceport, the world’s oldest in southern Kazakhstan that Russia leases.
The only place where the Soyuz rockets are produced is the Progress Rocket and Space Centre in the Volga River city of Samara – and Ukrainian missiles struck it on August 15. The attack ignited a fire and slightly damaged one of the facilities.
“So far, we see that the damage in Samara wasn’t critical,” Luzin said.
If it becomes critical, Russia would be unable to manufacture the Soyuz rockets, but the existing stash of rockets would still last a year, he said.
Communist Moscow never advertised the military component of its space programme, emphasising its “peaceful exploration of space”.
The USSR was first to send a dog, a man and a woman into space, and to launch the world’s first space station. In 1988, its Buran space shuttle became the first to complete an unmanned orbital flight and land automatically.
Its unmanned probes soft-landed on Venus and Mars and took the first photos of the moon’s dark side.
Some key figures of the Soviet space programmes were born in what is now Ukraine, and a string of crucial design bureaus and manufacturing facilities kept working there after the 1991 Soviet collapse.
Following Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and the subsequent breakdown in Russian-Ukrainian relations, Ukrainian aerospace facilities severed their longstanding ties with Moscow, disrupting decades-old supplies of booster rockets, guidance systems, electronics and other components.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine also deepened the international isolation of its civilian space programme, with Western governments and space agencies suspending or abandoning several planned missions and partnerships.
After the war began in 2022, the European Space Agency terminated its cooperation with Roscosmos on ExoMars, removing the Russian-built Kazachok landing platform from the mission designed to search for signs of past life on Mars.
The same year, Berlin switched off its X-ray telescope on Spektr-RG, a Russia-German space observatory that maps clusters of galaxies and surveys the universe for black holes.
For the sake of seizing insignificant areas in eastern Ukraine, “Putin will waste the Russian space programme the way he wasted the rest of the Soviet legacy”, analyst Mitrokhin believes.
Yet Russia has not been completely cut off from international space cooperation.
Despite the collapse of some partnerships, NASA and Roscosmos have continued to work together on board the International Space Station, while Moscow has turned to China and other non-Western partners for new projects.

The Ceuta border breach was leapt on by Europe’s right. That doesn’t absolve Spain | María Ramírez
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:29:48 UTC
22:29:48 KST

More than a month after an estimated 72,000 people suddenly crossed from Morocco into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, the city remains in chaos and the damage inflicted on the Spanish government is becoming clearer. Most of those who made the crossing have returned to Morocco. The scale of the incident was nevertheless extraordinary, and about 140 people are thought to have died.
Also extraordinary was the response of the 22 EU governments that rounded on the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, rather than demonstrate the solidarity one might expect from allies. Perhaps less surprising was the exploitation of the crisis by rightwing and far-right parties in Spain and beyond, Donald Trump’s attacks and the interventions of Russian state-linked actors and Israeli critics on social media to fuel division.
But this opportunism by Europe’s rightwing governments – Italy suspended its Schengen arrangements with Spain for no good reason – does not absolve Spain of blame. What has unfolded since 30 July is tragic for Ceuta, which has a permanent population of only about 84,000 people, and for the thousands of people, including an estimated 1,200 unaccompanied children, left on its streets and beaches. Sánchez’s government must take responsibility for some of the damage it is now belatedly trying to mop up.
On 1 August, in the aftermath of the border breach, Sánchez reassured the EU that “virtually all” of the people who had arrived in Ceuta had returned to Morocco. The overwhelming majority did indeed leave, but thousands did not – and they are still in the city. Official numbers have fluctuated. The Spanish government’s estimate is that 5,000 of those who arrived are still in Ceuta; the region’s local government has suggested it could be double that. For weeks, there was no accommodation available, and hundreds are still camped on beaches or near the overcrowded migrant centres.
People living near these centres complain they cannot leave their apartments out of fear, and that their children are unable to play on the beach or in the street. Businesses have had to close for days on end, incurring losses. Summer festivities had to be cancelled. Many migrants, including women and children, have survived on charity from local NGOs, the Red Cross and neighbours, and have little food, water and shelter.
Yet as the situation deteriorated, the Spanish government failed for weeks to appoint anyone to coordinate a response. This would have been essential in Spain’s decentralised system, with powers divided between the central government and local and regional authorities. Now Madrid is finally funnelling resources and money into the matter, but only after the situation had deteriorated dangerously.
Tensions have been evident in recent days, with local people crying in front of TV cameras, and politicians pleading for help. Protests directed against migrants have been constant. They have been mostly peaceful, but there have been outbreaks of violence. In one incident, a group of protesters tried to drive migrants off the beach and burned their tents before they were dispersed by the police with teargas. In another, military police were allegedly assaulted by a group from Morocco. At least 23 sexual assaults against migrants have been reported, including nine against children.
Ceuta was already fragile. The city, smaller than the site of Madrid airport, is home to a multicultural community that has been part of Spain since the 17th century. But even before this, its citizens complained about feeling abandoned. And now Morocco is reviving claims of sovereignty.
Sánchez’s defence of Morocco – telling parliament on Thursday that there was “no evidence” that Rabat had orchestrated events at the border – is at odds with popular sentiment in Ceuta and with most of the parties in parliament, including his leftwing allies Sumar, the minority partner in the governing coalition.
The Spanish government’s slow response and state of denial are damaging not only for Ceuta, but for Madrid’s own message on immigration. Spain has quite successfully promoted immigration as a force for good in recent years, even as most governments in Europe have moved in the opposite direction. What happened in Ceuta should not diminish the case for immigration as a factor driving economic growth and social dynamism, as Spain has shown over the past decade. But the mismanagement of Ceuta on the ground will inevitably impair that message.
Even now, the Spanish government is backtracking, tightening its migration rules and pointing to disinformation around a supreme court decision that protected migrants’ rights against speedy returns as a cause for the rush on Ceuta. It has said it will stop transferring unaccompanied minors out of the territory and distributing them around the country for their protection, and is approving restrictions in line with the hardline EU pact on migration and asylum pushed by rightwing governments.
Regional politicians, who are mostly conservative, refuse to help out. The conservative People’s party (PP), which is leading in the polls before next year’s general election, is always better at attacking the government than clarifying what it would do differently. But even some local politicians from the Socialist Workers’ party have recently joined demonstrations in solidarity with Ceuta.
The Ceuta episode has landed Spain with an almost impossible situation to resolve. But a combination of passivity and blaming everyone but Morocco has not helpedthe city’s residents, Sánchez’s political position or the positive case for immigration in Spain and beyond.
- 
  María Ramírez is a journalist and deputy managing editor of elDiario.es, a news outlet in Spain

Palestinians gather around a destroyed vehicle on a street after an Israeli military strike.
Israel has plans ready to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip but is waiting for the United States to figure out where to take them, the defense minister has said.
“There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration,” Defense Minister Israel Katz told a conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
The Israeli government “is organized and prepared to get them out, by sea, by air, by every way possible,” he said.
U.S. President Donald Trump, at the start of his second term, stunned much of the world by calling for all two million Palestinians to leave the Gaza Strip.
Trump spoke of developing the Mediterranean territory, devastated by Israeli bombardment since the 2023 attack by Hamas, into a luxury resort destination.
Trump walked back the idea following strong pushback including from Egypt, the only country other than Israel to border Gaza.
The proposal was also condemned by Palestinians themselves, for whom any effort to force them off their land would recall the “Nakba”, or catastrophe -- their mass displacement during Israel’s creation in 1948.
Katz, known for his outspoken remarks, said that Trump had only “frozen” the idea as he looks for countries to take in Palestinians, as Egypt is not an option.
“The plan hasn’t been cancelled; it is being discussed all the time, even now, and I think there is no other solution for everyone’s good,” he said.
“But for it to happen, we need the U.S. When will we get their approval? Whenever it becomes clear that Hamas is not meeting its obligations” under the ceasefire, he said.
Katz, without citing his source, said 80 percent of people in Gaza wanted to leave but that Hamas was preventing them.

BJP accuses Kejriwal, Mann, his wife of running a 'syndicate' to settle rape cases in Punjab. (Pradeep Bhandari, Bhagwant Mann)

Police detain 16 in renewed Yavne’el child-marriage investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:22:42 UTC
22:22:42 KST

Police detained 16 minors and adults in Yavne’el on Thursday over suspected involvement in illegal child marriages, marking the second major operation in the Lower Galilee town in three months.
Dozens of officers raided several locations after investigators received information indicating that minors had recently married or that concrete preparations had begun for illegal wedding ceremonies, police said.
The adults questioned were described as members of the minors’ immediate circles.
The raid followed an operation in June in which over 20 people were questioned over suspected involvement in arranging, conducting, and concealing underage marriages within what police described as a small, closed community centered in Yavne’el.
According to police, the ceremonies are generally held in the morning hours, with few participants. Locations are withheld until shortly before the ceremony, and phones and photography are prohibited to prevent documentation.
In many cases, police said, the religious ceremony is followed by a larger gathering presented publicly as an engagement party, which is not prohibited by law.
The methods make it difficult for investigators to establish that a marriage has taken place, particularly when there is no photographed ceremony, signed ketubah, or witness willing to give evidence.
During an earlier operation, officers found a young couple dressed as a bride and groom and recovered a ketubah, wedding rings, and a foil-wrapped glass hidden inside a water-system cabinet, according to police.
Israeli law bars marriages before 18
Israeli law generally prohibits marriage before the age of 18. A family court may grant permission from age 16 in exceptional circumstances when it finds that marriage is in the minor’s interests.
Absent such permission, adults who marry a minor, officiate at or assist with the marriage, or cause their child to marry can face up to two years in prison.
The central problem exposed in Yavne’el is the difficulty of detecting the ceremonies, protecting the minors involved, and producing evidence that can support criminal charges.
The Yavne’el investigation comes amid evidence of wider failures in the enforcement of Israel’s Marriage Age Law.
A May report by the Knesset Research and Information Center identified substantial, unexplained gaps between government records.
The Population and Immigration Authority said it referred 128 suspected cases to police in 2023, 95 in 2024, and 98 in 2025. Police, however, reported receiving 23 complaints from all sources in 2023, including seven from the authority, and 15 in 2024.
Those discrepancies have raised questions about whether information held by hospitals, schools, welfare departments, religious institutions, and the authority reaches police early enough to prevent underage marriages, rather than necessitating investigation after the fact.
Yesh Atid MK Meirav Cohen, who chairs the Knesset Committee on the Status of Women and Gender Equality, arrived uninvited at a Yavne’el Local Council meeting on Wednesday, one day before the police operation.
Cohen said she went to the meeting after council head Snir Arish failed to attend parliamentary hearings or participate in a committee visit to the town.
Arish accused the council and its welfare department of failing to protect children and alleged that boys and girls continued to be married under pressure within the community.
The council has previously rejected accusations of inaction. Arish said in July that the municipality continuously assisted law enforcement authorities and that its welfare department provided daily support to affected residents.
Yavne'el school principal alleged to have arranged marriages for minor daughters
Questions have also been raised about educational oversight after a school principal in Yavne’el was summoned for a hearing over allegations that she had arranged marriages for her daughters while they were minors, yet she remained in her position as the school year began.
The principal denied that an illegal marriage had taken place, saying that an event documented in media reports was a traditional henna ceremony and that her daughter would not marry before turning 18.
The Education Ministry said in August that it was examining the matter and would act according to its findings and legal authority.
Police said on Thursday that the investigation would continue in cooperation with other enforcement and welfare authorities.

====================================================================================================

New details reveal clashes that stopped beeper op. against Hezbollah days after Oct. 7 - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:22:20 UTC
22:22:20 KST

Readers of The Jerusalem Post are very familiar with the byline of Yonah Jeremy Bob.
As the senior military analyst and correspondent for the paper over the last half-decade (and before that, its legal correspondent), his stories have encapsulated and explained the dizzying pace of events the country has endured in recent years and have helped readers understand the implications and intricacies of the wars, campaigns, negotiations, and dilemmas that are a constant part of Israel’s landscape.
If we abide by the 1943 adage by American journalist Alan Barth that “news is only the first rough draft of history,” then the new book by Bob, together with Wall Street Journal editorial writer Elliot Kaufman, In The War Room: The Inside Story of Israel’s Fight Against Hamas and the Iranian Axis, is a final sculpted treatise that is a must-read for anyone who cares about the pivotal developments that led up to the cataclysmic events of October 7, 2023, and resulted in the ongoing battle against Iran and its proxies in Gaza and Lebanon.
It reads like a gripping, yet almost improbable espionage novel at times, and the proof in the pudding of Bob and Kaufman’s ability to weave an intriguing tale is that although we know what transpired in each successive development in the unbelievable timeline of events – whether the beeper and pager campaign against Hezbollah or the cataclysmic attack by Israel and the US on Iran’s nuclear facilities – readers feel compelled to turn the page such that it is as if they’re discovering the details all anew.
In the War Room provides an inside account of how Israel came back from its darkest hour after Oct. 7 to decimate Hamas and Hezbollah and command the skies over Tehran.
Inside the war room
The recurring focus of the book that provides the insider coverage most spectacularly is the ongoing meetings taking place between the masterminds of the Israeli campaign to change the post-Oct. 7 regional landscape and fight a multi-pronged war – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, then-defense minister Yoav Gallant, and then-war minister Benny Gantz.
Bob and Kaufman place the reader as a fly on the wall as the contentious trio makes fateful decisions, constantly switching allegiances, opinions, and strategies – with one eye on the war and the other eye on each other.
The prose shows the war leaders expressing both doubt and conviction about how Israel should proceed and maneuver amid Hamas intransigence, growing US opposition to Israel’s policies, internal pressure due to the ongoing hostage situation, and damning world opinion.
Doves became hawks and hawks became doves depending on the situation and the decisions to be made. One can almost feel the perspiration under their military-chic black buttoned-down shirts as they deliberated in tense sessions in the “Kirya,” where day and night don’t exist.
“Gantz, the supposed dove, along with Gallant and [then-IDF chief of staff Herzi] Halevi, once again pressed Netanyahu to green-light an invasion. They told the prime minister that there was no way to get additional Israeli hostages back from [Yahya] Sinwar without cornering the Hamas leader to a point where he would fear being caught. They also noted that so long as Khan Yunis was in the hands of Hamas, the terrorist group would retain the strength to operate as a national military organization.”
THE AUTHORS state that later in the war, after Netanyahu fired Gallant and Gantz quit, the war room transformed into the prime minister’s personal domain.
“For all the war room’s dysfunction and small-minded rivalries, for large portions of the war, Netanyahu, Gallant, and Gantz balanced each other’s views. This may have helped Israel avoid major errors and kept its relations with US Democrats and Western Europe from collapsing.”
Once Gantz quit and Netanyahu fired Gallant, the prime minister had no war room of substance to push back on his ideas – or those of his coalition partners. He did not think he would miss Gantz or Gallant, but on this, he did.”
Bob and Kaufman had unprecedented access to the actors, and the writing is based on two years of private interviews and briefings with the Israeli triumvirate, meetings with the top Israeli military and intelligence officials, and trips to combat zones on four fronts: Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, and the West Bank.
In addition, they interviewed top Biden and Trump administration figures, including former US National Security advisor Jake Sullivan and Trump administration envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff.
But instead of just a “then they said” account, the writers utilize their vast backgrounds and expertise to put you inside the heads of the main players and help the reader understand their motives amid the global chess game taking place, like this passage on Gallant:
“In the days after October 7, however, Gallant mainly was trying to decide – and then convince a notoriously hard-to-pin-down prime minister and cabinet – what Israel’s policy should be against Hezbollah.
“Armed by Iran with an extraordinary missile arsenal, the US-designated terrorist group had long cowed the Lebanese Armed Forces and shared Hamas’s goal of destroying the Jewish state. In support of Hamas’s invasion, Hezbollah started shooting rockets at northern Israel the very next day, on October 8.
“Gallant still believed, as he did before the war, that Hezbollah, not Hamas, posed the larger, perhaps existential threat to Israel.
“During his sleepless night, he came to two conclusions. First, Israel needed to execute a devastating strike against Hezbollah right away.
“A combination of intelligence, sabotage, artillery, and air power could cripple the terrorist group before it could use its well-trained troops and tens of thousands of sophisticated missiles to follow up Hamas’s attack with a far more powerful assault of its own. This would allow Israel to regain the initiative, shock the Iranian terror axis, and isolate Hamas in Gaza.
“Second, Gallant concluded that Netanyahu, his Likud party leader and boss in Israel’s coalition government, though renowned for his hawkishness, would be dead set against his proposal.”
The authors deliberately shy away from the non-military aspects of the war and how they dominated the Israeli discourse for over two years while the agonizing hostage saga played out.
There’s none of the anguish of the families, the protests against the government (except in how public pressure affected or didn’t affect decision-making), the tragic personal stories of the war or the drama and trauma the country went through watching on TV as hostages were released in gruesome Hamas-led ceremonies and then were reunited with their families. That’s the topic of another book.
The hostages are mentioned perfunctorily, as in this passage:
“From November 23 to November 30, 2023, the fighting paused. Hamas would return around 100 hostages in exchange for the release of more than three times as many Palestinian security prisoners from Israel. This deal – or ransom – was hammered out by Mossad Director David Barnea and Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim al-Thani, two men who influenced the course of the war from the shadows.”
Writing from an Israeli perspective
What’s also lacking in the book, to its great benefit, is a sense of even-handedness. Bob and Kaufman start from a belief that Oct. 7 was an atrocity that had to be answered. It’s written from a Zionist perspective and surely won’t be used as required reading in a US liberal arts Middle Eastern studies course.
Writing about October 17, 2023, the authors state:
“That day, Hamas said an Israeli air strike on Gaza City’s al-Ahli Arab Hospital had killed at least 500 Palestinians. That would be the headline in The New York Times and across the world. By the next day, however, it would turn out that the attack wasn’t Israeli, it wasn’t an air strike, it didn’t hit the hospital, nowhere close to 500 people were killed, and Hamas knew it.
“Israeli intelligence indicated that the culprit was a rocket launched by Islamic Jihad from a cemetery. It had fallen short, as the terrorists’ rockets often did, and landed in the hospital’s parking lot. President [Joe] Biden affirmed that finding less than 24 hours after the incident, a key early moment of support for Israel.”
But in the half-day period of uncertainty, the media leaped to echo the Hamas report. The BBC explained that the Israelis “said they are investigating, but it is hard to see what else this could be, really, given the size of the explosion, other than an Israeli air strike, or several air strikes.”
The world received the story essentially as Rep. Rashida Tlaib, the Michigan Democrat, put it on social media: “Israel just bombed the Baptist Hospital killing 500 Palestinians (doctors, children, patients).” The damage was done. The Oct. 7 attack was only 10 days old, but a new narrative was already forming.
WITHIN THE context of presenting the events from an Israeli perspective, and with Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran portrayed for what they are – bloodthirsty elements aimed at Israel’s destruction – they manage to provide a subjective account of what transpired, without bringing in their own political biases or opinions.
Discussing the prickly subject of whether Israel could have ended the war and brought the hostages home earlier, the authors just present the facts, ma’am.
“Israel had opportunities to conclude the fighting at earlier junctures. In the summer of 2024, after the invasion of Rafah. In March 2025, extending the second hostage deal. In each case, the prime minister refused, deciding to fight on for better terms.
“Gallant, Gantz, and Halevi had reservations, but were willing to accept the terms of the deals on the table. Halevi believed that Netanyahu had not sufficiently invested in negotiations about the second phase of the January 2025 hostage deal, involving the shaping of postwar Gaza.”
And:
“Critics will say the prime minister fought on only to keep power. Netanyahu would say that after October 7, Israel needed total victory to restore security and deterrence. The debate would then go on in endless circles about whether total victory was even possible, and whether the interest being pursued was national or personal.
“For a time, pushing forward worked to Israel’s advantage. Even against great pressure, Netanyahu prevailed to maintain the war to keep open the possibility of invading Rafah, defeating Hezbollah, and destroying the Iranian nuclear program and proxy axis should the right opportunities arise for him.
“But continuing beyond that? The quest to end the fight in Gaza on a similarly convincing victory would drain Israel – and cost it severely on the world stage.”
Israel-haters who will bristle at the stingy use of the word “genocide” in the prose may eschew the book as just some more Israeli propaganda. But for historians, diplomats, and anyone who’s passionate about Israel and the continuation of the Zionist endeavor, In the War Room will indeed be required reading.
Bob and Kaufman have written one of the definitive, in-depth, and easily readable accounts of one of the most amazing periods of Israeli history that will continue to reverberate around the region for decades to come.
Their ability to synthesize and analyze the big events and put them into perspective will be a valuable resource for scholars and researchers in years to come. And they never lose sight of the main reason that the book exists.
“Despite all the successes and theatrics Israel would pull off in Iran and Lebanon, October 7 remains the day of this war which has seared deepest into the Israeli mind. Hamas invaded from Gaza and packed an entire intifada’s worth of slaughter into a single day, setting everything else into motion.” ■
The reviewer is the former managing editor of The Jerusalem Post.
IN THE WAR ROOM: THE INSIDE STORY OF ISRAEL’S FIGHT AGAINST HAMAS AND THE IRANIAN AXIS
By Yonah Jeremy Bob and Elliot Kaufman
A Wicked Son Book/
Post Hill Press
352 pages; $32.50

Supreme Court president warns of physical violence against legal figures after vebal attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:22:13 UTC
22:22:13 KST

Supreme Court Chief Justice Isaac Amit warned on Wednesday that verbal attacks by public officials and on social media can pave the way for physical violence against judges and lawyers, calling for restraint as Israel’s election campaign intensifies.
“The path to physical violence first passes through verbal violence,” Amit said at a special Israel Bar Association conference in Tel Aviv, convened following the killing of attorney Arbel Feldman at his Rishon LeZion office last month.
Violence against legal professionals does not occur in isolation, Amit noted, arguing that degrading public discourse about judges inevitably reaches courtrooms and the lawyers working in them.
The conference had originally been intended to mark the opening of the legal year, Amit said, but was repurposed after Feldman was shot dead on August 4.
Amit described the killing as part of what he characterized as a wider period of verbal and physical violence directed at lawyers and other legal professionals because of their work.
Such violence risks damaging more than the individuals targeted, he said. Lawyers serve as the link between citizens, the law, and the state; threats may deter them from taking controversial or difficult cases, meeting clients alone, or representing them effectively.
Amit said some courts had closed proceedings to the public and used live broadcasts because of concerns about disturbances. In more serious cases, he said, court security personnel have escorted lawyers and litigants to their vehicles.
He also cited the June riot outside the Alon Shvut home of Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, in which protesters damaged the house and Sohlberg’s car while members of his family were inside.
Dozens were detained following the disturbance. Amit said the incident had been intended to intimidate Sohlberg and other judges over their judicial work.
He also referred to recent verbal attacks against Jerusalem Magistrate’s Court Deputy President Oren Silverman and Nazareth-Nof Hagalil Magistrate’s Court Deputy President Ruth Spielberg-Cohen, though he did not identify the speakers or statements involved.
Election campaign necessitates careful action by public figures
Amit placed particular emphasis on the election campaign, warning that heated political disagreement increased the responsibility of public figures and others to choose their language carefully.
“An election campaign is, by nature, a period of disagreement, criticism, and struggle over ideas and the direction of the country,” he said. “But precisely during such a period, we all bear greater responsibility to act with restraint.”
At the end of the conference, the Bar Association and five other professional organizations signed a joint charter titled “Workers Without Fear.”
The organizations agreed to establish a permanent forum addressing violence against workers and professionals, promote legislative changes and reporting mechanisms, and coordinate with the government, Knesset, police, and other enforcement authorities.
The signatories included representatives for teachers, nurses, social workers, public-health physicians, and public-transportation drivers. They also committed to responding collectively to serious attacks against members of any one of the participating professions.
Israel Bar Association head Amit Becher called Feldman’s killing the most severe expression of what he described as an expanding pattern of threats and violence against lawyers.
“Harming lawyers is harming the rule of law,” Becher said, calling for faster enforcement, deterrent penalties, and measures to protect lawyers facing credible threats.
The Bar Association will seek legislation equating an assault on a lawyer with an assault on a public servant, he said.
Representatives of the other organizations said the problem extended well beyond the legal profession. Teachers, nurses, social workers, doctors, and bus drivers described workers facing threats and assaults while providing essential public services, often without adequate staffing or protection.
Suspect indicted for murder of Arbel Feldman
Feldman, a father of three, was killed after a former client allegedly entered his office and shot him several times, according to police and prosecutors.
A prosecutor’s statement was filed on August 25, formally notifying the court that charges were being prepared. The following day, the Central District Attorney’s Office indicted Ahmad Alargov, 24, of Ramle, in the Central District Court in Lod.
Alargov was charged with murder under aggravated circumstances, carrying a weapon and ammunition, destroying evidence, and obstructing justice.
According to the indictment, Feldman represented Alargov in civil proceedings involving an approximately NIS 18,000 insurance claim following a road accident.
Prosecutors allege that Alargov became dissatisfied with the pace of the claim, armed himself with a loaded semiautomatic handgun, and fired six shots at Feldman at close range.
The indictment describes a dispute between Feldman and a former client and does not allege a political motive.
Amit nevertheless used the killing as the starting point for a broader warning about violence against legal professionals and the effect of hostile public discourse on the justice system.

Germany was investigating a suspected arson attack outside a defense firm in Munich on Thursday, days after two sabotage attempts on the power grid and a month after an airport drone attack that Berlin and its allies blamed on Russia.

The suspects, a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man, both Bulgarian, were arrested at a nearby petrol station, police in the state of Bavaria said.
Germany on alert after attempts on power grid

Germany has been the focus of European fears about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure this week.
Allies rallied round after Germany blamed a drone attack in August at Leipzig/Halle airport on Moscow as part of hybrid warfare meant to intimidate and divide countries that have supported Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
While investigations continue and the European Union weighs more sanctions, Russia strongly denies involvement and on Thursday said it would close Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centers, reciprocating similar moves from Berlin. Poland and Britain summoned Russian diplomats, as other European allies had.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul welcomed an "impressive display of solidarity" as he met Polish and French counterparts, adding: "I believe that its impact has not gone unnoticed in Moscow, either."
This week, police investigated two attempts to sabotage the electricity grid within 24 hours in the states of Brandenburg and North Rhine-Westphalia.
Interior minister warns of foreign powers using extremist group as proxies

On Sunday, a closely watched election takes place in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right, Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) holds a commanding lead in surveys.
At the meeting with Wadephul in Weimar, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said Warsaw had summoned the Russian ambassador to express a "strong condemnation of Russian state terrorism".
In Germany's northern neighbor Denmark, the national security and intelligence service PET said Russia was recruiting Danish citizens to help plan sabotage against Danish defense firms with ties to Ukraine.
The PET has uncovered examples of Russia trying to recruit Danes on social media and gaming platforms for tasks such as taking photos of companies or infrastructure that could be used in planning sabotage, a statement said.
German investigators are also still pursuing leads in Poland and Serbia related to the Leipzig drone attack, the Spiegel magazine reported on Thursday, citing security sources.
One suspect was linked to another act of sabotage at a hardware store in Lodz, Poland, in July 2024, Spiegel reported.
Investigators are also examining links between the Leipzig attack and the discovery of a drone and explosives at the Serbian-Hungarian border, Spiegel said.
The Federal Criminal Office did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. A court in the Serbian city of Subotica said proceedings were under way against two suspects.

Mladic died in UN custody in The Hague on August 27. The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, which succeeded the ICTY, had repeatedly rejected his defense team’s requests for early release on health grounds.
Milorad Dodik, leader of the ruling Alliance of Independent Social Democrats in Republika Srpska, described Mladic’s death in custody as a deliberate killing. Vucic said the Hague court had deliberately prevented Mladic from dying a dignified death in Serbia.

UK summons Russian diplomat over 'reckless' Leipzig drone attack

13:20:12 UTC
22:20:12 KST

Britain joined a wave of European condemnation of the Leipzig airport drone incident, as EU officials warned the bloc is now facing "state-sponsored terrorism" and a "hybrid war" with Russia.
Britain's Foreign Office summoned Russia's most senior diplomat in the country on Thursday to condemn what it called an "egregious and reckless attack" involving a drone at Leipzig airport last month.
"Today we summoned the Russian charge d'affaires to condemn the attack in the strongest terms," a spokesperson said in a statement, describing the incident, which involved an explosive-laden drone, as "the latest in a clear pattern of attempts by the Russian state to undermine our collective security."
The Leipzig/Halle Airport incident, on the night of 4-5 August, saw police use a robot to defuse a device found near a Ukrainian cargo plane, after months of suspicious drone sightings over German military and industrial sites had already put Berlin on alert.
A second drone, also carrying traces of an explosive substance, was reportedly found near the airport weeks later.
Germany's government has blamed Russia for the incident, with the country's interior minister saying it "fits the known pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe," and Berlin has since moved to close Russia's consulate in Bonn and its cultural centre in the capital.
Russia has called the allegations "absurd," with its embassy in Germany rejecting the accusations as "unsubstantiated" and warning of "consequences" over the German response.
'We will not tolerate it'
The UK's move follows a wave of condemnation from other European capitals and institutions. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, speaking at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Ireland, said: "It is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism."
She added: "The question is, what do we do about this?"
Kallas said the EU had summoned the Russian envoy, with member states doing the same.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the Leipzig incident marked "a new escalation" in Europe.
"This was an attack using military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil," she said after talks with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
"We will not tolerate it," Von der Leyen warned and said that such incidents had become a "new normal" for Europe as Russia steps up destabilising activities.
Poland's top diplomat, Radoslaw Sikorski, struck a similarly stark tone: "We do not seek conflict with Russia, but Russia seems to be at hybrid war with us.
"We are no longer in regular peacetime."

Science on the go: 10 EU-funded podcasts, from AI to climate change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:17:18 UTC
22:17:18 KST

Are you curious about science? Or are you just looking for new ways to expand your knowledge of EU science and innovation? Either way, we’ve got you covered!Podcasts are an engaging way to learn something new, and you can listen to them wherever you like – at home, in the office, on your commute or out and about.Give these podcasts developed by EU-funded researchers a listen to learn about a wide range of different research areas.ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE"Bits of Ethics" is a podcast produced as part of AIOLIA, a project which focuses on turning high-level EU AI Act ethical principles into practical tools. The podcast explores the gap between AI ethics theory and real-world practice, featuring episodes on topics like artificial love and AI avatars.CITIZEN SCIENCEThe European Citizen Science (ECS) podcast is a new initiative exploring the scope and impact of citizen science projects in Europe. In the first two episodes, you can explore the topics of inclusion and participation in citizen science and hear perspectives from different actors questioning current practices, motivations and success stories.CLIMATE CHANGEThe ScienceUs Podcast connects you with the researchers and practitioners who are shaping the future of climate change adaptation. Episode 1 features Thermo-staat, a Dutch project giving residents simple sensors to measure rising indoor temperatures. Episode 2 looks into EcoVoce, a Romanian project providing residents with a mobile app and digital mapping tools to monitor environmental issues.CLIMATE DISINFORMATIONThe Just Europe podcast series takes a closer look at the challenges we face on the path to a fair and inclusive Europe. The latest episode is on climate disinformation and features researcher Max Falkenberg of the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions-funded POLARCLIMATE project.DEMOCRACY AND EU ENLARGEMENTThe REUNIR project is analysing the instability of the EU’s eastern neighbourhood by evaluating threats to the resilience of candidate countries. In their podcast series, find episodes dedicated to the interference of external actors such as Russia.FOOD FRAUDThe EFF-CoP project aims to fight food fraud – the deliberate act of altering, substituting, mislabelling or counterfeiting food, ingredients, or packaging for economic gain. Listen to their “Authentic Appetites” podcast series, where each episode treats a different facet of their mission to enhance transparency in our food supply chains.FRESHWATER RESTORATIONBringing Europe’s Freshwaters Back to Life is the title - and the theme - of the MERLIN project’s podcast. It followed the project’s journey into freshwater restoration across Europe, offering a behind the scenes look at some of the continent’s ambitious projects carried out through cutting-edge aquatic science and conservation.LITERATURE AND GENDER The EUTERPE project studies how women’s writing across Europe moves between languages, borders and cultures, to create open resources and better understand what it means to be European today. Listen to their podcast series featuring interviews with doctoral researchers, conversations with writers, poetry readings and more.MIGRATIONThe Link4Skills project is investigating how cross-border migration can help address skill shortages across the world. Throughout 2026, project members will contribute to several episodes of the award-winning podcast Borders & Belonging to share insights into their research.SCANNING TECHNOLOGIESEach monthly episode of the CORDIScovery podcast touches on an EU-funded project, idea, or debate in science. The latest episode focuses on the world of new scanning technologies, which are identifying illegal items – from small packages to large shipping containers – more effectively than ever.Views and opinions expressed are those of the author(s) only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or European Research Executive Agency (REA). Curious about the European Research Executive Agency? Find out more on LinkedIn, X or Mastodon. Publication date1 September 2026AuthorEuropean Research Executive Agency

Unknown Publisher

22:16:54 KST

MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. Russia’s international reserves amounted to $774.2 bln as of August 28, 2026, having increased by $13 bln in one week, the Central Bank reported.
"International reserves amounted to $774.2 bln as of the end of the day on August 28, 2026, having increased by $13 bln, or by 1.7%, in one week mainly due to positive revaluation," the regulator said.
As of August 21, the country’s reserves totaled $761.2 bln.
Russia’s international reserves are highly liquid foreign assets available with the Bank of Russia and the Russian government. They comprise foreign currency, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), a reserve position in the International Monetary Fund, and monetary gold. Following the onset of Moscow’s special military operation in Ukraine Western countries slapped sanctions against the Bank of Russia. Apart from freezing Russia’s gold and foreign currency reserves, all transactions related to management of the regulator’s reserves and assets, as well as transactions with any legal entity, organization or body acting on behalf or at the direction of the Central Bank, were prohibited.

Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:15:26 UTC
22:15:26 KST

Nvidia will buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips.
Shares in Nvidia were slightly lower after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday.
Hugging Face, based in New York and backed by the likes of Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf.
Nvidia is already a major open AI player in the US with its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology.
Acquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to collaborate and test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the technology gap with top American and Chinese labs.
“Nvidia gains visibility into customer’s preferences and the AI models they use,” said Naveen Chhabra, principal analyst at Forrester. “They can see which models are trending, what datasets customer are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news.”
Demand for open-weight models has surged from businesses balking at the steep bill of deploying generative AI. Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai have emerged as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks including generating computer code at a lower cost.
There are fears that some US firms could become reliant on Beijing’s models even as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future. The Trump administration has scrambled to respond to the wave of open models from China, weighing whether to restrict their use while also worrying about stifling American businesses that have taken to using them.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, was a signatory of an open letter earlier this year from major tech firms that advocated for open models and warned against government regulation that would stifle their use. Huang pledged that Nvidia would keep Hugging Face open after acquiring it.
“Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” said Huang, adding that his company’s chips would not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face.
Under the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention program of up to $1bn for employees who join Nvidia.
For Nvidia, building up its open source business may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance on its costly and supply-constrained processors. Several Chinese chip-making firms have also made recent advancements that could further disrupt the balance of power within big tech, though they face strict international export controls.
It has been a volatile year in the market for chipmakers, with a chip stock selloff in July wiping $1tn from the market caps of leading firms. Nvidia shares bounced back in August, though, with a strong revenue forecast leading to the second-biggest one-day gain in market history – adding $442bn to the company’s market value.
Hugging Face has also been in the news recently after a hack by rogue AI agents that escaped OpenAI’s testing environment. Beyond hosting AI models, it offers datasets, software libraries and cloud services used to build and deploy AI applications.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

Ukrinform to present Commanders of Victory book at Lviv Book Forum
The presentation will take place as part of the Lviv Book Forum.
Among the figures featured in the book are current Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine Kyrylo Budanov, Deputy Head of the Office of the President Pavlo Palisa, Commander of the Bakhmut Ghosts sniper platoon Oleksandr “Ghost,” Head of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine Oleh Ivashchenko, Commander of the National Guard Oleksandr Pivnenko, and Commander of the Ukrainian Land Forces Hennadii Shapovalov.
The book aims to document the testimony of Ukrainian military commanders who are directly involved in the Russia-Ukraine war and make critical decisions on the battlefield, preserving their stories for future generations.
A distinctive feature of Commanders of Victory is that the entire book-production process – from preparing and editing the journalistic materials to design, layout and prepress – was carried out by the Ukrinform team. For the agency, this represents a new way of working with its own journalistic content and preserving it in book form.
The publication contains original autographs from the project’s subjects, along with handwritten quotations reflecting their personal life mottos. Another distinctive feature is a bookmark decorated with a spent shell casing. It was made by Ternopil volunteer Olha Konoval, the wife of fallen Hero of Ukraine Serhii Konoval.
The book is illustrated with unique photographs taken by Ukrinform correspondents, including images from the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia fronts. One photograph by the agency’s photojournalist Dmytro Smolienko – a picture of sunflowers – was included among the 100 best photographs of 2025 by the U.S. magazine Time.
During the presentation, the agency’s team will talk about the creation of the book, from the initial concept and preparation of the materials to design and printing. The discussion will also focus on the role of the media in documenting the Russia-Ukraine war and preserving the testimony of those directly involved in it. One of the Commanders of Victory featured in the book, whose name has not yet been disclosed, will also attend the event.
The special guest of the presentation will be Honored Artist of Ukraine, serviceman and lead singer of the band Antytila Taras Topolia, who will perform an acoustic set.
As reported by Ukrinform, the agency is publishing Commanders of Victory, bringing together more than 20 stories of Ukrainian commanders and their units. The book is based on interviews published by the agency over the course of a year.

China unveils second batch of 32 pilot cities for retail sector innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
21:13:42 CST
22:13:42 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Commerce, together with three other government departments, has jointly issued a notice announcing the second batch of 32 pilot cities for the national retail industry innovation and upgrade initiative, the ministry announced on Thursday.
The 32 cities include Qinhuangdao and Baoding in north China's Hebei Province, Wuxi and Yangzhou in east China's Jiangsu Province, and Kaifeng and Xuchang in Henan Province in central China, among others.
In November 2024, the Ministry of Commerce and six other departments released the implementation plan for the retail industry innovation and upgrade initiative. The plan aims to improve the country's modern commercial circulation system, build sound long-term consumption-boosting mechanisms, and accelerate the diversification of consumer services.
Under the plan, pilot cities will be selected annually for retail innovation and upgrading, existing retail facilities will be renovated, and successful practices will be promoted nationwide.
The goal is for a modern retail system to take initial shape by 2029, characterized by abundant supply, balanced distribution, diversified channels, high-quality services, smart and convenient services, and green, low-carbon development.
China announced the first batch of 38 pilot cities in June 2025. The first batch includes the likes of Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai and south China's Shenzhen.
This latest move underscores China's commitment to expanding domestic demand and boosting consumption as key drivers of economic growth, analysts said.
China aims to raise its total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan (about 8.85 trillion U.S. dollars) by 2030, according to the plan for expanding consumption during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
The plan, released in July, outlines 28 specific measures across several dimensions, including boosting consumption capacity, improving the consumption environment, and strengthening institutional mechanisms.
It prioritizes service consumption expansion in areas such as elderly care, childcare, culture, tourism, and health, reflecting a structural shift from goods-dominated consumption to a balanced goods-and-services model. The plan also calls for removing unreasonable restrictions in some sectors, including automobiles and housing, implementing paid leave policies, and strengthening social security safety nets to boost consumer confidence.
In the first seven months of 2026, China's total retail sales of consumer goods reached 28.77 trillion yuan, up 1.2 percent year on year. ■

The Brave Warriors will begin their Group G campaign against the Republic of the Congo on Sept. 24 before facing Comoros four days later.
The provisional squad comprises three goalkeepers, nine defenders, 12 midfielders and five forwards, bringing together experienced foreign-based players and talent from Namibia's domestic league.
Senior players Peter Shalulile and Deon Hotto are among those selected, alongside Riaan Hanamub, Aprocius Petrus, Prins Tjiueza and Bethuel Muzeu. The squad will be trimmed before the two fixtures.
The opening matches are expected to be crucial to Namibia's qualification hopes in a competitive group that also includes five-time African champion Cameroon.
Namibia will be seeking to build on its performance at the 2023 AFCON tournament in Cote d'Ivoire, where the Brave Warriors reached the knockout stage for the first time in the country's history after recording a landmark victory over Tunisia.
The main qualifying group stage for the 2027 tournament will be played across three FIFA international windows.
The first two matchdays are scheduled between Sept. 21 and Oct. 6, followed by another two in November, with the final rounds set for March 2027.
A total of 48 teams have been divided into 12 groups of four. The top two teams in Group G will qualify for the finals.
The 2027 AFCON tournament will be jointly hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from June 19 to July 17, 2027. ■

Lucas Museum in Los Angeles brings visual storytelling to life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
21:13:25 CST
22:13:25 KST

Guests visit the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art during the opening preview for media in Los Angeles, the United States, Sept. 2, 2026. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art was unveiled to the media Wednesday in Los Angeles, bringing together art, architecture and visual storytelling in the new cultural landmark. Located in the city's Exposition Park, the museum, designed by Chinese architect Ma Yansong, was founded by American filmmaker and "Star Wars" creator George Lucas and his wife Mellody Hobson. (Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua)
by Xinhua Writers Tan Jingjing, Gao Shan
LOS ANGELES, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art was unveiled to the media Wednesday in Los Angeles, bringing together art, architecture and visual storytelling in the new cultural landmark.
Located in the city's Exposition Park, the museum, designed by Chinese architect Ma Yansong, was founded by American filmmaker and "Star Wars" creator George Lucas and his wife Mellody Hobson.
The museum is dedicated to exploring the power of visual storytelling and showcasing the universal tradition of storytelling through images.
Covering about 27,800 square meters, the museum features more than 9,300 square meters of gallery space across more than 30 galleries.
Its inaugural exhibitions trace the history of narrative art through more than 1,300 works spanning painting, illustration, comics, photography, film and murals. The collection includes concept designs, props and costumes from the "Star Wars" films, as well as works by artists such as Vincent van Gogh, George Bellows and Jacob Lawrence.
Innovative technology is a dominant feature, including high-resolution images and 3-D scans, to present high-fidelity reproductions of artworks, architecture, and archaeological sites from around the world, allowing visitors to experience artworks and cultural heritage that might otherwise be difficult to access.
For Lucas, the museum is rooted in the enduring relationship between images and stories.
"Images have tremendous power, and stories have tremendous power," Lucas said at the event. "When you put those two elements together, they can create a society."
He said narrative art can unite people with common beliefs, enabling cooperation and achievements beyond individual capabilities.
In contrast to conventional rectangular buildings, the Lucas Museum features a sweeping, organic structure that appears to float above the park. Its curved architecture creates a fluid relationship between the building and the surrounding landscape.
Designed without a single straight line, the building creates a seamless transition between indoor and outdoor spaces -- an approach the architect has described as creating an environment or scene rather than simply designing a building.
"The museum merged like a natural feature of the landscape into Exposition Park, and the building invites everyone to participate in a journey of discovery and become part of the story of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art," Ma said.
Ma told Xinhua he was invited by Lucas to participate in the design competition 12 years ago, competing as the only Chinese architectural design team.
His team drew inspiration from traditional Chinese gardens and architecture, exploring how the concept of "harmony between humanity and nature" could be expressed through the museum's design.
Ma said the goal was to connect people, nature and architecture not only ecologically, but also through emotional and cultural connections.
In recent years, Chinese architecture has continued to innovate while drawing on its cultural heritage, gaining increasing influence internationally and offering new ideas for modern urban design and development, Ma said.
Tracey Bates, CEO of the museum, told Xinhua that the collection reflects a vision of narrative art -- stories that are illustrated and can be seen in a single frame.
"Many museums and galleries around the world have presented incredible works of this kind in particular areas, such as comics or graphic storytelling. But to have such breadth of collection presented permanently in an institution of this size is different and incredibly special," Bates said, adding that "We really want people to come to the museum, discover their own story here and truly engage with the museum."
She said the museum hopes to attract visitors from around the world, including from China, where there is a large community of "Star Wars" and George Lucas fans.
The museum will open to the public on Sept. 22. ■

China sees falling myopia rate among students
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
21:13:13 CST
22:13:13 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- The overall myopia rate among Chinese students stood at 49.9 percent in 2025, a 3.7 percentage points drop from 2018, the National Administration of Disease Control and Prevention said Thursday.
The figure also marked a continuous decline over the past five years, the administration added.
In 2018, China released measures to curb rising myopia among children and teenagers, urging coordinated action from schools, households, healthcare institutions and government bodies to tackle the issue.
Heavy academic workloads, insufficient outdoor time and excessive screen use had been widely cited as major barriers to curbing rising myopia among young people.
Earlier this year, the Ministry of Education rolled out new guidelines to develop "healthy schools," mandating at least two hours of daily physical activity for primary and secondary students and the extension of class breaks from 10 minutes to 15 minutes.
During this year's "two sessions" -- the annual meetings of China's top legislature and political advisory body, Education Minister Huai Jinpeng called for sustained work to ensure every student acquires at least one sporting skill to benefit them for life.
Huang Hong, a physical education teacher with 37 years' experience at Beijing Bayi School, said middle and high-school students there have seen a clear increase in PE class time in recent years.
The school has introduced over a dozen elective courses, including martial arts, fencing and boxing, ensuring that every student can find a sport they enjoy.
The "healthy school" framework also calls for comprehensive measures to prevent and control myopia, especially during key stages in kindergartens and primary schools, with the goal of accelerating the decline in China's myopia rates.
At a primary school in Pingli County in northwest China's Shaanxi Province, posture-correcting devices, eye-friendly lighting and a dedicated vision-care room have been installed to protect children's eyesight.
These efforts cut the school's student myopia rate by three percentage points from the level recorded five years ago, said Wu Jinpeng, the school's principal. ■
