Uber quits major African markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:00:24 UTC
22:00:24 KST

Uber quits major African markets
US ride-hailing company Uber has shut down operations in Nigeria and Uganda, ending a 12-year presence in Africa’s most populous nation and a decade of service in the East African country.
The withdrawals took effect on Wednesday following what Uber described as a “thorough review” of its business. The company did not disclose how many employees or drivers were affected, but said assistance would be available during the transition.
Uber said the closures were limited to the two markets and that it remains committed to Africa. The move coincided with a global Uber restructuring involving around 3,300 job cuts, equivalent to roughly 10% of its workforce. In a message published by the company on Wednesday, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said the restructuring would reduce costs and free resources for investment in growth and innovation as Uber seeks to “build the autonomous future.”
The company launched in Lagos in 2014 and Kampala in 2016. Its African operations have faced persistent disputes over driver earnings, commission rates, and regulation.
Nigerian drivers held strikes earlier this year over fares they said failed to keep pace with rising fuel and vehicle-maintenance costs. The Amalgamated Union of App-Based Transporters of Nigeria described Uber’s business model as exploitative and criticized the company for withdrawing without adequately consulting drivers, multiple local outlets reported on Thursday, citing the union’s national spokesperson.
The Nigerian exit also followed a dispute over access to airports operated by the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria. Uber denied that the issue prompted its departure, saying the decision reflected changing business priorities and investment plans. The shutdown leaves Bolt, inDrive, and the government-backed LagRide among Nigeria’s main alternatives.
In Uganda, Uber faced competition from platforms including SafeBoda and Faras, while drivers complained about low fares and high commissions. Local reports also cited rising operating costs and difficulties retaining drivers.
The latest closures extend the company’s retreat from the continent. Uber withdrew from Ivory Coast (Cote d’Ivoire) in 2025 and Tanzania in January 2026, following years of disputes with Tanzanian regulators over controlled fares and limits on platform commissions. It suspended operations in Morocco in 2018 because of regulatory uncertainty but returned in November 2025.
The latest exits limit Uber’s direct African presence to South Africa, Kenya, Ghana, Egypt, and Morocco. Its technology is also used in Mauritius by Taxi by ala-lila, a locally managed service powered by Uber.

US Orchestra Refuses to Cancel Russian Violinist Vadim Repin Despite Ukrainian Embassy Appeal

US Orchestra Refuses to Cancel Russian Violinist Vadim Repin Despite Ukrainian Embassy Appeal
The Annapolis Symphony Orchestra (ASO) has said it does not plan to cancel upcoming performances by Russian violinist Vadim Repin despite an appeal from the Ukrainian Embassy in the United States and protests from activists, The Violin Channel reported.
Repin is scheduled to perform with the orchestra at Maryland Hall in Annapolis on November 6 and 7. The program includes Soviet composer Dmitri Shostakovich’s Violin Concerto No. 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Representatives of the Annapolis Symphony Orchestra told The Violin Channel that the scheduled performances would go ahead as planned.
The orchestra noted that it had previously removed Repin from its program in 2022, immediately following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as cultural institutions worldwide were determining how to respond to Russia’s actions and whether to continue presenting Russian artists.
According to the ASO, the 2022 decision was not based on a conclusion that Repin personally supported Russian leader Vladimir Putin or Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
The orchestra said that after inviting Repin to perform again, it conducted what it described as a “careful review” of his public record to determine whether there was evidence that he personally supported the Russian government’s aggressive policies or Putin.
“We have found no evidence. As such, we have proceeded with our plans to feature Mr. Repin in the performance of Shostakovich's Violin Concerto No1.” the ASO stated.
On August 25, the Ukrainian Embassy in the United States called on the orchestra to cancel Repin’s appearances, citing his participation in events linked to the Kremlin.
The embassy pointed to Repin’s February 21, 2024, performance with the State Kremlin Orchestra at a concert organized by a Kremlin-affiliated foundation to mark Russia’s Defender of the Fatherland Day.
Ukrainian diplomats also said that following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Vadim Repin Arts Development Foundation received substantial funding from Russia’s Presidential Fund for Cultural Initiatives.
The controversy surrounding Repin’s international appearances has extended beyond the United States. International activists previously urged the Sofia Philharmonic in Bulgaria to cancel a scheduled performance by the Russian violinist, issuing an open letter ahead of his concert planned for May 2026.

Love Island USA Must Do More to Protect Black Women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:00:06 UTC
22:00:06 KST

Love Island USA would not exist without Black women. Their viral moments, reads at the fire-pit, and ability to shape pop culture in their image are the stuff of marketing executives' dreams. Within the timespan of a summer, Season 8’s core four—Trinity Tatum, Kayda Bosse, Aniya Harvey, and Melanie Moreno—gained millions of followers across social media platforms, signed deals with major talent agencies, and received widespread coverage across mainstream media publications.
The Love Island USA effect is not limited to these four women. The show has also brought notoriety and fame to their male partners and other Islanders, as well. But the breakout stars of the Peacock dating series are experiencing these phenomena on another level, with built-in fanbases that follow and support every campaign they take part in, both on and off social media. In a landscape where fame equates to followers and followers equate to money, these four Black women are raking in the profits and new opportunities their newfound fame has brought, and Black women are to thank for it.
But even as their fans prop them up, it often seems as though they are taken for granted by other Islanders, those cast members’ fanbases, and ITV America and Peacock, which have seen their bottom lines grow significantly as a direct result of the dating franchise. Despite their success, Tatum, Bosse, Harvey, and Moreno have been subjected to constant anti-Black racism and sexism, and the support network that should be there to protect them has been conspicuously absent: There’s been no statement of support or condemnation from the networks, while cast members defend their mistreatment of the core four rather than have their backs. What’s more, the harm to these women is experienced by Black women watching the show as vicarious racism—an indirect exposure to racial and gender discrimination—that elicits feelings of fear, sadness, and anger. (As of publication, representatives from Peacock and ITV America had not responded to a request for comment.)
On the Love Island USA Season 8 reunion, which aired Aug. 31 on Peacock, mistreatment on social media was a recurring theme among the Islanders, specifically the Black Islanders, who spoke about receiving death threats, racial slurs, and discriminatory harassment from fans of the Fiji-set dating franchise. “I don’t stand for racism towards me, towards Titi [Tierra Davis], and any of the other cast members, which is a big reason why I haven’t really been on social media,” said KC Chandler on the reunion stage. “I wanted to get my mind right and really focus on what matters to me, which is my family and my mental health.”
This was not the first time a Black Islander had expressed discontent on the Love Island USA reunion stage. Last year, breakout star Olandria Carthen tearfully spoke about the racism and bullying she experienced from fans of Huda Mustafa, including one who photoshopped her face onto the body of George Floyd. Serena Page, winner of Love Island USA Season 6, told podcast host Kamie Crawford that she talked to production staff about their decision to cast male Islanders who were not attracted to Black women, thus reinforcing the stereotype that Black women are undesirable. And these messages are sent to a massive audience: the most recent season accumulated nearly 19 billion hours of viewing—a streaming record for Peacock.
It is no secret that reality television has historically been unwelcoming and unsafe for Black women. Nor is Love Island USA the first unscripted television show to have a toxic fandom. But the lack of protections for these stars, in addition to being an ethical lapse with serious ramifications for their mental health, could pose a threat to the future of the franchise. Fans are loyal to Islanders more than to the show itself, and if the show’s biggest stars are no longer in its orbit, it becomes harder to keep their devotees in that orbit too. The trio of friends nicknamed PPG—Leah Kateb, Serena Page, and JaNa Craig—who catapulted the unscripted series into fame in Season 6, have publicly distanced themselves from the dating show. Carthen took a similar tack after last year’s reunion. And Moreno claimed not to have tuned in to the Season 8 reunion via an post on the official Shondaland Instagram page.
To be clear, Black women aren’t the only ones who seem to be moving on once their time on the show is done. “ I don't think these people want to be professional reality stars,” says Anna Peele, contributing editor at Vanity Fair and author of Enter the Villa: The Unauthorized Reality Behind Love Island. “ Huda [Mustafa] wanted to keep being on reality TV. I think some of the cast members who left earlier are going to be very happy to be [on its spinoff series] Beyond The Villa.” But for the most part, she explains, they want to pivot or branch out. “These people want to be models, hosts, presenters, DJs. I don't know if those are higher aspirations than being a reality star, but they are different aspirations. The way that you contort yourself is going to be different than continuing to feed the public interest in your private life.”
The franchise has perhaps inadvertently shown fans the downsides of being a part of it. Beyond The Villa became its first spinoff series following the breakout success of Season 6, which saw significant growth in the show’s stateside audience. The spinoff followed the fan favorites of that season as they adjusted to their newfound fame in Los Angeles. The show was meant to be an inside look into the lives of America’s favorite Islanders, but it wasn’t all glamorous. Viewers were privy to these young adults’ experiences of heightened anxiety, depression, struggles with their shifting personal and professional identities, and other issues related to their participation. And its window into Black female cast members’ experiences was grimmest of all. Season 2 of the spinoff did not feature runner-up Nic Vansteenberghe, Carthen, Mustafa, nor Allen “Ace” Steve Greene and Michelle “Chelley” Evelyn Bissainthe, after many of them expressed frustration over the way they were depicted. The spinoff was renewed for a third season, but the likelihood of Season 8's core four joining is slim to none—though contractual obligations mean other new opportunities may be temporarily limited.
Islanders are beholden to a one-year exclusivity clause, an industry standard in reality TV. “It gives the network or streamer veto power over any brand or commercial deals the talent may pursue,” McKinley Franklin explains in the Hollywood Reporter. “And it gives them a window to see if they want to sign up the talent in question for any future shows or spinoffs.” Jade Sherman, head of digital at Gersh—the talent agency that represents Vanderpump Rules alum Ariana Madix, who hosts Love Island USA, as well as Aniya Harvey—spoke about the clause to Variety. “Love Island is an incredible brand, and they try really hard to protect their IP. They’ve put things in place to do that, and it’s on us as representatives to be able to pivot and adapt to where their changing rules are,” she said.
Yet no discussion about the series’ record-breaking viewership or Islanders’ post-show deals is complete without acknowledging the impact of the discourse online. Islanders receive a psychological screening before they begin filming the show, and they have access to on-site psychological support in Fiji. But the support does not seem to adequately address one of the biggest threats to contestants’ wellbeing: fear of their fans. When Peele interviewed former Islanders for Enter The Villa and conversations touched on their hesitancy to step in when another Islander was being harassed, they described the fans as terrifying. “ There's a moral imperative to do the right thing and to do what's right. But they can't control them,” says Peele. Fred Johnson, a talent manager at Select Management Group, the agency that represents Love Island USA Season 7 fan favorite Jeremiah Brown, told The Ankler, “The audience that takes a typical content creator years to build pretty much arrives overnight” for an Islander.
There is a lot of power in being a fan favorite, but for Black women Islanders, it exacts a particular toll. Zari Taylor, faculty fellow at New York University and co-author of From Screen to Store: Exploring the Reality TV to Influencer Pipeline on Love Island, spoke to TIME about the double standard they face. "On the one hand, while Black women [are] emerging victorious, especially dark-skinned women, they have to go through something” in order to achieve that fan-favorite status. Taylor describes the process as a trial by fire, in which the Islanders have to walk through the hot coals of misogyny and sexism on the show itself. They have to take the male Islander back even after lies and betrayals during the Casa Amor segment of the show, when he is tempted by other women, and are often an object of pity from the audience.
It is impossible to fully curb racism and sexism online. But that doesn’t mean the franchise can’t take meaningful steps toward creating a safer workplace and post-show experience for Black women—one that might encourage them to invest in it rather than move away from it as quickly as contractually possible. When asked what changes could be made to improve the conditions for Black women on Love Island USA and those who watch it, Taylor had one clear starting point. “ Black women put a lot of effort into the show because we've had to fight for the representation that we have. Both franchises [Love Island and Love Island USA] have had a Black couple win or a Black woman win. [The producers of these shows] need to be more conscious of things like online misogyny influencing the people that come on, and misogynoir, misogyny in general, so that they can keep an eye out for it.” This includes in the casting process, when prospective Islanders are asked about their dating preferences.
Peele sees the addition of Ciara Miller as the host of Love Island: Aftersun, a recap show where the events of the episodes are discussed postmortem, as a sign that show is trending in the right direction. Her presence helps provide a space for conversations about dating as a Black woman on reality TV, led by a woman with personal experience. And Peele points to the possibility of age-restricted safeguards, barring fans under the age of 18 from participating in the discourse online, as Madix has noted that putting such restrictions on her own content significantly reduced negative interactions.
Love Island USA remains in a moment of major growth and unprecedented attention. Madix secured the series’ first Emmy nomination, for Outstanding Host for a Reality or Reality Competition Program. She will host Season 9 of the franchise, along with Love Island Games, in 2027. Viewership is growing: 35% of viewers this summer were new to watching the series. And the Season 8 reunion closed with an announcement that casting is already underway for the next crew of Islanders. But more eyeballs bring more scrutiny, and growth cannot be sustained without the very people who made it possible. Let’s hope that expansion brings more discussions about continuous protection for the Black women who will join the franchise in addition to those who came before. Because no amount of fame can compensate for the damage done by anti-Black racism and sexism. And the show is nothing without its brightest stars.

I Got a Brief Look at ‘Guild Wars 3,’ and I’m Excited
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Hardly a year goes by without me whistling the Guild Wars 2 loading theme, rewatching clips of the original to soak up that Pre-Searing Ascalon nostalgia, or subjecting my wife to yet another Grawl impression. (Gui-la-la!)
That's how monumental ArenaNet's MMORPG has been in my life. So you can understand my excitement when the game developer announced Guild Wars 3 earlier this summer, with a beta set to launch in late 2027.
I spent countless hours playing Guild Wars in middle school and high school, and an ungodly amount of time playing Guild Wars 2 with my roommates in college. Guild Wars always felt like the dark horse in the MMORPG world, never reaching the scale and attention of World of Warcraft or Final Fantasy XI, yet maintaining a massive user base with a cult-like following. (It uniquely did not require a monthly subscription.) You wouldn't hear anyone talking about it in the school cafeteria like you would the other two titles (I was not a Cool Kid). Still, it always had a grand scale of wonder, adventure, and lore that drew me in—props to my older brother for discovering the game and its many discs, and building a PC to run it.
Guild Wars 3's setting predates the events of Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2, which means you don't really need to know anything about the series to dive in. It marks the first time the franchise is heading to console with a PlayStation 5 release alongside PC. And while developers typically wind down support for predecessor titles ahead of a sequel, ArenaNet plans to maintain both the original Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2 for years to come. (It recently released the original game as Guild Wars Reforged with system enhancements and a mobile port.)
Details on the game—built on Unreal Engine 5 and in development for 4 years—are limited, but ArenaNet gave me a brief glimpse of early alpha footage showcasing gameplay components that have me excited to jump back into the world of Tyria.
Joy of Movement
Gliding is already a movement mechanic in Guild Wars 2, but when you stop and start running, the transitions are awkward and slow. All of that is becoming more fluid in Guild Wars 3, alongside some new range of movements. In some ways, it brings the game closer to an action RPG.
You can jump into a ravine, start gliding, and now wall-run to reach your desired destination, all in a series of fluid movements with no awkward transitions, though there is a stamina bar as a limiter. Colin Johanson, ArenaNet’s studio head, says this unlocks “truly expressive and free-formed joy of movement.” Much of this centers on character momentum—using speed, weight, and directional inertia—a philosophy massively multiplayer online games have historically avoided due to network latency and server-client synchronization issues.
Momentum doesn't only affect how you get around, but combat as well. For example, you can build up speed to ram into enemies and smash them into cliff walls to stun them—they can do the same to you—or use momentum to kick them off a ledge, King Leonidas-style. (What happens to their loot if they fall off a cliff? ArenaNet hasn't figured that out just yet.)
While the basic movement mechanics are the same across all character classes, each class has a unique spin on it. The Warrior class, for example, can sprint up a wall and use downward momentum to plunge their weapon and slam the ground, causing area-of-effect damage to nearby enemies.
I recall enjoying many of the collaborative fighting mechanics when Guild Wars 2 first debuted—like an Elementalist dropping a fire ring on the ground so an ally could shoot arrows through it to inflict burning damage. That's still a crucial component in GW3.
Warriors can angle their shield to act as a launchpad for allies, catapulting them into the air for elevated strikes. Rangers have an ability that creates an ice vortex, and a Warrior can jump in, ride the vortex's lift high, then plummet down to cause big (icy) damage. Some of these moves are GW3's new “contextual skills," which only show up during specific contextual windows. If a Warrior is in the air, that's when they can use the skill to bomb down and hit the ground with power.
In one encounter against spiders, a Warrior set his weapon on fire, which in turn lit his allies' weapons. They sliced through the spiders quickly, and the fire also spread through the webs to clear them out. Players can adjust and customize their builds on the fly in the open world, though some build aspects are restricted until they're back in main hub locations.
“Customizing your build to defeat different enemies more easily is also an important part of the Guild Wars franchise,” Johanson says. “It's one of the key pillars of Guild Wars 1, and we're bringing it back more heavily in the combat system in Guild Wars 3.”
Conditions you place on enemies are multiplayer stackable, so if one player starts freezing an enemy, the cold effect builds, and the enemy's animation slows down; their attacks are slower. As more people put more cold on the enemy, they'll move slower and slower until they become a block of ice that blocks their moves for a short period. If the enemy is low on health, a character with a knock ability like a Warrior can slam into the ice block and, if it kills the enemy, shatter them into tiny ice cubes, causing damage to nearby foes.
There's lots ArenaNet didn't talk about in this gameplay showcase, like the spirit mounts from the game's initial teaser—Johanson says there will be more to share in the future. Also, how will PS5 players, who can't really take advantage of the game's text-based chat systems on PC, communicate? But he confirmed that there will be a player-versus-player (PvP) mode, along with “high-trust coordinated dungeon-like experiences.” In general, combat will feature a “heck of a lot less” user interface over the screen than a traditional MMO.
ArenaNet says the scale is different compared to Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2, with the former sitting at the smaller scale of the MMO market and the latter sitting on the opposite end. “Internally, we call Guild Wars 3 more of a meaningful MMO, where it's more about each player on-screen really matters and makes a difference,” Johanson says.
That's because GW3 uses an evolved version of the megaservers from GW2, allowing for fewer loading screens and an open-world cap of roughly 20 players in active combat zones—a number that scales up significantly higher in social hubs, like cities and towns.
“We've seen very few new MMOs in the last decade, and the overwhelming majority of us are still playing the same games from 10 to 20 years ago,” Johanson says. “We see MMO fans constantly clamoring for something new and saying this genre desperately needs something new to move it forward right now, and I think that is when ArenaNet is at its best.”
Expect a slow trickle of information over the next year as the beta launch for Guild Wars 3 approaches. Until then, I'm going to dust off Guild Wars 2, which has been seeing its own sudden influx of new players. As the Norn say, “May the spirits guide you.”

Nvidia RTX Spark ‘Superchip’: The First AI PCs Are Here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Three months ago, Nvidia took the wraps off its RTX Spark “superchip” and a handful of future laptops that would use it. It felt like a consequential moment in the history of the PC, despite all the questions that remained.
And now, as announced at the IFA 2026 tech show in Berlin, we’ve had our first hands-on look at one of these laptops, as well as some announcements around RTX Spark-powered mini desktop PCs. Demand for running agentic AI workflows like OpenClaw locally on your computer keeps rising, and these new PCs look like they are designed specifically to feed it.
Nvidia Alternatives to the MacBook Pro
The laptop in question is the Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1, a 16-inch laptop with a 360-degree hinge. As I assumed it would, this thing looks incredibly premium, aiming to be a MacBook Pro competitor in every aspect. The OLED touch display has a sharp 2880 x 1800 resolution and a 120-Hz refresh rate. The whole chassis is surrounded by rounded metallic edges and some very thin display bezels. Other high-end features we don’t typically see include a six-speaker sound system and a 9.2-megapixel webcam.
But here’s the important bit: It’s 0.69 inches thick, just 0.03 inches shy of the 16-inch MacBook Pro. That’s possible thanks to Nvidia’s Arm-based chip under the hood, which combines a Grace CPU with “up to 20 cores” and a Blackwell RTX GPU with “up to 6,144 cores.” The CPU, GPU, and memory are packaged together into a single system-on-a-chip (SoC), sharing more in common with Apple silicon than a conventional Windows laptop. Based purely on core count alone, that would theoretically put the integrated GPU capability of this chip somewhere between an RTX 5070 Ti and an RTX 5080 as found on laptops available today. Those specs also indicate that lower-powered configurations will be sold, though we don’t know how broad the performance range will be. There was no mention of battery-life claims, though presumably one benefit of using an Arm-based SoC (rather than a discrete GPU) is greater efficiency and, thus, better battery life.
Personally, I don’t prefer laptops this large with 2-in-1 capabilities and number pads, so I’m happy that Lenovo is also offering a 15-inch model, the Yoga Pro 9n. While it wasn’t available to see in person, that’s the model I’m more interested in checking out. It shares a lot in common with the 16-inch model, such as the rounded edges, higher-resolution webcam, and very large haptic touchpad. But it has a smaller 15-inch OLED screen with a resolution of 2560 x 1600 and is thinner at 0.66 inches (at its thinnest point). Another unique feature is its Force Pad touchpad, which lets you use a stylus (such as the Yoga Pen Gen 2) to write or draw directly on it.
Interestingly, the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 can only be configured with up to 64 GB of memory, which is less than I thought these AI-focused PCs would offer. I suppose what makes the Yoga Pro 9n a “Pro” model is its configuration options up to 128 GB of memory, as it otherwise seems to have the same performance.
Lenovo’s device is just one among a new line of RTX Spark-powered laptops coming this fall, including the Dell XPS 16, Asus ProArt P16, and Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra. These larger laptops all seem focused on pleasing the creator and AI enthusiast demographic, though only one 14-inch model has been announced so far: the HP OmniBook X 14.
AI Boxes
The point of all these new PCs is to offer hardware that can capably run on-device AI models locally. That means less dependence on the cloud and more ability to run full agentic AI workflows without worrying about privacy. That’s crucial when an AI model handles sensitive personal data like your financial information, email accounts, or anything else you feel comfortable providing.
Acer announced its own mini PC solution, the Acer SFF RTX Spark, following up on Asus’ ProArt Mini PC shown off earlier this summer. Both are around the same size as the Mac Mini, but offer a “petaflop of AI performance,” up to 128 GB of memory, and the same RTX Spark superchip at its core. These mini PCs are interesting, coming just a week after the announcement of Apple’s M6 Mac mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio. These small, efficient desktop computers are going to (and already are) play an important role in the adoption of local AI.
Nvidia isn’t the only player here. Lenovo announced an AMD-powered ThinkCentre X Ultra, which also puts 128 GB of memory at the disposal of agentic AI models, alongside AMD’s Ryzen Max+ Pro 495 chip. This is another popular chip being used for local AI, such as on the Framework Desktop. You can even buy the AMD Developer Kit with 128 GB of RAM right now. The expected starting price of the ThinkCentre X Ultra is $3,699, which should give you an idea of how expensive these systems are getting. And note that’s the base model, not the maxed-out, 128-GB version.
Price remains the most crucial missing element. RAM has never been more expensive or more necessary, so I wouldn’t expect any RTX Spark systems to be cheap. The most affordable MacBook Pro (aside from the M5 base model) is $2,349, which gets you the M5 Pro and only 24 GB of RAM. For a 128-GB MacBook Pro, you’re currently looking at $6,139.

Where Can Russian Athletes Compete After the IOC’s Provisional Ban Lift?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Russia’s return to international sports competition was already well underway long before the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted its ban on the Russian and Belarusian Olympic Committees this July.
The shift began in September 2025, when the International Paralympic Committee voted against maintaining its ban on Russian and Belarusian athletes, paving the way for them to compete at the 2026 Milano-Cortina Paralympic Games, where Russian competitors won eight gold medals.
By December, the IOC recommended that international federations lift their bans on Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.
However, some individual governing bodies acted even earlier. The International Judo Federation became the first to restore full participation rights to senior Russian athletes in November of last year. World Taekwondo followed this January by approving the full return of both junior and senior athletes from Russia and Belarus.
Since then, eight additional Olympic sports federations have restored full participation rights to Russian athletes and teams, allowing the use of the Russian flag, national anthem and team uniforms.
Below is a list compiled by The Moscow Times detailing where and how Russian athletes can currently compete on the international stage:
Federations that allow full senior and youth participation
Archery: On August 14, World Archery reinstated Russian athletes, allowing them to compete under their national flag and bringing their status in line with Belarusian athletes, who were reinstated in May.
Aquatics: The World Aquatics Bureau lifted its ban on senior Russian and Belarusian athletes on April 13, 2026, two months after it lifted its ban on Junior athletes.
In its statement, World Aquatics President Husain Al Musallam said, “Over the last three years, World Aquatics and the AQIU have successfully helped ensure that conflict can be kept outside the sporting competition venues. We are determined to ensure that pools and open water remain places where athletes from all nations can come together in peaceful competition.”
Boxing: On July 30, World Boxing announced that it was restoring full participation rights to all Russian athletes.
"The Executive Committee accepted that Russian athletes would now take part in World Boxing competitions like boxers from any other national federation. However, World Boxing will strictly monitor the behaviour of Russian delegations during events as well as compliance with anti-doping protocols," the statement read.
World Boxing previously lifted its restrictions on Belarusian athletes on May 12.
Equestrian: The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) will lift restrictions on Russian riders and officials starting Oct. 5 and once again allow international competitions to be held in Russia, the governing body has said.
FEI had already approved a return to competition for junior athletes from Russia and Belarus on May 19, 2026, but did not change its stance that senior athletes should compete with neutral status at that time.
Fencing: The International Fencing Federation (FIE) reinstated Russian and Belarusian athletes on June 2, 2026.
“The decision reflects the FIE’s commitment to the fundamental principles of the Olympic Charter, including non-discrimination, equal treatment and the universality of sport, as well as the objectives and principles set out in the FIE Statutes,” FIE’s statement read.
On July 28, Russian fencer Pavel Graudyn won gold in the Men's individual sabre at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, marking Russia's first gold at a major championship since the International Fencing Federation lifted its restrictions.
Gymnastics: The Executive Committee of World Gymnastics released a statement on May 18, 2026, that it had decided to lift all restrictions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts.
On July 28, 2026, European Gymnastics voted to bring itself in line with World Gymnastics in allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete with their national symbols.
Handball: On July 15, 2026, the International Handball Federation (IHF) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian teams and officials, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
“The IHF reiterates its longstanding commitment to the Ukraine Handball Federation and continues to stand in solidarity with Ukraine. It strongly condemns the ongoing war in Ukraine and its devastating consequences. It is the IHF’s sincere hope that the conflict will soon come to an end, paving the way for a return to peace, the restoration of normal sporting relations and the resumption of peaceful international cooperation,” the IHF statement said.
“At the same time, the IHF remains committed to safeguarding the values of sport, promoting dialogue within the international handball family, and ensuring that its decisions continue to reflect the recommendations of the IOC and the interests of the global handball community”
Judo: The International Judo Federation, calling sport the “last bridge for reconciliation and peace,” was the first to allow Russian and Belarusian senior athletes back, doing so on Nov. 27, 2025.
“Athletes have no responsibility for the decisions of governments or other national institutions, and it is our duty to protect the sport and our athletes,” the federation’s statement said.
“Sport must remain neutral, independent and free from political influence. Judo, rooted in the values of peace, unity and friendship, cannot allow itself to become a platform for geopolitical agendas. The decision to reinstate full national representation reflects the IJF’s confidence in its ethical safeguards, as well as in the strength and integrity of the sport,” it continued.
Modern Pentathlon: The International Union of Modern Pentathlon lifted its ban on Russian athletes on July 13, 2026, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
Taekwondo: The World Taekwondo Council allowed Russian and Belarusian athletes back into the fold on Jan. 31, 2026, at a meeting in the United Arab Emirates.
Triathlon: Mikhail Degtyarev, head of the Russian Olympic Committee and the Russian Minister of Sport, said on Aug. 21 that World Triathlon had granted Russian athletes full participation rights.
World Triathlon lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian junior athletes in April 2026, while senior athletes continue to compete as neutral athletes.
"This was made possible by the restoration of the Russian Olympic Committee's status. Earlier in April, World Triathlon already admitted Russian junior and para-athletes," Degtyarev said.
Volleyball: The International Volleyball Federation (FIVB) announced on July 8, 2026, that Russian teams and athletes would be restored to the World Ranking with the same World Ranking points they had at the time of the initial ban.
“The FIVB remains deeply concerned about the ongoing war in Ukraine and strongly condemns all forms of violence. We continue to hope for a peaceful resolution as soon as possible and remain committed to supporting the Ukrainian volleyball community through the FIVB Volleyball Empowerment programme,” FIVB added.
Weightlifting: The International Weightlifting Federation decided on June 26, 2026, to reinstate Russian and Belarusian athletes.
“The IWF remains committed to promoting fair competition, safeguarding the integrity of the sport and ensuring that athletes have the opportunity to compete in an environment that respects the principles of neutrality, inclusion and excellence,” the decision read.
Wrestling: United World Wrestling announced on May 15, 2026, that Russian and Belarusian wrestlers would be able to compete without restrictions starting with immediate effect.
Federations that allow full youth participation
Baseball/Softball: On Jan. 19, 2026, the World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes. However, senior athletes remain banned.
Chess: The International Chess Federation (FIDE) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian youth chess players on Dec. 14, 2025. Senior athletes may compete under a neutral designation.
Curling: World Curling announced on Jan. 30, 2026, that, following the IOC’s recommendation, Russian and Belarusian junior athletes would be able to compete in international competition. Senior athletes remain unable to compete.
Sailing: The Russian Sailing Federation published a statement on June 9, 2026, announcing that the World Sailing Federation had approved a return to competition for Russian junior athletes.
Ski Mountaineering: The International Ski Mountaineering Federation (ISMF) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.

Turkish Cyprus ferry probe deepens as questions mount over captain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:59:54 UTC
21:59:54 KST

Police guard the entrace of the port of Kyrenia, in the Turkish Cyprus, during a rescue operation off the coast after a ferry capsized. (AFP Photo)
The investigation into the sinking of a passenger ferry off the coast of Turkish Cyprus deepened on Sept. 3, with growing questions surrounding he captain’s qualifications and the validity of his maritime license.
The ferry carrying 267 people sank on Aug. 30, shortly after departing from Kyrenia Port on the northern coast of the divided island.
Search and rescue teams on Sept. 2 recovered the body of one of 20 people who had been missing after the ferry capsized, bringing the death toll to at least nine.
The victim was believed to be a man in his 50s. Prime Minister Ünal Üstel did not disclose where the body had been found.
As the investigation intensified on Sept. 3, authorities determined that the captain had originally obtained a maritime license from Türkiye, but that it had expired after he failed to renew it following a 10-year hiatus from sailing.
The captain was later reportedly found to have used his old license number when contacting individuals in Greece and to have obtained a new license from Honduras in exchange for $3,500.
He subsequently secured a certificate of competency in Turkish Cyprus and operated the ferry using those documents.
The vessel’s second captain told a court that it was known before departure that Taşucu Port, the ferry’s intended destination in southern Türkiye, was closed.
He said the decision to set sail had been made at the captain’s discretion.
Expert reports prepared as part of the investigation indicated that the disaster could have been averted had the vessel returned to port slowly, immediately after it began taking on water.
The reports concluded that the accident could have been prevented had the captain not made an extremely sharp maneuver.
Passengers aboard the ferry at the time said they noticed the vessel was taking on water but alleged that the crew failed to take the situation seriously.
As search and rescue efforts continued following the disaster, Turkish Cypriot Transport Minister Erhan Arıklı was dismissed.
Arıklı, who heads the Rebirth Party (YDP), one of the coalition partners, subsequently announced that his party was withdrawing from the government in response to the decision.

When Drone Swarms Leave Seconds to React, Germany’s New IRIS-T Packs Eight Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:59:43 UTC
21:59:43 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
When Drone Swarms Leave Seconds to React, Germany’s New IRIS-T Packs Eight Missiles
German defense manufacturer Diehl Defence unveiled the IRIS-T SLS MK 4, a next-generation short-range air defense system, at the ILA 2026 air show in Berlin on September 3, according to ArmyInform, which cited analysts from the Belgian defense center Army Recognition Group.
The system is presented as the fourth generation of the combat-proven IRIS-T SLS platform. Diehl Defence, headquartered in Überlingen in western Germany, described it on its official website as a direct evolution of a system already tested in battlefield conditions—an implicit reference to its use in Ukraine's defense against Russian strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Diehl Defence's official product release, the IRIS-T SLS MK 4 "is a further development of the combat-proven IRIS-T SLS system" and represents a "high-performance solution in dynamic threat scenarios."
The IRIS-T SLS MK 4 consolidates radar, command-and-control systems, and a launch unit onto a single highly mobile vehicle.
Its effective engagement range reaches 12 kilometers, with altitude coverage up to 6 kilometers. The architecture is vehicle-independent, allowing the system to be mounted on different platforms to meet varied customer requirements, Diehl Defence noted on its official portal.
A key upgrade in the MK 4 standard is the increase in the number of ready-to-fire missiles from four to eight, effectively doubling engagement capacity compared with previous configurations.
ArmyInform, citing Army Recognition Group analysts, reported that this improvement is particularly relevant for countering swarm attacks involving drones and loitering munitions—scenarios in which reaction windows are measured in seconds.
Automation is another defining feature of the new system. Automated target detection, tracking, engagement planning, and firing sequencing reduce crew requirements while accelerating response times, according to Army Recognition Group specialists cited by ArmyInform.
This capability is described as especially critical against modern aerial threats such as cruise missiles and strike drones.
Defence Industry Europe, also cited by ArmyInform, reported that the missile hardware itself remains unchanged in the MK 4 variant. The system is expected to gain a fire-on-the-move capability in the future, allowing missile launches while the vehicle is in motion—a feature that would further compress response times in mobile operations.
The MK 4 standard was developed in alignment with NATO requirements and operational specifications, reflecting the alliance's growing emphasis on integrated, rapidly deployable short-range air defense.
The SLS system is already incorporated into the Ukrainian layered air defense concept and can integrate additional effectors, including the unmanned armed missile system or a combat station.

Ukraine’s 66th Brigade Says It May Have Just Destroyed One of Russia’s Last IFVs in Its Sector
Ukrainian FPV drone operators from the MARA Unmanned Systems Battalion destroyed what the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade described as possibly one of the last Russian infantry fighting vehicles remaining in its area of responsibility on the Lyman front.
The brigade published footage of the September 3 operation, showing MARA crews continuing their systematic campaign against Russian vehicles and personnel in the sector.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The battalion has been using FPV drones to repeatedly strike Russian equipment along the Lyman axis, gradually reducing the number of armored vehicles available to Moscow’s forces in the area.
In the latest operation, Russian troops riding motorcycles also came under attack from Ukrainian drone operators.
The most notable target, however, was a Russian infantry fighting vehicle.
According to the 66th Brigade, MARA operators destroyed what may have been one of the last remaining Russian IFVs in the brigade’s sector.
That assessment, if accurate, would highlight the extent to which Russian forces in parts of the front are increasingly relying on lighter and less protected transport as conventional armored vehicles become harder to sustain.
Earlier, Ukrainian drone operators destroyed two Russian 2S19 Msta-S self-propelled howitzers in the Vovchansk direction.
Ukraine’s 57th Separate Motorized Infantry Brigade reported that the two Russian artillery systems had been positioned behind the front line but were detected and destroyed by Ukrainian drone operators.

UK summons Russian envoy over 'reckless' Leipzig airport attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:58:19 UTC
21:58:19 KST

The UK has summoned Russia's charge d'affaires to condemn what it described as a "reckless" drone attack on Germany's Leipzig Airport on August 4.
The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) said in a statement on Thursday that it summoned the Russian diplomat after the attack, which London condemned "in the strongest terms".
"The UK stands in full solidarity with Germany following Russia's egregious and reckless attack on Leipzig airport," an FCDO spokesperson said.
The spokesperson stressed Britain's commitment to NATO allies and continued support for Ukraine, saying both remained "ironclad".
"Any attempt by Russia to undermine our united resolve is futile," the spokesperson said, describing the incident as the latest in what London viewed as "a clear pattern of attempts by the Russian State to undermine our collective security."
The FCDO said the Russian charge d'affaires was summoned to underline that Britain, together with its European and NATO partners, would continue to respond to such actions.
The spokesperson said the UK would "continue to expose Russian hostile activity at every level."
The statement came after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport and unveiled extensive measures and sanctions against Moscow.
France has also supported German proposals for sanctions over what it described as hybrid attacks in Leipzig and sought additional measures against vessels belonging to Russia’s “shadow fleet”.
Leipzig Airport is a major freight hub and a key logistics node for military cargo, including Ukrainian Antonov flights. Officials have described the foiled drone strike as an attempt to disrupt that support chain without launching a conventional military attack.
German authorities told media that the August 4 attempt on a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane was more serious than first reported. The drone had been rigged with explosives, and investigators later concluded that several drones were involved, not one.
Russia has rejected claims of assassinations, sabotage, drone incursions, and spying in countries allied with Ukraine, accusing Western governments of stoking “anti-Russian paranoia".

DSA03 OME part 3: ranges
DSA03.OME part 3 brings together all the Defence Ordnance, Munitions and Explosives (OME) Safety Regulator (DOSR) document suites relating to ranges.
Documents
Details
The document covers the following:
- the range safety management system to be used for the safe operation, maintenance and use of all Ministry if Defence ranges
- the design and construction of standard and non-standard military small arms and infantry weapon systems ranges
- the use of fixed wing aircraft and helicopter mounted weapon systems, and unmanned aircraft systems on ranges
- the policy and principles for the planning and conduct of demolitions, disposals, explosive ordnance disposal and battle simulation activities
Also included are:
- Range Safety Policy Letters (RSPLs) which contain changes or clarification of range safety policy
- Range safety notices and Range advice notes
- Defence ranges safety (JSP 403 volume 2)

How Israeli settler violence is altering Palestinian geography
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:56:10 UTC
21:56:10 KST

Breadcrumb
How Israeli settler violence is altering Palestinian geography in the West Bank
Nablus, occupied West Bank - At Joseph’s Tomb in Nablus, Israeli military vehicles enter the city ahead of groups of Jewish settlers. Roads are closed within minutes. Movement in the surrounding neighbourhoods comes to a halt.
Palestinian residents retreat into their homes as tear gas drifts into nearby streets and buildings. The visits usually last only a few hours. But the military operation around them can disrupt daily life across the area, clearing streets and restricting movement to allow settlers to reach the site.
The scale of the deployment is striking: soldiers, armoured vehicles, road closures and movement restrictions are mobilised to facilitate a temporary settler presence in the heart of a Palestinian city.
That makes the visits more than religious pilgrimages. They are also demonstrations of who can move through Nablus, who is required to stay inside, and which authority can impose those restrictions.
Joseph’s Tomb is, however, a special case. Although it lies inside Nablus, in Area A, the Oslo Accords established particular arrangements governing access to the site. Military-backed visits therefore do not represent the sudden extension of Israeli control over the Palestinian Authority-controlled city.
But the exception is politically significant precisely because it exposes the gap between jurisdiction on paper and power on the ground. The Palestinian Authority remains formally responsible for Nablus, yet when a visit is authorised, Israel can deploy troops, close roads and secure a route for settlers. Israeli military power ultimately determines who can enter and who can move.
“Turning religious and heritage sites into instruments of political conflict is a dangerous development, as it conflates the sacred with the settlement project and transforms collective memory into a means of generating violence and forcibly reshaping the geography,” Dr Mona Abu Hamdiya, a researcher in heritage and archaeology, told The New Arab.
When an exception becomes the norm
The closures eventually end, but their effects are less easily erased.
Families plan around incursions. Work is disrupted. Relatives can be separated. Streets that are normally open become inaccessible. Residents learn that, for several hours, the ordinary rules governing their city can be suspended.
Repetition matters. An event that is officially exceptional can, through repeated incursions, become part of the landscape of Palestinian life.
Joseph’s Tomb therefore offers a lens through which to view a wider transformation underway across the occupied West Bank. The question is not simply whether Israeli sovereignty has formally changed, but whether the space available to Palestinians is being progressively narrowed while Israeli access, settlements and infrastructure become harder to reverse.
The figures suggest this is no longer a marginal phenomenon.
According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,300 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties or property damage were recorded across the West Bank in the first seven months of 2026, an average of more than six a day.
More than 2,300 Palestinians had been displaced by settler attacks and related access restrictions since the beginning of the year.
By late August, OCHA had recorded 23 Palestinians killed and more than 1,040 injured in settler attacks in 2026. Palestinians are now being injured directly by Israeli settlers at a rate of more than three a day, compared with two a day in 2025 and one every three days in 2020.
The pattern is particularly stark in communities close to settlement outposts, where attacks are accompanied by restrictions on access to agricultural land, roads, water and electricity.
Qusra, near Nablus, illustrates how these pressures can converge. In August, settlers established a new outpost in Area B near three Palestinian families in the Ras Al Ein area. OCHA reported increased settler and military presence, damage to water and electricity infrastructure and severe restrictions on the families’ movement. By late August, two of the four roads connecting the area to Qusra were under Israeli control.
The mayor of Sebastia municipality, Mohammad Abdul Aziz Azem, described the pressure on Palestinian communities as part of a broader effort to empty land of its Palestinian inhabitants and confine them to increasingly restricted population centres.
“This is being pursued through organised terrorism supported by Netanyahu’s government, amid international silence and the absence of effective deterrent sanctions against the Israeli occupation government,” he told The New Arab.
Violence changes the map
The significance of settler violence lies not only in the immediate harm it causes, but in what happens afterwards.
A farmer who is attacked must decide whether returning to a field is worth the risk. A family facing repeated threats may stop using a road. A community whose water infrastructure is damaged becomes more dependent on outside assistance.
When such violence is followed by little accountability, and Palestinians subsequently face restrictions on accessing land from which they have been driven, temporary intimidation can create a lasting change in who uses the territory.
Yesh Din, which has monitored Israeli police investigations into ideologically motivated offences against Palestinians since 2005, found that 93.6% of the cases it tracked ended without an indictment. Only 3% resulted in a conviction.
“Settler violence is part of a comprehensive strategy aimed at determining the outcome of the conflict through the silent annexation of Palestinian land,” Dr Hosam Al-Dajani, a writer and political analyst, told The New Arab.
“This is being pursued by forcibly displacing the population through a series of measures imposed by the occupation, including escalating violence and targeting trees, property, people, and everything that connects Palestinians to their land,” he added.
From coercion to administration
On the ground, the process can be incremental. An outpost appears on a ridge. Settlers begin using surrounding land. Palestinians face threats or attacks. Access roads are closed or restricted. Roads, electricity connections and other infrastructure follow, while military protection makes the new arrangement more secure.
Eventually, what began as an unauthorised presence can acquire some degree of official recognition or state support.
OCHA reported in August that at least 26 settlement outposts had been established in Area B over the previous two and a half years, 19 of them since the end of 2024. Peace Now estimates that settlers have taken control of more than 100,000 dunams in Areas A and B, including through violence and threats that have restricted Palestinian access to land.
The process is increasingly accompanied by administrative measures.
Israel’s land-registration programme, approved in February 2026, is intended to complete title-settlement procedures covering 15% of unregistered land in Area C over five years. Israel says the process will clarify ownership. Critics, including Peace Now, argue that formalising land rights while Palestinians face restrictions on access risks turning inequalities created under occupation into an administrative record.
The concern is not simply that a registry might transfer land illegally. It is that the conditions under which evidence of ownership is produced are themselves unequal.
A Palestinian family may have inheritance documents, tax receipts and generations of knowledge establishing its claim to a field. But if repeated attacks or access restrictions prevent the family from regularly cultivating it, absence can begin to look like abandonment.
An outpost, meanwhile, may acquire roads, electricity, security and eventually official recognition.
Coercion can therefore precede administration. Violence does not have to be formally ordered by the state to alter the conditions under which land is subsequently governed.
"Settler violence is part of a comprehensive strategy aimed at determining the outcome of the conflict through the silent annexation of Palestinian land,” Dr Hosam Al-Dajani, a writer and a political analyst, told The New Arab.
“This is being pursued by forcibly displacing the population through a series of measures imposed by the occupation, including escalating violence and targeting trees, property, people, and everything that connects Palestinians to their land,” he added.
“The objective is to impose new facts on the ground in order to advance this strategy, which violates international law and resolutions of international legitimacy, particularly UN Security Council Resolution 2334,” Al-Dajani said.
Annexation without a declaration
Calls to annex the occupied West Bank have grown louder since the far-right government came to power, with ministers openly stating their intentions to seize the Palestinian territory.
Yet at an official level, and to international interlocutors, Israel says that security measures protect Israelis, that registration settles ownership questions, and that borders should be decided through negotiations.
But any future negotiations would not take place over a fixed landscape. While the political status of the territory remains unresolved, the land Palestinians can reach, the authority they encounter and the evidence they can produce to establish ownership are already changing.
Since 2023, the UN says more than 6,200 Palestinians have been displaced by settler attacks and related access restrictions since 2023, including more than 2,300 in 2026 alone. Forty-six communities have been completely displaced.
The cumulative effect is territorial change without a formal declaration of annexation.
“Palestinians face a major challenge that requires unity and cooperation in confronting this project. The threat is not only to Palestinian land but also to the Palestinian national political project itself,” Akram Atallah, a political analyst and columnist for Al-Ayyam newspaper, told The New Arab.
“It is also undermining the two-state solution, as the territory on which a Palestinian state is supposed to be established is being fragmented and brought under increasing Israeli control.”
Mohammed Saleem is a Palestinian journalist, writer, and political analyst.

Palestinian Christian forced out of dream home by Israeli occupiers attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:53:59 UTC
21:53:59 KST

- Priest Bashar Fawadleh says more than 16 families have left Taybeh in the past three years, while dozens more are considering emigration
Seven years ago, Bashir Naim, a Palestinian Christian, built his dream house, where he hoped to raise his children and grandchildren. But he lived there for only a few days before being forced out by violence from Israeli occupiers.
Naim spent more than $270,000 building the house in Taybeh, east of Ramallah, one of the most prominent predominantly Christian communities in the occupied West Bank.
He surrounded it with a fence and surveillance cameras in an effort to ensure his family's safety, but he says repeated attacks eventually turned home into what felt like a “prison.”
In recent months, the town has witnessed an escalation in occupier attacks targeting homes, farmland and livelihoods, prompting warnings from local and church officials that continued violence is pushing more families and young people to consider leaving.
Harassment that escalated into attacks
Standing outside his dream house, Naim told Anadolu that the approximately 421-square-meter residence was designed as a future home for himself, his wife, his two sons and their families.
"I wanted this house to be for me, my wife, my sons and my grandchildren," he said.
"I have two sons whom I wanted to marry off, and we were all going to live here," he said. 
Naim also set aside part of the property for his work repairing refrigerators and washing machines.
But as he prepared to move into the house, he said occupiers began repeatedly appearing around the property. What initially involved harassment during the day escalated into nighttime attacks.
According to Naim, the problem went beyond occupiers simply appearing near his home. The security measures he had installed were also targeted.
"They came at night, stole the surveillance cameras and cut off the internet service," he said.
The harassment then escalated, he said, to occupiers following him and his son and attempting to attack them.
"Every time we came to the house, they would follow us and try to attack us, until my son and I had to take refuge inside," he said.
As the incidents continued, Naim installed additional security measures around the property. But the precautions intended to protect his family instead made him feel as though he was living behind barriers rather than in the home he had spent years building.
"Look at all these precautions I have taken. My house has become a prison," he said, pointing to the fence surrounding the property.
Ultimately, Naim was unable to stay. After moving some of his furniture into the house, he and his son spent only four or five nights there before leaving.
Emigration only viable option
Instead of beginning a new life in the home he had built, Naim returned to his father's old house in Taybeh.
But for Naim, the consequences went beyond being forced to abandon his home.
The future of his family in Palestine itself has now become uncertain.
He said his two sons, who completed their studies at Birzeit University in the West Bank, are now considering emigration and asking him to obtain a passport so they can leave the country together.
His eldest daughter has already left for France and sought asylum there following the attacks against the family, he said.
"My children are now thinking about emigrating and pressuring me to obtain a Palestinian passport and leave with them," he said.
Following the family's displacement, the Palestinian Presidential High Committee for Church Affairs condemned what happened, saying Naim's family had been forced to leave their home because of continued "threats and attacks" by occupiers.
Not an isolated incident
Bashar Fawadleh, priest of the Latin Church of the Redeemer in Taybeh, said Naim's story is not an isolated incident but reflects the pressure facing residents as occupier attacks continue alongside restrictions on movement and worsening economic conditions.
"This citizen represents the Palestinian who wants to remain on his land and live in his home," Fawadleh told Anadolu.
According to Fawadleh, more than 16 families have left Taybeh over the past three years, while dozens of families and young people are currently considering emigration.
Fawadleh previously warned in August that occupier attacks were expanding to different parts of Taybeh, targeting homes, agricultural land and sources of income.
Asked whether the attacks specifically target Christians, he said the issue goes beyond religious identity.
"There is a deliberate targeting of Palestinians who want to remain on their land and continue living on it," he said.
According to Fawadleh, security concerns have forced some residents to spend nighttime hours monitoring their homes, land and vehicles for fear of attacks.
The attacks have also affected livelihoods. He said owners and workers at some businesses, including a quarry and a factory, have been unable to reach their workplaces for the second consecutive month.
Occupier attacks, military closure
In June, Taybeh Mayor Suleiman Khoury said occupiers had set fire to a mountainous area containing agricultural land in the town, burning portions of the area.
As attacks continued, the Israeli army on Aug. 10 declared Taybeh a "closed military zone" under an order issued by Central Command chief Avi Blot. Israel's public broadcaster claimed the measure was intended to prevent occupier attacks.
The order barred non-resident Israelis and foreigners from entering the area, while imposing no equivalent restrictions on Palestinian residents.
However, the mayor said at the time that the closure failed to provide the protection residents needed and instead harmed tourism and livelihoods. Residents and religious figures also said occupiers continued to reach the town's lands despite the order.
The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said occupiers carried out 628 attacks in August, compared with 1,402 attacks by the Israeli army.

Indian foreign minister pays 1st standalone visit to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:52:49 UTC
21:52:49 KST

Elena Teslova
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar paid his first standalone bilateral visit to Ukraine on Thursday, according to the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry.
Jaishankar met Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha in Kyiv, with the two discussing international peace efforts, Black Sea security and bilateral ties, the ministry said in a statement.
Sybiha briefed Jaishankar on what he described as "an escalation of Russian attacks," including strikes involving vessels, Ukrainian ports and port infrastructure.
The ministers discussed the peace process and the possibility of greater Indian involvement in international efforts to end the conflict.
“Prime Minister Modi recently said in Putin’s presence that it is time to put an end to the endless war. We support this position. Ukraine is ready to end the war and has realistic proposals. It is time to move to diplomacy,” Sybiha said.
India, meanwhile, reiterated its call for a diplomatic solution to the conflict.
"Solutions will not emerge from the battlefield," the Indian ambassador said at a news conference following the meeting, adding that it was for the parties involved to find a way to end the war.
"If India can be of any help in any manner, we are ready," the ambassador said.
The ambassador also said an Indian national was killed in an attack in Kyiv two days earlier.
Talks on broader relations
The talks also covered freedom of navigation, global food security and the two countries' broader bilateral agenda.
Sybiha said Ukraine viewed India as an important international partner and welcomed its potential role in broader diplomatic efforts.
“We expect further support from India for the principles of the UN Charter, Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, freedom of navigation and international law,” he said.
The ministers also discussed expanding trade, investment and business ties, including Indian participation in Ukraine's reconstruction.
Sybiha said bilateral trade currently stood at $2.6 billion and that there was significant potential for further growth.
The two sides are expected to discuss a date for a meeting of the intergovernmental economic commission aimed at expanding bilateral trade, he added.
Potential areas for cooperation include energy, infrastructure, transport, agriculture, pharmaceuticals, digitalization and machinery, according to Sybiha.
The ministers also agreed to promote scientific and technological cooperation, contacts between universities and research institutions, and educational and cultural exchanges.

Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:52:08 UTC
21:52:08 KST

Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.
The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.
“I can assure you that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.
Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.
Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.
But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.
In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”
As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.
On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.
Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.
In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”
It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.
However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.
Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

Increased leave, paternity leave, and combating workplace mobbing - a draft of the new Labor Code has been submitted to the Verkhovna Rada
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:51:53 EEST
21:51:53 KST

Increased leave, paternity leave, and combating workplace mobbing - a draft of the new Labor Code has been submitted to the Verkhovna Rada
Kyiv • UNN
The new draft Labor Code provides for the de-Sovietization of labor legislation, ensuring the dignity of employees in the workplace and reducing "labor bureaucracy."
A draft Labor Code that introduces amendments to a number of Laws of Ukraine has been registered in the Verkhovna Rada. In particular, it provides for extending the duration of leave, introducing parental leave for men, and combating psychological terror in the workplace. This was reported by UNN.
Details
According to the explanatory note, the purpose of draft law No. 16010, or the draft Labor Code of Ukraine, is to de-Sovietize labor legislation, regulate individual and collective labor relations based on the principles of freedom and equality, ensure decent work, and implement international standards for regulating labor relations into national legislation.
The Labor Code of Ukraine, adopted in 1971, is Soviet both in content and in spirit and demonstrates a clearly pronounced dominance of the regulatory function of the paternalistic state in the sphere of labor relations, which was characteristic of a planned socialist economy, under which the state was the actual employer in all economic relations. The current Code was developed with a focus on an industrial economy and the existence of large systemic enterprises that were the flagships of the economy. Under current conditions, when the number of workers in the production sector has decreased by more than threefold since 2000, there is an urgent need to adapt labor legislation to the needs of new relations and new sectors of the economy, which absorb the released labor force and adhere to a different philosophy of labor relations
It is also noted that attempts to adopt a new Labor Code over the past 20 years have been insufficiently effective because of the unchanged basic principles on which Ukrainian labor legislation is based.
In addition, it is noted that a characteristic feature of modern labor law is that it includes a significant number of subordinate regulatory legal acts. They contain numerous provisions that often conflict with the provisions of acts of higher legal force.
Such "labor bureaucracy" significantly complicates the application of labor legislation both for employers and for the protection of employees’ rights. Thus, the Code is a mixture of legal provisions adopted under different historical and economic conditions, most of which are outdated and cannot adequately regulate modern labor relations
The new Code also provides for increasing the minimum annual paid leave from 24 to 28 calendar days, and extending leave related to the birth and upbringing of children to men.
In addition, it specifically provides for strengthening the protection of employees from discrimination, mobbing, and harassment in the workplace. The Code regulates modern forms of employment: remote and home-based work, as well as work with an unfixed schedule.
We remind you
The draft new Labor Code proposes legally enshrining employees’ right not to respond to work-related phone calls, messages in messengers, or emails outside the established working hours.

A cartographic rebellion — users are massively downloading the app that refused to rename Lake Ontario
Kyiv • UNN
MapQuest kept the name Lake Ontario despite Trump's executive order. After that, 80,000 people downloaded the app, and its usage grew 50-fold.
Users are massively downloading the app that refused to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America" by order of U.S. President Donald Trump, reports UNN, citing Bild.
Details
Due to the customs conflict with Canada, U.S. President Donald Trump renamed Lake Ontario "Lake America" by executive order. The Canadian city of Toronto, with a population of over one million, is located on its shores, and many of its residents mocked this vengeful move by the American president as a genuine farce. However, U.S. digital services — Google, followed by Apple — evidently did not want problems with the White House and renamed the lake. But one company refused: MapQuest, a former pioneer of digital mapping, still labels the lake as "Lake Ontario".
Behind this rebellion is a tech boss who apparently is not afraid of confrontation with Trump: Michael Blend, head of MapQuest's parent company, System1. He does not hide the fact that he supports the Democrats. Blend donated $5,000 to former Vice President Kamala Harris when she ran against Trump. MapQuest General Manager Doug Berger also made his position clear. On social media, he stated: "We will not change the name!" Trump is even being slightly provoked: the statement refers in capital letters to "Big Beautiful Map" — an allusion to Trump's former posts on Truth Social.
Notably, the cartographic rebels were rewarded — with numerous new customers: MapQuest is now far ahead of Apple and Google in terms of app downloads. 80,000 people downloaded it onto their smartphones within a few hours. Use of the app increased 50-fold, the company reported.
Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario Lake America27.08.26, 20:56 • 13858 views
The rebellion against Trump thus turned out to be a gold mine. In the 1990s, the mapping service was a leader, but today MapQuest is more of a dwarf, especially compared with the two billion monthly users of Google Maps. It seems Trump unintentionally made the service "great again" — even if only for a short time.
