Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:25:06 UTC
20:25:06 KST

Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.
Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.
Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.
At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.
According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.
Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.
Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.
“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal electricity authority, told Reuters.
Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.
“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”
“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”
Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.
The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”
At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we are told there is a dry space inside. We are trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.
The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology available in Nepal right now, and we are taking help from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.
Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.
She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”
She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”
Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.
According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

Leave it to the experts, district councillor told after chaotic deer rescue

Chan said he discovered the trapped animal, crying out helplessly, as he passed by Hung Lam Drive in Tai Po Kau.

The clip also shows that, after the trio pulls the barking deer out of the fence, they lift it over the railing and drop it on the other side, causing it to briefly roll down a slope. It then quickly disappears into the forest.
Chan defended the trio’s approach, arguing the animal was trapped and bleeding. “I cannot leave it injured and bleeding like this,” he said.

A Sverdlovsk region judge has reportedly ordered the nationalization of Ventprom, Russia’s largest manufacturer of industrial ventilation equipment for mines, tunnels and metros.
Yekaterinburg’s Leninsky District Court on Aug. 17 ruled to transfer a 100% stake in the Artyomovsky Machine Engineering Plant Ventprom to the state, according to the Interfax news agency.
“Nothing has changed for us except the shareholder,” a Ventprom spokesperson told Interfax on Thursday.
The government seized the strategic factory after branding its former owners and associates an “extremist organization,” the regional news outlet Vecherniye Vedomosti reported earlier.
The Sverdlovsk region’s deputy prosecutor filed a lawsuit against eight individuals and two foreign companies in connection with the “extremist” designation. They include former Ventprom executives Oleg, Igor and Olga Gorshkov, as well as companies registered in Britain and Germany.
Court records published by Vecherniye Vedomosti show Google and Russia’s communications watchdog Roskomnadzor as being among third parties listed in the court case.
Defense lawyers declined to discuss specifics of the case with the news outlet due to client confidentiality. Unverified reports claimed the “extremist” designation stemmed from a bank transfer that was made to a Ukrainian citizen, as well as to the fact that Gorshkov has lived outside of Russia since 2023.
Vecherniye Vedomosti said Google was likely drawn into litigation since one of the Ukrainians listed in the case, Viktor Litovchenko, is a popular blogger on YouTube, which the tech giant owns. Neither Litovchenko nor the second Ukrainian, Natalia Prushinskaya, reportedly held shares in Ventprom.
Ventprom, which supplies ventilation systems to the Moscow, St. Petersburg, Novosibirsk and Minsk metro networks, as well as to Lukoil, Alrosa and Rusal, reported more than 3 billion rubles (almost $35 million) in revenue last year.

Maduro, wife want US drug charges dismissed on immunity grounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:24:00 UTC
20:24:00 KST

Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife asked a U.S. judge Wednesday to dismiss drug trafficking charges against them, arguing they are immune from prosecution as the former leader and first lady of a foreign country.
In papers filed in Manhattan federal court, lawyers for Maduro said a judge was required by law to reject the indictment because it cannot be brought against a foreign leader.
"No American court has ever presided over the criminal trial of a foreign leader who was recognized by their own country as the sitting head of state at the time the charges were brought," the lawyers wrote.
"That is not an accident of history. It reflects a rule older than the common law: heads of state are exempt from the criminal process of any national court but their own," they added.
Maduro and his wife are scheduled to go on trial on drug trafficking charges next June 1. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein has set oral arguments for Nov. 17 on motions to dismiss the indictment.
Maduro, 63, and his wife, Cilia Flores, 69, have been held at a Brooklyn jail since U.S. forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid in early January and brought them to New York.
In separate papers filed Wednesday, lawyers for Flores said she too has immunity from U.S. prosecution on sovereign immunity grounds.
"It is an attribute of Venezuela’s sovereignty, and only Venezuela may surrender it,” her lawyers wrote.
Maduro's lawyers said that even if Maduro were not entitled to sovereign immunity as the head of state, the case against him must be dismissed because he is also entitled to conduct-based sovereign immunity.
Meanwhile, the lawyers argued, Maduro "vehemently denies the allegations against him."
"If this case were to proceed to trial, it would be apparent that he has been falsely accused," they said.
Both have pleaded not guilty in a criminal case first brought six years ago against numerous alleged co-conspirators.
They face potential life prison sentences if a jury agrees that they were part of a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S.
Federal prosecutors are scheduled to file a response to the arguments later this month.
President Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
U.S. prosecutors claim Maduro carried out a conspiracy to move thousands of tons of cocaine into the U.S. by colluding with Venezuelan law enforcement to help drug kingpins.

Iran tests Trump with Gulf strikes as US touts Hormuz oil surge and battered carrier raises alarms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:23:40 UTC
20:23:40 KST

Iran launched a new round of missile and drone attacks against bases used by U.S. forces in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, testing President Donald Trump’s threat of retaliation even as Washington touted a sharp rise in oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and fresh images highlighted the strain on its naval forces.
Sirens sounded in Kuwait early Thursday, and several hours later the Iranian military said it had targeted Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base, which is used by U.S. forces. Tehran said another attack struck concentrations of American troops and radar systems at Al Minhad Air Base in the UAE. The United States did not announce fresh strikes on Iran overnight, despite Trump warning earlier this week that Washington would respond forcefully to further attacks.
The current escalation began Sunday when the United States struck launchers on Iran’s Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, saying they were preparing to deploy naval mines against passing vessels. Iran responded with missile and drone attacks on Gulf states, prompting a broader U.S. strike Tuesday against around 60 targets in southern Iran and the Hormuz area. Asked Wednesday about another response, Trump said he was “ready,” but added that the confrontation “will not last long.”
A U.S. official told CNN on Thursday that American forces expect operations around Hormuz to continue because Iran still retains the ability to threaten shipping. The official described the expected strikes as “mowing the grass,” aimed at steadily degrading Iranian capabilities. Recent U.S. attacks have targeted radar systems used to track ships, mine-laying capabilities and communications infrastructure.
US touts oil surge through Hormuz
At the same time, the Trump administration is portraying its naval operation in the strait as an increasingly successful effort to restore the flow of oil from the Persian Gulf. Two U.S. officials told CNN that American warships escorted 40 commercial vessels through Hormuz on Tuesday carrying a combined 18 million barrels of oil.
If accurate, that would be close to the roughly 20 million barrels that passed through the strait on an average day before the war. U.S. warships also shot down Iranian drones and intercepted anti-ship cruise missiles during the operation, according to the officials.
Washington says the figures show that Iran is losing leverage over one of the world’s most important energy routes. But maritime experts and industry figures remain skeptical. Shipping trackers still show relatively low traffic, while U.S. officials argue that many vessels are switching off their transponders to make them harder for Iranian forces to target.
A source connected to the maritime industry told CNN that he knew of no one who believed daily traffic had genuinely returned to the levels claimed by Washington.
Trump has meanwhile emphasized economic pressure as his preferred tool against Tehran. The United States continues to restrict Iranian oil exports and has threatened sanctions against countries that maintain economic ties with the regime.
Battered carrier shows toll of deployment
The campaign is also putting pressure on U.S. military resources. The USS Abraham Lincoln arrived this week at Laem Chabang in Thailand after completing 268 days at sea during its Middle East deployment, where it supported operations against Iran before being replaced by the USS George Washington.
Its roughly 5,000 crew members are now receiving a week of rest, but photographs taken after the carrier arrived showed extensive rust across large sections of its exterior.
Former U.S. Navy Capt. Carl Schuster told CNN that rust itself is common on warships, but said the unusually long deployment made regular maintenance difficult and allowed corrosion to spread. Based on the images, he estimated that removing it could require about 30 days of preservation work.
“Rust is like a contagious disease. It spreads,” Schuster said, warning that untreated corrosion can eventually weaken steel structures such as decks, passageways and railings.
The Lincoln’s condition adds to broader concerns over prolonged deployments, ammunition stocks and the strain on U.S. forces as Washington tries to keep shipping moving through Hormuz while maintaining pressure on Iran.
For Trump, the latest Iranian attacks sharpen that tension: Tehran is still testing Washington militarily even as the administration argues that its economic and naval strategy is beginning to work.

Interview: SCO offers unique model for global governance, says SCO secretary-general
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:22:22 CST
20:22:22 KST

BISHKEK, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) can serve as an example for modern global governance, SCO Secretary-General Nurlan Yermekbayev has said.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, he said that within the organization, decisions are made by consensus, countries have equal rights, and the interests of each participant are taken into account.
In the 25 years since its founding, the SCO has been advocating for strengthening multilateralism, abiding by international law, equal dialogue, and the development of a fair system of international relations, he said.
"The SCO has every opportunity to become a 'laboratory' for global multilateral cooperation -- a space where ideas of peace, security, development and dialogue take concrete forms," Yermekbayev noted.
In his opinion, one of the SCO's main achievements is the formation of a unique space of trust and cooperation among countries with their own historical, political and civilizational traditions.
"Over the years, member states have developed a sustainable culture of multilateral interaction based on equality, mutual respect, consideration of each other's interests, and the search for consensus," he noted.
He said the organization has established sustainable mechanisms to combat terrorism, separatism, extremism, transnational organized crime, drug trafficking and other modern threats, while offering substantial opportunities for cooperation in such fields as trade and investment, transport connectivity, energy, the digital economy, agriculture, environmental protection, education, science, culture, healthcare and tourism.
The secretary-general said the "Shanghai Spirit" of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations, and pursuit of common development is the important philosophical foundation for the SCO's development, allowing SCO countries to cooperate successfully.
"States from various regions see the SCO not as an instrument of geopolitical rivalry, but as a platform for equal dialogue, mutually beneficial cooperation, and the joint search for answers to common challenges," he said.
Yermekbayev emphasized China's significant role in the SCO's formation and development.
"Over the past 25 years, China has consistently supported the development of the organization and made a significant contribution to strengthening its institutional capacity," he said.
In this regard, it is of great significance that Chinese President Xi Jinping has put forward important concepts, such as building an even closer SCO community with a shared future, as well as building a common home featuring solidarity and mutual trust, peace and tranquility, prosperity and development, good-neighborliness and friendship, as well as fairness and justice, the SCO secretary-general noted.
"These concepts largely reflect the philosophy of the Shanghai Spirit, giving it new meaning applicable to modern conditions," he said.
Yermekbayev noted that the four global initiatives put forward by Xi -- the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative, and the Global Governance Initiative -- have been widely praised. "This is a complementary system of ideas and practical approaches aimed at addressing pressing contemporary challenges and building a just, peaceful, and sustainable world order," he said.
As the 2025 SCO Tianjin Summit marked the commencement of a new stage in the organization's development, Yermekbayev said, the decisions adopted at the meeting defined strategic guidelines for the organization until 2035.
"The SCO faces great opportunities," he said, expressing hope that the just-concluded Bishkek summit will inject new impetus into the SCO's development.
He also voiced hope that participants of the summit will work together, maintain strategic mutual trust, and safeguard peace and development interests, and that the SCO will make even more significant contribution to building a secure, just, and prosperous Eurasian region and the entire world. ■

No evidence Morocco planned Ceuta migrant surge: Spain PM

11:22:00 UTC
20:22:00 KST

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Thursday they have found no evidence that Moroccan authorities orchestrated or took part in a deadly border rush into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July.
Sanchez's comments in the lower house of parliament followed a police report that emerged this week saying that the mass entry into Ceuta was not a spontaneous migration event but a planned and phased operation designed to overwhelm border controls.
"I can assure you that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever," Sanchez said.
However, he said Morocco's Gendarmerie police did allow crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on July 30, when migrant arrivals peaked. Spanish authorities had yet to determine whether this was due to inaction or inability to contain the influx, Sanchez added.
The police report, seen by Reuters, alleged that Moroccan security forces were initially deployed in smaller numbers than usual near the Tarajal breakwater separating the enclave from the North African country and did not make a serious attempt to disperse the crowds.
Some uniformed Moroccan officers gave directions toward the crossing point, while other unidentified people appeared to guide or monitor the flow of people, the report said, but it did not identify individual officers or provide independently verified evidence of orders from Moroccan authorities.
Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Last Monday, Sanchez accused Russia and Israel of spreading disinformation about Spain’s migration policy that helped trigger the migrant surge into Ceuta.
He said that research by the EU's diplomatic service EEAS had indicated that Russian and Israeli networks had been behind the spread of disinformation in conjunction with far-right networks.
Sanchez added that it was clear that the two countries had used the crisis to criticize Madrid due to dissatisfaction with its position on the wars in Ukraine and Gaza, but gave no further details on the evidence he had of their involvement.
Over 72,000 migrants irregularly crossed from Morocco into the tiny Spanish territory between July 30 and 31 in an unprecedented surge at one of the EU's only two land borders with Africa, prompting alarm across the bloc. At least 100 people died in the attempt, according to Ceuta's local authorities.
Roughly 5,000 migrants, some seeking asylum, have remained in Ceuta, triggering near-daily protests from locals against the Spanish government's handling of the crisis and sporadic attacks against a makeshift migrant camp at El Trampolin beach, according to police reports.

No end to torture of Gaza doctor Abu Safia in Israeli prison: What to know

No end to torture of Gaza doctor Abu Safia in Israeli prison: What to know
Abu Safia, in custody for nearly two years, continues to face abuse inside prison, his lawyer says.
Jailed Palestinian doctor Hussam Abu Safia continues to face abuse in Israeli detention, according to his lawyer, raising renewed concerns about his safety inside prison.
Israel abducted Abu Safia on December 27, 2024 from Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza for defying Israeli orders to evacuate the hospital – one of the last remaining functioning medical facilities in the Gaza Strip at the time. Israel has killed hundreds of medics and destroyed or damaged almost all of Gaza’s hospitals as part of its genocidal war on the enclave.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UN experts urge Israel to free Gaza doctor amid reports of ‘severe torture’
- list 2 of 4Israeli court rules to keep prominent Palestinian doctor in detention
- list 3 of 4Jailed Gaza hospital chief in life-threatening condition, rights group says
- list 4 of 4UN inquiry urges release of Palestinian doctor jailed by Israel
Campaigners and the family of the Palestinian doctor have routinely highlighted his physical state inside the prison and called for his release. In July, a United Nations inquiry commission said Abu Safia faced “continued and severe abuse”, and last month, the director general of Gaza’s Ministry of Health called for urgent action to “save” the jailed doctor’s life.
So what is the latest testimony by the jailed doctor, and why does Israel continue to keep him in detention without charge?
What is Abu Safia’s latest testimony?
The jailed doctor’s latest testimony was conveyed by his lawyer Nasser Odeh, according to a statement on Wednesday by Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI). Odeh visited Abu Safia in the Rakefet detention facility inside Nitzan Prison in central Israel on Sunday.
Abu Safia said Israeli prison guards continued to beat him, deprive him of sleep and threaten him against sharing the conditions of his detention with his lawyer.
Guards have assaulted the doctor by “punching and kicking him and beating him with batons across his body, including sensitive areas”, according to the statement from PHRI.
Abu Safia is also “deliberately” deprived of sleep through the use of loudspeakers and other noise throughout the night, PHRI said.
What else has Abu Safia experienced during his detention?
Rights groups and his family have long said he shows signs of having been regularly tortured.
The doctor has been held in solitary confinement at the underground Rakefet facility, where he has been subjected to daily violence and beatings, his lawyer has said in the past.
At one point, his injuries were so severe – with “fresh and serious bruises on his head, around his eyes, on his ears, and on his neck”, that his lawyer had trouble recognising him, PHRI said in July.
In June, footage of Abu Safia appearing via videolink before an Israeli court showed him looking noticeably thinner in his face and around his abdomen.
On August 10, he was transferred from Rakefet to the prison service’s medical centre at Ramla prison, which PHRI has stated “in itself indicates serious medical needs that cannot be adequately addressed in ordinary prison wards”.
What are rights groups saying?
The jailed Gaza doctor’s testimony comes as PHRI pursues legal proceedings demanding that an independent physician examine him, a request that was submitted to the Israel Prison Service on July 7 but has not yet been approved, the organisation said.
Abu Safia has also petitioned an Israeli administrative court through the group, and the Israel Prison Service recently requested additional time to submit its response.
The Israeli rights group has said “there is no justification for further delay.”
When was Abu Safia arrested and why?
There have been no charges filed against the doctor, and he has not undergone any trial as he is being held under Israel’s combatant law, a policy it has used to hold Palestinians for prolonged periods without trial.
The Israeli forces abducted the doctor after raiding Kamal Adwan Hospital, which the Israeli military destroyed. He had refused to evacuate the hospital.
Amnesty International has called the combatant law “at odds with international law”.
“This law authorises the military to issue indefinitely renewable detention orders against anyone from the Gaza Strip suspected of posing a threat to state security or engagement in hostile activities, based on classified evidence and without having to produce an indictment,” Sara Hashash, Amnesty’s deputy regional director for the Middle East and North Africa, told Al Jazeera.
Before his detention, he had been a prominent voice highlighting Gaza’s decimated healthcare sector during Israel’s genocidal war and continued to work despite the death of one of his sons in an Israeli drone attack.
At least 13 other Palestinian doctors from Gaza have been imprisoned for more than a year and a half without charges or due process, according to PHRI.
“Our central demand remains unchanged: The release of the 14 physicians from Gaza, including Dr Abu Safia, so that they can reunite with their families and resume their medical duties,” the organisation said in its statement on Wednesday.
What has been the international response to Abu Safia’s arrest?
In July, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory called for Israel to immediately release Abu Safia. The commission also urged Israeli authorities to provide him with immediate independent medical care.
Leading human rights organisations, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, have also petitioned for his release and an end to his torture in Israeli custody.
“Amnesty International has expressed grave concern over reports that Dr Hussam Abu Safia has been subjected to severe physical and psychological abuse, prolonged solitary confinement, beatings and other ill-treatment in detention,” Hashash said.
“Amnesty International’s position is clear: Dr Hussam Abu Safia should be immediately and unconditionally released, as should all Palestinians who are arbitrarily detained without charge or trial,” she told Al Jazeera.
How have Palestinians been treated inside Israeli prisons?
The UN commission’s July report found that Israeli authorities’ reported conduct towards Abu Safia reflects a broader pattern of violations that it identified in previous reports. The commission has found that torture and ill-treatment of Palestinian detainees is widespread and systematic.
It has called on Israel to end its practices of arbitrary detention and torture and has urged that independent medical experts, the International Committee of the Red Cross and human rights monitors be given unhindered access to places of detention.
Hashash urged the international community to use all available diplomatic, legal and economic measures to pressure Israel to end arbitrary detention.
“In light of Israel’s persistent disregard for international law and its lack of cooperation with UN and other international human rights mechanisms, it is crucial that all states exert diplomatic and economic pressure on Israel to release Dr Hussam Abu Safia and all Palestinians it arbitrarily detains,” she said.
According to PHRI, Israel’s policy of torture in prisons against Palestinian detainees has killed at least 105 people since October 2023.
Israel is currently holding more than 9,400 prisoners, including 92 women and more than 370 children, according to Palestinian and Israeli rights groups.
Palestinians jailed by Israel have faced widespread abuse in custody, including routine beatings, starvation and sexual assault. Former Palestinian detainees have told Al Jazeera how they suffered dehumanising treatment by guards and soldiers, including torture and sexual violence.

China aims to raise its total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan by 2030, according to an implementation guideline released on Monday. ■

Gloria Steinem's Long and Revealing History With TIME
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:21:42 UTC
20:21:42 KST

Over the course of her long and influential life, Gloria Steinem went from being described in the pages of TIME as “one of the best dates to take to a New York party these days” and “smashing looking Gucci liberal” to being lauded as a “feminist icon.” If nothing else, the shift in the tone of her coverage in the magazine provides a window into the change in attitudes toward women that she helped engineer over the course of her 92-year life, which ended on Sept. 2.
Let’s add one more description to the list: durable dynamo. Steinem never outlived her ability to be relevant, inspiring several generations of women to organize and strive to be given the same opportunities as men. She never stopped blazing a trail for those who faced a particularly dense thicket and she never thought small. “I believe that things are a circle, not a hierarchy,” she said to TIME in 2011. “The kind of society we are striving toward is one in which things are linked not ranked. And one in which we understand that the women’s movement and the anti racist movement and the gay movement and the environmentalist movement, they’re all linked.”
Steinem was born on March 25, 1934, to a homemaker mother and a father with, she later said, only two points of pride: "He never wore a hat, and he never had a job. He was always going to make a movie, or cut a record, or start a new hotel, or come up with a new orange drink." She didn't spend a full year in school until she was 12, when her parents split and she ended up living with her mother, whose mental health was in a dire state, in East Toledo, Ohio. At 16, she was sent to live with an aunt in Washington. Before that, she says, "I'd never lived any place to invite anybody home to. I thought that people always ate out of refrigerators."
After graduating from Smith College in 1956, she spent two years in India on a fellowship (and also to get out of an engagement), then came home to work in Cambridge, Mass., for a group encouraging American students to attend Communist youth festivals abroad. It was later revealed to be CIA-funded, but Steinem was unfussed, saying she “was happy to use the Establishment's money against the Establishment."
In 1963, she famously published a first-person account of her glamour-free month undercover as a Playboy Bunny in Show magazine. It was her big break, and it also threatened to be her curse, since at first she almost exclusively got offered assignments along the same lines. This was the period when TIME thought it important to note an appearance in which she wore “a Luis Estevez creation that consisted of five widely spaced bands of chinchilla held together by transparent black net. In between was supposed to be little more than a bare bodkin.”
She later got hired at the fledgling New York magazine, where in 1968 her first story was about Vietnamese leader Ho Chi Minh’s stint as a New York City waiter and laundryman. As she steadily found her journalistic feet, she began to find her calling: to use her charm, wit and platform to promote equality. Steinem understood the fear that these ideas stirred up in people. “Women don't want to exchange places with men,” she wrote in an essay for TIME in 1970, shortly after the magazine identified her as “a trim, undeniably female, blonde-streaked brunette who has been described as 'the thinking man's Jean Shrimpton.' " She went on to add: “But we do want to change the economic system to one more based on merit. In Women's Lib Utopia, there will be free access to good jobs—and decent pay for the bad ones women have been performing all along, including housework.”
Inevitably, her activism moved beyond writing to organizing. In 1971, along with Shirley Chisholm, Bella Abzug, Betty Friedan and several others, she convened the National Women's Political Caucus to try to get more women into government offices. Shortly after that she co-founded Ms. magazine, which she described as “a how-to magazine; not how to make jelly but how to seize control of your life." TIME’s writers, by this time calling her “feminism’s superstar,” finally began to acknowledge her impact. A story about the 1972 Democratic convention—titled, alas, "Eve's Operatives"—opened with: “Gazing around the convention through her blue-tinted glasses, Gloria Steinem pronounced with satisfaction: ‘We've changed the population here. It almost looks like the country. What she meant was that women are 52% of the nation's population, and last week close to 40% of the convention delegates were women—a dramatic jump over their 13% representation at the 1968 Democratic Convention.”
There was a still way to go, however—both for women and for TIME. “Decorative as the women were in their bell-bottom trousers, miniskirts, jeans and hot pants,” the magazine went on to say, “they were not there to be on display but to seek power. Except for a couple of setbacks, they got enough to satisfy and even surprise them.” After the crushing loss of Democratic Presidential Candidate George McGovern to Richard Nixon, Steinem’s political campaigning took a backseat to her advocacy work. The 1977 women’s conference, which she has called "the most important event that nobody knows about," remained one of her proudest achievements, even as it sparked a conservative backlash and perhaps the founding of the religious right.
10 Questions for Gloria Steinem
As the decades passed, Steinem’s activism grew to encompass more than women’s equality. She campaigned on behalf of native people, was arrested while protesting apartheid, publicly opposed the first Gulf War, advocated for disarmament in Korea, spoke against child abuse, female genital mutilation and pornography, and was an early supporter of LGB rights. (It took her a little longer to endorse the transgender movement.) Her advocacy was always couched in pragmatism and compassion. She pointed out that the pedestal women were put on was "as much a prison as any small, confined space" and called her 2019 memoir The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off! Writing, her first calling, remained one of her great loves—"the only thing that, when I do it, I don't feel I should be doing something else." She published books throughout her career, many of which, including her first memoir, 1983’s Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, were bestsellers; her latest, An Unexpected Life, is due out this fall. (She often joked that she wished her books didn’t get republished so much because it would mean they were no longer relevant.)
By the '90s, Steinem had scored a TIME cover, albeit one about a pushback against feminism, after her book about female self esteem—Revolution From Within—was a bestseller. “As she tours shopping malls, Steinem is being mobbed by crowds that, according to one bookstore owner, exceed those of Oliver North and Vanna White, the backlash icons of American manhood and womanhood,” Nancy Gibbs wrote. As well as writing her own books, Steinem contributed to countless others, appeared in more than 120 films, help produce several documentaries and inspired the 2019 Off Broadway play, Gloria: A Life. She cast her gaze domestically, locally, nationally and globally, founding Equality Now, which aimed to elevate and protect the rights of girls and women internationally.
Somewhere around the turn of the century, the times—and TIME— caught up with Steinem; her ideas became mainstream and her words and activities were covered with the kind of reverence reserved for icons. In 2013, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Half a century after writing her Women's Lib Utopia essay for TIME, she annotated it, warning that women had made many advances but that the "time of greatest danger comes after a victory, and that’s where we are now." (She also noted that she found out later that she had been paid less than the men who wrote for the same issue.)
Through it all she kept one of her less acknowledged gifts intact: her sense of humor. She did not come up with the classic feminist saying that women need men like a fish needs a bicycle, but she popularized it. She was always threatening to get a back tattoo for her 70th birthday. So frequently was she asked about her beauty secret that she came up with the perfect reply: "Revolution," she would say. "It keeps you young."
In 2011, TIME asked what she would do if she only had two years to live. “It seems to me one of the uses of age is to help you know what you want to do and keep from wasting time,” she said. “And I have this unfortunate notion that I’m immortal, which doesn’t cause you to plan very well. I think it would be mainly about writing and seeing friends, my chosen family. And writing what I believe. And maybe living with elephants. I do still want to live with elephants.”

This is not a standard review but notes of developments spotted and noted quickly over the past two weeks, and some very limited comments. Expect this format next week, then return to standard after that.

My guess is the most significant development of the past two weeks will play out to be:
1st and 3rd Corps have been assigned the mission of holding Slovyansk and Kramatorsk against the expected Russian offensive. Both commanders are self-made generals – Denys Prokopenko (1st Azov Corps) and Andriy Biletsky (3rd Army Corps) – who rose through Azov’s ranks; in other words, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) put its first team and best players into the Donetsk region.
These are two of the AFU’s hardest-fighting corps – although, to be fair, probably the 30th Marine and 7th and 8th Airborne Assault Corps are to that level. The presence of USF brass at the outset of the planning makes crystal clear the Ukrainian intent: when Russia launches its big offensive, probably after the fall wet season, the most effective Drone Wall buzz saw will be in place to meet it. Three months is a long time to let Ukrainians prepare…
This command move was the work of Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapaty and President Volodymyr Zelensky and although I know it’s not fashionable to observe positive leadership by Zelensky, this is an unchallengeable example. The man clearly is pushing for a younger, more modern, and more agile AFU leadership.
Russia to Close Goethe-Institut Branches in Retaliation Against Germany
On Aug. 26 the Ukrainians ran a typical-for-them complicated air strike with all manner of moving parts and preparatory operations; it appeared to have worked and at least one Russian army HQ was blown up.
The Play-by-Play (Note: None of the images are by me, all are pulled from open sources, order of images isn’t really tied to the text)
- Aug. 15 – The Chongar railroad bridge collapses of its own accord, ending heavy rail transport between Crimea and the rest of the world. Probably the Russians will build a bypass, but for trucks. Under present circumstances, laying down new track is probably impossible because of the drones.
- Aug. 15 – Flamingo missiles hit the Progress plant in Samara twice. This is the center of Russia’s national space effort. The missiles appear to have hit a pair of production buildings that manufacture Soyuz components in hyper-sterile conditions. In one building, manufacturing lines opened to the elements include electrical equipment, instruments and printed circuit boards. The second building is final assembly. Usually, Flamingos miss or get shot down, but not this time, it seems.
- Aug. 16 – Massive fires at two Wildberries warehouses outside Moscow, 600+ drones involved in strikes
- Aug. 16 – Drones take out a Bastion launcher for hypersonics in Crimea. This is another early indicator that the Ukrainians are actively hunting Russian ballistic/hypersonic launchers because the Ukrainians are out of Patriot interceptor missiles.
- Aug. 17 – Zelensky replaced the commander of the Logistics Forces of the Ukrainian Armed Forces: Yury Pogrebnoi was appointed instead of Volodymyr Karpenko. This is another step in the overhaul of the AFU senior command. Pogrebnoi is 41 years old and comes from the Sumy region. He has served primarily in military logistics and technical support, and his prior job was deputy chief of logistics of Joint Forces East.
- Aug. 17 – Ukraine tests its first “Uravnitel” guided aerial bomb, and it is already being procured for the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Roughly, Uravnitel in Ukrainian means “equalizer.” The bomb was developed by DG Industry. It features a 250-kilogram (550-pound) warhead and is capable of striking targets at a range of up to 130 kilometers (80 miles). Keep this in mind if you decide to read through to the Aug. 26 entry. The Ukrainians say it costs three times less than the American JDAM.
- Aug. 18 – Yet another massed strike at Moscow, 600+ drones, Wildberries warehouse burned
- Aug. 18 – Fines issued in southern Russia for complaining about gasoline shortages. A court in Volgograd fined a local woman for griping about fuel station queues and outages, charging her under the article prohibiting participation in mass gatherings.
- Aug. 18 – Russian Banderole jet-powered drones hit the village of Pechenihy, Kharkiv region, 10 dead, 17 injured. The strike appears to have targeted wholly civilian structures: cafe, post office, shop, private houses.
- Aug. 19-20 – Russia launches its long-awaited “big” strike, 45 missiles of which about 12-15 are ballistic missiles. The weapons came in two waves. Kyiv was the primary target and a border checkpoint in Odesa was the secondary target. One ballistic missile destroyed the top two stories of a five-story Kyiv apartment building. As of midday Thursday the casualty count was 16 dead and 45-50 injured. As per Ukraine air force policy, no stats were published on how many ballistic missiles were intercepted; based on air war networks, the figure for that probably is somewhere between “none” and “zero.”
- Aug. 20 – Drones hit six cargo ships off Tuapse, leaving one burning seriously, four more were hit on Aug. 24-25.
- Aug. 20 – Sevastopol – Authorities announced power shortages are so bad that the city is switching to a 2/6 electricity rationing, i.e., about two hours with power and up to six hours without power. Things have been much worse outside Crimea’s cities, with some outlying villages reporting no power – not making this up – for a month so far. Sevastopol, as the administrative and imperial heart of Russian occupation of Crimea, had managed to avoid serious blackouts. Not anymore.

- Aug. 22 – Ukrainian forces hits Ozon warehouse, Samara, fires.
- Aug 22 – Substantial Russian strike, 200 drones, 10–20 missiles, Odesa and Kyiv targeted, seemingly railway and rail infrastructure primarily. Odesa was the primary target: 17 Banderol missiles, four Kh-59 and Kh-31 missiles, about 10 aerial bombs.

Two Russian army command HQs in Donetsk hit, heavy damage. 51 Army commander and staff reportedly killed in underground parking lot converted to command center; it appears six (!) SCALPs punctured the parking lot’s roof and blew up inside the command center.There was wide speculation that the second half of the strikes was carried out with US experimental JDAM-LR precision-guided bombs, which the US is only experimenting with and neither Washington nor Kyiv have mentioned as a possible sale to Ukraine. The key argument of the speculation was that the JDAM-LR can fly 150+ km and so might be launched safely outside the range of Russian air defenses, while the JDAM we know the Ukrainians have – JDAM-ER – only has a max range of 75 km or so and in practice the Ukrainian bombers can’t squeeze more than 45–50 km from the weapon, because they have to fly low to avoid Russian air defenses and glide bombs fly further if released at high altitude.If you’ve read this far you know the Ukrainians just tested their OWN JDAM-like glide bomb, and further, there was the SEAD strikes the Ukrainians had flown in SW Russia (next to Donetsk) in the past few days. So my sense is the Ukrainians either broke a hole in the Donetsk air defense coverage and sent a bomber into the gap, or, they waited for the Russian air defenses to go apesh*t from six incoming SCALP missiles and then timed the bomb drops for the point of maximum Russian air defense confusion. Or knowing the Ukrainians, they did both. But bottom line, this was a very sophisticated air strike that barely made news outside Ukraine.

- Aug 28 – SBU drones hit Engels airfield, Tu-95M bomber is hit and its wing blown in two. Rare destruction of irreplaceable strategic bomber.
- Aug 28 – Bloomberg reports Ukraine hit record number of Russia oil refineries 21 hit, it was 18 in July. Four of Russia’s 10 largest refineries hit during August. Very wide targeting including Tatarstan, Bashkortostan, Volga region, Yaroslavl and Moscow region. Russian crude processing is currently 3.8 million barrels/day for August; prewar August was 5.3–5.5 million b/d. Gasoline production down 20 percent on year, diesel production down 23 percent on year. Remember, the Allied bombing tactic that shut down the Wehrmacht was attacks against German fuel production. Damage is difficult to repair and it accumulates; meanwhile the military keeps drinking fuel.

Care workers and others fleeing UK modern slavery win visa reprieve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:19:19 UTC
20:19:19 KST

Care workers, chefs and others in danger of losing their migration status under post-Brexit rules if they leave an exploitative employer will be helped by new visa changes, the Home Office says.
Officials said if an employee was found to be a victim of modern slavery they would be allowed to work for any employer for the remainder of their visa.
The migration status of people on skilled worker visas was tied to a sponsoring employer, under a scheme introduced to fill post-Brexit labour shortages by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government in 2021.
It meant workers on that route, who have no recourse to public funds, risked having to leave the UK if they lost their job and could not quickly find a new sponsoring employer.
Campaigners have been warning the rule was being exploited by rogue employers, who use workers’ precarious status in the UK to underpay them, force them to put in long hours, or to force them into zero-hour conditions.
From Thursday, the restriction tying an individual’s immigration status to a specific sponsor will be lifted if they receive a positive “conclusive grounds” decision formally recognising them as a victim of modern slavery through the national referral mechanism – the UK’s framework for identifying and supporting victims of modern slavery and human trafficking.
The Salvation Army’s deputy director of anti-trafficking and modern slavery, Maj Heather Grinsted, said: “Allowing survivors to work for another sponsor for the remainder of their visa is a crucial way to help them rebuild their lives safely and with dignity.”
However, Dr Dora-Olivia Vicol, CEO of the Work Rights Centre, cautioned that while the changes “could be a gamechanger”, the impact depended “on how accessible the modern slavery framework is”.
She added: “For almost three years we have warned the Home Office that the sponsorship system instituted after Brexit is a recipe for labour exploitation, and have urged officials to free people’s visas from their employers’ control.”
Last week the Guardian reported that the number of employers being stripped of their licence to sponsor workers for abuses had hit record levels.
More than 6,600 sponsors have been stripped of licences since Labour came to power. Of these, more than 4,400 were in the year to June 2026, a 140% rise on the year before.
Modern slavery can include abusive working and living conditions, withheld wages, deception, intimidation, threats, violence, controlled movement, or confiscated passports.
Ministers say the rule change will help care workers, chefs, hospitality staff and others who came to the UK in good faith, but faced abuse.
Where evidence of criminality is identified, sponsors will be referred to the police.
The minister for migration and citizenship, Jo White, said: “No victim of modern slavery should be trapped with an exploitative employer because of their immigration status. These changes will give victims the freedom to leave abusive workplaces and rebuild their lives.
“While we support them, we are also cracking down on those responsible. Rogue sponsors who exploit workers will face the full force of the law.”
The government says it is also making it easier, through the immigration white paper, for sponsored workers to change employer, strengthening protections against exploitation.
A lack of safeguards had led unions and some councils to introduce their own provisions, with Unison working with care workers and councils to produce a migrant care workers charter.
Last year 111,000 skilled worker visas were granted, 76% fewer than at the peak in the year ending December 2023. The fall came after new overseas applications for care worker visas were stopped after July 2025.

Sadiq Khan cleared of car tax conviction caused by ‘scam’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:19:07 UTC
20:19:07 KST

A car tax conviction against the mayor of London has been withdrawn after it transpired that he was targeted by a “scam” that led to him being fined for failing to tax a car that was not his.
Sadiq Khan was found guilty last month under what has been described as a system of “conveyor-belt justice”, in which magistrates decide on hundreds of cases a day, sometimes spending less than a minute on each.
City Hall officials say the 24-year-old Nissan Micra did not belong to Khan or Transport for London.
The case was formally reopened at a magistrates court hearing at Hereford justice centre on Thursday and withdrawn by a panel of magistrates after a request from the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA).
Neither the mayor nor a representative from the DVLA were present at the court for the one-minute hearing.
A legal adviser told the panel of magistrates that they may be aware of the case since it was “widely publicised” on Wednesday, adding: “The DVLA have requested that the original matter, if you consider it to be reopened, be marked withdrawn.”
Chair of the bench, Mrs Digings JP, said: “We accept the reopening of the case as requested. Further to the request from the DVLA, we are going to mark the matter as withdrawn.”
The mayor has been the focus of protests in the past by motorists angry at the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone in London. Some said they planned to register cars in Khan’s name to make him liable for the £12.50 daily charge.
After the conviction emerged on Wednesday, a spokesperson for Khan said the mayor had been the target of “a scam, which is a crime”.
“It’s not the first time the mayor has been the victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle. Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware,” they added.
Khan had been convicted in his absence by a magistrate – who was sitting in a private hearing of the single justice procedure – and was ordered to pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs and to settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.

The USS Abraham Lincoln crew received their first rest-and-recuperation day on Wednesday after 286 days at sea, deployed in the Middle East, with photos showing significant surface rust amid reports of mental health concerns, deteriorating onboard conditions, and a possible redeployment until 2027.
The ship was docked in eastern Thailand, with busloads of sailors and Marines wearing civilian clothes, many smiling and waving, arriving hours later at a hotel in the resort city of Pattaya, about 150 km (93 miles) southeast of Bangkok.
On the eve of the Lincoln's arrival, Pattaya street vendors near the city's infamous "Walking Street" nightlife zone were excited by the prospect of a boost in sales.
"It's been so quiet these days," said clothes seller Kadsalin Ketpa, 43. "I hope with their arrival they would drive my sales up."
Food seller Saroch, 45, told Reuters that port visits by the US military were good for business. "They're here for drinks, having fun, and letting loose," Saroch said.
"Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our Sailors and Marines to rest and recharge," the commander of Carrier Strike Group 3, Rear Admiral Robert E. Loughran, said in a statement.
"What this strike group has accomplished is truly historic. I could not be prouder of the exceptional professionalism and expertise demonstrated by every member of this team during our operations."
Concerns of mental health amid reports of a new deployment
Shakeira Fairfax flew in from New Jersey and was waiting outside the Pattaya hotel to meet her 25-year-old daughter Jade, a crew member on the Lincoln.
She explained how there were moments during the long deployment after the start of the Iran war when morale was low, when contact was limited, and she feared for her daughter's safety.
"There was a period of silence," she said. "It was an uncertain time; it was a scary time. It was difficult, it was definitely difficult, but she has a support system," she told reporters.
"I just can't wait to see her smile. I can't wait to hear 'Mom'; I know that's the first thing she's gonna say," she said.
Pentagon expected to extend deployment amid supply chain disruptions report
And while the crew is expected to rest while the ship undergoes maintenance, a report by The Wall Street Journal revealed that the Pentagon plans to extend deployment in the Middle East until at least 2027.
Sources said the military presence is intended to preserve President Donald Trump's ability to choose between continued economic pressure, limited military operations, and broader escalation.
Some aides have warned Trump that expanding the conflict beyond the recent exchanges of strikes could hurt Republican candidates in the November midterm elections, according to the report. Trump has maintained that electoral considerations are not guiding his military decisions.
The decision also comes amid reports by The New York Times about problems in the logistics chain to supply troops in the Middle East, with strikes on critical bases in the region forcing the US to use naval routes for resupply missions.
According to the report, the operations in the region require some 420,000 meals per week, which are brought to the soldiers using some 30 million liters of fuel.
The report noted that the strikes on a key logistical base in Bahrain forced the US to use the island of Diego Garcia (located some 3,500 kilometers from the conflict zone) and Singapore (6,000 kilometers away) as logistical points.
Shir Perets contributed to this report.

Iran war drives gasoline prices in Germany to record high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:16:18 UTC
20:16:18 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
The price of gasoline has reached a record high following the resurgence of the Iran war, Europe’s largest automobile association (ADAC) said Thursday.
The nationwide daily average price for a liter of E10 gasoline surged to €2.215 ($2.57) on Wednesday, surpassing the previous record of €2.203 set in March 2022, ADAC added.
Furthermore, low water levels on the Rhine river have also recently had an impact on prices, as they have increased transportation costs.
E10 is the cheapest common type of gasoline in Germany. It is generally 5 to 6 cents cheaper than Super E5, which is allowed to contain less biofuel.
High gas prices are often followed by calls to ease the burden on drivers. From early May through late June, a fuel rebate of 16.7 cents per liter was in effect, which cost the federal government approximately €1.6 billion, according to an estimate by the Finance Ministry.
The government has so far refused to renew the program. Germany’s public finances are already in the red due to the debt-financed investment package.
Nominal price records do not reflect, in any case, what percentage of their income citizens actually have to spend on energy, food, etc. This is because both prices and wages are rising. The statistical offices therefore always report the inflation rate on an adjusted basis.
In August, inflation had risen again to 2.9% overall due to the war in Iran.

Hong Kong regulator reclassifies certain funds with exposure to private markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:12:03 UTC
20:12:03 KST

Hong Kong regulator reclassifies certain funds with exposure to private markets
The industry has increasingly focused on the risks of what was previously a booming private credit industry
Hong Kong’s market regulator has reclassified some of the city’s authorised funds with exposure to private market assets above a certain amount as complex products, raising the threshold for selling these products to retail investors.
Funds with exposures to direct or indirect private market assets amounting to 50 per cent or more of their net asset value would be recategorised.
The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) said that it observed some funds gaining indirect exposure to private market assets through layered structures and complex instruments, which might lack transparency.
This structure made it difficult for retail investors to fully understand the underlying risks, the SFC said in a circular released on Thursday.
Due to low liquidity, valuation challenges and higher credit risks, funds with exposure to private credit and private equity would need to enhance their transparency regarding underlying investments and associated risks, according to the SFC.
Funds classified as complex products are subject to the SFC’s selling requirements, which include ensuring product suitability, the regulator added.

China’s grey-zone game: Why India must prepare for ‘armed coexistence’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:09:58 UTC
20:09:58 KST

China’s grey-zone game: Why India must prepare for ‘armed coexistence’
Indrajeet Rai / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Sep 03, 2026, 19:47 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
India-China ties have thawed since the border skirmish in 2020.
Former foreign secretary Vijay Gokhale argues that China waits for a strategic opening, acts pre-emptively and then builds a narrative of self-defence.His new book, “China’s Wars: The Politics and Diplomacy Behind its Military Coercion”, examines past conflicts and China’s recent grey-zone tactics.In an interview with Indrajeet Rai, Gokhale explains why the India-China relationship has entered an era of “armed coexistence”, why a full-scale war is not the most likely outcome but cannot be ruled out, and how political uncertainty after Xi Jinping could produce global economic shocks or military adventurism. Edited excerpts:You describe China as an opportunistic power. What does that mean, and when does Beijing decide to act pre-emptively?By opportunistic power, I did not intend to suggest that China is very different from other major powers. In the case studies in my book, China waited for the international situation to turn favourable, or for some advantage to accrue from its relations with other major powers, before carrying out conflict with a neighbour or another country. It used opportunity strategically to achieve its goals.The Chinese idea of preventive deterrence or preventive conflict differs from the Western concept. In the West, deterrence is a counteraction intended to stop the adversary from escalating. In the Chinese context, it is pre-emptive: China acts even before the adversary has had the chance to act first. The aim is to deliver a political and psychological shock so the adversary desists or fears retaliation.The 1962 conflict is one example. There was no indication that India intended to launch a military assault. But China used the words of then PM Jawaharlal Nehru and an international situation dominated by the Cuban missile crisis to act pre-emptively against India.
China often depicts its own aggressive action as defensive and blames the other side. How central is this narrative warfare to its strategy?The Chinese Communist Party utilised China’s difficult circumstances after the collapse of the empire and projected itself as the only organisation capable of pulling the country out of its problems. It placed the blame for China’s declining economy and global influence on external circumstances. It played the victim’s card: China was perennially the victim, and the party was the instrument that would restore it as a major power.
China’s grey-zone strategy seeks to steadily pressure and exhaust rivals while avoiding the escalation of tensions into full-scale war.
The blame, therefore, was always placed on somebody else: The colonial powers, the United States in the Korean War, India in the 1962 war and the Soviet Union in the 1969 conflict. There was never an acknowledgement that some responsibility also fell on China.This is not limited to foreign policy. The party does not take responsibility for major domestic failures either: The Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution or the 1989 Tiananmen incident. Blame falls on an external force or a few bad elements, never the party itself.You argue that China is pursuing sustained grey-zone coercion. How does this work against India?Since 1979, China has not fought a real conflict. The leadership made economic development the priority, and successive leaders after Mao Zedong focused on reform and opening up.But China was not willing to give up the use of force; it changed the manner in which force was used. Instead of hot wars or major conflict, it engaged and continues to engage in very low-intensity military conflict, popularly known as grey-zone warfare.Grey-zone warfare uses threats or actual force while staying below the threshold that might tempt the rival to launch a counteroffensive. It punishes or deters, but stops short of making the rival feel compelled to push back with force. We see it along the Line of Actual Control, in the South China Sea and in the East China Sea.I have characterised the situation on the LAC after 2020 as the end of peaceful coexistence and the beginning of armed coexistence. Armed coexistence does not mean conflict. It means China will continue to take grey-zone military action around the LAC to keep us tied down and to exhaust us not only financially - because keeping forces and equipment at those heights costs a lot - but also in terms of men and material.This fulfils a key Chinese objective: Keeping India confined to South Asia.
Apart from the United States, there are few potential rivals in this century, and India is one. If you look at India, it's geographical location, its population size, its territorial size, its talent, it's economic potential. All of it lends a credence to the belief that India can become a major power in this century. And clearly, China would like to delay that possibility.Does that mean a large-scale India-China war is unlikely in the foreseeable future?Nobody can predict this definitively. China and its decision-making processes are opaque, and there are no alternative channels of information such as free media or civil society.China is a mature state focused on becoming the strongest economy and power in the world. On a rational cost-benefit analysis, the price of a major war with India could exceed the benefits. Logically, China would be reluctant to engage in such a conflict.At the end of the day, however, it is impossible to predict. We have to be prepared for the worst, while logically understanding that a hot conflict with India may not be in China’s interest in the foreseeable future.China’s capabilities against Taiwan have grown, while the US is distracted by several conflicts. Could Xi Jinping move on Taiwan to secure his legacy?An American commander of the Indo-Pacific Command, Admiral Philip Davidson, suggested that by 2027 China would have the military capability to launch an assault on Taiwan. Some interpreted that to mean China would attack by 2027, but he did not actually say this.China’s capabilities for an assault on an island have substantially increased: Landing craft, area-denial capabilities, communication systems and anti-ship missiles.It is one thing for a major power to bomb another country and destroy its infrastructure, and quite another to occupy or conquer it. That requires a very large commitment of forces and material, with no assured guarantee of victory.China’s demographic decline is already causing anxiety. An assault would mean mass casualties because boots on the ground would be required. After Galwan, India acknowledged within days that 20 soldiers had been martyred; China took much longer to admit fatalities. With Taiwan potentially producing casualties in the hundreds or thousands, Beijing will worry about the domestic impact.
This is where democracy, for all its weaknesses, becomes a strength. A democratic government has electoral and constitutional legitimacy to act, including in war. In China, the party claims it has popular support but has never tested that proposition. The reaction to large-scale war casualties is unpredictable.Xi has removed the age and term limits that helped institutionalise succession. What happens after him and why should India worry?Deng Xiaoping introduced two reforms that stabilised succession: Those above 68 could not continue in top party positions, and the president was limited to two five-year terms. This helped ensure smooth transitions from Jiang Zemin to Hu Jintao and then to Xi Jinping.Xi has abolished the age and term limits. In an authoritarian system, no leader will voluntarily give up power because enemies may find it easier to target him, and he cannot be certain a successor will not misuse authority against him.China could enter a period of political uncertainty and potentially turmoil as Xi ages and factions emerge in a contest for power. It is unclear whether this happens before or after his death, or whether he intends to stand for a fourth term.Because China is the world’s second-largest economy, domestic turmoil would affect its economy, military and diplomacy and create huge ripple effects abroad. Beleaguered regimes also sometimes use an external threat to divert attention. India must consider whether turmoil could produce military adventurism and how to preserve its national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity.China has few formal allies and did little visibly to support Iran. Does it lack the partnerships needed to become a global leader?China lacks the United States’ large network of treaty allies. But we should not underestimate the goodwill it enjoys. The Belt and Road Initiative has been welcomed as an alternative route to development. Western assistance often came with harsh conditions; China offers fewer and less onerous strings. Nobody gives aid for free, but China has built substantial diplomatic influence.There was little need for China to do more in the Iran war. It could neither persuade the United States to stop nor force peace. It protected its oil interests and relations with Iran and the Gulf countries without entering the mediation game.
When the conflict ends, Iran will rebuild using its oil and gas wealth. It is unlikely to trust the West, while China can build infrastructure at a scale few others can match. China needs energy; Iran needs infrastructure and money. That creates an enormous downstream economic opportunity and a win-win situation. Why would China get significantly involved now when there seems to be no clear way out of the conflict?As US-China rivalry intensifies, which side of the emerging world order should India prefer?India should not look at the world order through an either-or lens. The United States and China will both remain major powers. The question is how, in a triangular or quadrangular relationship, including the European Union if it acts as a union, we create an international framework relevant to this century.
India has objective advantages: Its location, demographics and consumer base; tested political stability; an independent military capability and growing defence industry; and talent.I do not see how India can fail to become a major power in this century. The international order is disintegrating and all states are hedging their bets; India is doing so too. The task is not to choose a US-led or China-led order. It is to help build an order in which India is one of the leaders.

Feminist Activist and Icon Gloria Steinem Dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:09:46 UTC
20:09:46 KST

Gloria Steinem, the feminist activist who inspired a generation of women and fought for gender equality, has died at age 92.
Her foundation announced the news in a social media post Thursday morning, sharing that Steinem had "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City the day before, surrounded by her loved ones.
"Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor," the statement read.
"Gloria loved the tradition of lighting signal fires on hills to light the way to the other side of the mountain. Lighting your own candle for Gloria makes you part of this global and celestial community circle."
Steinem was a celebrated writer and magazine editor, who became the face of the women’s movement.
In the 1970s, Steinem co-founded a number of trailblazing initiatives, including the Women's Action Alliance, a feminist organization dedicated to fighting sexism, Ms. magazine, a publication focusing on women’s issues, and the National Women’s Political Caucus, a multi-partisan grassroots organization aimed at increasing women’s participation in the political process.
Steinem avidly campaigned for women's reproductive rights and later supported the legalization of same-sex marriage. Much of her work centered on pushing for equal rights and pay for women.
"Feminism has never been about getting a job for one woman. It’s about making life more fair for women everywhere. It’s not about a piece of the existing pie; there are too many of us for that. It’s about baking a new pie," she wrote in a 2008 op-ed for the Los Angeles Times.
Steinem’s early years
Steinem was born in Toledo, Ohio, on March 25, 1934. The family moved a lot, somewhat due to her father’s profession as a traveling antiques dealer, and Steinem didn’t attend school full-time until she was around 12 years old. After her parents separated, Steinem lived with, and helped care for, her mother, who suffered from depression.
In her 2015 memoir, My Life On The Road, Steinem credited her mother for influencing her journey to activism.
“Depression is anger turned inward; thus women are twice as likely to be depressed,” she wrote. “My mother paid a high price for caring so much, yet being able to do so little about it. In this way, she led me toward an activist place where she herself could never go.”
The makings of an activist
Upon graduating from Smith College, Steinem pursued a career as a freelance journalist.
She completed an 11-day stint as a Playboy bunny to inform her exposé of the working conditions faced by the women in the job.
Her two-part story, titled “A Bunny's Tale," featured in Show magazine in 1963. (In 1985, ABC transformed the exposé into a made-for-TV movie starring Kirstie Alley as Gloria Steinem.)
By 1968, Steinem was a contributing editor at New York Magazine and used her platform to shine a spotlight on women's rights. Her 1969 article titled "After Black Power, Women’s Liberation," which attracted national attention, saw Steinem connect feminism with the Black Power movement.
In 1972, Steinem's newly-launched Ms. magazine created another national conversation when an article titled "We Have Had Abortions" showcased a petition signed by 53 prominent American women, including Steinem herself. It was published a year before the Supreme Court’s landmark Roe v. Wade decision established a woman’s right to an abortion.
Family, legacy, and recognition
Steinem continued campaigning for women's rights over the decades and authored critically-acclaimed books as a lead voice within the feminist movement.
Her 1983 collection of essays titled Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions blended political commentary with personal anecdotes. Her 1994 collection of essays, titled Moving beyond Words: Breaking the Boundaries of Gender, further explored the female experience and gendered stereotypes.
In 2000, Steinem, then age 66, married lawyer David Bale, the father of Oscar-winning actor Christian Bale.
"I hope this proves what feminists have always said—that feminism is about the ability to choose what's right at each time of our lives," Steinem said in a statement about the marriage, her first and only. David Bale died of brain cancer in 2003.
Steinem received numerous accolades over the years on account of her activism and global impact.
In 2013, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama.
“As a writer, a speaker, an activist, she awakened a vast and often skeptical public to problems like domestic violence, the lack of affordable child care, unfair hiring practices," Obama said at the time. “And because of her work, across America and around the world, more women are afforded the respect and opportunities that they deserve. But she also changed how women thought about themselves.“
Tributes pour in for feminist icon
Former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton remembered Steinem as someone who "pushed open doors not just for herself, but for literally millions of women behind her."
Paying tribute to the platforms Steinem created for others, Clinton said: "She wasn't going to be an astronaut, but she made it possible for Sally Ride to be an astronaut. She wasn't going to play college sports, but she stood behind the women in Congress who passed Title IX."
Meghan Markle posted a picture of herself and Steinem, highlighting how she was "celebrating the life and legacy" of her "friend and mentor."
"Privately, she was even better than you would imagine," Markle said. "Spending Thanksgiving with our family, introducing me to one of my best friends (forever the champion of female friendship), loving our children with her whole heart, counseling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit."
Former First Lady Jill Biden remembered Steinem as someone who "understood that women’s equality begins with the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, health, and futures."
Paying tribute to Steinem's activism, she continued: "For decades, she fought to make that freedom real for generations of women and girls. She spoke up when it was difficult, listened to those whose voices too often went unheard, and never stopped pushing our country forward."

Armenia does not consider the presence of Russia’s 102nd military base vital and would not oppose its withdrawal if Moscow decided to leave, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said on Thursday.
Speaking at a press briefing in Yerevan on his meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek on September 1, Pashinyan said Yerevan had not raised the issue of the Russian base with Moscow.
“We have not raised the issue of the Russian military base even once during this period, and it is not the case that we consider the presence of the Russian 102nd Military Base on the territory of Armenia to be a vital necessity,” he said.
Pashinyan also said transferring Russia’s rights under a concession agreement for Armenia’s railway infrastructure to a third country would be the best option for Yerevan.
The future of Armenia’s railway infrastructure was among the issues discussed by Putin and Pashinyan during their meeting in Bishkek on Tuesday, on the sidelines of SCO summit.
Putin said investment in the railway would depend on freight traffic, adding that opening additional routes could create new cargo flows and make further investment economically viable.
Russian military base
Putin also said the presence of the Russian military base was ultimately a sovereign decision for Armenia.
“If Armenia believes that the Russian military base is not needed, we will leave as early as tomorrow. We will not impose anything on anyone,” he said.
At the same time, Putin said Russia would remain if Armenia’s population wanted a Russian military presence and was prepared to continue working and cooperating with Moscow.
Armenia seeks closer regional ties
Pashinyan’s government has also pursued closer ties with Türkiye and Azerbaijan while seeking deeper integration with the European Union.
Yerevan has said it wants to establish diplomatic relations with Ankara and reopen the land border, while continuing efforts to normalise relations with Baku and expand regional connectivity.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has again dismissed reports that Russia is preparing a new military mobilization, calling the rumors an “information attack” aimed at disrupting upcoming State Duma elections.
