Flash flood survivors gather to receive utility aid from a temporary relief camp at Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on September 3, 2026. (AFP Photo)
Desperate families of missing foreigners were clinging to hope as they combed hospitals and morgues in search of clues, a week after catastrophic floods tore through Nepal’s Himalayan border region.
Outside Kathmandu’s tourist police headquarters, Sanjeev Rai was trapped in agonizing uncertainty.
The 53-year-old American flew to Nepal after learning that his wife, Jiwan Jyoti, was untraceable while returning from a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred peak revered by Hindus and Buddhists.
“The day I arrived I said, let’s find a helicopter, I’m going to look for her,” Rai told AFP.
But Timure, the village in Rasuwa district where she was when disaster struck, remains inaccessible and dangerous.
“I feel desperate, it’s been so many days,” he said.
Jyoti, an engineer at Intel, had embarked on the journey as a spiritual quest and an adventure to mark her 50th birthday.
Now Rai says he has all but abandoned hope of finding her alive.
“I’m no longer counting on survivors. I just hope the DNA samples will match. I want to be able to mourn.”
The Aug. 26 flood has become one of the deadliest disasters to hit the Himalayan nation in recent years.
The huge wave of debris has killed more than 1,200 people and left more than 4,750 missing in Nepal and China’s Tibet region, smashing towns, roads, bridges and multiple hydropower dams.
According to Nepali police, some 294 foreigners have been rescued, most of them Chinese and Indian nationals.
But 583 foreigners remain unaccounted for, many of them pilgrims who had spent months preparing for the demanding trek around Mount Kailash.

Nepal floods leave 22,000 children without safe water: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:20:46 UTC
19:20:46 KST

Nepal floods leave 22,000 children without safe water: UNICEF
More than a week after flash floods struck the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river basin in Nepal, at least 22,000 children urgently need safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene support, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Thursday.
Water systems have been damaged across affected districts, while toilets and other sanitation facilities have been damaged or destroyed, raising the risk of waterborne and infectious diseases.
“Every parent in these districts is now making the same calculation several times a day,” said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative in Nepal. “Where can I get water, and is it safe to give to my child?”
Crowded living conditions
Affected families are now living with host communities or in holding centres— crowded spaces that make it difficult to maintain safe hygiene practices.
This week, the World Health Organization (WHO) highlighted how flooding, displacement, overcrowding and stagnant water can increase the risk of communicable diseases such as dengue and scrub typhus.
“The risk of waterborne disease increases rapidly in these conditions, but it is preventable,” Ms. Akunga insisted.
Supplies reach communities
UNICEF has dispatched water, sanitation and hygiene supplies for around 19,000 people in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, among the hardest hit areas.
These items include more than 3,800 hygiene kits, 3,300 collapsible 10-litre jerrycans, 3,500 buckets, 3,500 one-litre mugs, 4,000 bottles of water treatment solution and more than 1,000 tarpaulin sheets.
Staff are also working with government counterparts and partners on disease surveillance, hygiene promotion and outbreak prevention.
Critical infrastructure destroyed
The flooding was triggered by a glacier collapse on the Nepal-China border on 27 August. The death toll has surpassed 1,100, according to international media reports.
Infrastructure such as roads, bridges, telecommunications networks as well as water systems were damaged, complicating access to communities and delivery of aid.
UNICEF estimates that at least 19 schools have been damaged, including eight that were completely and eight partially destroyed, while more than 10,000 school-age children need immediate psychosocial support and access to safe learning spaces.
Young lives upended
“Before all this, I used to spend most of my time in school and hang out with friends when I was free,” Swostik Paudel, a 14-year-old from Nuwakot, recently told the agency. “Mostly we would play football.”
Swostik is now living in a shelter with his parents and sister where he tries to remain connected to his former life.
“Some children have brought a football here,” he said. “Even though it’s punctured, we’ve been passing it around. Some friends have also been playing matches.”
Building back better
As access improves, UNICEF will scale up emergency water supply, household water treatment, water-quality monitoring, temporary sanitation and handwashing facilities, and essential hygiene and menstrual hygiene supplies in communities and holding centres.
Ms. Akunga said restoring safe water and sanitation “is not a one-week job”. She stressed that damaged water systems, pipelines, pumps, toilets and other sanitation infrastructure need to be repaired and rebuilt to withstand future floods.
“We need to make communities safer and more resilient,” she said. “Otherwise, we will be having the same conversation again after the next disaster, and it will be children paying the price yet again.”

Off-grid UK-Australian couple describe ‘anguish’ at removal of children by Italian court

2026-09-03

19:20:22 KST

A couple have told of their heartache, trauma and stress after fighting for two years for their right to parent their children as they choose in the glare of the world’s attention.
The three children of a Melbourne woman, Catherine Birmingham, and her British partner, Nathan Trevallion, were removed from their “dilapidated” off-grid home in Italy last year.
It sparked global conversations about state intervention and alternative lifestyles.
They were raising the children on a property in the woods in the Abruzzo region, where they grew their own food and homeschooled the children.
In September 2024, the family was hospitalised after eating poisonous mushrooms they had picked, which brought them to the attention of authorities.
In November 2025, the juvenile court ordered the removal of Utopia Rose, nine, and six-year-old twins Galorian and Bluebell to a residential care facility, citing a lack of hygiene, social interaction, toilet facilities and schooling.
Birmingham stayed with them until March, when she was ordered to leave under a new court ruling.
On Wednesday, an Italian court approved a staged process that would allow a “gradual reunification process”, and could eventually allow the children to leave the facility.
“The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out a gradual reunification process, allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately and, from October, for weekend overnight stays with their family,” their lawyer, Simone Pillon, said.
In a statement released on Thursday, the couple said the “long-awaited decision, which our entire family awaited with anguish, arrived with a harshness that broke each of our hearts”.
They asked whether forcing school attendance was “fair, legal, and respectful” of their parental rights and the rights of their children, saying they chose Italy for reasons including its homeschooling rights and support for family bonds.
The parents have said that doctors say the children’s health is at “serious risk” and “the only way to reduce this risk is to return them home immediately”.
“We are deeply concerned for their health,” the parents wrote.
“How will they be well if they are forced to travel back and forth from their home to the foster home, then to school, and then back to the foster home again, all while still being kept apart from their parents?
“How will they fare in the evening when, after an afternoon spent at home with their friends and pets, they must return to the foster home?”
Even Italy’s hard-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has weighed in. She expressed “alarm” over the children being taken into care, while the deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, compared the case to a kidnapping.
But the judiciary’s union said the court’s decision was based on factors including the children’s safety, sanitary conditions and education.
After the latest decision, social services will monitor the process and make an assessment before any permanent reunion can happen.
The couple wrote that the authorities wanted to impose a standard. “And those who don’t follow it lose their children,” they wrote.
“We are deeply saddened by this.
“We have continued to collaborate and engage with everyone, even under extreme trauma, stress, exasperation and concern for our children knowing their daily suffering but we will always demand respect for our parental rights and, above all, for our children’s rights, especially their right to health – mental, physical and emotional.”
The couple plan to appeal for a complete and faster reunification.

One in five children in 21 nations faced tech-facilitated sexual abuse: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:20:15 UTC
19:20:15 KST

One in five children in 21 nations faced tech-facilitated sexual abuse: UNICEF
About 20 million children aged 12 to 17 – one in five across 21 countries – were sexually exploited by perpetrators using technology such as social media, according to a UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) report released on Thursday.
Key points
- Nearly 60 per cent of cases occurred on social media
- Many children do not report abuse
- UNICEF calls for safer platforms and stronger laws
More than 15 million children in this age group were exposed to unwanted sexual content, nine million were asked to engage in sexual conversations or share sexual images against their will and four million had sexual images of themselves shared without their consent.
UNICEF said the total figures are likely much higher.
“The report reveals a painful reality,” UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said. “More than 20 million children across the countries studied were subjected to unwanted explicit sexual content or exploitation online, often in the digital spaces where they learn, play and connect with friends.”
Exploited on social media
Nearly 60 per cent of all recorded instances of exploitation in the report occurred on social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and WhatsApp, and 14 per cent happened on online games, with the platforms’ features often used to exploit trust.
Some 38 per cent of children first encountered the perpetrators online, and evidence shows abuse is often facilitated through intentional features that allow perpetrators to hide their identities.
In Montenegro, more than 80 per cent of reported cases involved social media.
Across the 21 countries, 57 per cent of exploitation cases involved perpetrators the children knew, including peers, friends and family.
Exploitation raises risks of self-harm
In interviews with researchers, children who endured sexual exploitation described impacts on their emotional wellbeing, sense of safety and trust in others, including fear, shame, confusion and isolation.
“I didn’t know how to react…I felt a little in shock,” said a young woman from the Dominican Republic after private images were circulated without her consent at age 14.
Children who experienced technology-aided sexual exploitation were four times more likely to report suicidal thoughts or behaviours and self-harm and reported significantly higher levels of anxiety, according to the analysis.
In Pakistan, the risk of self-harm was more than seven times higher for children who had been exploited.
Unsure where to turn for help
More than 40 per cent of cases of tech-facilitated abuse were never shared with anyone, while fewer than one per cent were reported to authorities.
The most common reason was children not knowing who to tell.
“These experiences cause profound emotional and mental distress,” UNICEF chief Ms. Russell said. “Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help. We cannot look away.”
Stakeholders must act
“All of us, including governments and technology companies, must do more to protect children online,” Ms. Russell said.
The researchers issued calls for help to prevent abuse:
- Tech companies should include stronger protections for children and improve their reporting systems
- Governments should strengthen accountability and enforcement mechanisms
- Societies should address harmful gender norms that normalise the sexualisation of girls and stigmatise survivors of sexual violence

To carry out the campaign, its organisers plan to involve media outlets, bloggers and Telegram channels with questionable reputations, including in exchange for financial reward. We urge you to trust only verified official sources of information."

- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps said that its deputy commander for combat operations, Stepan Kaplunov, had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of a residential building. G7: A new approach to development Development assistance G7 News Published on : April 30th 2026 Updated on : May 07th 2026 At a time when development policies are undergoing major changes, the members of the G7 are reflecting on how to build a renewed approach to development assistance based on mutually beneficial partnerships. This new approach to development is based on four main principles: resilience, sovereignty, effectiveness and coherence. The priorities are: Reaffirming solidarity with the most vulnerable countries to strengthen their resilience and help them anticipate food and public health crises and natural disasters to prevent them from developing; Strengthening the capacities of partner countries to finance essential sectors for sustainable development such as childhood, education, health, food security and nutrition; Improving the effectiveness of development assistance and promoting a new approach to development; Developing and updating the framework for international partnerships, to better take into account all of the flows contributing to development and include new partners. THREE QUESTIONS FOR ÉLÉONORE CAROIT, MINISTER DELEGATE FOR FRANCOPHONIE, INTERNATIONAL PARTNERSHIPS AND FRENCH NATIONALS ABROAD 1. How can the effects of the war in the Middle East on the most vulnerable countries be mitigated? The supply crisis caused by the closing of the Strait of Hormuz and the substantial, lasting damage to oil and gas infrastructure are posing major risks for the most vulnerable countries. These include the risk of an oil crisis, a food and humanitarian crisis, and worsening financial difficulties for partner countries. Along with our partners, we are working to identify solutions to help the most vulnerable countries faced with these crises, in particular food crises. We will also discuss the reconstruction of infrastructures in countries affected by conflict, as we wish to promote new methods of financing cooperation. 2. How can we reaffirm the need for solidarity with the most vulnerable countries? International solidarity must prioritize early childhood development, education, food security, nutrition, health and the fight against extreme poverty. France wants to support partner countries faced with the risk of health crises by proposing a new approach to health funding. This new approach aims to support domestic resource mobilization, the activities of national development banks and the coordination of health funding with the strategies established between partners countries and the World Bank. France also wants to strengthen the support of the G7 and its partners for the Global School Meals Coalition, an initiative launched by France and Finland in 2021 to ensure that every child worldwide has access to meals at school to allow them to properly learn and grow. France also wants to help increase the resilience of the most vulnerable countries to natural disasters by strengthening early warning systems. With this aim, France will announce a commitment of €3 million and will seek to mobilize its partners through the CREWS initiative. For more than a decade, the CREWS initiative has contributed to strengthening the resilience of 77 countries, including 80% of the least developed countries and small island developing States. Today, it has the capacity to support all of these countries with basic early warning systems. 3. How can the fall in development budgets be addressed? We wish to strengthen our partners’ funding capacities, key to their independence and sovereignty. We are working to support domestic resource mobilization as well as private capital and blended finance, and innovative mechanisms such as remittances and diaspora investments. We are supporting this approach in essential sectors advancing the sustainable development, sovereignty and resilience of partner countries, such as health, education and rural development. We are also stepping up dialogue with public development banks, which will come together on 29 April at an event convened by the Finance in Common (FiCS) network, as well as with the main foundations. The French G7 Presidency is the first to support the creation of a dedicated engagement group, the F7. World Press Freedom Day Freedom of expression Statement On : May 03rd 2026 On World Press Freedom Day, France condemns the attacks and acts of violence against journalists and media professionals. It pays tribute to those, too many again this year, who have been killed while carrying out their work around the world, in Palestine, Ukraine, Sudan and elsewhere. We honour the memory of Antoni Lallican, a French photojournalist, who was killed on 3 October 2025 in a Russian drone strike. Russia has made press freedom a target. During the high-level week of the United Nations General Assembly in September 2025, France, alongside 21 other countries, demanded the protection of journalists and media professionals in Gaza, in accordance with international humanitarian law. France called on the Israeli authorities to allow independent foreign media access to Gaza. In southern Lebanon, four journalists have died since March in strikes carried out by the Israeli army. The deliberate targeting of journalists, where established, constitutes a war crime. France supports the Lebanese authorities in their efforts to fully investigate these tragedies and ensure that justice is served. France is mobilizing the international community in support of an honest, free and regulated information space. The Partnership for Information and Democracy, launched with Reporters Without Borders, is supported by 57 countries. In October 2025, at the Paris Peace Forum, 34 States committed to multilateral action to safeguard information integrity and media independence. France has renewed its support for the International Fund for Public Interest Media (IFPIM). It supports the international rollout of the Journalism Trust Initiative (JTI), a certification framework promoting media outlets that meet standards of ethics and independence. In the face of restrictions on freedom of expression and press freedom in many countries around the world, and the spread of disinformation and increasing manipulation of information, France reaffirms that the freedom to inform and to be informed is essential to democracy. The release of arbitrarily detained journalists and media professionals is imperative. France continues to engage with the Algerian authorities to secure the release of Christophe Gleizes and his return to France.

G7 Trade Ministers - Boosting the resilience and fairness of global trade Foreign trade G7 News Published on : May 04th 2026 Updated on : July 22nd 2026 As global balances are reshaped, the members of the G7 wish to reaffirm their commitment to open, fair and rules-based global trade. Ahead of the Leaders’ Summit in Évian (from 15 to 17 June), the Trade Ministers of the G7 countries – Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States – will meet in Paris on 5 and 6 May. The aim is to identify common focuses to address the transformations of global trade and enhance cooperation between partners. THREE QUESTIONS TO NICOLAS FORISSIER, Minister Delegate for Foreign Trade and Economic Attractiveness, attached to the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs 1. What is the context surrounding this G7 Trade Ministers’ Meeting? This meeting comes amid major uncertainty for global trade. Supply chains are under strain, market volatility is rising and structural imbalances persist in the global economy. Geopolitical crises, particularly in the Middle East, are also stifling trade and energy flows, with a direct impact on supply conditions and prices. In this context, the G7 is an essential setting to engage in dialogue, coordinate analysis and identify common solutions in order to guarantee a more stable and predictable trade environment. 2. What can we say about global trade? Several trends are setting in. Firstly, certain non-market practices are continuing to create distortions that feed into industrial overcapacities, unfair competition and unnecessary trade pressures. Moreover, the vulnerabilities of value chains, including in strategic sectors such as critical minerals, are thrown into sharper relief, with excessive dependencies and risks of breakdowns in supply. Finally, the swift rise of e-commerce has brought new challenges as regards regulation, security and fairness. For example, we want to bring an end to the imbalances caused to our markets by massive shipping of small, low-value packages. 3. How will this meeting address these challenges? This meeting should bring tangible and coordinated progress. We are going to enhance our collective analytical capacity, improve transparency and sharing of information, and draw on tools to better address market distortion. We will also speed up work on the resilience of supply chains, including as regards critical minerals, by identifying vulnerabilities, diversifying supply sources and developing cooperation with trusted partners. Finally, we will foster initiatives to modernize the global trade framework, including WTO reform and better regulation of e-commerce. Our aim is clear: to build effective common responses to today’s challenges. Read here the G7 Trade ministers' Communiqué Photo: Archives/MEAE

More than 80 migrants feared dead after boat rescued off Canary Islands
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:19:03 BST
19:19:03 KST

More than 80 migrants feared dead after boat rescued off Canary Islands
- Published
More than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died in a boat which was adrift in the Atlantic Ocean for 27 days.
Spanish Maritime Rescue teams located the vessel some 65 nautical miles southwest of Gran Canaria's coastal town of Arguineguín on Wednesday and found 44 survivors, with five dead bodies also on board.
The boat is believed to have departed The Gambia in West Africa in early August with 127 occupants on board. Human rights activist Helena Maleno Garzón, founder of Spanish charity Caminando Fronteras, said 83 people had lost their lives.
Rescuers were forced to leave the five bodies they found due to the rough sea conditions, Maritime Rescue said.
The organisation was unable to verify how many people were originally on board.
The 44 survivors are men from sub-Saharan Africa, Maritime Rescue said in a statement.
"Once the rescue was complete, adverse weather conditions in the area - featuring 20-knot winds and 2.5m waves - made it impossible to recover the five bodies found on board the vessel," it added.
Three of the survivors were airlifted to hospital in critical condition.
The rest were transported by sea to Gran Canaria, where they disembarked in the early hours of Thursday morning.
Fernando Clavijo, head of the Canary Islands government, posted on X: "It is intolerable that lives continue to be lost. The Canaries cannot get used to or accept as normal the fact that the Atlantic continues to be a death trap."
The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings.
Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous journey each year seeking to reach Spanish territory despite the risks posed by rough seas, strong currents and long distances.

Gloria Steinem, feminist icon and co-founder of Ms. magazine, dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:16:31 UTC
19:16:31 KST

Gloria Steinem, the pioneering journalist and activist who became one of the most recognizable figures of the American feminist movement, has died at 92.
Steinem died Wednesday at her home in New York, surrounded by loved ones, according to a statement posted on her official Instagram account.
For more than six decades, she stood at the intersection of journalism, politics and activism, helping move issues such as abortion rights, workplace equality, political representation and violence against women into the center of American public debate.
Born in Toledo, Ohio, in 1934, Steinem graduated from Smith College in 1956 and later spent two years in India, an experience that helped shape her interest in grassroots organizing.
She began her career as a freelance journalist in New York, at a time when women were often pushed toward fashion and lifestyle assignments. Her national breakthrough came in 1963, when she went undercover as a Playboy Bunny for Show magazine and wrote about the working conditions faced by women in Hugh Hefner’s clubs.
In 1968, Steinem helped found New York magazine, where she worked as an editor and political writer. By the end of the decade, she had become deeply involved in the growing women’s liberation movement.
A major turning point came in 1969, when she attended a public hearing on abortion rights in New York. Steinem later said hearing women speak openly about their experiences changed the direction of her life. She herself had undergone an abortion at 22.
By the early 1970s, Steinem had become one of the most prominent faces of second-wave feminism.
In 1971, she joined activists including Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm and Betty Friedan in helping establish the National Women’s Political Caucus, aimed at increasing women’s participation in politics.
A year later, she co-founded Ms. magazine, which became one of the defining publications of the feminist movement. The magazine brought subjects including abortion, domestic violence, sexual harassment and workplace discrimination into mainstream discussion.
Steinem remained closely associated with Ms. for decades and went on to help found organizations including the Ms. Foundation for Women and the Women’s Media Center.
She was also a prolific author. Her books included Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, Revolution from Within, Moving Beyond Words and the memoir My Life on the Road.
Her influence extended far beyond journalism. In 2013, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest U.S. civilian honor.
Steinem continued speaking and writing about women’s rights well into her 90s, including after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022.
Her career spanned a profound transformation in women’s status in American public life. Many of the battles she helped define remain unresolved, but Steinem’s central legacy was helping turn women’s experiences from issues often treated as private into questions of politics, rights and power.

Five dead on migrant boat rescued off Canary Islands, aid group says toll may be higher

Five dead on migrant boat rescued off Canary Islands, aid group says toll may be higher
ARGUINEGUIN, Spain, Sept 3 - Five migrants were found dead aboard a boat rescued off Spain's Canary Islands, maritime rescue authorities said on Thursday, while a migrant rights group reported that survivors said dozens more had died during the crossing.
Three survivors were in a serious condition and were airlifted to hospital, while another 41 disembarked at the port of Arguineguin on Gran Canaria in the early hours of Thursday, Maritime Rescue said in a statement.
Helena Maleno, founder of Walking Borders, said on social media that survivors reported that 83 people, including three women and a baby, had died during the crossing. The boat had left The Gambia 27 days earlier.
Reuters could not independently verify that figure. Maritime Rescue said it could confirm only that five bodies were aboard the vessel when rescuers reached it. The bodies could not be recovered because of adverse weather conditions.
Canary Islands regional leader, Fernando Clavijo, said the tragedy underscored the need for a state policy on migration, especially after a deadly migrant surge in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta in July.
"It is intolerable that lives continue to be lost. The Canaries cannot get used to or accept as normal the fact that the Atlantic continues to be a death trap," he said on X.
The vessel had been spotted on Wednesday by a rescue aircraft about 65 nautical miles southwest of Arguineguin.
The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats seeking to reach Spanish territory despite the risks posed by rough seas, strong currents and long distances.
The number of migrants reaching the Canary Islands from West Africa has fallen so far this year by 57.4%, according to official data. REUTERS

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

The Israeli military killed two Palestinian teenagers in the occupied West Bank Wednesday night, the Health Ministry said, in an attack the army claimed was its attempt to control an alleged riot.
Omar Mohammad Naji al-Nassan, 19, and Khalil Rasem Khalil Shahada, 16, were shot dead by the Israeli army in the village of al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah in the central West Bank, the ministry said.
Amin Abu Alia, the head of the al-Mughayyir village council, told AFP "Israeli settlers ... tried to steal sheep from two homes" in the village and that following a confrontation, "the Israeli army imposed a siege on the village before raiding its center."
He said the Israeli forces placed snipers inside buildings, who "opened live fire on residents who tried to confront the settlers."
The Israeli army, meanwhile, claimed it had "secured the entrance" to the village "in order to facilitate the return of livestock belonging to Israeli civilians that had been found in the area of the village."
"During the forces' activity in the area, a violent riot broke out, during which ... hurled cinder blocks and stones at the forces," the army said.
"The forces responded by firing at key instigators in order to remove the threat," it said, adding that the management of the incident was under review.
The Palestinian Red Crescent reported that the two teenagers were critically wounded by live fire during clashes, al-Nassan in the neck and Shahada in the back, and were transferred to two hospitals in Ramallah, where doctors pronounced them dead.
Footage filmed by Agence France-Presse (AFP) inside the Ramallah medical center showed mourners gathering around one of the bodies shrouded in a Palestinian flag.
The mourners carried the remains outside the hospital and chanted "with our souls and our blood, we will sacrifice ourselves for you, martyr. We were created to live in freedom."
Since Oct. 7, 2023, Israeli forces have intensified violence and operations across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, with reports of killings, arrests, forced displacement, home demolitions and settlement expansion.
Attacks by settlers on Palestinians have increased and become almost daily. At least 1,105 Palestinians, including a number of militants, have been killed by fire from Israeli soldiers or settlers, according to an AFP tally based on Palestinian official figures.
In a separate incident, Israeli forces arrested 21 Palestinians, including a journalist, during raids across the occupied West Bank early Thursday, the Prisoners Media Office said.
In a statement, the rights group said that the arrests included seven Palestinians in Bethlehem province, nine in Nablus, four in Salfit and a journalist in Hebron.
In Bethlehem, Israeli forces arrested four Palestinians during raids on homes in al-Doha town, Dheisheh refugee camp and al-Fawaghra neighborhood, according to the statement.
The forces also raided Beit Fajjar town south of the province and arrested a father and his two sons after searching and ransacking their home.
In Nablus, Israeli forces arrested two Palestinians during a raid on Asira al-Qibliya village south of the city and another from Askar refugee camp, the statement said.
Three Palestinians were also arrested in Awarta town, two in Bazariya and another on Oman Street in Nablus city.
In Sebastia town northwest of Nablus, Israeli forces raided the area and arrested the mother and sister of a Palestinian prisoner before releasing them after field questioning.
In Salfit province, Israeli forces arrested four Palestinians from Qarawat Bani Hassan town after raiding their homes and ransacking their belongings. A vehicle belonging to one of those arrested was also seized.
In Hebron province, Israeli forces arrested a journalist from Idhna town west of Hebron.
The Prisoners Media Office said the latest escalation reflects a continuing "policy of abuse and arbitrary arrest" against Palestinians.
The group called on human rights and international organizations to intervene to halt what it described as violations against Palestinians.

More join British Armed Forces than leave for full year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:15:43 BST
19:15:43 KST

More people joined the Regular Armed Forces than left for the fourth consecutive quarter, giving Defence its longest uninterrupted period of recruitment growth over departures since 2021, the Ministry of Defence has said.
Figures published on 3 September show a net gain of 1,460 personnel in the year to 30 June 2026, with Regular strength increasing across all three Services. Royal Navy and Royal Marines strength rose by 440 over the year, the Army by 170 and the Royal Air Force by 840.
The number of full-time military personnel available to support Defence operations also increased by 1,450 compared with 1 July 2025. Fully trained personnel available for operations rose for a third consecutive quarter, including the first increase in Army trade-trained strength since late 2021, alongside further growth in the Royal Navy and RAF.
The MOD said intake has been rising while the number of personnel leaving has continued to fall since late 2023, producing the year-long period in which recruitment has exceeded departures.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: “There has never been a better or more important time to join our Armed Forces. Under this government, those serving and joining up now can be certain of increased investment in defence and our people. That means better equipment, better housing and better support for them and their families.
“I am determined that serving our nation gives people the skills and opportunities to thrive during their service and beyond, no matter their background.”
The latest figures follow a series of changes to military pay, accommodation and recruitment policy. According to the MOD, Service personnel have received a cumulative 14.1% pay rise since July 2024, while every full-time member of the Armed Forces is now paid at least the National Living Wage, said the Government.
The government also say in their announcement that they are investing more than £7 billion in military housing during the current Parliament. The MOD said recruitment rules have been changed to remove more than 100 policies which had previously prevented some applicants from joining, including restrictions involving hay fever, eczema, acne and fully healed injuries.
New entry routes have also been introduced for specialist roles, including the Cyber Direct Entry Scheme, intended to bring personnel with high-demand technical skills directly into Defence.
The MOD said rebuilding personnel numbers would take time after recruitment and retention targets were missed for 14 consecutive years, but the latest statistics show Regular strength increasing across each Service at the same time as trained strength continues to rise.
The Armed Forces remain a major provider of apprenticeships and vocational training, with military careers covering engineering, healthcare, cyber, digital and other specialist areas. The Army, Royal Navy and Royal Air Force have also regularly appeared among the leading employers in The Times Apprenticeship Rankings.

The lawsuit, filed at London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal on Sept 3, follows years of regulatory scrutiny over Apple’s App Tracking Transparency feature, which was launched in 2021.
Apple has said it introduced that feature to allow users to control whether to grant apps permission to track their activity across other companies’ apps and websites.
Lawyers bringing the new lawsuit against Apple, though, say the feature imposed stricter requirements on third-party app developers than on Apple’s own services, giving its advertising ecosystem a competitive advantage.
Ann Pope, a former senior official with Britain’s Competition and Markets Authority who is leading the lawsuit, said Apple’s policy “resulted in very significant harm to businesses that depend on Apple as a gatekeeper”.
“This action is important to protect the rights of British businesses that depend on Apple, to ensure that the rules that Apple applies are fair, and to compensate the losses that British companies have suffered,” Pope said in a statement.
Apple, which has previously said its App Tracking Transparency provides “important privacy protections”, did not immediately comment.
Apple’s App Tracking Transparency feature has been the subject of investigations across Europe, in particular in Germany where Apple in August agreed changes to rules on how app developers can use personal data for targeted advertising.
The German competition authority had accused Apple of abusing its market power, after Facebook-owner Meta plus publishers, advertisers and app developers – whose business models rely on advertising tracking – criticised the tool.
Regulators in France, Italy, Poland and elsewhere have also probed the App Tracking Transparency framework. REUTERS

Portugal's car market grew 11.3% in August, with electric vehicle sales surging 65.2% and now making up more than a third of new car sales.
Portugal's automotive sector has seen a strong recovery, with sales accelerating in August and 17,209 motor vehicles registered, 11.3% more than in the same month in 2025.
According to data released by ACAP – Associação Automóvel de Portugal, between January and August 2026 a total of 197,632 new vehicles were put on the road, representing growth of 10.3% compared with the same period a year earlier.
Up to August, registrations of light passenger vehicles totalled 169,323 units, a rise of 9.5% on the same period in 2025. In monthly terms, 14,086 new light passenger cars were registered, 8.4% more than in August 2025.
In the light commercial vehicle segment, sales in August posted a positive year-on-year increase of 21.8%, with 2,449 units registered. Cumulatively, the market reached 22,299 units, which represented an increase of 9.8% on the same period in 2025.
As for the market for heavy vehicles, which covers both passenger and goods transport, August 2026 saw an increase of 45.9% compared with the same month in 2025, with 674 vehicles in this category sold.
Up until August, registrations in this category totalled 6,010 units, representing market growth of 39.6% in the same period in 2025.
Demand for new vehicles has been driven above all by the steadily growing interest in electric cars.
According to ACAP figures, up to August 75.6% of newly registered light passenger vehicles were powered by alternative energy sources, with electric and hybrid models standing out. Around 26.8% of new cars were electric — a share that was higher in August, when electric cars accounted for 36.1% of sales.
In August 2026 alone, 10,391 new electric, plug-in and hybrid electric light passenger cars were registered in Portugal, an increase of 20.5% on the same month of the previous year.
Between January and August 2026, sales of electrified light passenger vehicles (electric, plug-in and hybrid) totalled 116,679 units, an increase of 29.4% compared with the same period in 2025.
Looking only at pure electric models in August, sales rose by 65.2% compared with the same month in 2025, with 5,079 new light passenger vehicles registered.
Over the eight-month period as a whole, sales of new electric light passenger vehicles increased by 43.1%, with 45,388 units registered, giving them a market share of 26.8% of all new light passenger vehicles registered in that period.

These latest confiscation orders from Area A show how Israel is now brazenly expanding its annexation agenda to areas that have been under the control of the Palestinian authorities since the Oslo Accords.
Heba Morayef, MENA Regional Director
In a recent report Amnesty International documented how the Israeli authorities have been accelerating annexation through a state-driven campaign of ethnic cleansing targeting Palestinian Bedouin and herding communities in Area C of the unlawfully occupied West Bank.

Under international law, an occupying power must not confiscate land in an occupied territory unless absolutely necessary for military reasons; this does not include illegal settlement expansion.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Thursday thanked his French and Polish counterparts for their strong solidarity after Berlin officially accused Moscow of hybrid attacks and an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport.
“The incident at Leipzig Airport has once again shown us in Germany that Russia’s aggression does not stop at borders—not at the Bug River, not at the Oder, and not even at the Rhine,” Wadephul told a joint press conference with the French and Polish foreign ministers in Weimar.
“We greatly appreciate the solidarity and support our partners have shown us since yesterday,” he said, referring to statements from EU and NATO partners. He added that the allies are united and determined to continue their efforts to deter Russia and provide support to Ukraine.

France vows ‘full solidarity’

"We obviously supported these measures," the French minister stated, adding: "We are ready to go even further if circumstances require it.”
Poland calls for more sanctions

“I am increasingly reluctant to speak about "hybrid warfare," because not everyone understands what it means. It refers to aggression falling below the threshold of an invasion, yet we are certainly dealing with state-sponsored terrorism here,” Sikorski said.
The minister said that many Russian diplomats in EU countries were actually intelligence officers, and called for stricter measures and travel restrictions in the countries where they are stationed.
“We estimate there are over 2,000 Russian diplomats in EU countries. And we estimate that at least 40 percent of them are performing tasks that are not consistent with diplomatic status,” he said. “They work for agencies that also carry out terrorist activities in our countries. Therefore, in a spirit of solidarity with Germany, we ought to implement all the necessary safeguards for our population.”

Grammy-winning jazz vocalist Cassandra Wilson dies at 70
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:12:20 UTC
19:12:20 KST

Dilara Hamit
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
American jazz singer and songwriter Cassandra Wilson, one of the most influential vocalists of the past four decades, has died at the age of 70 in her hometown of Jackson, Mississippi.
Wilson died peacefully at home surrounded by family, close friends and her longtime manager Robert Torre, according to a statement issued Wednesday. The cause of death was not disclosed.
"It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Cassandra Wilson, the Grammy Award-winning and legendary jazz artist," Torre said.
Known for her deep, melancholic contralto voice, Wilson blurred the boundaries between jazz, blues and folk while incorporating elements of pop, country and R&B into her work.
Time magazine named her "America's Best Singer" in 2001, praising her as a soulful, sensual and lyrical performer who carried forward the tradition of great jazz vocalists.
Jackson Mayor John Horhn described Wilson as an "extraordinary native daughter" and a singular musical voice.
"Cassandra Wilson carried the sound, spirit and history of Mississippi with her wherever her music reached," Horhn said.
Musician Jon Batiste said in a tribute that Wilson "sounded like the South," crediting her distinctive tone and phrasing, as well as her fusion of folkloric, R&B and diasporic music with experimental and popular styles, with having a major influence on him.
Born Cassandra Fowlkes in Jackson in 1955, Wilson began playing piano at the age of six and took up guitar by 12. After moving to New York City in the early 1980s, she met saxophonist Steve Coleman and became a founding member of the M-Base Collective.
She received widespread critical acclaim with her 1988 album Blue Skies and later signed with Blue Note Records, achieving a breakthrough with Blue Light 'Til Dawn in 1993.
Her album New Moon Daughter won the Grammy Award for Best Jazz Vocal Album in 1997, while Loverly earned her a second award in the same category in 2009.
Wilson received four Grammy nominations during her career.
She also contributed to recordings by artists including Steve Coleman, Gregory Osby, Luther Vandross, Regina Carter, Angelique Kidjo, John Legend and Ravi Coltrane. She appeared on The Roots' albums Do You Want More?!!!??! and Illadelph Halflife.
Wilson was one of the principal vocalists on Wynton Marsalis' oratorio Blood on the Fields, which became the first jazz composition to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music in 1997.
In 2015, Wilson marked the centenary of Billie Holiday's birth with a special performance at New York's Apollo Theater. That year, she released Coming Forth by Day, a tribute to Holiday and her final studio album.
She later joined Black Thought, Elvis Costello, DJ Premier, T Bone Burnett and Nathaniel Rateliff in the genre-spanning supergroup project Dopamine.
Wilson was named a National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master in 2022, one of the highest honors bestowed on jazz musicians in the US.

The 2,000-hryvnia banknote will be put into circulation on September 4 - the NBU explained why now
Kyiv • UNN
The new banknote will feature a portrait of poet Vasyl Stus. Its introduction was explained by the growth in salaries, prices, and the volume of cash.
On Friday, September 4, Ukraine will officially put into circulation a banknote with a denomination of 2,000 hryvnias, depicting the poet Vasyl Stus (1938–1985). The National Bank of Ukraine reports this, according to UNN.
Details
This will be the highest denomination in Ukraine. As noted by the NBU, the 1,000-hryvnia banknote was put into circulation in 2019, almost seven years ago. Since then, many events have taken place in Ukraine that have affected the economy. These include the coronavirus pandemic, as well as the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
The NBU cited the significant increase in the average monthly salary as one of the factors behind the introduction of the new banknote.
Since the introduction of the 1,000-hryvnia banknote seven years ago, the average monthly salary in Ukraine has tripled, while the price level based on the inflation index has doubled. This has created a need for a greater amount of cash, because while after the introduction of the 1,000-hryvnia banknote 10 banknotes of the highest denomination were sufficient to receive the average monthly salary, in 2026 more than 30 banknotes with a denomination of 1,000 hryvnias are needed for this
Another factor contributing to the introduction of the new banknote is the increase in the amount of cash from nearly 390 billion hryvnias in 2019 to more than 970 billion hryvnias as of July 1, 2026.
In addition, there have been changes in the structure of cash in circulation. Currently, banknotes with a denomination of 1,000 hryvnias already account for more than 55% by value. In global central banking practice, this indicates the need to introduce a banknote of a higher denomination
Let us recall
In honor of the 30th anniversary of the hryvnia, the National Bank of Ukraine put into circulation a commemorative silver coin, "Dedicated to the 30th Anniversary of the Monetary Reform in Ukraine."

Victims sue South African government over 1961 Sharpeville massacre that left 91 dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:11:37 UTC
19:11:37 KST

The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.
Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.
Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.
The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.
As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.
Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.
The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.
In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.
Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.
In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”
In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.
The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.
The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with the UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.
Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of about 20,000 rand for six years.
“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”
The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father, Samson, was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.
Mathinye did not initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”
Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but could not afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.
Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.
Sharpeville’s problems did not begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.
“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Culture
Details: In August alone, the Russians damaged 148 cultural heritage sites and 15 cultural institutions.

- cultural centres – 1,310: 285 destroyed and 1,025 damaged. The largest percentages are in Donetsk Oblast (19%), Kharkiv Oblast (15%) and Sumy Oblast (11.5%)

- arts education institutions – 195: 25 destroyed and 170 damaged. The largest percentages are in Donetsk Oblast (21%), Kharkiv Oblast (13%) and Kherson Oblast (9.7%)
- museums and galleries – 139: 20 destroyed and 119 damaged. The largest percentages are in Donetsk Oblast (17%), Kharkiv Oblast (11.6%) and Kherson Oblast (9.4%)
- theatres, cinemas and philharmonic halls – 56: four destroyed and 52 damaged. The largest percentages are in Kharkiv Oblast (12.5%), Kherson Oblast (10.7%) and Kyiv (12.5%)
- nature reserves – nine
- parks and zoos – 14: two destroyed and 12 damaged
- circuses – three damaged: one each in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv oblasts
- a film studio in Kyiv has also been damaged.

Emil Graesholm, PET’s head of counterintelligence, told public broadcaster DR that Danish companies were targets of “concrete Russian sabotage planning”.
“We see that Danish companies are also targets for concrete Russian sabotage planning, and that Russian intelligence services are actively preparing sabotage operations aimed at the defence industry in Denmark,” Graesholm said.
He also told Danish newspaper Berlingske that authorities had uncovered specific Russian plans for sabotage operations against companies in Denmark.
“Therefore, this is not just a warning that it might come to Denmark one day. We are already seeing the planning now. Very concretely,” he said.
The companies that could be targeted include defence firms linked to military aid to Ukraine, according to PET.
Recruitment efforts
PET said it had identified “concrete examples” of Russia attempting to recruit ordinary Danes through social media and other online platforms.
Those individuals could be asked to carry out tasks such as photographing companies or installations to help plan sabotage operations, the intelligence service said.
“It is extremely serious if ordinary Danes help Russian intelligence services — either intentionally or unknowingly,” Graesholm said.
Public warning
“It is such a concrete identification and preparation that we find it necessary to go out with the message that it is a threat that must be taken seriously,” he said.
The Confederation of Danish Industry said it was taking PET’s assessment seriously and was in close contact with relevant authorities.
“The changed threat picture calls for increased attention from companies, but also for calm and proportionality,” said Rasmus Anderskouv, the organisation’s head of security and preparedness.
No direct evidence
Despite PET saying Russia has become more willing to use hybrid measures, including physical sabotage across Europe, the agency also said it was not currently aware of “any specific instances of Russian physical sabotage in Denmark.”
Western governments have accused Russia of being behind several sabotage incidents, particularly those involving undersea cables and pipelines, but direct evidence linking Moscow to the incidents remains inconclusive. Russia denies the accusations.
The 2022 Nord Stream attacks in the Baltic Sea were initially widely attributed to Russia, until it emerged that the pipeline sabotage was linked to Ukraine.
On August 19 2026, German investigators arrested a Ukrainian man in relation to the undersea explosions.

China’s rare earth cerium drug can kill gout pains once and for all: scientists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:09:01 UTC
19:09:01 KST

China’s rare earth cerium drug can kill gout pains once and for all: scientists
Nanoparticle ‘sweeper’ drug eases joint inflammation and cartilage damage from the painful form of inflammatory arthritis in rat trials
One of the world’s most abundant rare earth elements could offer a comprehensive, long-lasting treatment for gout, a Chinese team has found.
More than 55 million people worldwide had gout in 2020, according to US health data, with the number expected to rise by 70 per cent by 2050.
The disease begins with raised uric acid levels in the blood, or hyperuricemia. Consistently high uric acid causes the formation of joint crystals that trigger severe, sudden pain attacks. If left untreated, this monosodium urate (MSU) crystal build-up can lead to joint deformities, kidney damage and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.
Researchers with the school of pharmaceutical sciences at Shanghai Jiao Tong University are now holding out hope, with a medication based on rare earth oxide nanoparticles that could target the cause of gout and relieve its severe pain.
Animal studies showed that the drug not only lowers uric acid levels but also reduces the formation of gout crystals, alleviates inflammation, and inhibits osteoclast or bone breakdown activity, thereby addressing all painful symptoms of gouty arthritis (GA), the team said.

Ukrainian helicopter gets new AI-assisted gun module against Shaheds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:08:18 UTC
19:08:18 KST

- The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation delivered a Khyzhak combat module for aviation use, funded through a joint project with Uklon.
- The module fires a stabilized 7.62 mm PKT machine gun and uses AI-assisted tracking to help engage drones, including Shahed-type strike drones.
The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation says it has delivered a remotely operated “Khyzhak” combat module for use in Ukrainian aviation, and that the system is now being used against Russian targets.
The foundation announced the delivery on social media, saying it purchased the module through a joint project with the ride-hailing company Uklon called “Pidsvity Voroha 2.0” (“Light Up the Enemy 2.0”). Video accompanying the post shows the module mounted on a helicopter and used against Russian Shahed-type strike drones.
“We are complicating flights for Russian Shaheds,” the foundation wrote. “The video shows the remotely controlled Khyzhak combat module, which the Foundation delivered for aviation. We purchased it as part of a joint project with Uklon, ‘Pidsvity Voroha 2.0.’ And now this module is successfully working against enemy targets, thank you for that!”
The Khyzhak module is built around a 7.62 mm PKT machine gun and can rotate 360 degrees horizontally and elevate up to 75 degrees vertically. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense codified the module and cleared it for use in the Armed Forces. The ministry said the machine guns mounted on the module can be loaded with either Soviet-pattern or NATO-standard 7.62 mm ammunition and that the platform is stabilized, allowing accurate fire while the vehicle carrying it is moving.
The module’s developers designed it to be modular. It can be installed on robotic ground platforms, mounted stationary, adapted for use on vehicles, or fitted to naval systems. The version shown in the foundation’s video represents an adaptation for aviation.
The module includes an artificial intelligence system for automatic target recognition and tracking, including automatic detection of drones. That capability allows operators to use the Khyzhak to engage small first-person-view drones as well as larger Shahed-type drones, which are roughly the size of a small Cessna aircraft, at close range.
The foundation did not disclose how many Khyzhak modules it has funded, which unit or units are operating the system, or the cost of the purchase made through the Uklon partnership.

Russia now hunts Kyiv by daylight too, Flash explains why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:07:52 UTC
19:07:52 KST

Russia has started launching its strike drones during the day, not only after dark. The reason is the new jet-powered Geran drones, which fire groups cannot take down, so for Russia there is no longer any difference between attacking by day or by night, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, President Zelenskyy's adviser on defense technologies, told Glavcom.
The near-hourly daytime raids are the new face of a campaign that culminated on 1 September, Knowledge Day, when Russia hit Kyiv and its region with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones and killed 12 people. That strike culminated a six-day assault on the capital that began on 27 August, two days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow. However, even after that, the attack continued. Sirens now sound across Kyiv and the surrounding oblast roughly once an hour, around the clock.
Why the shift to daylight
The daytime raids carry an added economic and psychological weight, he said. The threat of strikes forces shops and businesses to open and close unpredictably, snarls transport, and can halt rail service.
"They understand perfectly well that daytime attacks hurt the population and business," Beskrestnov said, adding that the state railway Ukrzaliznytsia is paralyzed.
Keeping the defenders on their feet
A further aim is to hold Ukraine's air defense in a permanent state of readiness, Beskrestnov said. Round-the-clock attacks mean radar stations and generators must run without pause.
"Radar stations and generators run constantly, and that also puts a strain on our troops," he added.
Kyiv remains a Russian prime target because it carries symbolic as well as military weight, as the capital houses the government, business, and warehouses, and a strike there would resonate far more than terrorizing a small town.
Russian forces first concentrated on districts nearer the drones' launch corridors — Kyiv's Left Bank, and the Brovary and Boryspil raions — before switching to the other bank to hunt for targets. As the cold season approaches, he expects Russia to intensify strikes on the energy infrastructure it has so far spared.

Norway seizes Russian ship to enforce $4.22 billion Ukrainian compensation claim
Norway said Wednesday it had seized a Russian ship as part of a Ukrainian effort to recover $4.22 billion awarded to state energy firm Naftogaz over Russia’s seizure of its assets in Crimea in 2014. The Professor Molchanov vessel was detained off the Arctic Svalbard archipelago after a Norwegian court ordered its arrest.
Norway has seized a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce a $4.22 billion compensation claim won by Ukrainian energy firm Naftogaz over Moscow's seizure of its assets when Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, officials said late on Wednesday.
The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was seized off the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard, according to Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz.
Read moreBelgium, France seize Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker in the North Sea
The Russian state news agency TASS quoted a foreign ministry spokesperson as saying the Norwegian action was "piracy".
The Svalbard governor's office issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held on Svalbard, adding:
"The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol".
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Russian ship to be held in Svalbard
It was not immediately clear how many passengers and crew were on the ship. Arktikugol ("Arctic Coal") is the Russian company that manages Moscow's assets on the archipelago.
Svalbard, a Norwegian territory since 1925, lies midway between the North Pole and the European mainland and is governed under a 1920 treaty that also allows citizens of signatory states, including Russia, to settle there without a visa.
The ship arrived on Tuesday in Barentsburg, a Russian-operated coal mining settlement on Spitsbergen, the largest island in the archipelago, with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them.
Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio, said the vessel had docked without incident and the expedition members had headed ashore.
News did not emerge until Wednesday evening that the ship had been seized.
"This seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Gorbunov wrote on KP's website.
"For the time being, the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg. It is completely unclear how long this ban will last."
Read moreFrance backed by Britain intercepts sanctioned oil tanker sailing from Russia
Court orders seizure of Russian properties in Svalbard
Naftogaz has previously won court orders to seize two Trust Arktikugol properties in Svalbard, including a rental guest house, but Russia has raised legal challenges.
Naftogaz has been pursuing Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for the expropriation of its property in Crimea.
A tribunal in The Hague in April 2023 ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.22 billion plus interest and legal costs.
"Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz Acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.
Norway said the matter was a legal one between Naftogaz and Russia and did not involve the Oslo government.
"As a party to the case, Russia can demand that the district court reassess the case," the Justice Ministry said.
Covington said it had been tracking the Professor Molchanov, a vessel used for commercial cruises, for months.
Anticipating its arrival, Naftogaz's lawyers applied to a court for the vessel to be arrested and compulsorily sold.
The application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which required the governor of Svalbard to enforce its order, supervise the ship and ensure that it is not moved.
Naftogaz has said it is coordinating enforcement across several jurisdictions, including the US, France, Britain and Finland, where Russian assets have been frozen.
Russia is appealing, saying no notice was given.
"We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world until the compensation awarded to Naftogaz and other Naftogaz Group companies is paid," the Ukrainian company said.
Barentsburg is one of two Russian settlements on Svalbard, along with Pyramiden. Together they have 392 residents out of a total population of 2,914, according to Statistics Norway.
The Svalbard Treaty restricts military use of the archipelago, but the islands are not a demilitarised zone.
Russia has frequently accused Norway of militarising the islands, which Oslo denies.

Lula adopts cautious Brazil election campaign, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:06:25 UTC
19:06:25 KST

Lula adopts cautious Brazil election campaign, sources say
BRASILIA, Sep 3 - Weeks before Brazil's October election, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is running one of the country's most cautious presidential campaigns in years as he tries to protect a razor-thin lead in the polls against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, advisers close to his campaign told Reuters.
The result has been an unusually subdued campaign, the sources said, amid concerns about misinformation, foreign interference, and accidentally unleashing damaging political narratives.
“The ability to mislead voters today is even greater than it was in 2022, so it’s a real concern. We have to be much more careful about what we do and say,” one adviser said, asking not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.
Polls show Lula holding a narrowing lead over Senator Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, with the latest polls showing a 1- to 3- percentage-point difference in the second round.
Inside the Planalto presidential palace in Brasilia, officials have been told to closely vet government actions to avoid accusations that state resources are being used for political purposes and to minimize missteps that opponents could exploit.
Ministers have been asked to delete social media posts, and state television has stopped broadcasting presidential events to avoid the risk of violating the Brazilian electoral law, the sources told Reuters. At the same time, official announcements and presidential events are being carefully reviewed to avoid misinterpretation, even if some officials see it as an overly cautious approach, they added.
"I think there's a certain amount of exaggeration in this concern with violating the law. Previous administrations had absolutely no concern about this," one source said. "The Brazilian legislation is clear that at some point the incumbent will be president and candidate at the same time."
Yet all that caution was not enough to spare Lula from a social media storm last week. During an interview, he said he had never met a lobbyist who is currently under investigation in a corruption probe, only for Instagram photos showing the two together to quickly resurface and circulate online.
His campaign claimed he is often approached by people asking for photos, but he maintains he has no relation whatsoever with the lobbyist.
His rival, Bolsonaro, has dealt with his own social media controversy as well. This week, a Brazilian magazine revealed that he had received a payment of $1.6 million from Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced former banker investigated for corruption in one of the largest fraud schemes uncovered in the Brazilian financial system. A previous payment of $24 million was revealed in May.
Lula's campaign, however, sees a much more challenging environment with the rise of artificial intelligence, which makes the distortion of information harder to detect, and an administration in Washington that seems to be encouraging a shift to the right in Latin America.
“The U.S. government today has a clear willingness to interfere in elections in the region,” one person close to Lula told Reuters, saying that the Trump administration views Brazil as the next target in a wave of right-wing victories "that they initiated in the region."
The State Department did not reply to a request for comment from Reuters, but the agency has previously rejected accusations of election interference by Brazil's government.
POLARIZATION
The reasons behind the subdued campaign, however, go beyond Lula's caution.
Analysts point to the polarization between Lula and the Bolsonaro camp as a factor contributing to voter fatigue, which ultimately translates into the general apathy seen on the streets.
"Both paths are familiar; they’ve already been tried," explained Cila Schulman, CEO of the Ideia Institute, a polling and public opinion survey think tank.
Senator Bolsonaro's campaign is also seeing a subdued public, one person who is close to the senator told Reuters, adding that their surveys show that voters across the political spectrum are tired of the political bickering, which is contributing to lower political engagement.
Brazil's electoral court, which oversees elections, has also forbidden platforms from showing content from candidates to users who do not follow them, adding to the challenge of reaching voters.
It's part of the reason why engagement in each campaign is confined to echo chambers, said Luis Fakhouri, director of strategy at Palver, a data intelligence firm that monitors social media. That, he added, could work in favor of Lula and Senator Bolsonaro, the two candidates leading the race.
"For Lula and Flavio's campaigns, if there's not much action, it is good for them. They're firmly in the lead, they don't need to rock the boat. The minor candidates are the ones that should try to heat up their campaigns," said Fakhouri. REUTERS

Katz said Israel was prepared for any further escalation.
“Israel is well prepared, defensively and offensively, for every possibility,” he said. “The IDF is ready to carry out the mission.”

Disposable fashion trend among Chinese tourists sparks waste and health concerns
One shop sells around 15,000 items per month, with bestselling products ranging from US$1.5 to US$7.5, comparable to a budget meal
The trend of wearing disposable clothing while travelling gained popularity among Chinese internet users this summer, drawing criticism for its environmental impact.
The term “disposable clothing” recently had gone viral on social media, with its hashtag accumulating 6.8 million views and 135,000 discussions on one platform.
People shared their experiences of wearing disposable clothing on their trips, highlighting it as an economical choice. One individual noted that she bought five sets of clothes for her seven-day journey, spending no more than 200 yuan (US$30) in total.
As the term implies, she had no intention of keeping the clothes after her travels.
Most disposable garments are designed for social media appeal, including vibrant long skirts, cloaks, and outdoor jackets that are deemed unsuitable for everyday wear.
A women’s apparel shop owner shared with the Chinese media outlet City Express that his store offers various clothing styles tailored to different occasions.
For instance, he stocks photogenic skirts for seaside adventures in May, traditional hanfu attire for the Dragon Boat Festival, and exotic skirts for travellers heading to Xinjiang.
The shop owner revealed that he sells around 15,000 items monthly, primarily to customers aged 18 to 30. His best-selling items range from 10 to 50 yuan (US$1.5 to US$7.5), comparable to the price of a budget meal.
