6 Taipei must-see galleries in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:55:25 UTC
18:55:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — From open-call showcases spotlighting emerging local talent to intimate botanical portraits, Taipei's art spaces are brimming with creative vitality.
Setting the tone, Whitestone Gallery’s contemporary art exhibition dedicated to the virtual pop icon Hatsune Miku drew massive crowds and long queues on opening day, underscoring the powerful convergence of youth culture and fine art.
Here are six gallery exhibitions to explore in Taipei this month.
"Song of Youth: Brushing the Sun"
After previously spotlighting European and US masters as well as young creators from China, Bluerider Art turns its focus back to local soil.
Selected from nearly 2,000 submissions by 500 applicants nationwide, this open-call exhibition presents nearly 60 works by 21 emerging Taiwanese artists born after 1985. The show highlights the dynamic interplay between heritage and experimentation in contemporary Taiwanese art.
The exhibition title draws from ancient poetry and Qu Yuan’s (屈原) classic Li Sao, blended with poet Rainer Maria Rilke’s mandate to “live the questions.”
Among the highlights are Wu Shang-wei (吳上瑋) and Lin Po-yang (林博揚). Li Hsiao-sheng (李曉昇) and Tsai Ming-tsan (蔡名璨) break traditional ink conventions. Chen Kuan-ray (陳寬睿) uses chemical pigments to generate natural rust on canvas.
Location: Bluerider Art Taipei Dunhua
Date: Aug. 1 – Oct. 4
"Objects of Desire: Where Micro and Macro Open in All Directions" and "Shelter Island"
Double Square Gallery is staging a compelling dual solo exhibition. Spanish artist Ana de Alvear, winner of the Edge Artist Award at Taipei Dangdai 2025, presents "Objects of Desire: Where Micro and Macro Open in All Directions."
Drawing inspiration from Susan Stewart’s cultural analysis “On Longing,” Alvear uses hyperrealistic colored-pencil trompe-l'œil techniques in series like “Moss and Void Labyrinth” to challenge spatial perception.
Sharing the gallery space, Taiwanese artist Chang Shan-hsueh (張善學) presents "Shelter Island," an inquiry into natural ecosystems and Taiwan’s historical role as a glacial refugium. Elevating flora from background motif to primary subject, Chang delivers vertical botanical portraits alongside his Datun Volcano Group landscape triptych.
At the center of the gallery sits a live installation of ferns cultivated on the artist's apartment balcony, transforming the concrete urban residence into a living sanctuary.
Location: Double Square Gallery
Date: Aug. 15 – Sept. 26
"A Pair of Underwear, A Pair of Socks"
A favorite in fashion and street-culture circles, Taiwanese artist Sangna Take (桑拿大可) makes his return to Eslite Gallery with his second solo show, "A Pair of Underwear, A Pair of Socks."
Named after fundamental daily garments, the exhibition reflects the unvarnished vulnerability and relaxed state of returning home and shedding societal roles. Featuring 34 new paintings and six ceramic sculptures, the exhibition reveals heavy stylistic influences from Nara Yoshitomo and Jean-Michel Basquiat.
Sangna Take departs from traditional centered compositions, intertwining his signature slacker boy figures with new characters such as fairies and anthropomorphic plants.
The exhibition also debuts Sangna Take's first official self portrait.
Location: Eslite Gallery
Date: Aug. 15 – Oct. 10
"Professional Amatures"
Curated by TKG+ Projects exhibition planner Huang Chung-li (黃仲笠), "Professional Amatures" emerges from an insider's critique of institutional art structures. The exhibition brings together five artists to examine how art market mechanisms define concepts of professionalism and value.
Lin Guan-ming (林冠名) uses photography to document stylized public visuals and labor. Hsu Chia-chen (許家禎) reinterprets Taiwanese sculpture history through public monuments and traditional molding.
Cheng Po-tsung (鄭帛囱) crafts intimate micro-paintings using everyday stationery, while Yang Hui-ching (楊惠青) showcases "blind drawings" cultivated from her background in art education and theater. Curator Huang Chung-li (黃仲笠) reclaims his identity as a painter with works that question formal canvas orthodoxy.
Location: TKG+ Projects
Date: Aug. 22 – Oct. 31
"Art of Miku"
Making its overseas debut at Whitestone Gallery, the "Art of Miku" contemporary art exhibition has entered its second stage, introducing a refreshed roster of artworks and international artists.
The showcase gathers more than 20 creators across diverse cultural contexts, including Auto Moai, Clasutta, Fabien Verschaere, and more. Through painting, sculpture, and multidisciplinary visual formats, the participating artists deconstruct and reframe the virtual idol Hatsune Miku, exploring the possibilities of virtual existence within contemporary art.
Online ticket reservations are required, with exclusive Taipei-edition merchandise available on-site.
Location: Whitestone Gallery
Date:Aug. 29 – Sept. 20
"The Binding Strand of" and "While Everything Falls Away"
Mind Set Art Center presents two concurrent solo exhibitions investigating materiality and sensory awareness.
Portuguese artist Rui Miguel Leitao Ferreira presents "The Binding Strand of," displaying 14 abstract paintings executed since 2020 that layer acrylics, repurposed canvases, and found objects.
Ferreira builds on geometric grid frameworks before allowing fluid paint application and exposed canvas seams to subvert the traditional flatness of modernist painting.
In dialogue with Ferreira's work, Taiwanese artist Huang Kuan-chun (黃冠鈞) presents "While Everything Falls Away."
Drawing on his background in sculpture and fiber arts, Huang stacks acrylic paint layers on glass before peeling them off to create freestanding "paint bodies." Inspired by Marcel Duchamp’s concept of subtle nuance, works like “Sky” are applied directly onto gallery windowpanes, allowing natural sunlight to filter through translucent paint films and dynamically evolve throughout the day.
Location: Mind Set Art Center
Date: Aug. 29 – Oct. 8

Putin says the war isn’t driving Russia’s falling birth rate
The war in Ukraine is affecting Russia’s birth rate, but it isn’t the main cause of the country’s demographic crisis, Vladimir Putin said at a plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum.
”SVO, of course, has some effect, but the SVO isn’t the reason. After all, Japan doesn’t have any SVO, and neither does South Korea, yet their birth rate is lower than ours. Yes, of course, we need to pay attention to all the factors. But that’s probably still not the main one,” Putin said.
Putin said there is no simple explanation for the falling birth rate: “We both know that in post-industrial societies the birth rate is low, while in countries with relatively poor populations it is high,” he said.
Putin said raising the birth rate will require new incentives for families and young women, along with a shift in “public consciousness.” He noted that Russia reversed the negative demographic trend and achieved a noticeable increase in the birth rate in the mid-2000s. “We have the experience, and we will definitely repeat it,” he said.
Rosstat stopped publishing monthly regional data on births and deaths in 2025, then completely removed the demographic section from its monthly report on Russia’s socioeconomic situation.
The move came amid a historic decline in Russia’s birth rate: an average of 3,012 children were born per day in March 2025, the lowest figure in nearly 200 years of record-keeping. Putin, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum, called demographics a matter of national security.

In the case involving the director of a language center in Khmelnytskyi, there are now nine child victims
Kyiv • UNN
Law enforcement officers have identified nine girls who were victims in the case involving the director of a language center. He is charged with 14 crimes committed between 2004 and 2025.
The number of child victims abused by the director of one of the foreign language learning centers in Khmelnytskyi has risen to nine. This is reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, according to UNN.
Details
Under the procedural guidance of the Khmelnytskyi Regional Prosecutor’s Office, a pretrial investigation is ongoing into the director of one of the foreign language learning centers in Khmelnytskyi, who is suspected of committing criminal offenses against the sexual freedom and sexual inviolability of children (Part 1 of Article 156 and Part 4 of Article 153 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine)
According to the available information, when the man was notified of the suspicion in August this year, there were two female victims, aged 13 and 14.
During the further investigation, law enforcement officers identified seven more underage and minor girls who had suffered from the suspect’s unlawful actions. At present, nine victims have been identified in the criminal proceedings, against whom 14 criminal offenses were committed between 2004 and 2025
This concerns the satisfaction of sexual desire with regard to minors (Part 2 of Article 153 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, in the versions in force at the time the criminal offenses were committed), sexual violence against persons under the age of 14 (Part 4 of Article 153 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine), engaging in sexual acts with a person under the age of 16 (Part 1 of Article 155 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine), and the sexual abuse of minors (Part 1 of Article 156 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
Investigators and prosecutors are currently verifying the circumstances of each episode and carrying out the necessary investigative and procedural actions. Other persons who may have suffered from the suspect’s actions are also being identified. Within the criminal proceedings, at the prosecutors’ request, a preventive measure in the form of detention without the right to bail was imposed on him.
Reminder
The 58-year-old director of the language center is suspected of sexually abusing 13- and 14-year-old female students during classes. The actions took place in 2018–2020 and 2023–2025.

Military recruitment and retention continues to improve as new statistics show yearlong improvement
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:54:29 BST
18:54:29 KST

Military recruitment and retention continues to improve as new statistics show yearlong improvement
More people joined the Regular Armed Forces than left for the fourth consecutive quarter, the longest such run since 2021.
New stats revealed today show that more people have joined the Armed Forces than left for an entire year. Regular strength increased across all three Services over the past year, with the Royal Navy/Royal Marines up 440, the Army up 170 and the RAF up 840.
Alongside rebuilding workforce numbers, the Armed Forces remains one of the UK’s leading routes into skilled careers, with opportunities across engineering, healthcare, cyber and digital roles, supporting growth in every postcode. The Armed Forces are also among the country’s leading apprenticeship providers, with The Times Apprenticeship Rankings consistently placing the Army, Royal Navy and Royal Air Force among the top five employers.
The Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has welcomed the progress on recruitment and retention, which comes after pay rises, £9bn funding to improve forces housing and a range of recruitment and retention reforms since 2024.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP, said:
  There has never been a better or more important time to join our Armed Forces. Under this government, those serving and joining up now can be certain of increased investment in defence and our people. That means better equipment, better housing and better support for them and their families.
I am determined that serving our nation gives people the skills and opportunities to thrive during their service and beyond, no matter their background.”
Today’s statistics also show other improvements, including:
- The number of full-time military personnel available to support Defence operations rose by 1,450 since 1 July 2025.
- The number of fully trained Tri-Service personnel available to support operations increased for the third consecutive quarter. An increase in fully trained personnel was first recorded as of 1 January 2026, the first such increase in trade trained strength since late 2021.
- Regular strength increased across all three Services over the past year, with the Royal Navy/Royal Marines up 440, the Army up 170 and the RAF up 840.
- Intake has increased steadily while outflow has continued to decline since late 2023, helping drive a net gain of 1,460 personnel in the year to 30 June 2026.
The government in 2024 inherited deep recruitment and retention challenges, with targets missed every year for the past 14 years. While rebuilding the workforce after years of declining personnel numbers will take time, the latest figures show signs of improvement, with more people joining than leaving the Armed Forces, strength increasing across all three Services and trained strength rising for a third consecutive quarter.
The Government is continuing to improve recruitment and retention through a range of measures, including:
- More money in the pockets of Service personnel, delivering a cumulative 14.1% pay rise since July 2024 and ensuring every full-time member of the Armed Forces earns at least the National Living Wage.
- Better homes for Service families, with over £7 billion being invested in military housing this Parliament, the biggest renewal of Forces accommodation in a generation.
- Improved recruitment practices, with the scrapping of more than 100 outdated recruitment policies, including rules that blocked applicants with hay fever, eczema, acne or fully healed injuries, while introducing novel entry routes into the military, such as the Cyber Direct Entry Scheme for high-demand specialist roles.
Whether joining straight from school, university or later in life, recruits can build careers in everything from engineering and healthcare to cyber and digital roles, developing skills and progressing on merit regardless of background.

Yair Netanyahu, Israeli PM’s son, angers UK right over Falklands comment

Yair Netanyahu, Israeli PM’s son, angers UK right over Falklands comment
Accusing the UK government of ‘hypocrisy’, Yair Netanyahu backs Argentina’s claims to the British-held Falkland Islands.
Comments by Yair Netanyahu, the son of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, backing Argentina’s claim to the British-controlled Falkland Islands have caused an unlikely row with Britain’s right wing – one of the United Kingdom’s last reliable pro-Israel groups.
The younger Netanyahu waded into the longrunning territorial dispute over the South Atlantic archipelago last week, writing on X in Spanish: “The Falkland Islands belong to Argentina.”
Britain and Argentina fought a war over the islands in 1982 and continue to dispute their sovereignty.
In follow-up posts, he said that Israel should support Argentina’s claim because the Argentinian government, under far-right President Javier Milei, is more friendly to Israel.
He accused the UK of “hypocrisy and hostility towards Israel with their recognition of ‘Palestine’”, as well as of perpetuating “antisemitism” and “blood libels”.
UK’s Restore Britain party clashes with Yair Netanyahu
His comments came days before United States President Donald Trump, also a close ally of Milei, said the US was reviewing its stance on the Falklands.
While Yair Netanyahu’s remarks appeared intended as a shot at the UK’s Labour government, which includes both centre-left and left-wing politicians, they have also angered right-wing British figures who are typically pro-Israel.
Rupert Lowe, head of the far-right Restore Britain party, responded directly to him on X, saying that the Falklands would “remain” British and that a UK government led by his party would “go to war if necessary to ensure it”.
“You have enough problems to be focusing on in Israel”, Lowe responded, while calling on the Israeli government to clarify its position on the Falklands.
According to YouGov, just 3 percent of people polled would vote for Restore if a general election were held tomorrow.
Sir Conor Burns, a former MP with Britain’s Conservative Party, called Yair Netanyahu’s comments “stupid” and warned they would be “damaging to Israel’s cause on the [British] right”.
Far-right British activist Tommy Robinson, formerly called Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, a vocal backer of Israel, shared a post on X calling British sovereignty over the Falklands a “true fact”, without mentioning the son of the Israeli premier.
‘Antagonised’ Israel’s defenders
Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer on security studies at King’s College London, said the remarks were the latest example of him causing “consternation amongst Israel’s self-declared friends in Europe.”
“Yair Netanyahu has antagonised the constituency in Britain most inclined to defend Israel,” Geist Pinfold told Al Jazeera.
While not an Israeli government official, Geist Pinfold said that he “is alleged to have far more de facto power behind the scenes thanks to Benjamin Netanyahu’s increasingly autocratic style of leadership”.
James Vaughan, lecturer in international history at Aberystwyth University, said that remarks could alienate some on the British right, though it is not a united bloc.
While Britain’s mainstream right-wing movements are generally pro-Israel, elements of Britain’s “extreme right” have historically been an “anti-Israeli force in British politics,” Vaughan told Al Jazeera, adding that there are signs of Restore Britain “reverting to older, anti-Semitic traditions”.
Last year, Restore Britain’s Lowe said of a camera that would film him, “In days gone by you’d call it a Jewish camera, but that would be politically incorrect. Because it’s so small.” He has also called for kosher – as well as halal – meat to be banned. He has rejected accusations of anti-Semitism.
Israeli officials stay mum
No Israeli government official has publicly endorsed Yair Netanyahu’s position on the Falklands.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has, however, previously invoked the islands while defending Israel’s illegal settlement policy in the occupied West Bank.
During a United Nations Security Council debate in February, Saar said that Israeli settlements in the West Bank were located “in the cradle of our own civilisation”, contrasting them with the Falklands.
“It is our country; it’s not 13,000 kilometres away from our country, like the Falkland Islands,” said Saar, addressing then-British Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper. “The Argentinians call it the Malvinas Islands – a dispute you haven’t solved with Argentina until today.”
Vaughan pointed out that the Falklands have long been a “thorny issue in UK-Israel relations”, including in the early 1980s, due to Israeli arms sales to Argentina.
“The fact that the current Israeli government is once again ‘playing the Falklands card’ is of little consequence in and of itself and probably tells us more about the current state of friendly relations between Israel and Argentina than anything else,” Vaughan told Al Jazeera.
Israeli officials have brought up other territorial issues when responding to criticism over Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestinian land.
On July 31, as Spanish authorities faced a wave of people rushing into its territory of Ceuta over the Moroccan border, Israeli ambassador to the United Nations Danny Danon goaded Spain over its control of the African enclave.
“Maybe before it continues lecturing us, it’s time it explained to the world why it [Spain] still maintains colonial enclaves in Africa,” Danon wrote in a post on X.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has noted that Israel is carrying out a genocide in Gaza, and Madrid has imposed sweeping measures, including a total arms embargo, against Israel.
Like the UK and other European countries, Spain also recognises Palestinian statehood.
‘Comprehensive reset’
Despite traditionally strong ties, there are signs of tension between Israel and Britain under Labour, which took power in 2024.
Under former Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer, the UK paused free-trade talks with Israel and suspended some arms export licences. The UK has also imposed sanctions on far-right Israeli cabinet members Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
The UK’s new leader, Andy Burnham, is currently weighing further measures relating to illegal Israeli settlements.
Israeli officials have derided the UK as relations deteriorate. Prime Minister Netanyahu recently referred to the UK as the “Islamic Republic of Britain”.
Vaughan said that the re-emergence of the Falklands issue is “indicative of underlying UK-Israeli tensions that are obviously rooted more in fundamental disagreements about Gaza, the West Bank and wider Middle Eastern conflicts”.

‘Military production can't be the answer’: Critics oppose Volkswagen’s defence plan with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:54:02 UTC
18:54:02 KST

Volkswagen's revived plan to produce military equipment at its Osnabruck factory with Israel's Rafael has drawn fresh opposition after reports that the state of Lower Saxony could step in to help overcome objections that had stalled the project.
The proposal comes as Volkswagen undergoes a sweeping restructuring amid falling profits, weaker demand in China and growing competition from lower-priced Chinese brands in Europe, with vehicle production at the Osnabruck plant set to end after 2027.
Thorben Peters, co-chair of the Left Party in Lower Saxony, said thousands of jobs at the factory, along with its industrial expertise and know-how, must be preserved without a shift to arms production.
"Replacing civilian production with military production cannot be the answer to the automotive industry's current crisis," Peters told Anadolu.
"The state of Lower Saxony, in particular, should not use public funds to participate in an arms-related joint venture. We reject the false claim that the only alternatives are unemployment or arms production."
Volkswagen confirmed in March that it was in talks with several defence contractors about the Osnabruck plant.
A blocked plan and a new workaround
The proposal has faced opposition from peace groups, labour movements and opposition parties for months, particularly over potential cooperation with Israel's state-owned defence firm Rafael.
In July, Qatar's sovereign wealth fund, Volkswagen's third-largest shareholder, blocked the plan.
Now, management has revived the idea with a structure that could overcome that obstacle.
According to recent German media reports, Volkswagen would transfer parts of the Osnabruck site to the state of Lower Saxony, which could then form a joint venture with Rafael to manufacture military equipment. 
The project could manufacture key components for Israel's Iron Dome air defence system, including launchers, transport vehicles and power generators.
The Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung reported that Lower Saxony could invest at least €200 million ($232 million) in the project.
The Left Party argues that if the state is prepared to spend public money to preserve production and jobs at the site, it should instead invest in civilian alternatives.
Peters said those could include special-purpose and environmentally friendly vehicles for public transport.
Volkswagen's supervisory board is due to meet on September 4.
Peters said his party opposes converting civilian industrial capacity to military production as a matter of principle, regardless of the nationality of the company involved.
In the case of Israeli defence company Rafael, however, he said the war in Gaza raises additional concerns.
"Given the massive human rights violations and serious allegations regarding breaches of international law in connection with the war in Gaza, there must be particularly rigorous scrutiny,” he said.
"The guiding principle for public investment must be that human rights and international law are non-negotiable."
'City of Peace' pushes back
The debate has particular resonance in Osnabruck, a city that has long promoted itself as a "City of Peace" because of its role in the negotiations that led to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, ending the Thirty Years' War.
The prospect of military production at the Volkswagen plant has sparked repeated protests in recent months, bringing peace activists, anti-war groups and local initiatives onto the streets.
The Osnabruck Peace Initiative argues that Lower Saxony should use any public money earmarked for the plant to support a socially responsible and environmentally sustainable transition rather than subsidise weapons production.
"Production for an Israeli arms company amounts to de facto support for the wars the state of Israel is waging against the Palestinians, Lebanon and Iran," Marie Dominique Guyard, spokesperson for the initiative, told Anadolu.
"Defence equipment for the Iron Dome plays a role in Israel's aggressive, offensive military activities, as it provides the protective shield enabling Israel to act aggressively toward its neighbours."
Speaking on behalf of the Osnabruck Peace Initiative, Guyard said the group's position is also informed by international legal proceedings concerning Israel's conduct.
She pointed to a 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that found Israel's continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory unlawful and said states must not provide aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by that presence.
She cited International Criminal Court arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant on war crimes and findings by a UN commission of inquiry and Amnesty International accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
But she also pointed to Osnabruck's own history to explain the depth of local opposition.
The city was repeatedly bombed during World War II, when it was home to arms-related industry. About 65 percent of Osnabruck was destroyed, including 95 percent of its historic old town.
For Guyard, the prospect of military production returning to the city some eight decades later makes the debate about more than the future of one Volkswagen factory.
"When arms factories are once again established in the city some 80 years after the last war, one can only despair at the decision-makers' disregard for history," she said.
“We do not wish to support such a disastrous development and will continue to build opposition to ensure that work in the city serves peace rather than war.”

Russia plans year-round navigation for Northern Sea Route — Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:53:26 UTC
18:53:26 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russia aims to make navigation along the Northern Sea Route year-round, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
"I would like to separately address the development of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor, which runs from St. Petersburg and Murmansk via the Northern Sea Route to Vladivostok and onward to countries in the Asia-Pacific region. In today's challenging global environment, amid risks to global shipping and trade, it is intended to ensure the flexibility and security of international supplies, open up new opportunities for transit and coastal shipping, and ensure uninterrupted northern deliveries to the Arctic regions of Russia. We aim to make navigation along the route year-round," he said.
The president noted that to achieve this goal, Russia is building icebreakers and ice-class vessels, service and rescue fleets, while also expanding its satellite constellation and strengthening port infrastructure.
"I would like to note a landmark event that will take place very soon. At Vostok Oil, one of our largest Arctic projects in the Krasnoyarsk Region, a trunk oil pipeline to the new Bukhta Sever terminal will be launched. The first oil batch will be shipped to customers along our Arctic sea routes," Putin said.
The president stressed that a comprehensive plan for the development of the Arctic and the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor should become a key initiative designed to integrate the logistics networks of the Far Eastern and Arctic regions. "It runs through 2050 and outlines which projects we will launch, in which industries and areas. I ask my colleagues to promptly finalize the comprehensive plan and begin implementing it," he said.
The Eastern Economic Forum is being held on September 1-4 in Vladivostok on the campus of Far Eastern Federal University. The forum is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Russian government. TASS is the general information partner.

After 264 days at sea, USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thailand’s notorious sex-tourism hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:50:42 UTC
18:50:42 KST

After 264 uninterrupted days at sea supporting the U.S. war against Iran, sailors and Marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln finally stepped ashore this week in Pattaya, the Thai resort city long associated with sex tourism and U.S. military shore leave.
Buses carrying crew members streamed into Pattaya on Thursday after the aircraft carrier docked at nearby Laem Chabang port. The Lincoln has now been deployed for 286 days in total, according to the U.S. Embassy in Bangkok, and is expected to leave Thailand over the weekend as it continues its journey home.
The stop gives the carrier’s roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines a rare chance for rest and recreation after a deployment that included a record 264 consecutive days at sea. The unusually long stretch had raised concerns about crew morale and shortages of key food supplies aboard the ship.
The Navy played down reports of serious problems, while President Donald Trump said last month that the deployment was “not nearly long enough.”
But the choice of Pattaya for shore leave also revives a much older connection between the Thai resort and the U.S. military.
Pattaya still has a strong reputation for sex tourism, despite years of efforts to remake itself as a more family-friendly destination with malls, resorts, parks and other attractions. Its modern nightlife industry has deep roots in the Vietnam War era, when tens of thousands of American service members were stationed in Thailand and flocked to what had previously been a quiet fishing community.
At the height of the Vietnam War, between 40,000 and 50,000 U.S. military personnel were stationed in Thailand, mainly in support of American air operations. Pattaya was close to the Sattahip naval base and U-Tapao airfield, where U.S. Air Force B-52 bombers operated. Bars, massage parlors and other nightlife businesses expanded around the steady flow of servicemen, helping establish the resort’s long-running sex-tourism reputation.
Prostitution remains illegal in Thailand, although the law is often loosely enforced. Paying for sex is also punishable under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, and U.S. Navy shore patrol personnel work alongside Thai police when large numbers of sailors are granted liberty in Pattaya.
On Thursday, however, many of the Lincoln crew members arriving in the city appeared focused on more conventional shore leave.
Vendors and travel agents gathered outside the Hard Rock Hotel, which served as a pickup and drop-off point for personnel coming from the carrier. Sailors climbed off buses carrying luggage as sellers offered souvenirs, transportation and other services.
Several service members told The Associated Press they were simply happy to be back on land.
Dozens were later seen walking through Pattaya’s Terminal 21 mall carrying shopping bags and escaping the afternoon heat.
A 20-year-old navigator serving aboard the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr., part of the Lincoln strike group, told AP that morale among his crew was high after reaching Thailand. He described his first Navy deployment as difficult but said he was relieved to finally be heading home.
Two other ships from the Lincoln strike group are also in Thailand. The Petersen docked at Sriracha in Chonburi province, while the cruiser USS Robert Smalls arrived at Map Ta Phut in neighboring Rayong province.
The arrival has also provided a boost for local businesses accustomed to U.S. military port calls.
A-ngoon Sombat traveled about 200 kilometers from Ayutthaya province to Pattaya to sell braided bracelets to visiting sailors, something she does whenever she hears that an American warship is arriving nearby.
“There are many vendors around. It’s really up to how lucky each of us are,” she told AP.
The carrier itself became a local attraction after docking Wednesday. Residents and tourists gathered outside Laem Chabang port to peer through a fence at the vessel, which is roughly the length of three American football fields.
American Keith Eldridge, who has lived in Thailand for five years, traveled from neighboring Chachoengsao province specifically to see the ship.
“When you get to look at something so big, wrapped up with so much technology, the radars, the sonars, the weapon systems, the propulsion systems, it is truly amazing that we can build it, float it, and we fight from it,” he told AP.
The Lincoln’s commanding officer, Capt. Dan Keeler, said the carrier would soon continue toward the United States, although it could make additional supply stops along the way. He declined to say exactly when the strike group is expected home.

Ukraine fits Abrams tank with Russian-style hedgehog armor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:50:31 UTC
18:50:31 KST

- Ukrainian forces have fitted an M1 Abrams and a BMP-1TS with "hedgehog" anti-drone armor made of unwound steel cable.
- The design, dubbed Yozh or Oduvanchyk in Ukraine, was pioneered by Russian forces in the fall of 2025.
Ukrainian forces have begun fitting their own armored vehicles with the same “hedgehog” anti-drone armor that Russian units pioneered last year, according to photos and video circulating from Ukrainian military channels.
The images show a Ukrainian M1 Abrams from the 225th Separate Assault Regiment and a BMP-1TS operated by the 58th Motorized Infantry Brigade, both covered in dense frameworks of unraveled steel or aluminum cable.
The armor, known also as “Yozh” (Hedgehog) or “Oduvanchyk” (Dandelion), is built from industrial cabling cut into uniform lengths and unwound into individual wire strands. The strands are bundled and welded onto a metal frame that is then bolted or welded to the vehicle’s hull and turret, producing a bristling covering that can extend a foot or more from the armor underneath.
The design first appeared on Russian tanks in the fall of 2025 and has since spread across the front. Iryna Rybakova, a press officer with Ukraine’s 93rd Mechanized Brigade, told RFE/RL that the covering is meant “to get drones tangled and not detonate, or detonate at a distance” from the vehicle’s hull. Most first-person-view kamikaze drones carry a fuse that protrudes from the warhead and triggers on impact. The wire strands are intended to snag or deflect a drone before that fuse reaches the armor plate underneath.
Ukrainian drone operator Yevhen, who fights under the call sign “Krym,” described a related mechanism to RFE/RL: when a shaped-charge warhead detonates away from the hull rather than flush against it, the resulting blast jet is less likely to penetrate. He said the same wire covering can also break up a vehicle’s silhouette, making it harder for reconnaissance drones to identify from the air.
Ukrainian troops initially mocked the appearance of Russian hedgehog vehicles, which have been compared to a vehicle “wearing a bulky, badly made wig.” One heavily armored Russian vehicle reportedly absorbed around 25 mine and drone strikes near Siversk before a 26th munition disabled it, according to Euromaidan Press. Despite the criticism, Ukrainian units have adopted the same approach for their own vehicles over the past several months, a pattern that has repeated with earlier Russian innovations such as “cope cage” and “turtle” armor.
Ukraine has fitted the covering to at least one M1 Abrams before. In February, an ex-Australian M1A1 Abrams belonging to Ukrainian forces appeared in Zaporizhzhia Oblast wearing a hedgehog frame of unwound aluminum cabling. That tank was later struck and disabled by a Russian FPV drone while stationary.
The tradeoffs of the armor are well documented on both sides of the front. The added weight strains vehicle gearboxes and drivetrains, and heavily covered vehicles have reportedly become stuck attempting to cross rivers and streams. One Russian tank crew member told a reporter that a hedgehog-equipped tank “didn’t even make it 10 kilometers before one of the drivetrain components failed.” Carlo Masala, a military expert at the Bundeswehr University in Munich, told RFE/RL the broader shift toward this kind of improvised protection “seems to be a new tactic to bring maneuver back into warfare,” as cheap FPV drones have made large armored assaults increasingly costly for both militaries.
The extent of Ukraine’s adoption of hedgehog and dandelion armor across its vehicle fleet has not been disclosed, and neither the 225th Separate Assault Regiment nor the 58th Motorized Infantry Brigade has released details on how many vehicles in their formations have received the modification.

Consul General of India in Los Angeles Ambassador Dr. K. J. Srinivasa and Ambassador of India to Azerbaijan Abhay Kumar undertook a series of high-level engagements in Karnataka
NEW DELHI: Consul general of India in Los Angeles Ambassador Dr K J Srinivasa and ambassador of India to Azerbaijan Abhay Kumar held a series of high-level meetings in Karnataka as part of a diplomatic visit aimed at strengthening the state's global outreach and exploring partnerships in technology, investment, innovation and industry.The two ambassadors called on Karnataka governor Thaawarchand Gehlot and CM D K Shivakumar, with discussions focusing on the state's growing international profile and its strengths in technology, innovation, industry and skilled human resources.They also met senior members of the Karnataka government, including Electronics, information technology and Biotechnology minister Priyank Kharge, Large and medium industries and Infrastructure development minister M B Patil, energy and tourism minister K J George, and transport minister Byrathi Suresh.
Focus on technology, investment and innovation
The discussions centred on expanding Karnataka's global footprint, facilitating investment and technology partnerships, promoting its startup and innovation ecosystem, and strengthening links with international technology and business centres.The meetings also explored opportunities to showcase Karnataka's tourism potential and skilled workforce while developing stronger technology, education, innovation and investment linkages with global partners.
As part of the visit, Srinivasa and Kumar visited Sarvam AI in Bengaluru, where they interacted with the company's leadership and were briefed on India's evolving artificial intelligence ecosystem, including indigenous foundational models and multilingual AI.The interaction also explored opportunities to strengthen international technology partnerships and connect India's innovation ecosystem with technology hubs abroad.
Aerospace, defence and advanced manufacturing
The ambassadors also visited the Karnataka Aerospace Park and Centum Electronics, where they reviewed the state's capabilities in aerospace, defence electronics, advanced manufacturing and high-technology innovation.The engagements highlighted opportunities for international investment and technology collaboration, as well as stronger links between Karnataka-based companies and global manufacturing and innovation networks.The visit covered sectors including artificial intelligence, frontier technologies, aerospace and defence, advanced manufacturing, clean energy, tourism, startups and entrepreneurship.For the consulate general of India in Los Angeles, the visit also provided an opportunity to identify areas for closer cooperation between Karnataka and the US West Coast, particularly Southern California, in AI and emerging technologies, aerospace, higher education, startups, clean energy, investment and innovation.
The consulate said it would continue working to facilitate institutional and business linkages between India and stakeholders in its jurisdiction and support efforts to promote trade, investment, technology, education and people-to-people partnerships.

Gold’s surge in August marks fastest monthly gain in over half-year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:49:48 UTC
18:49:48 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Gold rose 10% last month, its fastest monthly gain in seven months, amid the US Treasury’s expanded long-term bond buyback operation, weakening expectations that the Fed would hike rates and a relative easing of geopolitical risks.
During this period, demand for the US dollar increased as its safe-haven feature came to the fore amid uncertainties, leading to selling pressure in commodities, especially precious metals.
Gold gained 12.4% in January and 8.5% in February but began to decline with the outbreak of the US-Israel-Iran war at the end of February.
Gold fell 11.3% in March, 1% in April, 1.8% in May and 11.7% in June before gaining 0.9% in July.
The US Treasury expanded its long-term bond buybacks, US inflation slowed, employment in the country weakened Fed rate hike expectations and geopolitical risks relatively eased in August, driving gold up 10% at the end of the month to $4,449 per ounce.
Silver saw a similar trend, as the precious metal rose 15.4% in August to $66.5 per ounce due to easing rate hike expectations, also marking its fastest rise in seven months.
Zafer Ergezen, a futures and commodity markets expert, told Anadolu that the US Treasury’s announcement drove up gold prices, as did central bank gold purchases.
Ergezen stated that there have been very large-scale gold purchases resembling those of a major institutional investor or a central bank.
He mentioned that the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) purchased 19 metric tons of gold last month and that these central bank purchases could continue in September.
He added that the US dollar, bond yields or oil prices did not significantly decline last month, noting that the rise in gold prices last month could have been a result of reactive buying.

Advertisement

You go to bed Kuwaiti, you wake up stateless
Unknown

Breadcrumb
You go to bed Kuwaiti, you wake up stateless
Since the decrees withdrawing Kuwaiti nationality began to pour down, Sunday, the day on which the official gazette Kuwait al-Youm appears, has become a day of anxiety. Kuwaitis feverishly await its appearance, snap it up immediately to see if their name is in it, or if they are to remain Kuwaiti for another week.
Since 2024, with the accession of Sheikh Meshaal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah to the ruler’s throne, the campaign of re-examining and withdrawing nationality has acquired new dimensions. Indeed, the new Emir announced that he meant to put an end to the cases of fraudulent nationality acquisition - the use of forged documents, false declarations, etc. – and to track down cases of dual nationality, forbidden by the law of the land.
The net turned out to be cast wide, since several categories of citizens naturalised quite legitimately were caught in it: people whose residence In Kuwait since 1965 or before had been one of the criteria for naturalisation on the basis of the 1965 census; people who had been granted citizenship in recognition for “eminent services” rendered to the nation”; women having acquired it through marriage to a Kuwaiti; as well as certain children of a Kuwaiti mother and foreign father who did not acquire citizenship automatically through their mother but could be naturalised. These citizens had started families. Their children and grandchildren were born and had grown up under these perfectly legal regulations.
Now those who cannot point to a “nationality of origin” risk becoming stateless, and swelling the ranks of the hundreds of thousands of biduns, the “withouts”, the approximately 10% of the population who are stateless. Mostly from the bedouin tribes, these residents did not acquire Kuwaiti nationality when the country became independent in 1961. They are now deprived of most of the rights of citizens, mainly the right to vote, and to access various other privileges such as property ownership and state support.
This radical change in the notion of citizenship has far-reaching consequences since it affects by extension the children and grandchildren of the excluded, who may became excluded themselves. It is still too recent for its effects to be to fully measured (some will be specified by decree) and to understand its deeper reasons. However, the consequent stiffening of nationality policy appears to be the fulfilment of the promise “to give Kuwait back to its original inhabitants, cleansed and rid of its impurities” made by the new sovereign when he ascended the throne.
A broad aim
Kuwait’s nationality law makes a sharp distinction between citizens “of origin” and citizens “by naturalisation”. That distinction is reaffirmed by the 2026 reform: Kuwaitis of origin are defined in particular on the basis of their establishment in the country before its creation in 1920 and the resulting affiliation, along with continuity of residence, while people having acquired the nationality through naturalisation – as well as their descendants in certain cases – remain legally bound by this status. The rules for withdrawal or revocation are not identical in these different categories and in certain cases specified by law, may have consequences for the descendants. According to the new dispositions, naturalised citizens no longer have voting rights, and are no longer able to stand in elections or be appointed to any representative body.
Among those affected by the withdrawal of nationality are prominent figures in Kuwaiti public life: doctors, professors, historians, athletes and former diplomats. Some have represented Kuwait or contributed for decades to its institutions and cultural and scientific life. Such is the case with Bader al-Awadhi, former Kuwaiti ambassador to the United Kingdom, deprived of his Kuwaiti citizenship by filiation in January, a repercussion of the posthumous withdrawal of his father’s nationality. Since May, this high-ranking civil servant has been a citizen of neighbouring Bahrain.
These revocations have also hit people known for their political stances.
How to live?
An official decision can take just a few lines. Its consequences may begin the very next day. Losing Kuwaiti nationality isn’t just a matter of losing one’s passport. Citizenship is linked to a vast array of rights, services and accesses: voting, education and scholarships, certain public sector and military offices, housing, health care, pensions, subsidised welfare benefits, certain banking services, inland travel, stability of one’s judicial status. The question which the excluded person asks is not “What have I lost?” but “How can I live?”
After their citizenship has been withdrawn, the person concerned can only travel for a short time on their Kuwaiti passport. When that has expired, someone who hasn’t been able to get a passport corresponding to their original nationality or some other travel document, may find themselves unable to leave the country.
According to several witnesses, the regularisation procedure involves great pressure to hand over their nationality documents, to have their fingerprints taken and sign documents connected with their change of status. They explain that the non-fulfilment of these procedures can have consequences for their family’s access to certain benefits, especially in the areas of education and health. So for many families what is involved is not merely an administrative formality but an unavoidable step if they want to leave their children’s daily lives undisturbed.
The latter are in some cases the first collateral victims if one of their parents should lose their Kuwaiti nationality: it’s called “revocation by dependence”. Their number is unknown but some estimates put the total at 200,000.
Consequences for employment, housing, property
The change of status also directly affects work. Public service jobs reserved for Kuwaiti citizens are no longer open to these people. In the military and security sectors, where only citizens can be engaged, certain employees may be transferred to civilian functions, in the best of cases. Access to certain management or supervisory positions may also be restricted. When the person concerned is also the family’s main breadwinner, these modifications have a direct effect on the economy of the whole family.
The change of status may also entail major financial burdens, in particular for people who have benefitted from a public real estate loan. Several people questioned about this explain that they were informed by the Kuwait Credit Bank that they could be obliged to pay back all the remaining capital due in a relatively short time, which might amount to more than $100,000.
Housing is also a major source of worry according to many witnesses. Several people deprived of citizenship explain that they no longer benefit from the same property rights or public facilities as a Kuwaiti citizen. In the event that the accommodation had been obtained via some state agency, some families say they have had to look for a trustworthy Kuwaiti citizen in whose name to register their property.
The wall of regularisations and appeals
For many, regularising their situation does not simply mean filling out some administrative forms: it means having to reconstruct, in just a few months, a judicial status and daily security which up till then had been taken for granted.
In practical terms, the “deprived” have to establish a “nationality of origin”, then regularise their legal situation within a limited amount of time. But how do you find a “nationality of origin” when you were born in Kuwait, when your father and grandfather were also born there and when your family lived there under the British protectorate? How can you demonstrate your connection with another state in which no one in your family has ever lived and from which your family may not possess a single document?
Today several thousand people, including those with nationality revoked by dependence, are simply unable to claim a “nationality of origin”. Their official status is that of “non-Kuwaiti”. This does not yet mean that they are legally stateless, but this status shows that no other nationality has been established.
In Kuwait, nationality issues count as “acts of sovereignty”
The shock of the announcement is compounded for many by not knowing the reasons. In many cases, no precise or personalised justification is provided, which in itself makes any attempt to lodge an appeal useless. An online portal for complaints was opened by the authorities in May 2025, but it has been deactivated since the beginning of 2026. So in practice anyone who has been deprived of their nationality in 2026 has no access to that means of recourse, any more than those who lodged an earlier appeal.
In Kuwait, nationality issues are treated as “acts of sovereignty”, which drastically limits the criteria for submissions to the courts in the event of an appeal. The possibilities for review are slight indeed, despite appeals from human rights organisations and UN experts in favour of legal oversight and more effective channels for appeal.
Becoming an “illegal resident”
The fear of statelessness is very real in a country which officialised this status shortly after independence, considering as “irregular residents” the tens of thousands of (mostly) bedouins who were not registered with the nationality committees set up under the Nationality Act of 1959, shortly before independence in 1961.
People stripped of their nationality without recourse talk of “civil death”, witnessing as they do the disappearance of the rights that structured their place in society, while remaining physically present there. “What am I after losing my nationality?” What seemed to constitute one’s life in the city has suddenly taken the form of a stack of files to be updated: ID papers, education, employment, travel, accommodation, income, as well as the children’s rights.
I am still attached to my country, though the way I’m defined has been changed on paper. I look at the country where I was born and grew up and for the very first time, I ask myself a question I would have thought impossible: If I am no longer Kuwaiti, what am I?

Putin's autocratic regime not enough to freeze assets of Russia-linked companies, EU's court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:41:42 UTC
18:41:42 KST

Autocratic rule alone is not enough to freeze the assets of Russia-linked firms, the EU's top court has said in an influential ruling on Thursday. National authorities need solid, objective proof of actual control.
The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled on Thursday that Russia's autocratic regime is not, on its own, enough to justify freezing the assets of a company indirectly linked to someone under EU sanctions, as any such measure must be backed by objective and solid evidence.
Brussels has currently blacklisted around 3,000 entities and individuals considered to be part of the Russian industrial-military complex that is participating in the invasion of Ukraine, pending extension on 15 September.
The judgment sets clear limits on how far national authorities can go when freezing the assets of entities not directly listed under EU sanctions, but alleged to be linked to a sanctioned individual.
The case concerns Inter Rao Lietuva, a Lithuanian electricity company that Lithuanian authorities placed on the national asset-freeze list despite it not being directly targeted by EU sanctions against Russia.
Lithuanian authorities argued that the company's ownership structure made it sufficiently connected to sanctioned individuals to justify the freeze: 51% of its shares are owned by Rao Nordic, a Finland-registered company wholly owned by PJSC Inter RAO, a major Russian state-controlled energy firm.
Since the company was ultimately controlled by the Russian state, the authorities concluded it was under the indirect control of President Vladimir Putin, who is himself subject to EU sanctions.
The CJEU rejected that reasoning, ruling that restrictive measures must rest on proven control over the entity concerned, supported by objective and sufficiently solid evidence.
As a result, the judgment concludes that the mere fact that Russia's political system is autocratic and oligarchic — giving Putin virtually unlimited power — does not by itself amount to sufficient evidence of his control over the company.
At the same time, the national authorities might take into account all relevant information to assess the effectiveness of the control, even of an informal nature, by another person or entity subject to EU sanctions.

Italian Grand Prix declared heat-hazard race

Unknown Publisher

10:41:30 BST
18:41:30 KST

Italian Grand Prix declared heat-hazard race
- Published
The Italian Grand Prix has been declared a heat-hazard race as high temperatures continue in the country following the summer heatwave.
A heat hazard is an official designation for an event where it is forecasted that temperatures will be more than 31C at some point during the race on Sunday.
The ambient temperatures around Monza, north-east of Milan, are expected to be in the mid-30C region all weekend.
They peaked at 36C on Wednesday afternoon near Milan's Linate airport.
The ruling means drivers can use a system that flows cooled liquid, such as glycol, through a system of pipes in a fireproof top worn under their overalls.
The cooling kit is not mandatory, but any driver who chooses not to use it has to carry 5kg of ballast in their car to ensure they do not have a competitive advantage.
- Ferrari upgrade a step but not all we need - Hamilton 
  - Published3 hours ago
- How to follow Italian Grand Prix on the BBC 
  - Published7 hours ago
Italy is the second race this year to be declared a heat hazard. The first was Austria early in the summer heatwave.
Some drivers prefer not to use the cooling kit because of discomfort, and because there have been issues with the coolant running out before a grand prix is finished.
In that case, the liquid ends up at car temperature, which is considerably higher than ambient.
Temperatures in the cockpit of an F1 car can be more than 40C, and drivers are wearing several layers of fireproof clothing in addition to a balaclava and helmet, so overheating is a serious concern.

IN BRIEF: Russian Foreign Minister on Ukraine conflict, Europe’s military buildup

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov spoke about the West’s position on the Ukraine settlement, NATO and European Union policies, and Germany’s militarization during a lecture organized by the Znanie Society at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
He also addressed the status of the Russian language and the Ukrainian Orthodox Church in Ukraine, and the situation in the Asia-Pacific region.
TASS has compiled the foreign minister’s key statements.
West’s position on Ukraine
The West’s position on Ukraine is disgraceful, as it disregards key provisions of the UN Charter: "The UN Charter states in its first article that everyone must respect human rights regardless of race, sex, language or religion. Moreover, Ukraine’s constitution still states that the state guarantees the rights of Russians and other national minorities. Nobody cares about that. They passed laws that contradict the UN Charter and the constitution, and everyone says these are supposedly European values. I consider the West’s position absolutely disgraceful."
EU and NATO policies
The North Atlantic Alliance is unlikely to survive much longer, as its attempts to find new reasons to extend its existence cannot continue indefinitely: "I don’t think the North Atlantic Alliance will last much longer. Its attempts to find new reasons to extend its existence, including by expanding its dominance into Southeast and Northeast Asia under the slogan of ‘containing China,’ cannot continue indefinitely. The Taiwan issue continues to gain momentum, and this effort will eventually run out of steam. Once again, voters will ask: What are we doing there?"
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is a "fuhrer" pulling Europe back toward Nazism: "We call European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen "Fuhrer Ursula." She is trying to pull powers and responsibilities into the European Commission that, under decisions by the European Union as a whole, were never transferred to Brussels and remain with national governments. This tendency is becoming increasingly pronounced."
The European Union’s "open-door" policy has triggered a migration crisis for the bloc itself: "The dominance of newcomers is becoming a problem for domestic development. It is causing discontent among the native population, which is forced to pay taxes to support people who have arrived. Ukrainian citizens also fall into this category. EU countries have provided them with subsidies and benefits since the beginning of the special military operation, when they fled their country, and in some cases, these benefits significantly exceed the unemployment benefits available to those countries’ own citizens."
Merz’s militaristic ambitions
Lavrov was stunned by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s militaristic ambitions: "I was simply appalled. We saw the metastases of Nazism reemerging in Germany previously. But when Chancellor Merz said he would make Germany Europe’s leading military power again, I was simply appalled." "If this man does not understand what the word ‘again’ means in this context, that is of course very sad for Europe and extremely dangerous. Europe is once again becoming a source of ideas about national and racial superiority."
Berlin has chosen to try to influence Russia by "strengthening support for fugitives": "The steps Germany has taken mean only one thing. Instead of maintaining open contacts that allow people to convey their culture and views, the Germans chose to support these fugitive agents."
Germany is once again trying to "place everyone else under its control" and prevent individual EU countries from maintaining normal relations with Russia: "Germany is again trying to bring everyone else under its control and suppress any moves toward normal relations with Russia that still exist in some EU countries, even though there are only a few of them."
Status of the Russian language in Ukraine
Washington and "nobody at all" have never told Kiev that the Russian language must be "restored" or that the Ukrainian Orthodox Church (UOC) should not face persecution: "Washington, and nobody else, has ever sent any signals to the Kiev regime that the Russian language must be restored or that the canonical church should not be targeted."
Russia raised these issues with US officials during contacts, asking how they could support those engaged in "this purely racist, Nazi activity": "They say: there will be negotiations, and we will include all of this on the agenda. That is wrong. There are things that cannot be made conditional. The right to language and religion is one of them."
AUKUS activities
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is ignoring risks associated with AUKUS, the military alliance of Australia, Britain and the United States, under pressure from the collective West: "We approach this issue carefully because failure to comply, or incomplete compliance, with IAEA standards carries the risk of spreading military nuclear technologies. Unfortunately, the current IAEA leadership seems to treat this rather lightly, clearly under extremely strong pressure from the United States and Britain."
Situation in Asia
Military cooperation among the United States, Japan and South Korea is growing: "Military cooperation among the United States, Japan and South Korea is expanding, with South Korea and, more recently, Japan under Prime Minister [Sanae] Takaichi increasingly interested in adding nuclear components, creating a risk of weapons of mass destruction proliferation."
Russia hopes that President Donald Trump will be able to ease tensions around the Korean Peninsula, but the substance of the US policy in the region is to contain North Korea: "The Korean Peninsula also plays an important role. Despite the zigzags in President Trump’s policy toward the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, he recently said that he gets along very well with Kim Jong Un, that they are friends and that he is ready to meet and communicate with him. But of course, the US is pursuing a policy of containing the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea on the Korean Peninsula. God willing, they will manage to ease tensions."
The Asia-Pacific region poses the West with a range of challenges in terms of preserving its dominance: "They do not hide this. Everyone that develops relatively independently is facing pressure from the West. I am not even talking about China, Russia or the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, but even countries that remain relatively independent and continue to maintain trade, economic, cultural and educational ties with Russia despite the pressure are facing it, again based exclusively on the West’s philosophy of dominance."
RIC format
The work of the RIC format, comprising Russia, India and China, is being revived: "We are restoring this three-way format now. It has operated quite regularly all these years since 1998 without interruption, except during the COVID pandemic."
Russia has numerous plans with India and China, particularly in nuclear energy: "We have a great many plans with both China and India. I would single out nuclear energy."

Russian Teachers Instructed to Identify Disloyal Students During Weekly Patriotic Classes

Updated guidelines from the Ministry of Education of the Russian Federation for the 2026/2027 academic year instruct teachers to record these incidents in specialized forms following lessons, as reported by The Moscow Times on September 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Teachers are also required to complete a self-assessment section where they answer "Were there situations when students demonstrated lack of understanding or disagreement with value orientations? How were they resolved?", while also tracking student passivity.
The official document states that the objective is to provide educational staff and school administrators with data to evaluate the impact of lessons, adjust teaching practices, and assess the "formation of value orientations" and "personal results."
Schools are required to measure these personal outcomes twice a year, at the beginning and end of the term. Individual institutions can choose their own schedule and tools, with school psychologists, deputy directors for guidance, and homeroom teachers tasked with gathering and evaluating the collected data.
In late May, the Ministry of Education released 3 surveys for school students, pedagogical university students, and teachers under 35 years old. These surveys examined views on civic, patriotic, and moral standards, traditional values, the mandatory weekly classes, and willingness to participate in patriotic activities.
Students were asked to evaluate historical figures like Lenin, Stalin, and Brezhnev on a 4-point scale, as well as answer questions about social media usage and their ability to verify information, including content from foreign agents.
University staff were required to submit their completed surveys through the state messenger app Max, while school surveys were distributed directly by teachers.
Conversations about Important Things became a required part of the school curriculum in September 2023, with officials framing the weekly sessions as a way to build patriotism and love for the country.
The lessons cover Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and regularly feature guest speakers, including combatants, former prisoners, and private military company fighters. Schools have also implemented a mandatory Family Studies course that encourages students to have large families and emphasizes sacrifice for the nation.

Britain wants laser armed ground vehicle drones
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:39:27 BST
18:39:27 KST

Britain is seeking counter-drone technology that could lead to autonomous laser weapons mounted on Army vehicles and, later, uncrewed ground vehicles, with £5 million available immediately through a new Ministry of Defence competition, the department has said.
Project PANOPTES, launched by UK Defence Innovation on behalf of the MOD, is intended to develop an integrated Counter-Uncrewed Aerial System force-protection capability able to deal with massed and low-cost aerial threats without rapidly exhausting conventional ammunition stocks.
The MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
Although the competition is open to a range of technologies, laser directed-energy weapons are specifically identified as an area of interest. The MOD said: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The intended configuration would place the counter-drone capability on a military ground platform. According to the procurement documents: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
The system is intended to protect deployed forces against complex and saturation attacks involving small uncrewed aircraft, including simultaneous threats designed to overwhelm local air defences or force troops to expend comparatively expensive missiles and ammunition.
The MOD stated: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus covers representative Class 1 UAS and other small aerial targets. These could include individual drones as well as repeated, sequential or simultaneous attacks used for surveillance, targeting, disruption or attempts to exhaust defensive systems.
A later objective would move the capability onto an unmanned ground platform. The MOD stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
UK Defence Innovation has confirmed that Project PANOPTES is open to UK-based innovators and that a share of £5 million is available immediately. Stage 1 will act as an initial screening process, with applicants outlining their proposed technology before successful teams are invited to develop more detailed proposals.
The first phase is not intended to produce a complete operational counter-drone system. The MOD said: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
Successful technologies could then be matured through later phases into demonstrable Minimum Viable Products before selected systems are developed into Minimum Deployable Capabilities for an initial operational user group.
The notice states: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record.”
The wider procurement has an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, rising to £150 million including VAT. That figure is not an approved programme budget. The MOD stated: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.”
Stage 1 submissions are due by midday on 23 September. A launch webinar will be held on 9 September to provide potential suppliers with further information on the operational requirement before the competition moves into its subsequent stages.

Ukraine Urges EU to Block Russian Ballistic Production With New Sanctions
Ukraine has formally proposed a specialized "anti-ballistic" sanctions package to European partners designed to prevent Russia from manufacturing ballistic missiles.
The initiative was presented by Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha during his visit to Ireland, where he attended an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in the Gymnich format, according to the press service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian estimates show that Russian forces currently hold approximately 600 to 630 ballistic missiles in stock, with a production capacity of around 100 missiles per month, potentially reaching up to 1,300 ballistic missiles annually.
“After every massive attack on Ukraine, new sanctions packages must be implemented so as not to give Russia pauses to adapt,” Sybiha emphasized.
Sybiha discussed the upcoming 22nd EU sanctions package with European officials, stating that it should inflict severe damage on the Russian economy.
Air defense enhancement was another major focus of the discussions. The foreign minister stated that establishing a reliable "air shield" over Ukraine remains a top priority and noted that there is now a "confident understanding of the partners' further steps."
Additionally, Ukraine outlined a list of critical pre-winter requirements to its partners. Kyiv is currently awaiting the delivery of essential equipment alongside financial assistance.
On April 23, 2026, the European Union officially approved its 20th package of sanctions against Russia, introducing over 100 individual restrictions and increasing pressure on the energy sector and the "shadow fleet."
The Council of the EU confirmed the measures, which targeted key economic sectors funding Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, introduced new actions against financial institutions in third countries, and restricted companies supporting the Russian military-industrial complex.
Furthermore, the package established a framework for future bans on maritime transport of Russian petroleum products, expanded the list of restricted vessels, and prohibited terminal services for Russian liquefied natural gas.

Rescue efforts continue as Nepal-China flood death toll rises to 1,280
Authorities in Nepal use helicopters and zip lines to reach remote flood-stricken villages amid widespread destruction.
Rescue teams in Nepal are working around the clock to reach workers trapped inside hydropower facilities more than a week after flash floods devastated entire communities in the Himalayas.
Last week, a cascade of rocks, mud and water that scientists believe came from a glacier collapse near the Langtang Lirung mountain peak swept away villages, roads, and bridges in Nepal and Tibet.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Death toll from devastating floods in Nepal and China surpasses 1,000
- list 2 of 3Nepal buries unidentified flood victims as families await answers
- list 3 of 3Photos: Nepal begins burying flood victims in mass graves
More than 1,280 people have been killed, and over 5,600 are still missing on both sides of the China-Nepal border, including at least 550 foreign nationals, authorities said on Thursday.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said 1,252 bodies have been recovered. Hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped inside hydropower plants, including some in tunnels, near the country’s border with China.
In neighbouring Tibet, Chinese authorities have reported 21 deaths and 541 people missing.
“We still hope there are some survivors inside,” Sanjay Kc, an officer from the Nepalese army engineering department, said, in front of bulldozers trying to remove huge piles of mud blocking the entrance of a tunnel in the Rasuwa district, one of the worst affected areas in Nepal. “Because it’s a big power house inside, so it’s a big room, and we feel that the whole power house is not flooded,” he told Al Jazeera.
Families of those missing are gathering each morning hoping for news about their loved ones. For many, the wait is excruciating.
“Every day I come here hoping to find my father,” said Pratik Rana, the son of a missing engineer. “But every day at sunset I feel my hope fades away… [A] father is equally important for everyone, but for me he was a precious part of my life.”
In other affected areas, authorities are using all available tools, including zip lines and helicopters, to rescue people trapped in remote villages. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) estimated floods and mudflows have left at least 2.2 million tonnes of debris.
In the capital Kathmandu, forensic teams are working to identify bodies.
Al Jazeera’s Jessica Washington, reporting from a DNA testing facility in the city, said many of the bodies being found are in a state of decomposition.
“Forensic teams on the ground told us that there are some things that can help with the identification process, such as tattoos and jewellery, but many bodies were found in such a state that it’s very challenging to identify them.”
On Wednesday, the country’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said authorities would continue searching for survivors while also starting rehabilitation and rebuilding efforts.
Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the NDRRMA, told the Reuters news agency that about 20,000 houses would have to be rebuilt, including 7,500 that have been destroyed.
“There is no point in rebuilding the houses in the same locations, as that would expose people to the same risks,” Upreti told the news agency, adding that authorities were trying to identify safer areas to relocate the communities and build up new settlements. As of Monday, the UN said more than 3,400 displaced people were living in 27 displacement sites in Nuwakot and Rasuwa, mostly in schools.
Nepali authorities have pointed to the role of major greenhouse gas emitters that have a “historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal”, said Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal. He added that the government has officially filed a “formal climate compensation claim letter” to international partners.
