Bring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reserves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:00:49 UTC
18:00:49 KST

On a bitingly cold night in Lapalala Wilderness nature reserve in South Africa’s Limpopo province, Duncan Kanyakera watches as instructor Jacques Viljoen deploys a thermal drone in search of a lone cheetah. Once the drone has disappeared into the inky sky, Kanyakera, from Tsavo in Kenya, and 20 other conservation professionals from across Africa turn their attention to the open-air screen in anticipation.
Many of the students – from 11 African countries as far flung as Benin, Liberia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar – witnessing the demonstration have earned their places at Lapalala after performing well on an online training programme for protected area technicians (PAT) run by the Connected Conservation Foundation (CCF). Also on the course, are five members of Peace Parks staff in training.
“Data and technology are critical to modern conservation,” says CCF’s Sophie Maxwell. “Cameras and collars and software like EarthRanger have transformed the fight against poaching … But then an elephant knocks over a pole and you are back to square one.”
Since 2015, the CCF has installed state-of-the-art tech systems in parks across Africa with remarkable success, helping to protect nearly 10m hectares (25m acres). “Parks with tech solutions are safer and more biodiverse and they have better relationships with communities,” says Maxwell.
Over the years, the CCF has “identified a critical gap”, says Carien Soldatos who oversees the PAT training programme: “Tech is fantastic, but it all depends on having trained technicians on the ground. Without people who know how to use, repair and maintain them, the fanciest gizmos in the world aren’t much use.” While there are such people in some parks, they are sorely lacking in many parts of Africa.
After searching everywhere for a tech course aimed at conservation professionals, the CCF decided to create its own. Their 10-module course, which launched in July 2025, was a global first. In the first year, 680 people from all over the world finished at least one module. Those who completed all 10 modules were invited to interviews, with the top 16 chosen to attend the practical component at Lapalala.
In less than 10 minutes, the heat sensor technology in the drone launched by Viljoen locates the cheetah resting with her cubs. Once he has locked its location, the operator sends a pin to the park’s on-duty field rangers, who rush to the scene. “I was stunned,” says Kanyakera. “There was no moon and the cheetah was miles away from us. But we could see exactly what was happening as the rangers got out of their vehicle and checked up on her.”
Kanyakera, who works for the Taita Taveta Wildlife Conservancies Association (TTWCA) to support a network of 35 conservancies and ranches in Kenya’s vast Tsavo landscape, recognised immediately how handy a drone would be back home. Human-wildlife conflict is a challenge in Tsavo: “If an elephant gets into a corn field, it causes havoc,” he says. “And then you have the problem of humans retaliating.”
The aim, says Kanyakera, is to keep humans and animals apart via designated wildlife corridors. But this gets tricky in the dry season when animals and humans alike are drawn towards water. Currently, if Kanyakera gets reports of an elephant near a village, he has to first work out where the elephant is and which direction it is moving in, before deploying rangers to intervene. This can take hours.
“With a drone, we could find the elephant in minutes,” he says. “The noise of the drone alone would probably be enough to scare the animal off. And if that doesn’t work, I can deploy rangers much more accurately.”
While a night-vision drone is the most exciting item on Kanyakera’s Christmas list, the course has also shown him how simple changes could drastically improve the tech “stack” back in Tsavo. This has a lot to do with the course design, explains Maxwell: “Each day, they build a new element of the stack,” she says, “before breaking it down at the end of each day and building it again the next morning to add another layer. It’s all about building muscle memory.”
And it seems to be working. “As soon as I get home, I’ll reconfigure our camera traps to make the most of AI,” says Kanyakera who also has his sights set on re-equipping the ops room in Tsavo. “In the past, we would just Google and make a decision. Now I know so much more, I can target what I really want. The learnings from this course can make a big difference to the people and animals of Tsavo.”
The course – which featured guest lectures and practicals from nine experts on topics including connectivity, communication, power systems, monitoring sensors, hardware integration and GIS visualisation tools – is having an impact far beyond Tsavo.
Effort Zivengwa, who works at the Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority head office in Harare, is part of a tech team responsible for 11 national parks. “We were content with what we were doing,” he says. “But, after completing this course, I think we have to do more. We are already using EarthRanger and we do have sensors, but they are not integrated.
“We have park headquarters and lodges that don’t have internet access,” he adds. “Using point-to-point internet can fix that problem easily.” The learning module on solar power further shifted his understanding of what is possible. “We have a lot of remote stations,” he says. “But the sun shines everywhere.”
Mabel Nokhuthula Piki, who teaches wildlife monitoring skills at the Chinhoyi University of Technology in central Zimbabwe, has also found the course empowering. “My students didn’t comprehend that tech was important. They couldn’t get the link between saving animals and computers. But now I am going to change their minds,” she says. “It is impossible to understand the value of tech until you have seen it.”
The CCF is planning to run a second practical course with another batch of students in the first quarter of 2027. What is more, says Soldatos, “we will be supporting five participants from the first course with internships and/or hardware donations”. The lucky five have not yet been chosen, but Kanyakera, Zivengwa and Piki are all in the running.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Testing-interface suppliers are expanding production capacity to keep up with growing orders, CTEE reported Thursday.
Semiconductor makers are facing higher testing requirements as AI and high-performance computing chips become more complex. Their higher cost means defects during packaging or testing can result in greater losses, prompting customers to place greater emphasis on testing quality and validation, according to CTEE.
WinWay Technology Co. is working on more than 10 projects related to co-packaged optics, a packaging technology that integrates light-based components with computing chips in the same package. The company said the need to move large amounts of data at high speeds is driving greater interest in CPO as AI chips become more powerful.
Small-volume production of related testing products is expected to begin in the second half of next year, followed by larger-scale production in 2028. Its work spans several stages of the testing process.
The company is developing socket solutions, which connect chips to testing equipment, as well as probe cards used for wafer-level testing. It is also expanding its capabilities for testing both wafers and packaged chips.
WinWay’s socket production capacity is expected to remain tight through the first quarter of next year. Additional facilities are scheduled to come online gradually in the second and third quarters.
Chunghwa Precision Test Tech Co. is also seeing strong orders from customers in AI and high-performance computing. The manufacturer said its production capacity remains relatively tight, with orders visible through 2027.
As AI chips become more complex, Chunghwa Precision said customers are seeking more services beyond wafer-level and final testing. System-level testing is becoming more important, while burn-in testing, which simulates prolonged operation to identify potential failures, is also seeing greater interest, according to Odi Morgan.
Meanwhile, customer planning horizons are becoming longer. Chunghwa Precision said some customers are no longer discussing capacity requirements for just one year, but are instead planning for two or three years, or even longer. The trend is particularly pronounced among AI and HPC customers, according to Anue.
To support future orders, Chunghwa Precision is expanding its manufacturing footprint. A new plant and additional equipment are expected to be ready in 2029, while several projects are currently under development and validation.

NATO warns Russia over submarine build up ‘We see them’
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

18:00:47 KST

NATO says it is closely monitoring the expansion and modernisation of Russia’s submarine force in the High North, including new-generation nuclear-powered cruise missile submarines operating from the Kola Peninsula, according to Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum.
In a statement published on X, the NATO command drew attention to developments around Russia’s Northern Fleet and said the Alliance was treating the growth of its undersea forces seriously.
Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum stated: “Something is moving beneath the surface. Russia is expanding and modernising its submarine force, with the Kola Peninsula remaining a key hub for the Northern Fleet.”
The Kola Peninsula in north-west Russia contains several of the Northern Fleet’s principal naval bases and provides access to the Barents Sea and wider North Atlantic. The area is central to Russian submarine operations in northern waters and hosts both nuclear-powered attack submarines and strategic ballistic missile submarines.
NATO specifically referred to the development of newer nuclear-powered guided missile submarines, saying: “Among them: new-generation nuclear-powered SSGNs, bringing serious long-range strike and sea-denial capabilities into the High North.”

SSGN is the designation commonly used for nuclear-powered submarines equipped primarily for cruise missile operations. Russian boats in this category can be employed against surface ships and land targets, depending on their weapons fit and tasking, while retaining the endurance associated with nuclear propulsion.
The command stated: “They may be invisible beneath the waves. But not for us. We see them, we watch the developments closely and yes, we take these developments seriously.”
The Northern Fleet is responsible for Russian naval activity across the Arctic and High North and operates from bases concentrated around the Kola Peninsula. Its submarines can reach the Norwegian Sea and North Atlantic through waters bordering NATO members Norway and Iceland and areas routinely monitored by allied maritime patrol aircraft, surface vessels and submarines.
Undersea activity in the High North has remained an important part of NATO maritime planning because the region connects Russia’s northern bases with the wider Atlantic. Allied forces regularly conduct anti-submarine warfare training in northern European waters, while maritime patrol aircraft and naval units contribute to surveillance and tracking activity.
Joint Force Command Brunssum is one of NATO’s operational-level joint headquarters and is responsible for planning and conducting activities across part of the Alliance’s northern and eastern area.

Taiwan begins 3rd phase of flexible migrant caregiver pilot program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:00:30 UTC
18:00:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Applications for the third phase of a pilot program that allows families to hire migrant caregivers for flexible, part-time care services have opened.
The Ministry of Labor's Workforce Development Agency said the “Diverse Companion Care Pilot Program” is designed to meet urgent and short-term care needs, per CNA. Under the self-paid program, residents can apply to participating nonprofit organizations for care services.
Thirteen nonprofit organizations currently provide services in 16 cities and counties, giving the program coverage for more than 70% of the country. The agency said it has received numerous complaints from residents in areas where the service is not yet available.
Hu Hsin-yeh (胡欣野), deputy director of the agency's Cross-Border Workforce Affairs Center, said applications for third-phase pilot organizations will be accepted through Sept. 24. The program aims to extend services to all 22 cities and counties, she confirmed.
Only nonprofit organizations that have been legally registered for at least five years are eligible to apply, according to the agency. Applicants must submit a care-service plan and documents demonstrating relevant service experience, among other requirements.
The labor ministry will evaluate applications through a selection panel, with proposals scoring at least 70 points considered qualified. Results are expected to be announced by Dec. 4, with new organizations potentially joining the program as early as the beginning of next year.
The program serves people with disabilities, serious illnesses, recent medical treatment or surgery, or long-term care needs at levels 2 to 8, per UDN. Services include assistance with basic daily activities.
As of the end of July, the program had provided more than 100,000 hours of care, with one-time services and once-a-week services the most common, CNA reported. The cumulative number of service users had surpassed 10,000.

MAD’s lucas museum of narrative art opens in LA this month: take an early look inside
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:00:22 UTC
18:00:22 KST

After more than a decade in development, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is preparing to open in Los Angeles on September 22, 2026. Designed by Ma Yansong of MAD with Stantec, and set within an approximately 52,600-square-meter campus landscape by Mia Lehrer of Studio-MLA, the five-story, 27,870-square-meter institution takes shape in Exposition Park as a continuous, curving volume hovering above the ground. Founded by George Lucas and Mellody Hobson, the museum will be dedicated to narrative art — images that communicate stories, beliefs and collective memory across painting, illustration, comics and cinema.
For MAD, however, the project begins before visitors encounter any of those works. Rather than treating the museum as an isolated object sitting on a conventional plinth, the architecture pulls much of its mass upward, allowing gardens, paths and sheltered public areas to continue beneath and around it. Conceived without a single straight line, the smooth exterior draws on the tree canopy of Exposition Park, producing a building that appears less deposited on the site than caught somewhere between landscape and sky. Its skin is assembled from more than 1,200 uniquely shaped curved panels of fiberglass-reinforced polymer, selected for their ability to produce the building’s flowing geometry while remaining considerably lighter than alternative materials.
That apparent lightness requires some fairly muscular engineering. At the center of the building, a central arch spans 56 meters to form a suspended plaza beneath the museum, creating a shaded gathering space connected to the surrounding park. From here, visitors can enter through north and south lobbies, while an elliptical Oculus hovers four stories above the plaza, opening a view from the ground toward the sky. The gesture turns what could have been the building’s most monumental moment into an absence.
Inside, the architecture becomes progressively brighter and more vertical. Sweeping arches define the main lobby, where daylight enters through large glazed openings and glass elevators carry visitors toward the galleries and restaurant above. The lower floors also contain two theaters, a horseshoe-shaped research library and learning space overlooking the park, ten studios and classrooms, a shop, café and an approximately 930-square-meter gallery. The movement through the museum is therefore not simply from room to room, but from landscape to sheltered plaza, from plaza to luminous interior, and finally upward into the exhibition spaces — a sequence that makes circulation part of the building’s storytelling.
the lucas museum rises above exposition park | image by Iwan Baan, courtesy of Lucas Museum
WHEN ROCKWELL MEETS COMICS
More than 9,290 square meters of the museum are devoted to galleries, drawing from a collection of over 40,000 works assembled by Lucas and Hobson. Its inaugural exhibitions alone will unfold across more than 30 galleries and bring together over 1,300 works. Their range deliberately collapses distinctions that museums have traditionally kept apart: paintings and popular illustration sit alongside comics, children’s books and cinematic art, with figures including Frida Kahlo, Norman Rockwell and Charles White forming part of a much wider history of images made to tell stories. The museum’s proposition is simple but surprisingly disruptive: illustration does not need rescuing from popular culture to qualify as serious art.
The curatorial structure extends that idea. Rather than primarily sorting works through movements, periods or mediums, galleries explore recognizable human themes such as family, love, work, play, childhood and adventure. A dedicated cinema installation, Star Wars in Motion, will examine vehicles from the first six films through concept designs, props and costumes, while another inaugural exhibition turns the lens back onto the building itself, presenting Ma Yansong as a narrative artist through drawings, renderings and photographs of the Lucas Museum and other MAD projects. Two cinematic theaters expand the narrative beyond static images, while a free research library, learning spaces, dining, retail and areas for public programs turn the building into something broader than a sequence of exhibition rooms. Architecture and curatorial strategy arrive at roughly the same conclusion: categories are useful, but stories have a habit of ignoring them.
MAD shapes the museum as a continuous curved volume
A 52,600-SQUARE-METER GARDEN AROUND THE ARCHITECTURE
The landscape by Studio-MLA is therefore less a decorative perimeter than the second half of the project. Gardens and planted spaces extend across the approximately 52,600-square-meter campus and slip beneath the elevated architecture, softening the conventional boundary between museum and park. Replacing what was previously an asphalt parking lot, the landscape introduces more than 300 trees alongside indigenous and drought-tolerant planting, a hanging garden, amphitheater, meadow and a fountain conceived as a dramatic waterfall. Its contoured topography draws on California’s foothills, valleys, mesas and canyons, turning the landscape itself into another form of narrative. In a part of Los Angeles already populated by major civic institutions, including the California Science Center and Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, the project uses its footprint somewhat paradoxically: building something enormous while trying to occupy as little of the ground as possible.
When the Lucas Museum opens on September 22, its collection will inevitably attract much of the attention — particularly the meeting of fine art, illustration, comics and artifacts linked to Lucas’s own cinematic universe. Ten monumental sculptures spread through the freely accessible park extend that collection outdoors, ranging from works by Fernando Botero and Prune Nourry to bronzes depicting Princess Leia, Yoda and Grogu. Yet MAD’s building makes a parallel argument through architecture. If narrative art is supposed to belong to everyday culture rather than remain trapped inside traditional hierarchies, the museum housing it cannot quite behave like an ivory tower either. Here, the tower has effectively been lifted out of the way, leaving a park underneath.
more than 1,200 curved FRP panels form the exterior
WHEN THE PEOPLE’S ART TAKES OVER
The inaugural exhibitions push that argument further, spreading narrative art across subjects and formats that rarely share the same museum floor. More than 30 galleries move between children’s literature, manga, comics and graphic stories, photography, murals, science fiction, romance and myths of the American West, alongside dedicated presentations of artists including Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, Maxfield Parrish, Frank Frazetta and Thomas Hart Benton. Other rooms turn to everyday life — childhood, family, love, school, sport and work — while works by Judith F. Baca, Diego Rivera and JR bring large-scale public storytelling into the mix. Taken together, the opening program gives architectural form to what George Lucas has described as ‘the people’s art’: images made not simply to be looked at, but to circulate, communicate and tell stories.

Face Recognition Is Becoming the Norm for Dating Apps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

In 2025, AI deepfakes flooded Tinder. According to the company, 98 percent of the content-moderation actions on the app were focused on combating fake accounts, scamming, and spam, pushing the company to expand its moderation efforts for its 60 million global users.
The problem is not unique to Tinder. The spread of AI-generated fake accounts has become a rising concern for dating apps, as things like chatfishing and voice cloning have gotten more widespread across the industry.
Among current online daters in the US, nearly half have been targeted by a dating scam, with US romance scams surpassing $4 billion between 2015 and 2025, according to the FBI.
The issue has forced just about every dating platform to adopt stricter authentication tools to ward off scammers. More and more, apps are asking that you surrender your most unique attribute in order to ensure that you’re a real person: your face.
More than a dozen major dating apps and sites use face recognition to verify users, often relying on liveness checks, 3D authentication, video selfies, or biometric ID to demonstrate humanness.
To combat the issue, Tinder launched the mandatory face-screening tool Face Check for new members in October 2025. “It’s not a feature. It’s a statement about what human connection online should require,” Yoel Roth, head of trust and safety for Match Group, which owns Tinder, said to WIRED in an email. Match Group tells WIRED that it is also starting to require Face Check for existing users in several of Tinder’s core markets, including the US and UK.
As face verification slowly transforms into a prerequisite for participation across the industry, the collective drive to combat bad actors has created a necessary and equally concerning new standard where “proof of human” profiles may soon be the norm.
Underpinning the shift, however, is a grim irony: In attempting to solve the problem of knowing whether someone is real, Big Dating is potentially creating more opportunities for privacy and security risks by forcing users to give up biometric data, while also legitimizing a culture of surveillance.
One company pushing for the use of ID-verification tech in dating apps is Tools for Humanity. The AI company created World ID, an iris-scanning biometric verification system, and partnered with Tinder in April, though it’s still optional for users. The most distinct feature about World ID is that confirmed users receive a “verified human” badge on the app after undergoing the process, which requires them to scan the colored part of their eye using the company’s orb device. They are given an identification number as their official World ID.
“In the near future, any dating app, like most online platforms in general, will need some sort of proof-of-human system like this,” says Tiago Sada, chief product officer at Tools for Humanity, adding that the way the majority of dating platforms handle verification is “super creepy, because you have to give your personal data to every single app that you want to use.” As stipulated by World’s policy, the orb does not share or retain any data; it is able to verify users without ever sending their data to a server. Once your image is confirmed, the orb sends the coded image to your phone before permanently deleting it, the company claims. Likewise, Face Check collects and stores an encrypted map of information about the shape of the user’s face, not the actual picture, Match said.
But even as dating apps claim that your biometric data is safe, security continues to be a significant concern.
Dating apps are subject to occasional data breaches, and while the inherent premise in these ID systems is that verification equals trust, cybersecurity researcher Katie Moussouris says that they are mostly a smoke screen. “Normalizing the idea that a face scan provides any assurance of identity or age is security theater.”
A liveness check requiring face scanning and live video only indicates a person was present at sign-up and does not guarantee that the person was not using AI to alter their appearance in real time. Likewise, an ID scan indicates an ID was presented, not that it belongs to the person who presented it. “Neither should be confused with trust,” Moussouris says. “A verified profile can still belong to a romance scammer who took over an account or created one using AI tools.”
And while passwords and usernames are interchangeable, faces are not, which makes them unique targets for attacks. More than that, biometric verification sets a risky precedent, says Woodrow Hartzog, a technology law professor at Boston University who previously served on the Massachusetts special commission on facial recognition.
“When we get accustomed to having our face scanned for everything we do online, it is really dangerous, not only potentially for the privacy risks but also to acclimate an entire population into thinking that that is normal behavior,” he says. “Facial recognition is the most dangerous surveillance tool ever created.”
Existing privacy laws are not equipped to deal with biometric verification on dating apps, according to Hartzog. He believes policies should ensure that less invasive options are used when they're available. In the case of biometrics, for example, your face, which can be monitored everywhere you go, is much more dangerous to collect than your thumbprint.
Utah’s State-Endorsed Digital Identity law, which went into effect in May, was one of the first major attempts at that. It limits the kinds of data that can be requested to only what is absolutely necessary while establishing a “duty of loyalty,” meaning platforms and providers cannot engage in practices that “conflict with the best interests of an individual” or “result in a disproportionate risk” to them. The law attempts to mitigate situations where people might have to present ID every time they log online, and also includes significant rules on the entity that’s collecting the data. The American Civil Liberties Union called it “the nation’s strongest digital identity bill.”
“Look at how easy it is to channel people's choices into agreeing to have their faces scanned as a condition of a good or service,” Hartzog says. “The more we can lean into policy frameworks that require strong protections from the company—rather than putting the onus on the person whose face is being scanned or who has to reveal their identity—then the better off I think we’ll be.”

Threats to civilian ships and aircraft constitute ‘state terrorism’ – Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:59:53 UTC
17:59:53 KST

Threats to civilian ships and aircraft constitute ‘state terrorism’ – Putin
The seizing and targeting of Russian civilian vessels constitute acts of “state terrorism,” President Vladimir Putin has said, warning that these actions are making peace talks with Ukraine more difficult.
Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Thursday, the Russian president denounced the recent captures of Russian civilian vessels and pointed to Kiev’s threats against passenger aircraft.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky previously stated that the “safe days” in Russian skies are over, addressing foreign airlines, insurers, and governments whose aircraft continue to use Russian airspace.
“This, of course, is a manifestation of state terrorism,” Putin said, adding that these actions “undoubtedly complicate the possibility of bilateral peace negotiations.”
He also warned that “those who remain silent and do not pay attention to this become accomplices in international terrorism,” referring to Kiev’s Western backers.
Putin’s remarks came a day after the Norwegian authorities seized the Russian research vessel the Professor Molchanov in Svalbard at the request of Ukraine’s state-owned Naftogaz. The ship was detained while docked in the Russian settlement of Barentsburg.
The Professor Molchanov is a Russian state-owned research vessel that operates regular passenger and cargo services between Murmansk and Svalbard, carrying scientists, workers, their families, tourists, and supplies to Russian settlements on the archipelago. Moscow has said the seizure will be challenged in court.
The detention follows a series of Western seizures of Russian-linked vessels accused of belonging to a so-called “shadow fleet,” although the Professor Molchanov itself was seized in connection with a legal claim by Ukraine’s Naftogaz against Russia. Moscow has rejected the “shadow fleet” label as having no basis in international law and accused Western states of using sanctions as a pretext to interfere with civilian maritime trade.
Putin warned last month that attempts to seize Russian ships and sell their cargo amounted to “piracy and robbery,” saying Moscow is prepared to respond in kind in any part of the world.

====================================================================================================

Israel teaches students how to vote, but not how to make an informed political choice - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:52:05 UTC
17:52:05 KST

Many students in Israel will encounter an Education Ministry worksheet titled “Who should I vote for?” – a sensible question, indeed. Made accessible in a modern format through a QR code, it invites students to rank the qualities they want in a party and in a Knesset member.
A valuable exercise, no doubt, but it stops just short of where a young voter needs the most help.
How does a student discover which party actually reflects the priorities they identify as important? Where should they look for reliable information? How should they judge a promise against a party’s record, or decide between two plausible arguments?
The worksheet offers little guidance. It does not ask students to compare platforms, check promises against performance, evaluate the reliability of sources, identify manipulation, or weigh conflicting evidence. This format carries forward a gap that has existed in election education for years, and the same gap appears in the election materials we reviewed in an Israel Democracy Institute analysis ahead of the election for the 26th Knesset.
First-time voters will account for about 10 percent of Israel’s eligible electorate. For those still in school, election season may be one of the few chances to practice political judgment in a setting where learning comes first.
The public isn't entirely convinced. In an IDI public opinion survey conducted in July 2026, 27 percent of Israeli adults said they wanted schools to avoid election-related topics, 34 percent favored teaching only the formal process, and 33 percent supported open discussion of parties’ positions on major issues.
Education Ministry encourages mock elections, lessons on voting
Nonetheless, Israel's Ministry of Education has laid some useful groundwork, encouraging mock elections, discussion of civic participation and lessons on the importance of voting. Yet these efforts fall short of encouraging meaningful democratic participation, focusing on electoral procedure, with less attention paid to helping students develop well-informed political judgment.
Partisan campaigning is prohibited, rightfully so, and schools are expected to expose students to a range of positions. One way that students are exposed to these positions is by holding panels with representatives from political parties, a longstanding practice that illustrates both the promises and limits of the current system.
The Ministry sees these encounters as ways to expose students to a range of views and give them practical experience in democratic participation. But the Israeli public is divided on the value of such panels, especially across religious groups, whose members often attend separate school systems in Israel.
In an IDI public opinion survey conducted in July 2026, a small majority of secular Israelis (55%) said they support holding such panels, while a majority from all other religious subgroups, traditional, national religious, and Haredim, said they oppose such panels, with Haredi opposition the highest at 82%.
Moreover, the educational value of the panel depends on whether schools truly give students the opportunity to encounter a broad range of positions and whether they are given the tools to compare and assess what they’re hearing.
These tools are limited, as reflected in our review of the topics suggested for classroom discussion in the Ministry of Education’s election materials: “the economy,” “security,” “law,” “welfare,” and Israel as a “Jewish and democratic state.”
While these categories appear to invite political discussion, their broad and abstract framing largely strips away the concrete controversies that define electoral debate. The judiciary, for example, is subsumed under “law,” while Jewish-Arab relations do not appear among the suggested topics at all.
That is a serious gap because political choices are made through disagreement.
A student who says security is a top priority still has to choose among parties that may all claim to protect Israel while offering very different strategies. A student who cares about Israel’s Jewish and democratic character has to consider what those principles require when they come into tension.
The same is true of economic policy, the judiciary and relations between Jews and Arabs. Schools can help students work through those competing claims with evidence, context and an understanding of the tradeoffs involved, while remaining nonpartisan.
Teachers lack training, support for appropriate classes
Many teachers currently lack the training and institutional backing to lead that kind of conversation. They fear complaints from parents, administrators, and public figures if a lesson is perceived as political, and indeed, ministry guidance spells out restrictions in detail and gives far less attention to the practical work of running a balanced debate.
When the cost of a misstep feels high, and the guidance feels vague, silence and avoidance become the safest choice.
Controversial questions can be discussed in a nonpartisan classroom. The quality of the discussion depends on the sources chosen, the accuracy with which competing views are presented, the way unsupported claims are challenged and the teacher’s willingness to let students reach their own conclusions.
These are professional skills, and the ministry can set clear standards for them.
Schools also have something that campaigns and social media rarely offer: time and structure. A teacher can slow a claim down, ask where it comes from, put competing proposals side by side, and require students to understand an argument before dismissing it.
That kind of classroom work would give young voters practice separating slogans from evidence and strong opinions from well-supported ones.
Political literacy should become an explicit part of election education. Students need recurring practice with real sources and competing policy proposals. They should learn to trace a promise, examine a record in office, test a claim against evidence, explain an opposing position fairly, and reconsider a view when the facts change.
Israel’s schools already teach students that voting matters. The harder lesson is how to reach a decision worth owning.
The choice of which party to vote for is ultimately a personal one, but the capacity to make an informed and independent choice is part of the democratic civic competence that must be developed long before Election Day.
Meital Baron and Daphna Cahana-Dolev are experts at the Israel Democracy Institute's Education Policy Program.

The new British government plans to announce in the coming weeks a comprehensive package of economic sanctions and other measures designed to prevent the Israeli expansion of West Bank settlements.

He spoke during his first question-and-answer session with lawmakers since he and the government he represents were sworn into office in July.
Miliband added that the new measures would include a ban on goods produced in the settlements and targeted sanctions on British institutions and individuals.
“We are looking, indeed, at our wider economic relationship with the occupied territories, and the different tools we have to tackle it,” Miliband explained. “We do not want British companies financing, constructing, or advertising new settlements. The work we are now undertaking is how we can stop that.”
Sa'ar warns of potential Israeli retaliation
Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar warned Tuesday that if the UK acted against his country, the Jewish state would take retaliatory steps against Great Britain.
“We are prepared, and I hope they will not make the mistake of doing this. If they do, there will be a reaction,” Sa’ar said in a podcast interview with the Hebrew news website Ynet.
Tensions between Israel and the UK have been escalating in light of Israeli military actions in Gaza and the West Bank following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack.
The UK’s decision under the last government to recognize Palestinian statehood in 2025 inflamed the situation, which is expected to get worse should Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu win the October 27 election in Israel.
Any government that Netanyahu forms is expected to be right-wing and to continue the policies of the existing government, just as the UK under Miliband and the new Labour prime minister, Andy Burnham, are more willing than their predecessors to go head-to-head with Israel on the issue.
Miliband already floated the idea of targeted sanctions after Israel’s Lands Authority opened bids for 1,234 homes in the largely underdeveloped E1 section of the West Bank settlement of Ma’aleh Adumim in August, a move that he said would undermine any two-state solution to the Israel-Palestinian conflict.
Miliband went further on Tuesday when fielding a number of questions from lawmakers frustrated about the lack of UK response to Israeli actions in the West Bank, such as terror activity by Israelis against Palestinian civilians and continued settler building. This includes the opening of E1 bids last month.
The foreign secretary explained that his words reflected the policies Burnham had considered even before he entered Downing Street in July, such as a ban on trade for goods produced in the settlements. “We are obviously working across government and with our allies on these measures,” Miliband said.
Israel has said that it has a right to build settler homes in Area C of the West Bank, which is under Israeli military and civilian control and where all the settlements are located. Under the Oslo Accords, the West Bank was divided into three areas, with sections A and B under the auspices of the Palestinian Authority.
ICJ issued advisory against construction in Area C
The International Court of Justice in 2024 issued an advisory opinion explaining that such construction in Area C is illegal, affirming a long-held stance of the UN and many nations, including the UK
Concern has been particularly high with regard to the E1 project, which would add 3,400 homes to the municipal boundaries of the city of Ma’aleh Adumim by building on an underdeveloped hilltop. The Palestinian Authority and the international community, including past US administrations, have warned that the project would block contiguous Palestinian development in that area and thus make a Palestinian state untenable.
Miliband referenced that viewpoint when speaking to the House of Commons on Tuesday, explaining that E1 development had long been considered a “red line,” because the project “cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable.”
He affirmed the UK’s commitment to a two-state resolution, explaining that his government would not stand idly by while that vision was being destroyed by Israeli actions on the ground in the West Bank.
In a harshly worded attack on the UK and Miliband in August, Sa’ar on X warned that the UK’s statements on Israel were fueling antisemitism in Great Britain and emphasized that the Jewish people had a right to build anywhere in their ancestral homeland.

Deputy commander of Russian Volunteer Corps describes detention in secret prison, where he was threatened with "disappearing forever"
Stepan Kaplunov, Deputy Commander for Combat Operations of the Russian Volunteer Corps The Russian Volunteer Corps is a military and political organisation established in 2022 that consists of Russian volunteers who have been fighting for Ukraine since 2014. , has described details of his abduction by Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) officers and explained why, under pressure and threats in a secret prison, he was forced to admit to having links with the Russian FSB.
Source: Kaplunov in an interview with Radio NV
Details: According to Kaplunov, he was abducted on 23 August near his house. He was handcuffed, had his eyes taped shut and was taken to a secret prison.
"For the first two days, I was interrogated more intensively. On the third day, they hardly spoke to me at all. As far as I understand, most likely the aim was to discredit the Tymur Special Unit [special-purpose unit within Defence Intelligence of Ukraine – ed.], including our commander directly – Tymur. I was accused of having links with representatives of the FSB. I later attributed this connection to my immediate superior, Dmytro – Commander Dmytro Ivanov. So this was not about WhiteRex [Russian Volunteer Corps commander Denis Kapustin – ed.]. Accordingly, I was not subjected to physical violence, apart from the abduction itself at the beginning. Nevertheless, there were remarks that I could disappear forever. In other words, there was talk of digging holes. We all understand what that means," he said.
Kaplunov said that, while in that difficult situation, he fully agreed with the version that he "had a connection with the FSB and subsequently attributed this contact to my immediate commander, Dmytro".
"Although in reality nothing of the sort had happened. I went along with it because of my situation and under psychological pressure," he stressed.
Kaplunov added that during his detention he was held at two different locations, but was released after nine days.
"I cannot tell you about events in the outside world, interaction between the services, communications and so on. After nine days, I was simply told: 'Get out.' I was also transferred – either to one vehicle or two. After that, I was taken to the place where, roughly speaking, I had been abducted, but I was not warned in advance that my flat would also be searched," he said.
Asked whether Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President, had contacted Kaplunov during that period, he replied: "Not at all."
"I know that Kyrylo Oleksiiovych is following this situation closely and keeping his finger on the pulse, but directly – no," Kaplunov said.
Background:
- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps said that Kaplunov had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of the building where he was living.
- On the morning of 2 September, reports spread on social media about a shootout said to be between Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) and the SSU in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi District, and that it was somehow connected to Kaplunov's disappearance. As of 10:00 on the same day, Ukrainska Pravda reported that the standoff was still ongoing.
- Later, officers from the State Bureau of Investigation and the head of the SSU's Special Operations Centre Alpha arrived at the scene. According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, three DIU officers were injured in the confrontation.
- Meanwhile, the SSU said that together with DIU, it had foiled a terrorist attack against a leader of a Russian opposition political national movement who had arrived in Ukraine.

Australian researchers create floating titanium metamaterial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:42:40 UTC
17:42:40 KST

- RMIT-led researchers built a 3D-printed titanium lattice that floats and stays buoyant even after significant structural damage.
- The material was 70% stronger than stainless steel or high-density plastic used in marine infrastructure at the same density.
Australian researchers have built a 3D-printed titanium structure that floats in water and keeps floating even after significant damage, according to a study led by RMIT University.
The material is a lattice made of hollow, interconnected titanium struts filled with polyurethane foam. Researchers said it withstands seawater exposure and is stronger than the stainless steel or high-density plastic currently used in jetties, buoys and floating sensors.
“Although metallic lattices can be incredibly light, with densities less than one-tenth the density of water, their open, interconnected spaces allow water to enter, causing them to sink,” said Dr. Jordan Noronha, lead researcher at RMIT’s Centre for Additive Manufacturing. “This has made these strong, lightweight structures unsuitable for marine infrastructure, until now.”
“By filling only the hollow titanium struts with polyurethane foam, we created a structure that allows water to flow through it while remaining buoyant even after significant cracking and damage,” Noronha said.
The researchers said the work is the first reported demonstration of a floating metal-hybrid lattice metamaterial. Samples floated in freshwater for more than two months during testing, according to the study.
To design the structure, the team introduced a measurement they call skeletal density. Conventional density calculations count all the open space inside a lattice, including space that water can fill and that therefore does not help the structure float. Skeletal density instead counts only the titanium walls and the sealed, foam-filled channels, the parts of the structure water cannot enter.
“This gives engineers a simple design rule: if the skeletal density is lower than that of the surrounding liquid, the structure will float, even when water flows through all its external openings,” Noronha said.
In compression testing, the titanium structure was 70% stronger than stainless steel or high-density polyethylene at the same overall density, the researchers said. In a two-week corrosion test using seawater from Melbourne’s Port Phillip Bay, the lattice lost 0.15% of its mass and less than 1% of its strength.
The structure also kept floating after damage that included cracking, failure at connection points and the fracture of an entire lattice layer, according to the study. It sank only after being severely crushed and compacted.
“Tiny, sealed cells in the foam trap gas and prevent water from flooding the hollow struts,” Noronha said. “In this way the foam acts as a distributed barrier that helps the structure remain afloat after damage, unlike conventional hollow marine structures, which can rapidly fill with water after cracking.”
The team built a 3D-printed marine buoy to test the concept and placed it in a turbulent seawater tank, rotating it up to 45 degrees. The researchers said the buoy remained stable without a sealed casing, protective coating or added flotation.
Project leader Distinguished Professor Ma Qian said the next steps include scaling up the demonstration parts and testing long-term performance under realistic marine and deep-sea conditions. Qian said the structure’s properties can be tailored by changing the material inside the titanium framework, opening potential uses beyond marine infrastructure in areas such as energy absorption, thermal management and vibration control.
RMIT’s Centre for Additive Manufacturing led the project with the Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers in France. The Australian Research Council and RMIT’s School of Engineering supported the research.
The study, “Breaking the surface: buoyant metal-polymer open-cell hybrid lattice metamaterials,” was published in the journal Advanced Materials.

West trying to draw India into ‘games’ against China – Lavrov
Western countries are trying to draw India into a confrontation with China by pushing a more military role for the Quad grouping, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok. 
Lavrov said India feels “very uncomfortable” in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) grouping, arguing that the US and Japan have sought to add a military component to it. 
“They are conducting maritime security exercises and are keen to draw our Indian friends into games against another great friend of ours – the People’s Republic of China,” Lavrov said.
The Quad grouping of India, the US, Japan, and Australia focuses on cooperation in the Indo-Pacific. Its activities cover areas ranging from trade and critical technologies to maritime security, with the four countries also taking part in the annual Malabar naval exercise.
At a meeting hosted by India in May, Quad foreign ministers launched a maritime surveillance initiative aimed at increasing information sharing and maritime domain awareness. India is also due to host the grouping’s next Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission, intended to improve interoperability and knowledge-sharing.

Lavrov linked the grouping to what he described as a broader Western effort to weaken the central role of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) by creating smaller blocs in the region.
He said Western countries are also trying to establish a “second Quad,” comprising the US, Japan, Australia, and the Philippines – instead of India – with the aim of fragmenting ASEAN unity.
The four countries already cooperate in a separate defense format, sometimes referred to as the SQUAD. Their defense ministers agreed last year to deepen maritime and air activities and strengthen what they described as regional deterrence and response capabilities.
Lavrov has raised similar concerns before. In May last year, he accused NATO of trying to draw India into ”anti-China intrigues,” while calling for the revival of the Russia-India-China (RIC) trilateral format.
India has pushed back against suggestions that participation in the Quad is directed against Beijing, saying it pursues an independent foreign policy based on national interests.
Lavrov also accused NATO of seeking to expand its presence and infrastructure in Asia. The US-led military bloc has stepped up cooperation with Australia, Japan, South Korea, and New Zealand in areas including maritime security, cyber defense, and emerging technologies.

Muhammad Ameer Hamza measures a cotton plant at a laboratory of Shihezi University in Shihezi City, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Aug. 24, 2026.
Muhammad Ameer Hamza hails from Depalpur, Pakistan. He is now pursuing a PhD in crop science at the Agricultural College of Shihezi University in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region.
Under the guidance of his supervisor, Yang Desong, Hamza conducts research in the university laboratory. He also works in cotton fields with Yang to learn about soil salinity and alkalinity, cotton field management and drone-based plant protection. Hamza said he has been impressed by technological applications in Xinjiang, such as water-saving irrigation and unmanned operations. He could apply what he has learned when he returns to Pakistan.
For Hamza, life in Xinjiang is not lonely. His supervisor gives him advice on daily life in addition to academic guidance, and he has Pakistani and Chinese friends. In his spare time, Hamza sometimes goes out with his friends, strolling through the streets and enjoying the city's vibrant atmosphere. Hamza said he is happy to study with his classmates at the university and integrate into local life.
Xinjiang is China's largest cotton-producing region. In recent years, the region has developed rapidly in cotton breeding, mechanized harvesting, and green pest control, providing valuable experience for agricultural development in similar climates. (Xinhua/Aman)

Ancrages - France strengthens its partnership with the African diasporas
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

Ancrages - France strengthens its partnership with the African diasporas Africa Economic diplomacy Communiqué On : April 17th 2025 On Wednesday, April 16, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot traveled to Marseille for the second edition of the Ancrages Forum, which is dedicated to promoting entrepreneurship between African countries and France. The forum, which was organized by the association Les Déterminés, with support from the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, brought together several hundred participants from the African diasporas and all of France. The Minister took this opportunity to reaffirm France’s commitment to the African diasporas, which play a key role in the dialogue, innovation and development that takes place between the two shores of the Mediterranean Sea. To this end, the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs has put together an African Diasporas Action Plan involving the entire diplomatic network, both in France and at our embassies in Africa. The plan comprises several foundational projects backed by our public service providers and partners: The MEET Africa and Pass Africa programs have already supported over 3,000 entrepreneurs to date. In Marseille, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs announced the launch of the third edition of the Pass Africa program. In 2025, it will provide support to 20 new entrepreneurs – the future business success stories spanning France and Africa; The Choose Africa program, the flagship initiative for funding the African private sector, has funded over 40,000 African businesses and several hundred thousand micro-entrepreneurs for a total of €3.5 billion. Choose Africa 2 (2023-2027) will bring the private sector new backers and support French businesses looking to expand into Africa. The DIASDEV program aims to reduce the cost of money transfers and develop innovative financial products for the diasporas. This program has likewise been renewed for 2025. The Digital Africa program helps African digital entrepreneurs roll out high-impact tech innovation by providing them with technical, financial and institutional assistance. The Minister recalled that the House of African Worlds (MansA) will be unveiled this June in Paris. MansA, which will be home to conversation, innovation and debate, will feature contemporary African art and also serve as a lab for entrepreneurship that allows people to create connections and share stories. On June 21, the day of the Fête de la musique, the Quai d’Orsay will highlight the African diasporas at a unique evening event where the diasporas’ talent and musical creativity will have pride of place. A third edition of the Ancrages Forum will also take place at the end of 2025. Furthermore, the Minister stated that he is looking forward to the second edition of the Democracy Forum of the Innovation Foundation for Democracy (FIDEMO), which will be held in Dakar, Senegal, from June 19-22, following on from the forum’s exciting first edition in Cape Verde last year. In addition, the Minister reiterated the importance of the African Art Forum, the second edition of which will be taking place in Lagos, Nigeria, in October 2025. A major event on the cultural calendar, this forum offers the chance to highlight all the French and African initiatives under way in the cultural and creative industries. Lastly, the Ancrages Forum in Marseille is an important part of the 2026 Mediterranean Season, which is dedicated to the ties that bind together the peoples of the Mediterranean. This cultural, civic-minded season, which is coordinated by the Institut français, will make its mark throughout France, the Maghreb and the Middle East.

Ancrages forum: supporting entrepreneurship in Africa
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

Ancrages forum: supporting entrepreneurship in Africa Africa Economic diplomacy Communiqué On : April 16th 2025 The Ancrages forum, the flagship initiative for revitalizing relations between Africa and France, will take place at the Palais du Pharo in Marseille on 16 April 2025. Spearheaded by the Les Déterminés association with the support of the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, this year’s event will highlight the talent, initiatives and innovation of young people who work between France and the African continent. Supporting entrepreneurship in Africa The Ancrages forum is a pioneering event that combines economic diplomacy, diplomatic action of local governments, and practical promotion of the various support programmes offered by the State for creative projects and entrepreneurship in France and Africa. Among these facilities are Choose Africa, conducted by the Agence Française de Développement (AFD) and BPI France, which has already led to investment of €2.5 billion in five years to support young innovative African businesses. Other facilities include the Meet Africa, Pass Africa and Digital Africa programmes, which offer these businesses rooted in many areas financial support and assistance in the crucial launch and scaling up phases of their growth trajectory. While the Ancrages forum is led by Les Déterminés, all government operators have contributed to its success, such as the Agence Française de Développement/AFD and BPI France (economic aspects), France Volontaires (youth mobility), Business France (export) as well as regional bodies. Marseille: global city and epicentre of actors from African diasporas On 16 April 2025, the Ancrages forum will take place in Marseille, at the Palais du Pharo. Marseille was a natural choice for this second edition. The southern city is a crossroads for initiatives, led by the diasporas, shaping the bridges between France and the African continent (Forum Europe Afrique, Emerging Valley, Cuisines Africaines). To encourage boldness and commitment, Ancrages Marseille will welcome business leaders, creators, athletes and scientists, demonstrating the diversity of success stories and trajectories. It also aims to build genuine connections between talents, businesses and institutions to support entrepreneurship and employability. MEETING SPACES Ancrages Marseille is also an immersive experience, with: An “Agora” village organized around specific themes, where participants can meet entrepreneurs, develop their networks and access practical, suitable resources. Inspiring accounts from role models that transformed their experience into a real strength. Round tables to work out the challenges of today and tomorrow. Participatory workshops to discover the programmes proposed by France’s government agencies (Bpifrance, Groupe AFD, Business France, France Volontaires, Institut Français, MansA - Maison des Mondes africains) and better understand the opportunities that exist to start a business, invest or get involved. The event is open to the public and 3,000 visitors are expected. Ancrages Marseille is part of a process of collective mobilization and embodies a shared ambition, which is to create a positive and inspiring narrative for young people from the diasporas by highlighting exemplary trajectories and fostering genuine opportunities. A look back at the first Ancrages forum The first edition of the forum took place in 2024 in Lille, and brought together more than 2,500 participants and mobilized a large ecosystem of committed actors, with some 9 million people reached on social media. It enabled the launch of the “Fonds Maghreb” facility to assist the development of French businesses in the central Maghreb region (Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia). Find out more about the launch of the “Fonds Maghreb” (in French) Sign up for the forum: https://www.forumancrages.com/ Follow the initiative on social media: https://www.instagram.com/ancrages.forum/

China outlines new five-year plan for sports powerhouse drive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:41:16 CST
17:41:16 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on building a leading sports nation during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Xu)
BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- China aims to expand its sports industry to more than seven trillion yuan (1.04 trillion U.S. dollars) by 2030 as part of a new five-year plan to build the country into a sports powerhouse, officials said Thursday.
The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), approved by the State Council in July, also targets increasing per capita sports venue space to about four square meters and raising the proportion of residents who regularly exercise to around 40 percent, General Administration of Sport director Gao Zhidan told a State Council Information Office briefing.
Gao said the "Year of Deepening Governance" campaign rolled out earlier this year will tackle bottlenecks in the development of the sports industry. This includes sustained efforts to root out corruption, combat "toxic fan culture" and build a well-regulated sports governance system.
In elite sports, Gao said China will shift from a "prioritized breakthrough" strategy to a "comprehensive development" model centered on the "633" project. The initiative calls for consolidating China's strengths in six traditionally successful sports, including diving and gymnastics, developing three foundational sports comprising athletics, swimming and water sports, and revitalizing basketball, volleyball and football.
Zhang Xin, director of the administration's Competitive Sports Department, said authorities will make greater use of market mechanisms to develop elite sports by allowing enterprises, universities and social organizations to play a larger role in training and competition, while attracting talent, capital and technology from a wider range of sources.
Chen Xingnian, director of the Mass Sports Department, said the national fitness plan for 2026-2030 will focus on making services more targeted, inclusive, intelligent, integrated and better regulated.
More than 5,000 small-scale fitness facilities, including micro-sports parks and multipurpose courts, will be built or upgraded over the five-year period, with resources prioritized for densely populated areas where demand is greatest.
On the sports industry, Yang Xuedong, director of the Sports Economy Department, said the administration will streamline event approval procedures to reduce costs and improve spectator experiences while developing 100 high-quality outdoor sports destinations.
New technologies, including artificial intelligence and big data, will be used to develop smart fitness services and virtual sports, Yang said.
Gao also reviewed China's progress during the 14th Five-Year Plan period, saying public fitness had become increasingly popular, Chinese athletes delivered the country's best overseas Olympic performance at Paris 2024 and the sports industry maintained strong growth.
"We have successfully forged a path to building a sports powerhouse with Chinese characteristics," Gao said. ■

Malta government seeks to calm tensions after acquittal in journalist murder trial

Acquittal in journalist murder trial stirs tensions in Malta
VALLETTA, Sept 3 - Malta's government has urged calm after the acquittal of a businessman accused of commissioning the 2017 murder of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
The 53-year-old journalist and anti-corruption activist was killed in a car bomb attack outside her home in October 2017. Her murder set off a political firestorm in Malta as well as focusing international attention on its police and judiciary.
The verdict in her murder trial, delivered late on Wednesday, has angered the victim's family, and drawn criticism from press freedom group Reporters Without Borders, which said it was "beyond outraged" by the acquittal.
Roberta Metsola, the president of the European Parliament and a former Maltese politician, pledged to continue the fight for justice.
"When they assassinated you, in broad daylight, outside your family home, we promised that we would not let them sweep it under the carpet," she wrote in a Facebook post addressed to "Dear Daphne".
"That promise holds today. We will not give up and we will not give in," she added.
Prime Minister Robert Abela, returned to power in May, did not comment directly but his government urged restraint in a statement issued late on Wednesday.
"At this sensitive moment, the government appeals for prudence in public comments that could do more harm than good," it said in a statement.
Three men have been convicted of carrying out the killing and two others for supplying the bomb after earlier trials and are now serving lengthy jail sentences.
However, businessman Yorgen Fenech, heir to a property empire that includes hotels and casinos, was acquitted on Wednesday by an 8-1 jury vote on charges of complicity in murder and the lesser charge of criminal association to commit murder.
TRIAL EVIDENCE TO BE ASSESSED
Prosecutors cannot appeal the verdict, except in exceptional circumstances involving points of law.
Judge Edwina Grima, who presided over the trial, has ordered that evidence be sent to the Police Commissioner to determine whether third parties should face criminal proceedings.
During a trial that began in July, the prosecution had alleged that Fenech wanted Caruana Galizia dead because she was about to reveal information about him.
In his defence, Fenech accused Keith Schembri, who served as chief of staff to former prime minister Joseph Muscat, of being behind the murder plot – an allegation Schembri denies.
Caruana Galizia's son Matthew expressed dismay, writing on Facebook: "Terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from. They had a great responsibility to deliver justice. And washed their hands of it."
The opposition Nationalist Party held a "silent demonstration" outside Abela's office overnight, during which party leader Alex Borg called for a recall of parliament from its summer break. REUTERS

China tightens border checks against polioviruses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:41:04 CST
17:41:04 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's customs authority has rolled out enhanced screening and quarantine measures for travelers and goods arriving from polio-affected countries or regions.
The measures were announced after the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that the risk of international poliovirus spread remains a Public Health Emergency of International Concern.
Effective from Thursday, travelers from polio-affected countries who have been in contact with polio cases or display symptoms such as fever, sore throat, cough, vomiting, diarrhea, neck stiffness, limb pain or flaccid paralysis are required to proactively declare their condition to customs upon entry, the General Administration of Customs said in a statement.
The administration also ordered sanitation treatment for inbound vehicles, containers, goods, luggage, and parcels that are, or may be, contaminated if they originate from polio-affected countries or regions.
The measures will remain in effect for one year and will also apply to any additional countries or regions that the WHO may designate as polio-affected during this period. ■

LISBON, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- The CAE-PAE Forum on Marine Technology and Ocean Engineering was held here on Wednesday, bringing together experts and scholars from the Chinese Academy of Engineering (CAE), the Portuguese Academy of Engineering (PAE) and the marine sector to discuss China-Portugal cooperation in marine technology and ocean engineering.
The forum featured discussions on marine engineering, maritime transport, shipbuilding and port engineering, with a focus on technological innovation in marine engineering and the sustainable use of marine resources.
Participants exchanged views on technological development and cooperation prospects in areas including marine engineering equipment, intelligent shipping, green ships, smart ports and marine renewable energy.
Experts and scholars from the two countries shared research findings and practical experience and explored ways to strengthen joint research and the commercialization of technological achievements.
During the forum, the CAE and the PAE also signed a memorandum of understanding on cooperation, marking a new stage of institutionalized cooperation between the two academies.
Sebastiao de Azevedo, president of the PAE, said the signing of the memorandum marked an important milestone in the China-Portugal cooperation in science, technology and engineering. It will further promote long-term cooperation between the two leading academic institutions, facilitate exchanges among researchers, experts and industry, and inject new impetus into China-Portugal cooperation in marine technology.
Chen Jianfeng, vice president of the CAE, said China and Portugal have achieved fruitful results in cooperation in marine science and technology, the blue economy and marine governance.
He called on the two sides to focus on frontier areas such as marine engineering, intelligent shipping and green ships, strengthen joint research and the commercialization of technological achievements, and promote high-quality development of the maritime economies of both countries.
He also called for greater cooperation on global issues including marine ecological conservation and the blue economy, to contribute China-Portugal expertise and solutions to global marine sustainable development.
Yang Yirui, Chinese ambassador to Portugal, said in a video address that Portugal was the first Western European country to sign a memorandum of understanding with China on jointly building the Belt and Road and the first EU member to officially establish a Blue Partnership with China.

He noted that the forum brought together leading academicians and experts in marine engineering as well as industry leaders, and would give a strong boost to the cooperation between the two sides in the maritime sector.

Carlos Guedes Soares, winner of China's International Science and Technology Cooperation Award in 2025 and an academician of the PAE, said he has been involved in China-Portugal cooperation in the maritime field for more than three decades and has witnessed mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries.

Singapore employers remain cautious on wages, hiring despite improved outlook
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:38 CST
17:40:38 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Singapore employers are expected to maintain a cautious approach towards wage increases and hiring in 2027, even as the business outlook has improved modestly, a survey conducted by the Singapore National Employers Federation revealed on Thursday.
The Survey on Wage and Employment Outlook 2026/2027 found that rising manpower costs remained employers' biggest workforce challenge, cited by 83 percent of respondents, up from 79 percent in 2025.
Concerns over the rising cost of upskilling and reskilling workers also increased, with 30 percent of employers highlighting the issue, compared with 23 percent a year earlier.
However, labor market tightness has eased. Fewer companies reported difficulties attracting and retaining professionals, managers, executives and technicians, at 41 percent, compared with 47 percent previously. Concerns over shortages of local high-skilled talent also fell to 35 percent from 42 percent.
Despite the easing, attracting suitable talent remained employers' top human resource priority, cited by 59 percent of respondents. Companies are also placing greater emphasis on exploring and adopting artificial intelligence, with 48 percent identifying this as a priority for 2027, up from 39 percent for 2026, alongside efforts to upskill and reskill employees.
The survey showed a modest improvement in business sentiment, with the proportion of employers expecting uncertain prospects in 2027 falling to 63 percent from 72 percent in 2026. Meanwhile, 65 percent of companies expect to perform well, compared with 63 percent a year earlier.
The outlook, however, remains uneven across sectors. While some export-oriented industries are benefiting from stronger external and technology-driven demand, domestically focused sectors such as retail trade and food and beverage services continue to face softer consumer demand and rising operating costs.
The survey, conducted between June and August 2026, gathered responses from more than 300 companies employing close to 160,000 workers across 20 industries. ■

Kommersant: Russian oil companies failed to fulfill about 60% of gasoline exchange contracts — due to Ukrainian attacks on refineries
Russian oil companies failed to fulfill about 60% of gasoline supply contracts on the St. Petersburg exchange between May and September, according to estimates from industry sources who spoke to the Russian business daily Kommersant.
About 20% of the deals fell through entirely, ending in default or cancellation, while another 39% remain unfulfilled. Of those, 24% have exceeded the standard 30-day shipment window.
Lukoil and Rosneft accounted for the bulk of the unfulfilled contracts, at 46% and 28%, respectively. A source told Kommersant that Ukrainian drone attacks hit their refineries hardest.
The source said oil companies prioritized state tasks first, such as supplying defense and industrial enterprises, leaving gas stations “on one of the last lines” of that list.
Independent gas stations are the exchange’s main buyers of fuel. Russian law requires vertically integrated oil companies to send a portion of their output there.
Russia’s second fuel crisis wave began in August, driven by Ukrainian drone strikes on oil refineries. Gasoline prices rose and lines reappeared at gas stations, just as they had in June.

Russia plans to make navigation along the Northern Sea Route year-round, President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday, outlining a series of measures aimed at expanding transport, energy and technological infrastructure in the Far East and Arctic.
Speaking at the plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Putin also said the first oil shipments from the Vostok Oil project would begin soon, while cargo traffic along the Transarctic Transport Corridor is expected to double by 2030.
"Based on the experience gained, we are launching a business support system that is unprecedented in scale and scope. Starting from January 1 next year, a single preferential regime will begin to operate throughout the Far East and the Arctic," he said.
Russia has been developing the Northern Sea Route as a major Arctic shipping corridor connecting its northern ports with the Pacific region. Putin has repeatedly identified extending navigation along the route as a key element of Russia’s Arctic development plans.
The president also ordered efforts to develop the use of low-altitude drones to transport civilian cargo in the Far East.
"With the development of unmanned aircraft, the sky at low altitudes is becoming as busy a transport artery as railways and waterways. And it is already necessary to set standards for autonomous transportation of civilian goods using drones," he said.
He also proposed allowing Far Eastern regions to reinvest infrastructure loans they repay into the implementation of master plans in their territories.
Russia also plans to expand communications infrastructure, with the goal of bringing communication links to all regional capitals in the Far East by 2030, Putin said.
'Deficit and surplus come in waves'
Putin also commented on the Russian budget deficit.
According to him, "proficit and deficit come in waves," and taking into account Russia's low state debt, as of now there are no grounds to worry.
"As for the deficit, the surplus, it's all coming in such waves.
"There is a shortage now. But I am sure that gradually, solving first of all the tasks of maintaining a healthy macroeconomics, we will solve all these issues," he said.
The Eastern Economic Forum is organised to discuss the development of the Far East, and transport connectivity, technology and international economic cooperation are among the central themes of the business programme.
Putin’s remarks came as China and Russia continued discussions on expanding economic cooperation in the Far East.
Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang told Putin on the sidelines of the forum that prospects for cooperation in developing the region were “broad and promising,” according to Xinhua news agency.
